Although after the prokeimenon at Sunday Vespers there was no reading in antiquity either, just as now, yet, as we have just seen, in the time of St. Symeon of Thessalonica (15th c.) the sacred ministers sat at the high place for the duration thereof;

whence cometh the present (unwritten) custom of their standing at this time at the high place.

## Manner of Execution of the Prokeimenon

Besides the introductory acclamations, the prokeimenon is distinguished from other hymnographic compositions by the external ceremonial setting of its chanting. In the execution of the prokeimenon the most conspicuous part is taken by the canonarch, who thus steps forward in divine worship at especially solemn moments: at **"The Lord is God"** or Alleluia (see Chapter 27 of the Typikon). After the acclamations before the prokeimenon, "the canonarch, having made a bow unto the superior, intoneth the prokeimenon and the verses, while the clergy [singers in the choir] chant the prokeimenon; the reader (= canonarch), having his arms folded upon his breast, standing in the midst of the temple, awaiteth the conclusion of the prokeimenon; and having made a bow, departeth unto his place."

## According Unto Ancient Typika

The stepping forward of the canonarch at the prokeimenon is the remnant of the former chanting of it and of its verses by a single singer prior unto the singing by the people (whence also the name—canonarch); for this reason in the above-cited passage of the Euchologion of the 8th–10th centuries, in place of the canonarch there is the chanter; see Introductory Chapter, p. 295; cf. at present at the Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts **"Let my prayer arise"**. Concerning the canonarch at the prokeimenon, manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon speak in the following manner: the 13th-century Georgian MS—instead of "canonarch"—"he who must recite the prokeimenon"; Greek MSS: "the appointed (*tachtheis* [Gr. ταχθείς]) monk"; ancient Slavic MSS: "another monk" (that is, in comparison with the one who read **"O Gladsome Light"**). Instead of "intoneth" [saith], ancient Greek MSS have nothing; later ones (from the 14th c.) and printed Greek editions: "singeth" (*psallei* [Gr. ψάλλει]), and so also Slavic MSS. Instead of "while the clergy chant", the Georgian MS hath: "the people the same"; the most ancient Greek MSS: "when we chant"; later Greek, printed Greek, and Slavic MSS have nothing, that is, they speak of the chanting of the prokeimenon and its verses by the canonarch alone. Greek and Slavic MSS before "having folded his arms" have: "having turned toward the west". The Old Believer Typikon hath all as our own, only before "having folded his arms": "having turned toward the west" [^2249].

*(Orig. p. 566)*

## The Prokeimenon of Sunday Vespers

The prokeimenon of Saturday-Sunday Vespers is sung more solemnly than at weekday Vespers. It is sung according unto the order of a Great Prokeimenon, although it is not titled "Great"; namely, it is sung with three verses, and consequently 4 1/2 times. Besides the present Vespers, such an execution is possessed by the prokeimenon at Vespers of the Twelve Great Feasts of the Lord, during Bright Week, and at Vespers of the Sunday days themselves of the Great Fast [Lent]. In this regard Saturday-Sunday Vespers is placed higher than Vespers even of the Twelve Great Feasts of the Theotokos, which hath no Great Prokeimenon, and is equalized with Feasts of the Lord. The difference with the latter is only that the Great Prokeimenon there is sung at Vespers not on the eve of the feast, but on the feast day itself (with the exception of that case when the feast falleth on a Saturday); this is because Vespers is considered as pertaining unto the following day only from **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"** (see Typikon, Cheesefare Sunday); at Sunday Vespers, however, it is otherwise, because the portion thereof before **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"** falleth upon such a semi-festal or pre-festal day as Saturday; whereas the festal celebration of Sunday itself, having no afterfeast, must cease earlier than on the Twelve Great Feasts. Great Prokeimena are assigned unto Vespers, and not unto Matins, by virtue of its ancient connection with the Divine Liturgy and the agape.

Already the Studite Typikon possessed Great prokeimena, that is, with three verses—yet only for Pascha, the Nativity of Christ, Theophany, and also at Matins of Great Saturday—the first before the paroemia; the second at this Matins with two verses [^2250]. All other prokeimena according unto this Typikon have but a single verse, including **"The Lord is King"** (*Gospod' votsarisya*) at Sunday Vespers [^2251]. So also the 13th-century Georgian manuscript of the Jerusalem Typikon; Greek and Slavic manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon, however, as well as printed Greek editions, direct the prokeimenon **"The Lord is King"** to be sung with two verses—the first two of the present ones, and in Greek this prokeimenon is termed *distichon* (*distychon* [Gr. δίστιχον / printed δίστυχον], two-versed), evidently in distinction from the great and ordinary ones [^2252]. Later Slavic manuscripts are silent concerning the verses [^2253]. The Old Believer Typikon is like our own. Greek and Slavic manuscripts say nothing concerning the concluding **"The Lord is King"**; the 13th-century Georgian manuscript, however, after its single verse unto the prokeimenon, hath: "the chanter: **'The Lord is King'**, the people the same". Yet the half-singing of the prokeimenon for the concluding time, without doubt, goeth back unto profound antiquity, as musical tradition and the analogy of the Roman Catholic Church demonstrate (see Introductory Chapter, p. 308).

The prokeimenon of Sunday Vespers is sung in Tone 6, the most mournful of the tones, without doubt for the same reason that in this tone there is sung also the first sticheron of the Paschal service (**"Thy Resurrection, O Christ Savior"**): the joy of the *(Orig. p. 567)* Resurrection breaketh forth for the first time through the grief over the death of Christ. In manuscripts the tone is not indicated.

As regards content, the prokeimenon of Sunday Vespers **"The Lord is King"**, with its verses: **"The Lord is clothed..."**, **"For He hath established the world..."**, **"Holiness becometh Thy house"**, borrowed from Psalm 92 [LXX 92; MT 93], doth not speak as directly of the Resurrection as the Matins prokeimena, yet on the other hand it speaketh of it from an interior aspect, indicating its profound essence in the royal glorification and, as it were, strengthening of the Lord, in the consolidation of the world that was disintegrating from sin, and in the founding of the Church. The immediate sense of the words of the psalm taken for the prokeimenon and constituting, presumably, the glorification of God for some victory (in the LXX the psalm is inscribed: "A song of praise of David")—is that God, as Creator of the world, is also its King, and His royal vesture is creation itself, revealing both His glory (majesty) and power (He is clothed with strength); as such, God is able to secure also the dignity, that is, the holiness, of His singular dwelling-place upon earth—the temple, preserving it from desecration.

The psalm was used among the Hebrews on Friday, as the joyful day of the completion of creation and the eve of the Sabbath (see Introductory Chapter, p. 11), whence probably cometh its inscription in the LXX: "On the day before the Sabbath, when the earth was founded" [LXX Ps. 92:1 incipit]. In the Syriac Liturgy of St. James it is recited upon the dismissal of the 'hearers' (catechumens) before the Symbol of Faith [Creed] (cf. with us at the Proskomedia) according unto an order similar unto the chanting of the prokeimenon with us—the priest: **"The Lord is King, He is clothed with strength, alleluia"**, followed by a brief glorification of the Son of God as the Bread of Life; the deacon: **"The Lord is clothed with strength and hath girded Himself, for He hath established the world which shall not be moved, alleluia"**, with a glorification of like content; the priest: **"Holiness becometh Thy house, O Lord, unto length of days. Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit"**; the deacon: **"The Lord is King"** [^2254]. In the Roman rite of divine worship this psalm is used at Sunday Lauds (Introductory Chapter, p. 315). At Chanted Vespers it must have constituted the 2nd antiphon, whereof by the 15th century there remained only the refrain **"The world"** (*Vselennuyu*) (Introductory Chapter, p. 341), yet at that time Chanted Vespers already possessed the present Sunday prokeimenon (Introductory Chapter, p. 342). Studite and Jerusalem Sunday Vespers possessed such a prokeimenon from the very beginning.

# PART 2 OF VESPERS

The subsequent order of Vespers, as has been said, is of a more prayerful than laudatory content. This second and principal part of Vespers hath much in common with the Divine Liturgy: the very same litanies (and at festal, most ancient Vespers, in that very *(Orig. p. 568)* same sequence); in ancient Vespers and Matins this resemblance was further augmented by the presence of prayers for the catechumens, those preparing for illumination [the photizomenoi], penitents, and the like. In Vespers this resemblance is even greater than in Matins: the conclusion of Vespers—**"Now lettest Thou"** [Canticle of Simeon], the Trisagion, and the troparion—coincideth fully with the conclusion of the Liturgy, a conclusion which, moreover, is performed by the priest already secretly [inaudibly], after the prayers of thanksgiving after Holy Communion. Thus, the second part of Vespers, like the conclusion of Matins [^2255], is, properly speaking, a Liturgy without the Gifts, yet by no means utterly devoid of the prayerful grace of the true Liturgy, inasmuch as the priest here (after the Entrance) approacheth the very same throne of grace. And it containeth prayers already for the faithful alone.

# THE AUGMENTED LITANY (*EKTENĒS HIKETEIA*)

## Its Content

This part of Vespers (as also of Matins) begins with one of the most fervent supplications known unto the Typikon, termed in common parlance the Augmented Litany (*sugubaya ekteniya*) [^2256], and in the liturgical books "fervent supplication" (*ektenēs deēsis* [Gr. ἐκτενὴς δέησις]) [^2257]. The short prayers offered up hitherto in several litanies are elevated in their intensity across the 12 petitions (reckoning with the exclamation) of the present litany: the faithful are invited to offer them up with all their soul and with all their mind, and begin their supplication with a petition for being heard and for mercy in general. The Augmented Litany is a prayer for the faithful alone, as St. Symeon of Thessalonica likewise defineth its content: "for faithful kings, for the local hierarch, for the superior of the monastery, for the guardians of the temple, for the Orthodox standing present, and for the faithful everywhere" [^2258]. With particular distinctness the litany prayeth for the tsar [sovereign], namely for 10 needs of his: for the strength of his rule ('might' [*derzhava*], *kratous* [Gr. κράτους]), victory (in warfare), longevity ('abiding' [*prebyvanie*], *diamonēs* [Gr. διαμονῆς]), peace, health, salvation (eternal), yet greater ('more abundantly' [*naipache*], *epipleon* [Gr. ἐπιπλέον]) divine assistance ('to help' [*posobiti*], *synergēsai* [Gr. συνεργῆσαι]) unto him, and full success ('to prosper *(Orig. p. 569)* [him]' [*pospeshiti*], *kateuodōsai* [printed *kateuodōsoa* / Gr. κατευοδῶσαι]) [^2259] in all things, and the complete subjection ('under his feet' [*pod noze*]) unto him of enemies domestic (*echthron* [Gr. ἐχθρόν]) and foreign ('adversary' [*supostata*], *polemion* [Gr. πολέμιον]); then a separate petition for the empress [queen] and a separate one for the heir and the reigning house (without uniting the former with the petition for the tsar, and the latter with the petition for the authorities and the military, as in the Great Litany); for the spiritual authority (the Holy Synod and the local bishop) together with all our brethren in Christ (= *adelphotētos* [Gr. ἀδελφότητος], more precisely 'brotherhood' = the 'clergy' [*prichte*] of the Great Litany); for the armed forces; a new petition in comparison with the Great Litany for the departed—and first of all for the founders of the monastery ('builders' [*sozdatelekh*], *ktētorōn* [Gr. κτητόρων], ktitors), who are termed on account of this their work blessed (almost saintly) and ever-memorable (*aeimnēstōn* [Gr. ἀειμνήστων]), and thereafter also for all the departed, yet of them first, naturally, for those buried right here; after this petition as it were for the departed brethren of the monastery—a petition for the present brotherhood and all their needs (which are enumerated with the same distinctness as in the petition for the tsar—8, among them for 'visitation' [*poseshchenie*], *episkepseōs* [Gr. ἐπισκέψεως], special mercies of God, then not only for 'forgiveness' [*proshchenie*], but also for the complete 'remission' [*ostavlenie*] of sins); constantly narrowing the circle of those interceded for, the Augmented Litany in its final petition concentrates upon the immediate participants in the present divine service, upon those having relation unto this given temple alone: its benefactors and more specifically its adorners ("those who do good works" [*dobrodeyushchikh*], *kalliergountōn* [Gr. καλλιεργούντων]), those who bear the more arduous (manual) labors in it ("those who labor" [*trudzhdayushchikhsya*], *kopīōntōn* [Gr. κοπιώντων] [^2260]), those who sing (*psallontōn* [Gr. ψαλλόντων]), and those simply standing in the temple; by its final words: **"that await of Thee great and rich mercy"**, the petitions of the Augmented Litany return unto their beginning and express the entire essence of their content. The ecphonesis of the litany appeals not unto God in general with His might and power, as do the preceding litanies, but in accordance with the general thought of the litany—unto His "mercy" (compassion—more specific than unto goodness in general, as in the Litany of Supplication) and love for mankind. The Vesperal Augmented Litany possesses as complete a form, and not one truncated at the beginning (which occurs at Matins), as at the Liturgy; yet in comparison with the Liturgy it hath not the petition **"For our brethren the priests..."** (which pertaineth more unto the Liturgy), but in exchange for it, in another position, the petition: **"Furthermore we pray for mercy, life..."**, a petition of more general content; thereafter it abbreviates one petition of the Liturgy's litany: in the petition **"For the blessed and ever-memorable holy Orthodox patriarchs, and pious tsars and right-believing tsaritsas"**, this beginning is omitted, and it proceeds directly unto **"the founders"**.

*(Orig. p. 570)*

## History of the Augmented Litany

In the Liturgy of the Apostle James in all manuscripts thereof, beginning with the most ancient 10th-century Messina MS, continuing with the 11th-century Rossano MS and the 12th-century Sinai MS (No. 1040), and concluding with the 14th-century manuscripts (Paris National Library Nos. 2509 and 476), there is a litany close unto our Augmented Litany, appointed immediately before the Gospel following the Epistle and the Alleluia (whereas immediately after the Gospel there is a litany close unto our Litany of Supplication). In all these manuscripts, excluding the Sinai MS, this litany is nearly identical. It possesses its most complete form in the most ancient 10th-century Messina MS, according unto which we set it forth, with variants from the remaining ones apart from the Sinai MS (the 5th MS hath only the opening words of the petitions):

"After the Alleluia the priest stands up. The deacon recites the litany (*ektenēn* [Gr. ἐκτενῆ / έκτενήν]; other MSS instead of all this: 'And the deacon', 'The deacon', 'The deacon before the Gospel'): **'Let us all say: Lord, have mercy. O Lord Almighty, God of our fathers, we pray Thee, hear. For the peace of the whole world and the union of all the Holy Churches, we pray, hear'** (other MSS:

'let us pray', *deēthōmen* [Gr. δεηθῶμεν], without 'hear', and so on until the 17th petition): **'For our holy father N.** (other MSS: **For the salvation and protection of our most holy father N., Patriarch), all the clergy, and the Christ-loving people, let us pray. For our most pious and Christ-loving emperor [tsar], all the palace and armed forces, and their victory, we pray** (absent in Rossano and Paris 1). **For the holy city of Christ our God and the imperial city [reigning city], every city and countryside, we pray** (absent in the same). **That we may be delivered from all affliction, wrath** (in the same: + **danger** [*napasti*], *kindynou* [Gr. κινδύνου / printed κυνδύνου]) **and necessity, captivity, [and] bitter death** (in the same: + **and from our iniquities**), **we pray** (Rossano: **let us pray**; Paris: **we pray Thee, hear**). **And** (absent in Paris 2) **for the people standing present and awaiting the rich and great mercy that cometh from Thee, O Lord** (the italicized words are absent in other MSS), **we pray Thee, have compassion and have mercy.** (Paris 1: + Instead of **'Have mercy on us, O God'**, this:) **Save, O God, Thy people, and bless Thy heritage** (other MSS: + **Thy**), **visit Thy world with mercy and compassions, exalt the horn of Christians, and send down upon us Thy rich mercies** (instead of the italicized words other MSS: **by the power of the Precious and Life-giving Cross**), **through the intercessions of our All-Holy** (Rossano: **All-Pure**) **blessed Lady, the Theotokos and Ever-Virgin Mary** (instead of the italicized words other MSS: **of the Forerunner and Thy Apostles**) **and of all Thy saints; we pray Thee, O Most Merciful Lord, hear us sinners praying** (other MSS: + **unto Thee**) **and have mercy. People: Lord, have mercy (thrice)** (absent in Paris 2)" [^2261].

The litany, therefore, represents a repetition of the Great Litany (just as in the Liturgy of the *Apostolic Constitutions* the litany close unto our Great Litany and appointed before the consecration of the Gifts is repeated also after them), but with the addition at the beginning and end of intensified prayerful and mournfully penitential petitions. Such additions were bound to multiply also in subsequent monuments, in later liturgies; such an element in this litany doth indeed increase, yet it is concentrated preeminently at its beginning. Even more than the Great Litany, the Augmented Litany possesses one common history across all liturgies, coinciding unto literal exactness, as we shall see, *(Orig. p. 571)* in the Liturgies of the Apostle James, Basil the Great, and John Chrysostom within the very same manuscripts, while differing endlessly within one and the same liturgy in different epochs. Therefore, the following (if not preceding) formula thereof after the one cited above may be acknowledged in the order of development as that given in an ancient redaction of the Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom:

"Deacon: **'Let us all say with our whole soul and with our whole mind let us say.'** Ecphonesis of the priest: **'O Lord Almighty, God of our fathers, rich in mercy and good in compassions, Who willest not the death of a sinner, but awaitest conversion and repentance, that he should turn and live.'** Deacon: **'For this holy temple...'** and further the petitions of the Great Litany down unto **'That we may be delivered...'** Inaudible [secret] prayer: **'O Lord our God, accept this fervent supplication'** (the present prayer). Deacon: **'That the Lord may be merciful, favorable, and gracious, let us pray.'** People: **'Lord, have mercy'** (and thereafter all petitions end with **'let us pray unto the Lord'** and **'Lord, have mercy'**). **'That the Lord God may hear the voice of the supplication of us sinners. For all those who have labored before us** (*prokopiasantōn* [Gr. προκοπιασάντων]) **and have consecrated** (*aphierōsantōn* [Gr. ἀφιερωσάντων]) **us. For the people standing present and awaiting rich mercy from Thee'**" [^2262].

Subsequent redactions of the litany fashion several deaconal petitions out of the opening prayer of the priest, and also abbreviate and modify the borrowings from the Great Litany. Thus, the Euchologion of the Sinai Library No. 1040 of the 12th century provides such a litany, identical for the Liturgies of the Apostle James and of Chrysostom:

"**'Let us all say fervently** (*ektenōs* [Gr. ἐκτενῶς]) **with our whole soul and... O Lord Almighty of heaven, God of our fathers... Rich in mercy and good in compassions, we pray Thee. Who willest not the death of us sinners, but grantest life and repentance unto conversion unto Thee, we pray Thee. That we may be delivered... Have mercy on us, O God... For our most pious and God-preserved emperors [tsars], their might... Furthermore we pray for our Archbishop N., his health, salvation, and remission of his sins. Furthermore we pray for the servant of God N., priest, the honorable priesthood, the diaconate in Christ, and all the sacerdotal rank, their health, salvation... Furthermore for the servant of God N. and all his people, their health... Furthermore for all our kinsmen according unto the flesh and brethren, and those who have charged us, the unworthy, to pray for them, and those who love us and hate us, Orthodox Christians, their health... And for the people standing present and all our brethren, for those travelling abroad, in infirmity, in captivity, and possessed by unclean spirits, and those sailing upon the sea, and all Orthodox Christians,** **their health... Furthermore we pray for the remission of sins and the blessed memory and repose of all departed Christians, lying here and everywhere Orthodox.' The priest intones the ecphonesis: 'For Thou art a merciful and man-befriending God...'**" [^2263].

Apparently at the very same stage of development, that is, of separation from the Great Litany, stands the Augmented Litany in the Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom in the Sinai Euchologion of 1153, No. 979:

"**'Let us all say... O Lord Almighty... Who willest not the death... Rich in mercy... Have mercy on us... Furthermore for our most pious and God-preserved emperors [tsars] and to subdue under their feet... Furthermore for the estate and peace of Christians, the deliverance of captives, the healing of the sick, and for the repose of those fallen asleep in faith... Furthermore for the servant of God N., his health...** *(Orig. p. 572)* **Furthermore for the servant of God N., his repose... Furthermore for those who bear fruit...** [^2264] **Furthermore that the Lord God may hear the voice...'**" [^2265].

Even fewer elements from the Great Litany and greater proximity unto the present Augmented Litany are found in the most ancient of Greek Euchologia that provide the litanies (and not merely the prayers of the priest), in the Euchologion of the Imperial Public Library No. 226 (from the collection of Bishop Porphyrius Uspensky, brought from the Sinai Library) of the 9th–10th centuries. Only the opening words of the petitions are present:

"1. **Let us all say: Lord, have mercy.** 2. **With our whole soul and with our whole mind.** 3. **O Lord Almighty.** (4?) **Who willest not the death of a sinner.** 4. **For this holy temple and with...** 5. **For our father and bishop.** 6. **For the most pious and God-preserved.** 7. **To help and subdue under their feet every...** 8. **That we may be delivered and to subdue.** 9. **For the people standing present.** 10. **For all those in need of...** (*chrēzontōn eis* [Gr. χρηζόντων εἰς]). 11. **Have mercy on us, O God, according unto Thy great [mercy].**" Thereafter follows an unclear rubric: "and immediately the litany: 1. **Furthermore that He may be merciful, and gracious, and acceptable** (*eudekton* [Gr. εὔδεκτον]), and the remaining litanies."

Free from elements of the Great Litany and advancing, apparently, further along the path of abbreviations is the Augmented Litany in the Slavic *Sluzhebnik* manuscript of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 604 (343) of the 12th century and the St. Sophia Library at the St. Petersburg Theological Academy No. 520 of the 14th century:

"1. **Let us all say with our whole soul.** 2. **O Lord Almighty.** 3. **O Good One, rich in mercy.** 4. **Who willest not the death of a sin[ner].** 5. **For those standing present.** 6. **Have mercy on us, O God.** 7. **Furthermore for the right-believing...** [^2266] 8. **And furthermore we pray for the bishop** (only in the second). 9. **And furthermore [that He may] hear...**" [^2267].

From the 15th century in both Greek and Slavic *Sluzhebniki* there is established approximately the present composition of the Augmented Litany and the present order *(Orig. p. 573)* of petitions within it, at least for the first 4 petitions; the remaining petitions also all appear from this time, yet with great fluctuations in their number, sequence, and sometimes in text. Thus, in the 1st petition certain Greek MSS have instead of "with our whole mind"—"in all our mind"; certain Greek and Slavic MSS omit "our", while certain ones add at the end "all". In the 2nd petition **"O Lord Almighty"**, certain MSS add after "hear"—"us". In the 3rd petition certain Greek and Slavic MSS after "Thy mercy" or after "we pray Thee" add + "O Lord". In the 4th petition for the sovereign [tsar], the most ancient have: **"For our most pious** (anc. Slav.: **'pious'**) **and God-preserved emperors [tsars]** (anc. Slav.: **'princes'**)" without names [NN.]; the Greek sometimes instead of "God-preserved" hath "Christ-loving"; certain Greek MSS alongside one petition for the emperors have also others in the form: "for the most pious and Christ-loving (instead of: 'God-preserved') emperors", wherein the objects of the petition are no longer indicated: "for their might, victory", but only the names (sometimes also of the empress); presumably this petition was for the so-called "lesser emperors" [*reges minores*]: the heir or the caesars. In later Slavic MSS and the first printed Moscow editions there are three petitions for the tsar, separated by a petition for the patriarch (following the first petition for the tsar); in the last of them the tsaritsa [empress] is also commemorated. In Slavic texts the titles of the Sovereign were subjected unto the same changes as in the Great Litany. Instead of "to help" [*posobiti*], the ancient translation hath more accurately: "to direct" [*napraviti*]. The petition for the archbishop (at present for the Holy Synod) is not present everywhere; in the most ancient: **"furthermore we pray for our archbishop"**, or: **"bishop"**; certain Slavic: **"patriarch"**, sometimes with the rubric: "and he commemorateth whom he willeth" (Greek); certain Slavic: + "N., for health and salvation"; "and for all our brotherhood in Christ" appears only in later MSS and printed editions. In later Slavic MSS and the first printed Moscow editions, instead of the archbishop there is commemoration of the patriarch, and this petition cometh after the petition for the tsar and before the reigning house. The petition for the armed forces appears only in later printed editions. Unto the petition for the patriarch certain MSS add or place in its stead a petition for the clergy in such forms: **"Furthermore we pray for the whole episcopate of the Orthodox"**; or: **"Furthermore we pray for the Orthodox** **bishops, the honorable priesthood, the diaconate in Christ, all the clergy and people, their health and salvation"**, sometimes with the rubric: "and he commemorateth the living in order"; or: **"Furthermore we pray for our brethren the priests..."** In place of the petition for the archbishop and clergy, or following directly after it, certain MSS have a petition for the abbot [hegumen] in the form: **"Furthermore we pray for our father N. and all our brotherhood in Christ"**, or: **"Furthermore we pray for the servant of God, our father Hegumen** (or: **'hieromonk'**) **N. and all our brotherhood in Christ, for health and salvation"**; sometimes: **"our brotherhood and all who serve and have served in this holy monastery."** After the petition for the clergy, certain Greek MSS have a petition for the departed in the form: **"Furthermore we pray for the blessed dormition** (*koimēseōs* [Gr. κοιμήσεως]) **and repose of the soul of the servant of God N."**, sometimes with the addition: "he saith [this] for the dead." The subsequent petition in the present litany for the ktitors (**"founders and benefactors"**) and all the departed appears from the 14th–15th centuries, and initially in such brief redactions: **"Furthermore we pray for the founders"** or **"ktitors"** (the conclusion is unknown), or: **"... for the ever-celebrated** (*aoidimōn* [Gr. ἀοιδίμων]) **and blessed founders"**, **"for the blessed and ever-celebrated..."**, *(Orig. p. 574)* or: **"Furthermore we pray for the blessed dormition and repose of the ever-memorable and blessed founders of this holy monastery"**, and so forth, as at present, sometimes with the note: "and he commemorateth whomsoever he willeth of the departed." Thereafter in Greek MSS there customarily follows the petition: **"Furthermore we pray for the servant of God** (or: **'Thy'**, or simply: **'servant'**) **N., his health"** (unfinished), or: **"For mercy, health, and salvation, remission of the sins of the servant of God"**, or: **"Furthermore we pray for mercy, peace, life** (or: **'life, peace'**), **health, salvation (+ visitation, pardon) and remission of the sins of the servant of God N."** (evidently of a private individual who requested commemoration). In Slavic MSS, however, in place of this there sometimes stands a petition, or even two, for the tsar in the form: **"Furthermore we pray for the mercy of God, for help, and for furtherance, and for strengthening, and for assistance, and for vouchsafing victory and triumph over enemies unto our right-believing and Christ-loving tsar and grand prince N., for the welfare of the armed forces, for peace, and for tranquility, and for the ordering and remission of sins of all Orthodox Christianity, let us all say."** This second petition on the litany for the tsar (found here, however, in only a few later MSS, for instance St. Sophia Library No. 899 of the 17th c. and printed Moscow editions of the 17th c.), evidently stands here in connection with the petition for the entire people, whose prosperity is linked unto the royal governance. Furthermore: the same MSS and editions after this petition have yet another petition for the tsar and tsaritsa, yet no longer concerning governance, but concerning their personal well-being (perhaps in the capacity of descendants of the ktitors). Thereafter both Greek and Slavic MSS have an independent petition **"for (+ all) who serve and have served** **in this holy monastery (+ for health and for salvation)"** (MSS of the 15th–16th c.), the primitive form whereof, apparently, was: **"for our fathers and brethren who labor and serve"** (unfinished) (MSS of the 14th–15th c.), sometimes with the addition: **"and for the people standing present and awaiting great and rich mercy from Thee."** Sometimes in its stead: **"for all the brotherhood... (and for all Christians?)"**. In the most ancient (15th c.) MSS, in exchange for this petition, and in somewhat later ones (15th–16th c.) together with it, after it, stands the present final petition, which in its primitive form must have contained a petition only for those who bear fruit (see above, p. 572); the Euchologion of the Imperial Public Library No. 109 of the 12th–13th c. reads it, however, in an unfinished form: **"and for those who bear fruit"**; others: **"for all those standing present"**; it receives its present form in MSS of the 15th–16th centuries after the following accretions, designated by brackets: (**"Furthermore we pray"** or **"and"**) **for those who bear fruit (and do good works) in this holy (and all-venerable) temple, (those who keep vigil, labor, and sing, and) for the people standing present, who await rich (or: 'great', later both) mercy from Thee (or: 'from the Lord')** (later Slavic MSS: **"for health and for salvation"**). After this petition in certain MSS of the 14th–16th centuries there was yet a final petition: **"(Furthermore we pray also) (for all the brotherhood and) for (all) (pious and) Orthodox Christians"** (later Slavic: **"for health and for salvation"**) [^2268]. The litany *(Orig. p. 575)* in the Liturgies of Basil the Great and John Chrysostom sometimes differs in composition, preserving in the former traces of greater antiquity [^2269].

Alongside such comparatively extensive redactions of the post-Gospel litany, there runs through a series of Greek manuscripts a homogeneous brief redaction that reduced the litany initially unto 5 petitions, and subsequently unto 4. Thus in certain MSS [^2270] of the 11th–12th centuries: **"Let us all say... O Lord Almighty... Have mercy on us, O God... Furthermore we pray for the remission of sins of N. the hieromonk and of all the brotherhood in Christ... Furthermore we pray for all who serve and have served in this holy monastery..."** Sometimes there were added here petitions for the emperor [tsar] and the archbishop, while the final petition was replaced by: **"for the people standing present and awaiting rich mercy"** [^2271]. Such a brief redaction, apparently, became predominant in Greek MSS and was adopted into the first printed Greek editions of the 16th century in even lesser volume: the petition for the abbot (hieromonk) was replaced by the petition for the emperors in the present redaction, while the final petition 'for those who serve' was omitted [^2272]. With the onset of Ottoman [Turkish] rule among the Greeks, there began to be excluded from the Augmented Litany, as also from the Great Litany, the petition for the emperors, being replaced by: **"Furthermore we pray for pious and Orthodox Christians."** In the present Old Believer *Sluzhebnik* (printed without alteration from the edition of 1601 under Patriarch Job), the Augmented Litany hath the following composition:

"**'Let us all say...'** (without 'our'). **'O Lord Almighty...'** (without 'hear and have mercy'). **'Have mercy on us...'** ('we pray Thee, O Lord'). **'Furthermore we pray for our right-believing and God-preserved sovereign [tsar], grand prince N...'** ('abiding' and further all in the genitive case; instead of 'to help'—'to direct, let us all say'). (Here the Prayer of Fervent Supplication). **'Furthermore we pray for our Patriarch N., for health and salvation. Furthermore we pray unto the Lord our God to have mercy upon our lord, the right-believing and Christ-loving tsar and grand prince N., and his right-believing and Christ-loving tsaritsa, the grand princess N.; multiply, O Lord, the years of their life and send them noble children as inheritance of their line, and deliver them from all affliction, wrath, and necessity, and from every sickness of soul and body, and forgive them every transgression voluntary and involuntary, let us all say. Furthermore we pray for the mercy of God, for help, and for visitation, and for strengthening, and for assistance, and for vouchsafing victory and triumph over enemies unto the right-believing and Christ-loving tsar and grand prince N., for the welfare of the armed forces, for peace, and for tranquility, and for the ordering, and for the remission of sins of all Orthodox Christianity, let us all say. (If it be a monastery, say this:) Furthermore we pray for our father Hegumen N. and for all our brotherhood in Christ, for health and for salvation. Furthermore we pray for all who serve... for health... (If it be outside a monastery, let us append also this:) Furthermore we pray for the people standing present and awaiting the great** *(Orig. p. 576)* **mercy that cometh from Thee, for health and for salvation. Furthermore we pray for those who give alms, for health, for salvation. Furthermore we pray for all the brotherhood and for all Christians, for health and for salvation'**" [^2273].

The difference between the Vesperal litany and the Liturgy's litany among the Old Believers consists only in the 2nd petition for the tsar, where there are no words concerning childbearing; at the Presanctified Liturgy after the 2nd petition for the tsar there is a similar petition 'for our lord, the right-believing and Christ-loving tsarevich prince N. and the right-believing tsarevna, grand princess N.', and there are no petitions for the abbot and for those standing present [^2274]. In the present Athens *Euchologion* there is the following difference from our litany: instead of the Synod, a petition for the archbishop without the brotherhood; following directly after it, the petition 'for our brethren', where there is added + 'hierodeacons and monastics'; in the petition for the ktitors, emperors [tsars] and patriarchs are not mentioned; there is the petition **'For **mercy, life...'** In the Constantinople edition everything is the same, only the petition **'For mercy...'** stands prior unto the ktitors; and in the petition **'For mercy...'**, instead of the brethren: 'of all pious and Orthodox Christians who dwell and abide in this city, the wardens [*epitropoi*] and parishioners [*enoritai*] of this holy church with their wives and children, and the servants of God NN.' (the latter also in the petition for the ktitors for the departed) [^2275].

## The Threefold "Lord, Have Mercy"

The threefold **"Lord, have mercy"** in the capacity of the people's response unto the petitions of the Augmented Litany became a distinctive feature of the post-Gospel litany scarcely at an early date. Yet in general the threefold **"Lord, have mercy"** was customary in the Church from the most ancient times and served as an expression of the most fervent prayer. In the Syriac Liturgy of the Apostle James it serves as the response of the people unto the invocation of the Holy Spirit for the consecration of the Gifts [^2276]. In Greek manuscripts of the Liturgy of the Apostle James, at the end of each of the three longest litanies before the prayer there stands the rubric: 'People: Lord, have mercy (thrice)', whereas beneath the first petition of the same litanies there sometimes stands: 'People: Lord, have mercy.' In the litany occupying the place of our Augmented Litany, there is only the first rubric, while the second is omitted [^2277], presumably as self-evident. Consequently, in the Liturgy of the Apostle James the threefold **"Lord, have mercy"** was an appurtenance of the final petition of each great litany, while all the remaining petitions of these litanies, including the litany corresponding unto our Augmented Litany, had a single **"Lord, have mercy"**. (A remnant of this practice in the present Augmented Litany is the single **"Lord, have mercy"** at the first two petitions). In the Liturgies of Basil the Great and John Chrysostom, Greek and Slavic manuscripts make no rubrics regarding the people's response unto the petitions of the litanies, excluding one MS of the 12th–14th centuries, wherein it is noted after the litany *(Orig. p. 577)* **'Let us all say'**: 'The people at the end: Lord, have mercy (12 times)' [^2278]; in Greek printed editions at each petition of the Augmented Litany, as also of the Great Litany, there stands: 'Choir: Lord, have mercy', and at the last: *Eis polla etē, despota* [Gr. Εἰς πολλὰ ἔτη, δέσποτα; Many years, Master]; the latter is explained by the custom indicated by certain Greek MSS of the 11th–13th centuries, for the hierarch or priest to sign with the cross and bless (*staurōnei, sphragizei* [Gr. σταυρώνει, σφραγίζει]) the people before the ecphonesis of this litany; the first Slavic printed editions have no such rubrics, nor do the Old Believer ones. For the first time Slavic printed editions, beginning with the Moscow *Sluzhebnik* of 1653, appoint such responses unto the petitions of the Augmented Litany as are customary at present, that is, for the first two—a single **"Lord, have mercy"**, and for the remainder—the threefold response (editions, for example the Moscow edition of 1655, that have at the end of the litany a petition for the tsar, appoint for it a 12-fold **"Lord, have mercy"**) [^2279].

## The Augmented Litany at Vespers

At Vespers the Augmented Litany, it must be supposed, was for the most part of the same composition as at the Liturgy. This is evident already from the fact that many manuscripts do not provide its text in the order of Vespers; where it is provided, however, it coincides with the liturgical text of the Augmented Litany of that same epoch. Thus in a 16th-century Georgian MS of the Tiflis Ecclesiastical Museum No. 450, in the order of Vespers, which bears traces of the Chanted Office [*asmatike akolouthia*], after the prokeimenon there is the following litany:

"**'Let us all say... O Lord Almighty... Rich in mercy... Who willest not the death of a sinner... For this holy temple... For our archbishop... That He may help and subdue unto him... For this city... For seasonable weather... For those who sail, travel... That we may be delivered... And for all who require help from God... Protect, save...'**" [^2280].

The 3rd and 4th of these petitions are indicated at the Vesperal litany also by certain Slavic MSS of the 13th–15th centuries [^2281]. In the order of Vespers that has preserved fewer traces of the Chanted Office than the preceding Georgian MS, according unto a manuscript of the Patmos Library No. 105 of the 13th century, the Augmented Litany has the first three petitions as at present, and thereafter:

"**'Furthermore we pray that the Lover of mankind, God, may be merciful, good, and gracious unto our transgressions... For our most pious and right-believing emperors [tsars], their might, victory, abiding... For the servant of God N. and all our brotherhood in Christ, their health, salvation...'** Here he commemorates the living, whomsoever he willeth. **'For the health, salvation, and remission of transgressions of all... And for our emperors who have been in pious memory... For the departed fathers, hegumens, and brethren... Furthermore we pray for those who remain and those who are departing, for the healing of those lying in infirmity, for the repose, relief, and blessed memory, the remission of sins of all who have fallen asleep before us...'**" [^2282].

*(Orig. p. 578)*

In these and in the majority of manuscripts prior unto the 12th century, at the Vesperal Augmented Litany is appointed a prayer, common with the liturgical one [^2283]. The first printed Greek editions have the Augmented Litany at Vespers with the following difference from the present one. The petition for the armed forces: **"Furthermore we pray for the remission (of sins) and strengthening of the Christ-loving armed forces"**; there is a petition: **"for the priests, hieromonks, and all the sacerdotal and monastic order"**; the petition for the ktitors ("founders") doth not contain a commemoration of all Orthodox Christians.

Subsequent Greek editions exclude the petitions for the emperors [tsars], the armed forces, and "for the priests..." [^2284]. As in certain Greek 16th-century manuscripts, so also in the first printed editions, the Vesperal Augmented Litany is distinguished by greater volume in comparison with the liturgical one, which breaks off at the petition for the emperor (see above, p. 575).

In the first printed Slavic editions, the Vesperal Augmented Litany likewise differs from the liturgical one, yet not so much in volume as in composition. Thus, in the Kyiv *Sluzhebnik* of 1629 the first petition in the liturgical litany is divided into two, whereas at the Vesperal litany, as at present, it constitutes one; at Vespers the petition "for the priests" is absent; in the petition for the ktitors only at the Liturgy is there the addition: "and for all Orthodox", while the petition "for those who bear fruit" begins only with "those who stand present" [^2285].

In the first printed Moscow editions, for example that of 1647, the difference between the Vesperal litany and the liturgical one consists only in the petition for those who serve and have served, which is redundant in the latter; in the Moscow *Sluzhebnik* of 1658 the present difference is already present in all exactitude. In present-day Greek editions there is no difference between the Vesperal and liturgical litanies. Likewise in the Old Believer editions, the difference consists only in the 2nd petition for the tsar, where at the Liturgy there are no words concerning childbearing; and at the Presanctified Liturgy, after the 2nd petition for the tsar, there is a similar petition "for our sovereign, the right-believing and Christ-loving tsarevich prince N. and the right-believing tsarevna, grand princess N.", and there are no petitions for the abbot and for those standing present [^2286].

## Who Recites the Augmented Litany at Vespers

The Augmented Litany at Vespers, unlike the Great Litany, the Typikon directs to be recited by the deacon, both in view of the greater solemnity of this part of Vespers, and because the priest hath already entered the altar to stand before the Holy Table and offer our prayers there, whereas litanies are recited upon the ambo.

In this requirement of the Typikon all ancient manuscripts thereof agree, although the majority of them, as we have seen, give the same direction also regarding the Great Litany.

*(Orig. p. 579)*

# "Vouchsafe, O Lord" (*Spodobi, Gospodi* — *Kataxioson, Kyrie*)

Following the prayer for the faithful, which the Augmented Litany represents, at Vespers there follows a prayer for needs, and first for the immediate ones prompted by the approaching evening. A prayer of this kind is divided into two prayers: a simple [lay] one and a sacerdotal one—**"Vouchsafe, O Lord"** (*Spodobi, Gospodi*) and the Litany of Supplication.

**"Vouchsafe, O Lord"** (*Kataxioson, Kyrie* [Gr. Καταξίωσον, Κύριε]) is rather a hymn than a prayer; by its prayerful-laudatory content **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"** cannot strictly be called either a prayer or a hymn, for which reason it is always named solely by its opening words. By its content and its place at Vespers, this hymnographic prayer resembles the Great Doxology at Matins, with which it literally coincides also in the majority of its individual expressions. At daily Matins it is appended in the same form as at Vespers unto the correspondingly modified and abridged Great Doxology. Like the latter, it is composed of biblical expressions verbatim or with slight necessary modifications. In comparison with the Doxology, it is of a more suppliant and not so festive a character.

In **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"**, the prayer for a sinless evening, which we entreat on account of the blessed Name so glorified by ancient righteous men (**"Blessed art Thou, O Lord, God of our fathers"**—from the Song of the Three Holy Children: Dan. 3:26), so as not to disrupt the eternal harmony of this praise—this prayer, naturally the first for a Christian at the arrival of evening, transitions into a more general prayer for the mercy of God in accordance with our hope (**"Let Thy mercy, O Lord, be upon us..."**—Ps. 32:22 [LXX]). Let this mercy be expressed first of all in the arduous instruction in that which can justify man before God. The sentence of Ps. 118:12 [LXX]: **"Blessed art Thou, O Lord..."**, as containing this fundamental petition, is repeated thrice, yet not verbatim as at the Great Doxology, but with modifications in the text adapted unto the Persons of the Holy Trinity, thereby supplying that which is lacking in **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"** in comparison with the morning Doxology: an address by Name unto the Persons of the Holy Trinity and Their glorification. The particular prayer for instruction in the will of God returns once more unto the general prayer for the mercy of God, a prayer already expressed in a stronger form, with even greater assurance: **"O Lord, Thy mercy endureth for ever..."** (Ps. 137:8 [LXX]), an expression which, like the subsequent concluding doxology, hath nothing in common with the Great Doxology. The conclusion of the prayer **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"** (**"Unto Thee belongeth praise..."**) resembles the ecphonesis of the Great Litany and represents, like the prayerful beginning, not a borrowing from Holy Scripture, but a brief hymn of praise unto the Holy Trinity, composed independently by Christians and tripartite in Her honor.

## History of the Prayer

In the *Apostolic Constitutions*, alongside the morning doxology, almost literally identical with the first part of the present Great *(Orig. p. 580)* Doxology, there is cited with the superscription (in later redactions): "Evening Prayer", the following prayer-hymn:

"Praise the Lord, ye servants, praise the Name of the Lord. We praise Thee, we sing unto Thee, we bless Thee for Thy great glory, O Lord King, Father of Christ, the Lamb without blemish, Who taketh away the sin of the world. Unto Thee belongeth praise, unto Thee belongeth song, unto Thee belongeth glory: unto God and the Father through the Son in the All-Holy Spirit, unto ages of ages. Amen" [^2287].

This hymn, therefore, constitutes the foundation and primitive form of **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"**. Remarkable is its strict analogy with the morning doxology: only the angelic New Testament praise at the beginning is replaced by psalmody (Ps. 112:1 [LXX]). Immediately following this prayer, the *Apostolic Constitutions* cite the Canticle of Simeon the God-receiver [*Nunc Dimittis*]. However, in the very order of Vespers provided by the *Apostolic Constitutions*, this prayer, as also **"Now lettest Thou Thy servant depart"**, is not indicated—among other reasons (see Introductory Chapter, p. 137), perhaps also because this prayer had not yet received widespread dissemination. The Typikon of the Great Church of Constantinople likewise did not know it, not only in its ancient redactions, but also in the Chanted Office [*asmatike akolouthia*] of the 15th–16th centuries (see Introductory Chapter, pp. 339, 342). Yet the eastern type of daily services, having borrowed it, evidently from the Syrian Church (the homeland of the *Apostolic Constitutions*), already knew it in the 6th century: in the account of the visit of Sophronius and John Moschus unto Nilus of Sinai, **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"** at Vespers occupies its present place, as it doth also in the Holy Sepulchre Typikon of 1112 and in the most ancient manuscripts of the Studite Typikon (ibid., pp. 295, 355).

In the Coptic Horologion, where this prayer is placed not in the order of Vespers, but in an appendix unto the Horologion among the seven night and day prayers, and in the 14th-century Ethiopic Horologion for the Coptic Church, where it constitutes only the 2nd part of the morning doxology, it possesses a greater volume than with us, and the following differences from our redaction:

after **"Let Thy mercy, O Lord..."**: **"For the eyes of all look with hope unto Thee... in due season. Hear us, O God... of the earth. And Thou, O Lord, shalt preserve us and keep us from this evil generation unto ages. Amen. Blessed art Thou, O Lord, teach me Thy statutes.** (Ethiopic: + **Blessed art Thou, O Lord, make me to understand Thy judgments). Blessed art Thou, O Lord, enlighten me with Thy righteousness. O Lord, Thy mercy... forsake not... Lord, Thou hast been our refuge from generation unto generation...** (and further as with us in the festal Great Doxology down to:) **unto them that know Thee and Thy righteousness unto the upright in heart** (Ethiopic: + **O Lord, Thy mercy**—a second time). **Unto Thee belongeth holiness** (Ethiopic: **praise**), **Unto Thee belongeth song, unto Thee belongeth glory** (Ethiopic: **holiness**)..." [^2288].

## Manner of Performance

Occupying at Vespers a position analogous unto the Great Doxology at Matins, **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"** would seem to require also the same manner of performance, that is, chanting. Yet in accordance with the lesser solemnity of Vespers in comparison *(Orig. p. 581)* with Matins, this prayerful hymn is not sung here, but read; in view of its importance, however, the Typikon entrusts its reading unto the superior, assigning it unto the number of the ten most important prayers read by the superior (see Chapter 7 of the Typikon, "Note" [*zri*]), although it permitteth its reading also unto a reader (in this 2nd chapter, whereas in Chapter 7 no such permission is given).

The reading of **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"**, notwithstanding its hymnic-laudatory character and analogy with the Great Doxology, is an echo of the fact that for this latter doxology also in the Studite Typikon there was appointed chanting close unto reading (see Introductory Chapter, p. 368; see below, "The Great Doxology").—Manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon speak thus regarding the manner of performing **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"**: 13th-century Georgian—"the people: Vouchsafe, O Lord"; the most ancient Greek (Moscow Rumyantsev Museum, Sevastyanov collection No. 491/35 of the 13th c.)—"we: Vouchsafe, O Lord"; later Greek (Moscow Synodal Library No. 381 of the 14th c.): "the appointed monk"; Slavic (for example, Kyiv Museum No. Aa 194 of the 16th c.)—"we say".

# The Litany of Supplication (*Prositel'naya Ekteniya*)

A supplement unto the prayer **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"** is the following litany, wherein the petitions of this prayer are both expanded and intensified by being offered through the sacred ministers. This litany is called in popular parlance the "Litany of Supplication" [*prositel'naya*], and in liturgical books by its first word the Litany of "Let us complete" (*Plērōsōmen* [Gr. Πληρώσωμεν]). Such an opening indicates that it is concluding in the service. As remarked above, it serves as an addition unto the Augmented Litany in the respect that the latter contains petitions for persons, whereas this one is for the objects needed by those persons. And just as the petitions of the Great Litany concerning persons receive further development in the Augmented Litany, although concentrating upon the faithful alone, so also the brief petitions of the Great Litany concerning human needs here become more detailed and at the same time are elevated in their content, namely, being restricted unto the realm of spiritual needs alone. And by its structure the Litany of Supplication begins where the Great Litany concludes ("Help us, save us"). Beginning its supplication from that petition with which the Great and Little Litanies conclude, the Litany of Supplication divides our needs into six classes, speaking first of immediate needs (a sinless evening, morning, or day), and thereafter of enduring and ever more important ones: it entreats a guardian of sinlessness—an Angel [^2289], the conditions for further sinlessness—pardon of past sins [^2290], other favorable conditions for righteousness—such as *(Orig. p. 582)* the present evening, and of the entire evening ("the remaining time") of our life, and its sunset—our end [^2291]; after the recourse unto the intercession of the saints, common with the Great Litany, the litany points out the pledge of the fulfillment of prayer in the goodness and love for mankind of God (cf. above, p. 569).

## History of the Litany

Deaconal proclamations almost literally coinciding with our Litany of Supplication are found in the order of Vespers and Matins provided by the *Apostolic Constitutions*, and at the present place in those services. Specifically, following the introductory psalm, the prayers for the catechumens, energumens, candidates for illumination, and penitents, and after their dismissal from the temple at Vespers and Matins, according unto this 4th-century monument (see Introductory Chapter, p. 136), there was appointed a prayer for the faithful with proclamations of the deacon close unto our Great and partially Augmented Litanies, and thereupon the deacon says:

"Save and raise us up [^2292], O God, through Thy Christ (*dia Christou* [Gr. διὰ Χριστοῦ]). Having arisen, let us entreat the mercies of the Lord and His compassions; an Angel of peace [^2293], good and profitable things, a Christian end, a peaceful and sinless evening and night, and all the time of our life without condemnation, let us entreat. Let us commit ourselves and one another unto the living (*zōnti* [Gr. ζῶντι; printed ζώνη]) God through His Christ."

At Matins the same proclamation of the deacon was read somewhat differently:

"Save them, O God, and raise them up by Thy grace. Let us entreat of the Lord His mercies and compassions, this morning and day peaceful and sinless, and all the time of our sojourning, an Angel of peace, a Christian end, a merciful and gracious (*eumenē* [Gr. εὐμενῆ]) God. Let us commit ourselves and one another unto the living God through His Only-Begotten" [^2294].

Similar petitions were customary also in the time of St. John Chrysostom: "Arise (*egeiresthe* [Gr. ἐγείρεσθε]). Entreat the Angel of peace, ye catechumens. Entreat all that is set before you (*prokeimena* [Gr. προκείμενα]) peaceful: a peaceful present day and all the days of your life. Entreat Christian ends for yourselves, that which is good and profitable" [^2295]. Among the complete liturgies, the Litany of Supplication hath its briefest form in the Armenian Liturgy; here it is appointed after the Gospel and Creed before the dismissal of the catechumens and the Cherubic Hymn; it begins: **"Again and again"**, and besides this introductory petition it hath before the special petitions yet another (concerning the hearing of prayer and a righteous life). There are four petitions with the response "Grant, O Lord":

"That we may pass the hour of this holy sacrifice and the present day in peace, *(Orig. p. 583)* let us entreat of the Lord. An Angel of peace and guardian of our souls, let us entreat of the Lord. Pardon and remission of our sins, let us entreat of the Lord. The great and sovereign power of the Most-Holy Cross unto our help, let us entreat of the Lord."

The conclusion of the litany consists of three petitions identical with those of the Armenian Great Litany (see above, p. 519) [^2296]. No longer is the corresponding litany in the Malabar (Nestorian) Liturgy, where it is appointed at the very same place.

> **Deacon:** "By prayer and supplication we entreat the Angels of peace and love (plural). People: Unto Thee, O Lord (such is the response unto all four petitions). By night and by day and all the days of our life, we entreat perpetual peace for Thy Church and a sinless life. Remission of sins and that which conferreth benefit upon our life and is well-pleasing unto Thy Divinity, let us entreat. The mercies of the Lord and His goodwill, ever and at all times, let us entreat. Let us commit ourselves and our souls unto the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. People: Unto Thee, O Lord God. The priest—the prayer" [^2297].

In the Liturgy of the Apostle James in Greek manuscripts, the Litany of Supplication is appointed immediately after the Gospel before the dismissal of the catechumens; it begins:

"Let us apply ourselves diligently (*scholazōmen ektenōs* [Gr. σχολάζωμεν ἐκτενῶς]). In peace let us pray unto the Lord"; and after three or four petitions common with the first petitions of the Great Litany: **"For the peace from above...** (absent in the Messina MS). **For the peace of the whole world... For the salvation and protection of our most holy Patriarch N., all the clergy, and the Christ-loving people, let us pray unto the Lord. For the remission of our sins and forgiveness of our transgressions, and that we may be delivered from all affliction, wrath, danger, and necessity, and the assault of enemies, let us pray unto the Lord"**, the present six special petitions follow in the same order, yet with the following variant readings in relation unto the present ones: in the 1st petition—"that we all may pass the whole day perfect, holy, peaceful, and sinless, let us entreat of the Lord";
in the 5th petition, instead of "in repentance"—"in health"; in the 6th petition "peaceful" is absent, and after "fearful"—"and dread" (*phriktou* [Gr. φρικτοῦ]). (Thus, the abbreviation of the Jerusalem Liturgy of the Apostle James in the Constantinopolitan Liturgy touched, but very little, also upon the Litany of Supplication). Yet in the Sinai MS of the Liturgy of the Apostle James (No. 1040 of the 12th c.), of these variant readings there is only the 3rd (no "peaceful"). The response unto the petitions is not indicated. Thereafter **"Commemorating our All-Holy..."** (with John the Baptist and the choirs of saints) [^2298]. In the Slavic translation of the Liturgy of the Apostle James according unto MS of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences No. 26 of the 17th century, the special petitions, of which only the opening words are given here, stand in the following order: 2, 4, 6, 1, 3, 5 [^2299]. In the Liturgies of Basil the Great and John Chrysostom, as also at Vespers and Matins, the Litany of Supplication in ancient *Sluzhebniki* hath in comparison with the present ones the following variant readings: in the first petition "holy" is sometimes omitted (Greek MS of the early 17th c.), while "faithful" is added (Slavic MS of the 16th c.); 2nd petition in ancient Slavic: "mercy and remission" [*milosti i ostavleniya*]; besides these two concepts, Porphyrius's Euchologion of the 9th–10th centuries hath also *kai syngchōrēsin* [Gr. καὶ συγχώρησιν] (forbearance), and instead of "remission" a Greek 16th-century MS hath it; instead of "transgressions" *(Orig. p. 584)* the ancient Slavic translation hath "scandals" [*soblaznov*]; in the 4th petition in one Greek 15th-century MS: "to grant unto Thy world"; in Slavic of the 14th–15th centuries: "unto the whole world"; the ancient Slavic translation instead of "peace" hath "humility"; the same also in the 5th petition; ibid.: "the remaining year" or "the remaining years"; in the 6th petition: "to end our life in a Christian manner"; instead of "painless"—"sinless"; instead of "judgment seat" [*sudishchi*]—"judgment" [*sude*] (inaccurate) [^2300].

As regards the relation of the Litany of Supplication unto Vespers, it is remarkable that the *Apostolic Constitutions* do not have it in the order of their Liturgy, but only at Vespers and Matins; consequently, this is a litany created for these services. At Vespers, moreover at its present place, it is indicated by the earliest manuscripts of Euchologia and Typika that provide the detailed order of Vespers from the 11th century; they indicate it under the name *Plērōsōmen* [Gr. Πληρώσωμεν], or *Plērōsōmen meta tōn aitēseōn* [Gr. Πληρώσωμεν μετὰ τῶν αἰτήσεων], or *aitēseis* [Gr. αἰτήσεις], in Slavic **"Let us complete our prayers"** [^2301]. Yet certain Typika and Euchologia of the 11th–12th centuries indicate it after **"Now lettest Thou Thy servant depart"** (Nicholas-Casole Typikon, Sinai Library Euchologion No. 973; see Introductory Chapter, pp. 368, 377). Presumably this was the most ancient place of the Litany of Supplication, since with it is closely linked the Prayer of the Bowing of Heads, and the latter in the most ancient Euchologia is preceded by the dismissal prayer (see Introductory Chapter, p. 344).

## The Bowing of Heads (*Glavopreklońenie*)

The Litany of Supplication, being in its conception the final prayer of the service, concludes with the impartation of peace, that is, the actual bestowing by God through the priest of that wherewith the supplications at Vespers (as at every service) began, and which is regarded as the sum of all blessings (in biblical usage "peace" signifieth also salvation; cf. the angelic hymn at the Nativity of the Savior; see above, p. 511). The prayer itself here, at its conclusion, reaches its summit in that action is joined unto words, that besides words it is expressed also in the action of the bowing of heads, which replaces the penitential bending of the knees. Over those who have bowed their heads at the invitation of the deacon, there is read secretly by the priest (as are all his prayers at the services) a special "Prayer of the Bowing of Heads": **"O Lord our God, Who didst bow the heavens and come down"**, wherein the priest entreats God to look upon those who by this action express their submission unto God and their hope, to preserve them always and in the approaching night from every enemy, the devil, and evil thoughts; in the ecphonesis of the prayer: **"Blessed and glorified be the majesty of Thy Kingdom"**, God is naturally glorified as King.

### History of the Bowing of Heads

The Prayer of the Bowing of Heads replaced the ancient imposition of hands by the bishop at the end of the service upon each worshiper, as was the case, for example, in the Jerusalem Church of the 4th century (see Introductory Chapter, p. 142) and at Vespers and Matins in the *Apostolic Constitutions*, where the prayer at this imposition of hands is also cited, *(Orig. p. 585)* being of homogeneous, though not identical, content with the present one (ibid., p. 136). The present prayer is already read in manuscripts of the 10th century, yet certain manuscripts have in its stead other prayers of the bowing of heads. Thus, the Euchologion of the Sinai Library No. 957 of the 9th–10th centuries: **"O Lord our God, Who sittest upon the throne of glory and beholdest the abysses, looking down with a merciful eye upon our humility: bless all of us who have bowed our heads unto Thee, and exalt our horn in Thy goodwill; blessed be the all-holy name of Thy love for mankind."** The Euchologion of the Paris National Library: **"O Holy Master, who have bowed the neck of our body unto Thee, we pray: grant us ever with an upright and unswerving mind to look upon the heavenly glory and to be exalted unto Thy majesty; for Thine is the majesty and Thine is the Kingdom"** [^2302].

# The Litiya (*Litiya* — *Litē*)

Following the Litany of Supplication and the Prayer of the Bowing of Heads linked with it, wherewith Vespers properly concludes, there is inserted into it a special additional, non-obligatory part, called the Litiya. *Litiya* (from Greek *litē* [Gr. λιτή], earnest supplication), according unto constant ecclesiastical usage, signified supplication outside the temple. The present Typikon knows four kinds of litiya, which according unto their degree of solemnity may be arranged in the following order:
a) "litiya outside the monastery", appointed on certain Twelve Great Feasts and during Bright Week before the Liturgy;
b) litiya at Great Vespers connected with a Vigil;
c) litiya at the conclusion of festal and Sunday Matins;
d) litiya for the reposed following daily Vespers and Matins.

By the content of their hymnody and prayers and by their rite, these kinds of litiya differ greatly from one another, yet what they have in common is specifically the procession forth [exit / *iskhozhenie*] from the temple. This exit in the first kind (of those enumerated) of litiya is complete, while in the remainder it is partial. Yet both there and here it is performed most immediately with the aim of expressing prayer not only in words, but also in bodily movement, changing its place to revive prayerful attention; a further aim of the litiya is the expression—by departure from the temple—of our unworthiness to pray within it: "we pray, standing before the doors of the holy temple, as before the doors of heaven... like Adam, the publican, the prodigal son" [^2303]. Hence the somewhat penitential and sorrowful character of the litiya prayers. Finally, in the litiya the Church goes forth from her grace-filled communion into the outer world—in the literal sense—or into the narthex [*pritvor*], as that part of the temple contiguous with this world, open unto all who are not yet received into the Church or are excluded from her, for the purpose of a prayerful mission in this world. Hence the all-popular and universal character (concerning the whole world) of the litiya prayers [^2304].

*(Orig. p. 586)*

## General History of the Litiya

By its original purpose, the litiya, having something analogous also in Roman cult (see Introductory Chapter, p. 354, note 2), was a supplication in times of public calamities in the places stricken or threatened by them (ibid., p. 152); such was the litiya also in the Typikon of the Great Church of Constantinople, and in the Western Church (ibid., pp. 353–354) only unto such supplications was the name litiya assigned.

Yet alongside these litai there existed already in the 3rd century supplications very close unto them of a joyfully festive character, consisting, like those, in processions outside the city, unto which, however, the name of litai and litanies was not assigned. These processions received special development in the Church of Jerusalem, where they were performed, presumably, at first on feast days unto the holy places commemorated by the festive events (ibid., p. 251ff.), and then, already in the 4th century, became a regular part of every Sunday Vespers; this litiya (likewise not called so) consisted in a simple repetition of the second, prayerful part of Vespers in various holy places (ibid., p. 142). The present litai before the Liturgy are a remnant of the festal Jerusalem litai, while those at Vespers and Matins are a direct heritage of the Sunday-Vesperal litiya there, which, under the influence of the Great Church and ancient universal practice, adopted elements from the penitential-prayerful litiya.

## The Procession unto the Litiya

The litiya at Great Vespers [^2305] is composed of three elements: rites, hymns, and prayers. The rite of the litiya consists in the solemn exit of the clergy and people into the narthex. Since "the narthex is appointed for the penitents and catechumens", the Church, "as if bearing the image of penitents and catechumens, humbling herself before God and entreating His mercy, performs a certain part of the service in the narthex" [^2306]. "Standing before the sacred temple, as before the doors of heaven, we entreat Him" [^2307]. This exit is so essential an attribute of the litiya that in Slavic manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon, instead of the term *litiya*, the term "procession" [*iskhozhenie*] is constantly used [^2308]. This *(Orig. p. 587)* exit is performed according unto an order close unto the Vesperal Entrance. The priest [^2309] with the deacon, as there, go forth through the north doors, with the Holy Doors closed (according unto the *Sluzhebnik*) [^2310]. The deacon walks beside the priest [^2311], holding the censer. Before them are carried two candlesticks [*manoualia*, Gr. μανουάλια]. The singers ("we") follow after the clergy. All this is performed during the singing of the stichera appointed for the litiya. Upon arriving in the narthex, the deacon "censes the holy icons (there), the superior, and the choirs, and stands in his place", that is, before the priest slightly to the right.

## The Procession according unto Ancient Typika

Studite typika did not know the litiya at festal Vespers.

The most ancient redactions of the Jerusalem Typikon indicated an exit for the litiya into other churches and oratories (*eukteria*) of the monastery, and in conclusion into the narthex of the main church, wherein on the way to each of these churches its stichera were sung, and in each of them one petition of the litiya litany was pronounced. Thus the Georgian Shiomgvime manuscript of the 13th century and two of the library of the Monastery of St. Sabas near Jerusalem of the 16th century [^2312]. As regards the rite of the exit, it had the following development:

Georgian:
"The priest goes with the censer, preceded by a lighted taper."

Greek MSS and printed editions:
"We chant the idiomelon, performing the litiya (*litaneuontes* [Gr. λιτανεύοντες]) into the narthex (*en tō narthēki* [Gr. ἐν τῷ νάρθηκι]), preceded by the priest with the censer and a lamp (*lampados* [Gr. λαμπάδος])", in printed editions "lamps" [^2313]; of censing in the narthex no mention is made.

"Order" (*Diataxis* / *Chin*) of Patriarch Philotheus:
"At the singing of them (the stichera of the litiya), the deacon, having entered (the altar) and taken the blessing as usual, goes forth together with the priest through the northern side with the Holy Doors barred, preceded by lamps, and having passed through the beautiful doors, and after them all the brethren, they take their stand in the narthex; during the singing of the brethren, the deacon censes all as usual; and upon the completion of the stichera, having taken his stand in the customary place, he says: Save, O God" [^2314].

In the most ancient Slavic MSS:
"The priest and deacon make the procession into the narthex, a taper going before with the censer, and we following them; and the priest having passed the church doors and having censed crosswise, stands there, and the choirs stand according to their order" [^2315].

Later MSS replace the one taper with "2 candlesticks" [*2 svetil'nikoma*]; concerning censing *(Orig. p. 588)* they add "the abbot and the brethren" [^2316]. Still later ones: "the priest goes forth with the deacon through the Holy Doors—and there censes (the priest?) the holy icons and the superior" [^2317].

Old Believer: the same, but the deacon censes + the brethren [^2318]. Present Greek Euchologion: "we chant the stichera, performing the litiya (*litaneuontes* [Gr. λιτανεύοντες]) in the narthex, preceded by the priest and deacon with lamps and censer" [^2319].

## Stichera of the Litiya

The exit unto the litiya of Sunday Vespers (customary) is performed during the singing of the "sticheron of the temple". The singing of such a sticheron is natural during a solemn procession through the temple; and it is natural to remember during the entire Vigil at least once the saint in whose honor the temple is dedicated (ancient typika, as we shall see, speak here of singing the sticheron specifically of the temple saint), even as he is remembered also in the liturgical chants once (in the troparion after the Entrance), and who is conceived of as spiritually co-present with the faithful and participating in their service, "sealing the singing and initiating the celebration" [^2320]. Which of the temple stichera to sing at the litiya, the Typikon does not specify [^2321]. In the Octoechos, in the service of Tone 1, it is noted: "we chant the idiomelon sticheron of the Saint of the monastery, making the litiya into the narthex, at which we chant the stichera of Paul of Amorion or what the superior wisheth." It is assumed that the temple, as was almost always the case in antiquity, is dedicated unto a saint, and from his stichera there is indicated for singing an idiomelon, as the most solemn in melody, wherever it may be appointed in the saint's service; for the most part, idiomela are appointed at "Glory, Both now" of *Lord, I have cried* or of the Aposticha. As regards the stichera of Paul of Amorion, placed in the Octoechos at *Lord, I have cried*, which are Theotokia in content, the Typikon nowhere assumes their singing at the litiya, since in the rubrics concerning Sunday service on Triodion Sundays it constantly speaks of chanting at the litiya only one sticheron of the temple, not counting the Doxastikon from the Triodion and the Theotokion [^2322]. "Upon the completion of the stichera," continues the Typikon in the present place, allowing the possibility of singing at the litiya also several stichera (which happens upon the coincidence with Sunday of certain commemorations), "Glory, Both now: Theotokion"; which Theotokion is not specified, but in the Triodion Sundays there is always specified here a Theotokion according to the Tone of the last sticheron (at Glory), and for the most part from the Sunday aposticha *(Orig. p. 589)* Theotokia [^2323]. Consequently, even when singing at the litiya one sticheron of the temple (on an ordinary Sunday), the Theotokion unto it must be taken from the aposticha Sunday ones according to the Tone of the sticheron. But if the temple is dedicated unto the Lord or the Mother of God, then as Theotokion at the litiya there can serve again only one of the stichera of the feast unto which the temple is dedicated [^2324], because...

...then the litiya sticheron of the temple belongs unto the number of those which are generally never joined with ordinary Theotokia; perhaps in view of this the expression of the Typikon concerning the Theotokion at the litiya is so indefinite. Ancient copies of the Typikon on this point—concerning litiya stichera—were more definite; in particular, some of them indicate chanting at the litiya the sticheron of the temple according to the Tone of the Octoechos, that is, choosing from the temple stichera a sticheron of that Tone which falls upon the given Sunday, in order to maintain musical correspondence with other parts of the service (see below). The sticheron of the temple at Sunday litiya is not sung on all Twelve Great Feasts, their forefeasts and leavetakings, the Forefeast of the Nativity of Christ, Palm Sunday, Thomas Sunday, Sunday of the Myrrh-bearers, and the 7th Sunday after Pascha (see there).

## Stichera of the Litiya according unto Ancient Typika

The Georgian 13th-century MS of the Typikon, as noted above, indicates at the litiya the stichera of those saints unto whose church the litiya is directed; hence, perhaps, the Typikon's general requirement to sing at the litiya the sticheron of the temple; several stichera (not one) are indicated for each church in the Tone of the day; in the narthex of the main church after them: Glory, Both now: Theotokion; Greek MSS and printed editions: "we chant the idiomelon of the Saint of the monastery (*tou kata monēn* [Gr. τοῦ κατὰ μονῆς]) in the Tone of the day; Glory, Both now: Theotokion" [^2325]. In the most ancient 14th-century Slavic MSS of the Typikon: "we begin the idiomelon (other MSS: idiomela) of the saint whose church it is, corresponding unto the present Tone in the Octoechos (15th-c. MS adds: 'if he hath', that is, presumably, if the saint hath stichera of such Tone, and if not, then of another Tone), they sing also the other idiomela of the Saint whose church it is, Glory, Both now: sticheron of the Annunciation, Tone 8: **Be glad, ye heavens**"; instead of italics, 15th-c. MS: "and upon the completion of the stichera, Glory, Both now: Theotokion"; 16th-c. MS: "we chant the stichera of the saint whose temple it is, in the Tone of the day, if he hath them; and upon the completion of the stichera, Glory, Both now: Theotokion" [^2326].

Old Believer Typikon: "and we chant the sticheron of the saint whose temple it is; *(Orig. p. 590)* then the stichera of Paul of Amorion or of the saint, if he hath them—" "—and upon the completion of the stichera, Glory to the saint, if the saint hath one, or of the morning aposticha we chant the Glory (that is, the Glory can be taken from the aposticha stichera unto the saint at Matins, since the evening aposticha one is sung as the first litiya sticheron?), and if there be none, Glory, Both now: Theotokion; but if it be a temple of Christ or of the Mother of God, Glory, Both now: of the temple" [^2327].

## The Litiya Prayers

After the stichera at the litiya there follows a supplication, called "prayers" (*molitvy* in the *Sluzhebnik*; the Typikon calls so its first part: **"Save, O God"**), but which is in structure a litany of 5 petitions with an ecphonesis.
