This litany in its petitions is more extensive even than the Augmented Litany and fuller than the Great Litany.

It begins with a general petition in the words of Ps. 27:9 [LXX]: **"Save, O God, Thy people, and bless Thine inheritance"** for the whole people (*laon* [Gr. λαόν]—"people") as the allotment (*klēronomian* [Gr. κληρονομίαν], "inheritance") of God, and for the whole world of God, with the addition, however, of a special request for Orthodox Christians ("exalt the horn"—give them pre-eminence before others for the good of the world itself); at the same time, immediately at the beginning of the litany (not at the end, as at the Great Litany), there are presented unto God as intercessors all the saints, the whole Church is moved unto prayer, including the Church Triumphant—with detailed indication of the choirs of saints and naming of the most important (in contrast unto the general reference unto such intercession in the Great Litany), namely: the Mother of God, the Cross, the Angels, the Forerunner, the apostles, hierarchs, martyrs, venerable ascetics, the righteous, and the temple saint. The same petition, besides evening litiya, is pronounced at festal and Great-Fast Matins before the canon.

After this general and introductory petition, the litiya litany transitions unto more particular prayer for the various classes of people and their special needs, beginning, according to the apostle's commandment, with the sovereign; the petition for the sovereign is the same as in the Augmented Litany, but in view of the greater size of the petitions in this litany and their fewer number, there are combined with it into one general second petition also the supplications of the Augmented Litany for the reigning house.

The 3rd petition is for the spiritual authority and all who are most in need of God's help: for all afflicted Christians (perhaps an echo of difficult times of Christianity), for the local temple or monastery, for the indispensable condition of all well-being and development—peace and stability...

...("estate" / *sostoyanie*) [^2328] of the world, especially of the Holy Churches (repetition of petitions from the Great Litany), more particularly concerning the various kinds and degrees of afflicted condition: concerning those of the brethren engaged in hard labor (*kopiontōn* [Gr. κοπιώντων], "those who labor") and lower services ("those who serve"; *diakonountōn* [Gr. διακονούντων]), which do not permit them even presence in the temple or cause absences from the monastery ("concerning those who remain behind", *apoleiphthentōn* [Gr. ἀπολειφθέντων], properly left behind by order at work, "and those traveling", *apodēmias* [Gr. ἀποδημίας; printed ἀποδημίοας], being on a journey), concerning the sick, the depar*(Orig. p. 591)*ted, their "repose" (*koimēseōs* [Gr. κοιμήσεως], that is, resting, properly peaceful lying), "respite" (*aneseōs* [Gr. ἀνέσεως], that is, resting from earthly labors), "blessed memory" of them on earth and "remission (*apheseōs* [Gr. ἀφέσεως]) of sins", concerning captives and those engaged in various services now and formerly.

The 4th petition—for the whole (external) world (return unto the beginning) and its deliverance from physical calamities: famine, pestilence, earthquake, flood, fire,—and civil: war and civil strife; in general for the mercy of God and turning away from us of God's wrath, both already bearing down upon us and possible in the future ("the threat... that hangeth over us", *apeilēs* [Gr. ἀπειλῆς], threat) [^2329].

The 5th petition—for the hearing of prayer. After this petition in the *Sluzhebnik* is the note: "Then he commemorates whom he wishes, living and dead, secretly." Instead of the usual ecphonesis, consisting merely in glorification of God and serving as the conclusion of a prayer, unto this extraordinary litany there is joined as an ecphonesis an entire priestly prayer, beginning with the words of Ps. 64:6 [LXX: "Hear us, O God our Savior, the hope of all the ends of the earth..."], unto God as Savior and hope of all the ends of the earth and the sea, for hearing and mercy, with the doxology of the Augmented Litany.

Since the litiya is a special service inserted into others, unto its litany there is joined the impartation of peace customary at the end of services, and it concludes as a dismissal prayer with the prayer of the bowing of heads unto Jesus Christ [^2330], as the All-Merciful (*polyelee* [Gr. πολυέлеε]) Master, for the acceptance of prayer, sheltering, driving away of enemies, pacification, and showing of mercy unto us and the world. In this prayer the priest appeals unto the intercession of the same saints unto whom the deacon appealed at the beginning of the litiya, whereby this prayer is also an expansion of the last petition in the Great Litany, **"Calling to remembrance our All-Holy, Immaculate"**. Unto the petitions of the litiya litany, in view of the special fervor of its supplications, surpassing in this respect also the Augmented Litany (ever-increasing fervor of supplications), the choir responds dozens of times **"Lord, have mercy"**, moreover not an identical number of times, but in accordance with the complexity of the petition: unto the 1st—40, unto the 2nd—30, unto the 3rd—50, and unto the two last, as supplementary—3 times each,—various symbolic numbers being taken. The final prayer of the litiya the Typikon and *Sluzhebnik* require to be pronounced in a loud voice and listened to, in accordance with the special fervor and sorrowful-penitential character of the litiya prayer, not merely with bowed heads as ordinary concluding prayers, but prostrate upon the ground, while it, as a prayer of blessing, is pronounced facing west (concerning turning to the west the *Sluzhebnik* makes no mention).

## History of the Litiya Prayers

The fundamental prayer of the litiya, **"Save, O God, Thy people"**, originated, perhaps, from a brief prayer with the same beginning in certain liturgies, for example, the Liturgy of the *Apostolic Constitutions*: before the consecration of the Gifts: "Save Thy people, O Lord, and bless Thine inheritance, which Thou hast gotten and acquired by the Precious Blood of Thy Christ and called a royal priesthood and a *(Orig. p. 592)* holy nation" (cf. in the Liturgy of Basil the Great and Chrysostom at the end of the Liturgy). In the Liturgy of the Apostle James, such a prayer, completely in the present redaction with minor variants (see above, p. 570), constitutes the last petition of the litany corresponding unto our Augmented Litany; in that same liturgy in the Great Litany in one petition "concerning every Christian soul... in need" (see above, p. 525). The frequently mentioned Georgian manuscript of the 13th century, Greek MSS of the 13th–14th centuries, and, apparently, all Slavic MSS, even of the 16th century, have only the first three petitions; likewise the first Slavic printed editions, ending with the Moscow *Sluzhebnik* of 1647 and the Old Believer Typikon; in the Kyiv *Sluzhebnik* of 1629 there are in small print also the two last petitions with the note that they are "found in the Greek only"; while in Greek editions, already the earliest, the two last petitions are present.

The first petition in the most ancient Greek MS of the 13th century (Moscow Rumyantsev Museum, Sevastyanov collection No. 491/35) contains among the saints only the Most-Holy Theotokos, the Cross, the Forerunner, the apostles, the saint N. (of the day or temple?) "and all the saints"; likewise the printed Greek edition of the Typikon, but with omission of the Cross and addition of the bodiless powers; Greek MSS of the 14th century add after the apostles: "our venerable and God-bearing fathers, the holy and righteous Ancestors of God Joachim and Anna"; likewise the most ancient Slavic MSS of the 14th century (Moscow Synodal Library No. 328/383), but without the Cross; Slavic MSS of the 15th century, restoring the mention of the Cross, add the Holy Archangels; Slavic MSS of the 16th century further add: "the holy right-victorious martyrs"; for the first time later Greek MSS and the first printed editions of the Euchologia append after...

...the apostles: "our fathers among the saints and great ecumenical teachers and hierarchs (*hierarchōn* [Gr. Ἱεραρχῶν]) Basil the Great, Gregory the Theologian, and John Chrysostom, our father among the saints Nicholas, Archbishop of Myra in Lycia, Wonderworker" [^2331].

In Slavic printed editions they began to supplement this prayer with saints even further. Peter Mohyla inserted after St. Nicholas: "the holy three hierarchs of Kyiv: Peter, Alexis, and Jonah, Russian wonderworkers"; after Joachim and Anna: "our venerable and God-bearing fathers Anthony and Theodosius of the Caves"; and after the mention of the Most-Holy Theotokos added: "if it be a temple of the Theotokos, say this: for the sake of Her honorable and glorious N." [^2332].

In the Moscow *Sluzhebnik* of 1647 the last addition is retained, all named saints are placed after the Ancestors of God Joachim and Anna; between the 3 Hierarchs and Nicholas are inserted Athanasius the Great and Cyril of Alexandria; unto the 3 Hierarchs of Kyiv are added John, Archbishop of Novgorod, and Leontius, Bishop of Rostov; then are named the venerable Anthony, Theodosius, Euthymius, Sabas, John of the Ladder, Sergius, Barlaam, Nicon, Paphnutius, Nicetas of Pereyaslavl, Demetrius of Priluki, Zosimas and Sabbatius, Alexander of Svir, the fools-for-Christ Maximus and Basil of Moscow, but the Caves venerable fathers are not mentioned.

The Moscow *Sluzhebnik* of 1658 returns unto the brevity and order of the Greek printed edition, adding only after St. Nicholas the 4 Moscow Hierarchs (with Philip).

Certain Slavic MSS and the *Sluzhebniki* of Peter Mohyla and Moscow 1647 have "the Christian horn". Ancient Slavic MSS of the Typikon instead of "All-Immaculate" [*Vseprechistyya*] have *(Orig. p. 593)* "All-Blessed" [*Preblagoslovennyya*], later ones "All-Immaculate and All-Blessed"; likewise the Moscow *Sluzhebnik* of 1647; Peter Mohyla's has "Immaculate"; Moscow 1658 as at present. Instead of "protection" [*predstatel'stvom*]—"intercession" [*zastupleniem*] all down to the Moscow *Sluzhebnik* of 1658, where the former is in the margin.

The 2nd petition for the sovereign underwent changes identical with those at the Augmented Litany. Petitions for the empress and heir are not yet present in the Moscow *Sluzhebnik* of 1658.

The 3rd petition (concerning the Synod and Archbishop) began in Greek and later Slavic MSS: "Furthermore we pray for the remission of sins of the servant (Slav.: unto the servant) of God (Greek: N.) the abbot (Slav.: + our father) and of all our brotherhood in Christ." (Prayer for forgiveness of sins corresponds unto the purpose of monastic life) [^2333].

Typika: ancient Slavic MSS, for example No. 328/383 of the Moscow Synodal Library of the 14th century, before this petition have a special one for the bishop: "Furthermore we pray for our Bishop N., for health, salvation, and remission of sins", as in Greek MSS and in the Moscow *Sluzhebnik* of 1647; but in the *Sluzhebnik* of Peter Mohyla of 1629:

"For the servant of God, our most venerable father Archimandrite N. or our father, the honorable Abbot, Hieromonk N.; and in a secular church say thus:... for our God-loving Bishop N., or: for our Most Reverend Metropolitan N.; and if it be a stauropegion, say: for our Most Holy Archbishop, Ecumenical Patriarch N.";

in the Moscow *Sluzhebnik* of 1658:
"for our Most Holy Archbishop of Moscow N., Patriarch of all Great and Little Russia, then: for our Bishop N., if there be one";

in the Greek Venice 1622 and in Goar (1740): "for our Archbishop or Bishop N." (concerning the abbot there is nothing in the 3 last). After "our fathers and brethren who serve", ancient Slavic MSS have: "in this monastery and everywhere, for Orthodox Christians of the true faith" [^2334].

Instead of "those who remain behind" (*apoleiphthentōn* [Gr. ἀπολειφθέντων]), Slavic MSS and editions down to 1647 have "those who are sent" (+ "on service"). Instead of: "for the repose, respite, blessed memory, and remission of sins", ancient Slavic MSS of the 14th century have: "for the reposed of remission of their blessed memory of remission of sins", some of the 15th century: "for the reposed respite of their blessed memory remission" [^2335];

*Sluzhebnik* of Peter Mohyla: "for the repose, respite, for blessed memory and remission..."; 1647: "for rest, and for respite and blessed memory, and remission..."; 1658: "for the repose, respite of blessed memory and remission" (consequently, some MSS understand "repose" [*uspenie*] in a collective sense = the reposed, while others understand "of blessed memory" as a title of the reposed).

After "let us say"—"all" in Slavic down to the edition of 1647. Petitions 3 and 4 are not in Georgian, Greek, and Slavic MSS of the Typikon and Greek printed editions, but in their stead is the note "and he commemorates (if he wishes) (as is the custom) (*hous legei* [Gr. οὓς λέγει]) the living and dead (secretly)"; neither are these petitions in the Slavic Moscow *Sluzhebniki* down to 1658; in Greek printed editions they are present with the following variants in comparison with ours: "that this holy monastery and every city and country may be preserved", after "merciful"—*eumenē* [Gr. εὐменῆ] ("favorable/propitious"—see above, p. 591), "righteous" without "and" [^2336]; in Peter Mohyla: "that this holy monastery and every monastery and every city, village, and country may be preserved"; "flood" + "hail"; Moscow *Sluzhebnik* of 1658 as at present, only: "that this holy monastery *(Orig. p. 594)* and every city may be preserved".

*Sluzhebnik* of Peter Mohyla after these petitions has the note:

"and having thus taken the commemoration book [*pomennik*], he commemorates whom he wisheth of the living and the reposed; and the choir sings 'Lord, have mercy' in a protracted chant [*provolokom*];—And if there be a drought, say also this: And that He may send rain... And if in excessive rains for fair weather, say this: And that the measureless and untimely pouring of rain may cease...".

The present Greek *Euchologion* following the first 3 petitions hath a note such as our *Sluzhebnik*, without "secretly" (concerning the commemoration of the living and the dead according to desire), and then the 2 present petitions with a variant in the first: + *eumenē* [Gr. εὐμενῆ]. The Old Believer Typikon and *Sluzhebnik* do not have these petitions or the note concerning the commemoration of the living and the dead.

At the final prayer, the most ancient Greek MSS (Sevastyanov) of the Typikon and printed editions following "the apostles" have only: "the Saint of the monastery (printed: 'Saint N') and all the saints"; later Greek (No. 381): "our holy and God-bearing fathers, the holy Ancestors of God Joachim and Anna, and the holy [patron] of the monastery, and all the saints"; the latest Slavic MSS (No. 678 of the 15th c. and Aa 194 of the 16th c.) have no difference in comparison with "Save, O God". The *Sluzhebnik* of Peter Mohyla following "the apostles" immediately places the martyrs and the venerable (in "Save, O God" at the end), omits (in comparison with "Save, O God") Basil the Great, Gregory the Theologian, and John Chrysostom, and adds following the Russian hierarchs: "the holy, glorious great martyr John the New, who is of Suceava" (14th c., see June 2). The Moscow *Sluzhebnik* of 1647 hath no difference from "Save, O God"; that of 1658 places the martyrs and the venerable before the hierarchs. Printed Greek *Euchologia* and the present printed one following the apostles have: martyrs and venerable, the 4 hierarchs, "the holy and glorious great martyr George the Victorious, Saint N., whose memory we celebrate, the holy and righteous Ancestors of God Joachim and Anna, and all the saints." In the Old Believer Typikon and *Sluzhebnik* there is no difference from "Save, O God".

## Bodily Posture during the Final Prayer ("O Master Great in Mercy")

Concerning the posture of the body during the final prayer (**"O Master Great in Mercy"** [*Vladyko Mnogomilostive*]):
The Georgian MS: "while we bend our knees";
Ancient Greek (Sevastyanov): "while they bow their heads and lie upon the ground";
Later Greek (No. 381): "while they bow their heads, turning unto the people from east unto west he says the prayer";
Printed Greek: "lying upon the earth";
Ancient Slavic MS (14th c. No. 328): "while we bow ourselves unto the earth and lie upon our knees";
15th c. (No. 678): "while we bow our heads";
16th c. (Aa 194) adds: "the priest turned unto the west";
Printed Greek *Euchologion*: "while all bow their heads and lie upon the earth";
*Sluzhebnik* of Peter Mohyla: "while the brethren and we bow our heads, the priest turned with his face unto the west, and the deacon standing at his right hand and holding his orarion with three fingers of his right hand, having bowed his head";
Moscow 1647: "with uncovered head";
1658: "while all bow their heads and bend down unto the earth."
Old Believer Typikon: "the priest, turning unto the west, prays aloud, while we bow our heads"; Old Believer *Sluzhebnik*: "with uncovered head" [^2339]. The hesitation concerning kneeling is explained by the ancient canonical prohibition of the latter on Sundays.

## The Litiya according to the Present Typikon of the Great Church

The litiya according to the present typikon of the Great Church departs considerably from the usual type. Its order is given not in the Typikon, but in the *Hieratikon* [Gr. Ἱερατικόν] (the priestly *Sluzhebnik*).

For the litiya the priest with the deacon go forth into the middle of the temple, where the loaves are already prepared for the blessing. The deacon, upon the completion of the "litiya troparion of the saint celebrated on the morrow," says: "Have mercy on us, O God... Lord, have mercy (thrice). Again let us pray for pious and Orthodox Christians. Again let us pray for our Archbishop N. Again let us pray for mercy, life... of the servants of God who celebrate this holy feast and His servants—and commemorates the names of those who have offered the loaves.—Again let us pray that this holy church or monastery and this city, or village, or island, and every city and country may be preserved from famine... Each choir chants 'Lord, have mercy' thrice 12 times. Again let us pray that He may hear... Lord, have mercy 3." The bishop, vested in epitrachelion and small omophorion, or the priest says: "Amen. Hear us, O God...". The choir: "Amen. Peace be unto all. Bow your heads...". At the bowing of the heads of all, the bishop or priest says: **"O Master Great in Mercy"**, with the mention following the apostles: *(Orig. p. 596)* "our fathers among the saints, the great hierarchs and universal teachers Basil the Great, Gregory the Theologian, and John Chrysostom, Athanasius and Cyril, Patriarchs...

...of Alexandria, Nicholas of Myra, Spyridon Bishop of Trimythous the Wonderworker, the holy glorious great martyrs George the Trophy-bearer, Demetrius the Myrrh-streamer, Theodore of Tyre and Theodore the General, Menas the Wonderworker, and the Hieromartyr Charalampus", martyrs, venerable monastics, Joachim and Anna, "Saint N., whose memory we also celebrate." Immediately thereafter, upon the singing of **"Rejoice, O Virgin Theotokos"** [*Bogoroditse Devo*], the blessing of loaves takes place, and Vespers concludes with the dismissal troparia of the Sunday and of the saint [^2340].

## The Return from the Litiya

The litiya returns into the temple in the same order in which it went forth thence, during the singing of the aposticha sticheron: "having raised ourselves upright (rising from knees or lifting the head after the bowing of heads), we sing the Sunday sticheron and enter into the temple, the candle-bearers going before, singing also the remaining stichera, which are alphabetical." The stichera are sung by both choirs together (see below), for which reason they stand in the middle of the temple in a semicircle before the table with the loaves. The priest, "preceded by lamps, goes through the Royal (that is, Beautiful) Doors and, as it were, enters into heaven. After the superior, under his leadership, the others follow, walking as if after Jesus Christ. And both choirs, having united into one and standing in the midst as a sign that our heaven has been opened and through Christ the Angels have entered into communion with us, chant the stichera of the aposticha" [^2341].

### According unto Ancient Typika

More detailed is the *Sluzhebnik* of Peter Mohyla: "the priest with the deacon, lamps going before them, enter into the church, and the brethren and all the people follow them." The Moscow *Sluzhebnik* of 1647: "the priest with the deacon depart into the holy altar and close the doors", that is, the Holy Doors. Yet the *Sluzhebnik* of 1658 generally states "enters into the church." In agreement with the *Sluzhebnik* of 1647 is the Old Believer *Sluzhebnik*, but their Typikon is like ours [^2342].

# The Aposticha (*Stikhovny* — *Eis ton stichon*)

The stichera "at the verse" (*eis ton stichon* [Gr. εἰς τὸν στίχον], more rarely *ta aposticha* [Gr. τὰ ἀπόστιχα]), or "aposticha" [*stikhovny*], represent the second and concluding series of festal chants at Vespers, which for this reason must already be elevated above the preceding series—the stichera at *Lord, I have cried*. Just as the prayers of Vespers continually increase in intensity with its progression, so also do the chants. Indeed, the aposticha stichera more fully extol the cele*(Orig. p. 597)*brated event by the very fact that they are joined not unto a daily psalm, but unto special verses (adapted unto the feast), whence their name is derived. Furthermore, they are called so also because at the litiya the stichera are without verses [^2343]. They dominate over the psalm (that is, over these verses) by opening their series without a psalm verse. On many feasts these stichera are more ecstatic than those of *Lord, I have cried*; for example, on Pascha they are the famous stichera **"A sacred Pascha"** [*Paskha svyashchennaya*]; they are chanted in the more intricate tones (3, 5, 7) and possess the most artistic and moving melodies (**"O House of Ephratha"**, **"When from the Tree"**). It is for this reason that they are performed by both choirs united in the middle of the temple, which for Sunday Vigil follows naturally from the preceding description (for ordinary Vespers this is specifically noted—see Chapter 9 of the Typikon).

## History of the Aposticha

An aposticha sticheron, as yet only one, is presumably intended in the famous narrative of the visit unto Nilus of Sinai by Sophronius and Moschus (7th c.) under the name of "troparion at *O Gladsome Light* or at *Vouchsafe, O Lord*": troparia are there called also the stichera at *Lord, I have cried*, while the term "sticheron" does not yet exist in this monument (Introductory Chapter, 295). Under their present name and in the quantity of several, the aposticha stichera are mentioned by the *Hypotyposis* (9th c.) under the name *stichēra tou stichou* [Gr. στιχηρὰ τοῦ στίχου] [^2344], by the most ancient Studite typika, and by the Evergetis Typikon; the most ancient Greek manuscript of the Jerusalem Typikon calls them "stichera *tou stichou*" [Gr. τοῦ στίχου] [^2345].

## Sunday Aposticha

The aposticha stichera at Sunday Vespers are appointed in the number of 4, greater by 1 than for all other feasts, even the Twelve Great Feasts, excluding Pascha. They have their own Theotokia, extolling the Incarnation of Christ [^2346] or...

...containing supplications unto the Mother of God for deliverance from afflictions—without relation unto the event of the Resurrection, even as the Dogmatika—which is why they serve, like the latter, as Theotokia also for the feasts of saints (polyeleos and vigil rank); the melodies appointed for them are more solemn than for weekday Theotokia, close unto the melodies of the Dogmatika. As verses for the aposticha stichera there serve the same verses of Psalm 92 from which the Sunday evening prokeimenon is composed, that is, **"The Lord is King..."**, **"For He hath established the world..."**, **"Holiness becometh Thine house..."** (see above, p. 567). In the series of Sunday aposticha stichera, the first of them are noticeably distinguished from the remainder: they are homogeneous in structure and content with the first three stichera at *(Orig. p. 598)* *Lord, I have cried* and, in any case, more ancient than the other aposticha. These latter, called "alphabetical stichera" [*stikhiry po alfavitu*], as beginning in succession with the letters of the alphabet, constitute thanks to this for all tones one unified whole, divided into 8 sections. They are somewhat longer and more detailed than the first stichera. Ancient manuscripts of the typika attribute them unto St. John of Damascus.

### History of Sunday Aposticha

The Studite-Alexis Typikon knows only one Sunday apostichon, naturally, the 1st of the present ones; for the Sundays of the Triodion it prescribes doubling it and singing after it the Triodion sticheron; consequently, on ordinary Sundays it was tripled. Studite typika of the Calabrian and Sicilian recensions, besides this sticheron, name also 3 alphabetical stichera, the former also naming the author: "John." The Evergetis Typikon indicates after the 1st two alphabetical ones, designating them by the name of "John the monk of Damascus." The Georgian manuscript of the Jerusalem Typikon indicates 3 alphabetical stichera with the name of St. John, assigning the 3rd at "Glory". Greek manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon call them *anatolika ta kata alphabētou* [Gr. ἀνατολικὰ τὰ κατὰ ἀλφαβήτου], assigning unto them also the present verses [^2347]. The alphabetical arrangement of the stichera suggests the thought that they were originally all intended for a single service and, presumably, played in it the same role as kontakia. Their Theotokia are called by Western Studite typika *tou alphabētou* [Gr. τοῦ ἀλφαβήτου], and by the Evergetis Typikon *deuterotheotokia* [Gr. δευτεροθεοτόκια].

## Cancellation and Abbreviation

In view of the special significance of the aposticha stichera, under no...

...coincidences are they ever replaced at Sunday service by others, nor are they abbreviated, nor multiplied in number by the addition of other stichera. An exception is December 24 and the Sundays from Pascha unto the Ascension (see there).

# "Now lettest Thou Thy servant depart" (*Nunc Dimittis* — *Nyně otpushchayeshi*)

Having provided a series of psalms both specially evening ones (103 and 140 with the following), regular ones (the 1st Kathisma), and specially festal ones (verses of Psalm 92), and having joined unto the psalms Christian hymns adapted both unto the evening hour (**"O Gladsome Light"**, **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"**) and unto the feast (stichera), Vespers, nevertheless, would not have exhausted its psalmodic-hymnographic material had it not added unto all this yet something from the cycle of the so-called Biblical Canticles, which at Matins under the form of the Canon occupy so prominent a place.

*(Orig. p. 599)*

This lack Vespers supplies by the prayer-canticle of St. Simeon the God-Receiver from Luke 2:29–32: **"Now lettest Thou Thy servant depart"** (*Nunc Dimittis* / *Nyně otpushchayeshi*) [^2348]. Full of thanksgiving and tranquility before the face of death, flowing from a constant thought not of oneself, but of the world and the people, of their enlightenment and salvation, this "prayer" of Simeon is fitting for the evening, which reminds us of the twilight of our life (like **"O Gladsome Light"**, it calls the Savior the Light). Notwithstanding the highly poetic character of this prayer-canticle, the Typikon appoints for it not singing, but reading (as, presumably, the righteous Simeon himself performed it: "blessed God and said"). The Typikon acts likewise with other frequently repeated hymns (see above, p. 560). In return, it is "spoken by the superior", whereas the subsequent Trisagion is read by the reader (at daily Vespers it is permitted that the reader pronounce it as well). According to Symeon of Thessalonica, "one of the officiants, as it were Simeon the God-Receiver, pronounceth it with reverence" [^2349].

## History of Its Usage

**"Now lettest Thou Thy servant depart"** is mentioned among the evening hymns immediately following the "prayer" close unto our **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"** by the *Apostolic Constitutions* [^2350], and in the present place of Vespers—in the famous narrative of the visit unto Nilus of Sinai (7th c.) and in Horologia of the 8th c. It is possessed by Coptic and Abyssinian Vespers. Armenian Vespers, like its other services, likewise hath a Biblical Canticle. Roman Catholic worship hath this canticle at Compline with the antiphon ("Save us"), while at Vespers it hath the Canticle of the Theotokos (Introductory Chapter, pp. 295, 300, 301, 317). Anglican worship, which hath no Compline, placed the *Nunc Dimittis* at Evening Prayer [^2351]. According unto the Studite Typikon, *Now lettest Thou Thy servant depart* was chanted "in a raised voice" [*v"ly*] (see above, p. 560).

The most ancient manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon say nothing concerning the manner of executing *Now lettest Thou Thy servant depart*; yet judging by the fact that they attach this hymn unto the preceding account of the singing of the aposticha stichera without any intermediate rubric or with "then" (*eita* [Gr. εἶτα]), they presumably assume its singing.

## The Trisagion

Unto *Now lettest Thou Thy servant depart* is joined the Trisagion and its accompanying prayers through the **"Our Father"**, which thus conclude the service, its prayerful portion. This is also natural for such a prayer as the "Our Father" (cf. the Divine Liturgy), while the preceding prayers prepare for it. These prayers are pronounced already by the reader.

### The Trisagion at Ancient Vespers

With these prayers Vespers concludes (without a troparion) in the most ancient Horologion of the Sinai Library of the 8th–9th centuries (Introductory Chapter, 298). According unto the most ancient *(Orig. p. 600)* Roman rite, services concluded with the "Our Father" as a collect (the general dismissal prayer—ibid., 308). Germanus of Paris († 576) in his *Expositio brevis antiquae liturgiae gallicanae* [Brief Exposition of the Ancient Gallican Liturgy] observes that the "Our Father" occupies the final place at the Liturgy, "so that our every prayer may be concluded by the Lord's Prayer" [^2352]. The Studite Typikon appoints for these prayers the same singing as for *Now lettest Thou Thy servant depart* and the troparion (see above, p. 560). The Jerusalem Typika act as with *Now lettest Thou Thy servant depart* (see above, p. 599).

## The Dismissal Troparion of Vespers

The chants of Vespers, increasing in their solemnity, conclude with the highest of all kinds of ecclesiastical hymnody—the troparion, the very name of which (*troparion* [Gr. τροπάριον], from *tropos* [Gr. τρόπος] = *ēchos* [Gr. ἦχος], tone, melody) points unto the special complexity and richness of melody for it. In each tone the troparic melody constitutes the crown of all other melodies, of which perhaps only the prokeimenon can vie with it. Therefore the troparion in all services among the series of other hymns occupies the most honorable place, opening their series, as at Matins, concluding it, as at Matins and Vespers, or replacing all other kinds of hymnody, as at the Divine Liturgy and at the Hours (at...

...the latter together with the kontakion). By the place which the troparion occupies at Vespers, it is called "dismissal" (lit. *apolytikion* [Gr. ἀπολυτίκιον]). "Dismissal" troparia sometimes differ from the ordinary ones—thus, besides Sunday, in which also the final troparion of Matins is special, on Great Friday, where the dismissal troparion—of Matins, however—is **"For our sake crucified"**, while the ordinary one is **"When the glorious"**.

### History of the Dismissal Troparion

The troparion is the most ancient ecclesiastical chant, wherewith the history of ecclesiastical hymnody began its development (Introductory Chapter, 328–329). In the typikon of the Great Church of Constantinople, which preserves the greatest number of traces of ancient practice, this is even the only chant. By such poverty of hymnographic material this typikon resembles Roman worship, wherein there is usually one hymn for each service and no more than two or three for each of the most important feasts. The hymn (*hymnus*) of Roman Catholic worship thus corresponds unto our troparion: it is there the only hymn not borrowed from Holy Scripture; very rarely, however, do the antiphons in Roman worship also present verses of original composition, not biblical.

The dismissal troparion in Patmos *Euchologion* No. 105 of the 13th century is appointed after a special "prayer of dismissal", and this prayer was adapted unto the feast; thus, the *Trebnik* of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 371/675 gives a series of such prayers for different choirs of saints and Twelve Great Feasts, calling them "prayer after the dismissal" or "dismissal prayer" [^2353].

*(Orig. p. 601)*

# "Rejoice, O Virgin Theotokos" (*Bogoroditse Devo*)

The troparion of Sunday Vespers (**"Rejoice, O Virgin Theotokos"** [*Bogoroditse Devo*]), according to the custom of the Orthodox Church which concludes each series of chants with a hymn in honor of the Mother of God, is dedicated unto Her. This is done also upon the same foundation on which the katavasia on Sunday is usually Theotokion (see below). For such a troparion there were chosen the most joyful words heard by the Mother of God and handed down unto us—the salutation unto Her of the Angel and of righteous Elizabeth; consequently, the troparion is composed of biblical (Luke 1:28, 42) divinely inspired words, which, nevertheless, are surrounded and interwoven with ours ("Theotokos [^2354] Virgin", "Mary", "For Thou hast borne the Savior of our souls"). The fundamental thought of the hymn, inviting the Mother of God unto joy ("rejoice" in the Hebrew and Greek languages, however, had the meaning generally of a greeting, corresponding unto Latin *ave* and Russian *zdravstvuy*, even as this word is rendered here in the Latin translation), is not without relation unto the event of the Resurrection, for which reason it has been assigned exclusively unto Sunday Vespers and unto Lenten Vespers—upon different grounds. There might also have been intended the ancient tradition that the Annunciation took place in the evening [^2355]. The Sunday troparion is not sung also on account of the conjunction of Vespers with Matins, at the very beginning of which it is appointed.

## History of the Troparion "Rejoice, O Virgin Theotokos"

The prototype of the troparion **"Rejoice, O Virgin Theotokos"** is given in the commemoration prayer at the ancient Liturgy of the Apostle James; in the series of various commemorations (after the transubstantiation / consecration of the Gifts) in the most ancient copy of this Liturgy (Messanensis of the 10th c.) there is also this: "Remember, O Lord, the archangelic voice saying: Rejoice, Thou that art full of grace, the Lord is with Thee, blessed art Thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of Thy womb"; in later copies (Rossanensis of the 11th c.) unto these words there is added: "For Thou hast borne the Savior of our souls"; in still later ones (Paris Library No. 2509 of the 14th c.) before the angelic words there is omitted: "Remember, O Lord, the archangelic voice saying"; in still later copies (Paris Library No. 476 of the 14th c.) before the words, which had thus taken the form of an independent chant-prayer, there is added the rubric: "the priest subjoins (*synaptei* [printed: *synantei*, Gr. συνάπτει]) and says this thrice." Since these words at the Liturgy of the Apostle James were pronounced by the priest immediately before **"Especially for the Most Holy..."**, the Liturgies of Basil the Great and John Chrysostom derived therefrom in...

certain of their manuscript copies (for example, in the Cryptaferrata MS *Falascae* of the 13th c.) also designate these words as a prayer of the priest following the words *(Orig. p. 602)* **"Especially"** [**"It is truly meet"** / **"All of creation rejoices in thee"**] (instead of **"All of creation rejoices in thee"** or **"It is truly meet"**, or alongside the second during its singing); at the Liturgy of the Apostle Peter (in the Rossano MS of the 11th c. only) these words are likewise set as a prayer of the priest before **"Among the first remember"**, herein with the addition following **"Full of grace"** of **"Mary"**, which is not found in the above-mentioned MSS [^2356]. — As regards the troparion at Vespers, in the Horologion of the Sinai Library No. 863 at the end of Vespers no troparion is appointed. According unto Western Studite typika at Vespers there was also, apparently, no troparion. So too at Coptic Vespers. According unto the Alexis-Studite Typikon, at Saturday-Sunday Vespers the appointed troparia were: **"Baptist of Christ, and the rest"**, replaced for a celebrated saint by his troparion. So too at Ethiopian Vespers, besides a troparion analogous unto **"Rejoice, O Virgin Theotokos"**, there are appointed hymns similar unto **"Baptist of Christ"**, **"Pray for us"**, and **"Beneath Thy Compassion"**. The Evergetis Typikon: "a dismissal troparion, and if the saint hath none, the Sunday troparion of the tone" [^2357].

Something analogous unto our Theotokion troparion is presented by the Biblical Canticle of the Theotokos [the *Magnificat*] at Roman Catholic Vespers. The troparion corresponding unto **"Rejoice, O Virgin Theotokos"** there enters into the composition of the usual beginning, and furthermore, preceded by four verses with responsories and with a special prayer following it, is pronounced thrice at dawn, at noon, and in the evening; such a private devotion, called the *Angelus*, arose in the 12th century, at first for the evening [^2358], probably under the influence of the opinion that the Annunciation took place in the evening. The text of the prayer in the Ethiopian Horologion hath the following variant reading from ours: "Rejoice, O Virgin, who hast found grace, Holy Mary"; among the Roman Catholics: "Hail (Lat. *Ave*, Polish *Zdrowaś*), Mary, full of grace — [the fruit] of thy womb Jesus. Holy Mary, Mother of God, pray for us sinners, now and at the hour of our death" [^2359].

## Manner of Execution

The troparion **"Rejoice, O Virgin Theotokos"** [*Bogoroditse Devo*] is set in Tone 4, the usual tone for the troparia of feasts. In view of the solemnity of the moment, the troparion is sung thrice, which is otherwise appointed only on the Twelve Great Feasts and feasts similar unto them. The censing of the loaves performed during the singing of the troparion also contributes unto this solemnity, having, however, as its immediate purpose the sanctification of the loaves.

### According unto Ancient Typika

Ancient MSS of the Jerusalem Typikon concerning the execution of the troparion: the Georgian MS: "and we [sing] the troparion Rejoice, O Virgin Theotokos, 3 times"; Greek Sevastyanov and No. 381: "and we [sing] the dismissal [troparion], Tone 4 (No. 381: Tone 5), Rejoice, O Virgin Theotokos, saying it thrice." The Order [*Diataxis*] of Patriarch Philotheus: "when the final dismissal [troparion] is sung aloud and slowly (*argōs* [Gr. ἀργῶς]), *(Orig. p. 603)* the deacon — censes." The remaining typika and *Sluzhebniki* are as the present one, or close to it. The present Greek *Euchologion* before the blessing of loaves appoints the singing of the dismissal troparion of the day and the Theotokion. According unto the Constantinopolitan *Hieratikon* [Gr. Ἱεраτικόν], the priest, censing the loaves, having before him the deacon with a lamp, sings **"Rejoice, O Virgin Theotokos"**, and the left choir sings the conclusion of the troparion: **"For Thou hast borne the Savior of our souls..."** [*Yako Spasa rodila yesi...*]; such a distinctive singing of this troparion according unto the Constantinopolitan Typikon is explained by the fact that besides it, at the end of Vespers the dismissal troparion is sung (the blessing of loaves and **"Rejoice, O Virgin Theotokos"** take place before the aposticha stichera) [^2360].

## Curtailment and Omission

**"Rejoice, O Virgin Theotokos"** [*Bogoroditse Devo*] at Great Vespers is sung thrice only on those Sundays with which no other great commemoration is combined; in these latter cases, however (for example, on the Sundays of the Fathers, certain Triodion Sundays, on forefeasts, afterfeasts, and leavetakings—not all, however), **"Rejoice, O Virgin Theotokos"** is sung twice and the troparion of the commemoration or saint once (on the forefeasts of the Transfiguration, the Entry into the Temple, the Annunciation, and the leavetakings of the latter two, however, **"Rejoice, O Virgin Theotokos"** is sung thrice). At a great concurrence of commemorations with Sunday, such as: on the 7th Sunday after Pascha, on the Sunday of the Holy Fathers [Genealogy / Ancestors of God] (if, however, it falleth not on December 31), if December 24 falleth on a Sunday, or March 25 on the 3rd Sunday of Great Lent, — **"Rejoice, O Virgin Theotokos"** is not sung at all.

# THE BLESSING OF LOAVES (*Blagoslovenie khlebov* — *Artoklasia*)

Having replaced the Liturgy and the agape meal, Vespers must provide the worshippers also with sustenance, even such as the sanctity of the temple permits. This is accomplished in the form of offering unto the worshippers blessed bread and wine, together wherewith there are blessed (as it were for the morrow's meal) oil and wheat. Unto this end, while the litiya is still being celebrated, there is prepared ("having been previously prepared" — *proeutrepisthentos* [Gr. προευτρεπισθέντος]) a "four-legged stand" (*tetrapodion* [Gr. τετραπόδιον]) [^2361], or, as it is subsequently termed, a "table", a small table, upon both sides of which the litiya candlesticks are placed; upon the small table is placed a dish (*diskos* [Gr. δίσκος]) with wheat (*sitos* [Gr. σῖτος]) and five (according unto the Gospel number) "loaves, whereof (Gr. ὧν; in the Slavonic *yezhe* refers not unto "dish", but signifies generally "which") we have the custom to make offerings unto the church", that is, with prosphora; upon both sides of the dish are two vessels (*angeia* [Gr. ἀγγεῖα]), unto the left (naturally, from the perspective of the worshippers [^2362], in accordance with which the icons also are arranged in the temple) with wine, and unto the right with oil; judging by the fact that in the prayer of blessing *(Orig. p. 604)* wine is named first, it is placed on the left only in order that, when pointing in this prayer unto the loaves, wheat, wine, and oil, a natural cruciform motion may be made with the right hand [^2363]. The deacon during the singing of the troparion, having taken a blessing from the priest, censes round about the table—wherewith the consecration of objects is frequently accompanied—and in view of such a specific purpose of this censing, besides the table he censes only the superior standing in his place (as one spiritually participating in the sacred ministration) and the priest (who performs the consecration), and thereafter once more the table ("the loaves") from the front only. The superior or, as is customarily done, the priest pronounces the prayer (understood to be following the preliminary "Let us pray to the Lord", "Lord, have mercy") "with a loud voice" [*veleglasno*], as hitherto only a single prayer has been pronounced—the final litiya prayer. The prayer beseeches the Savior, Who showed in the miracle of feeding the five thousand all the power of His blessing, for the same blessing and (wonder-working) multiplication of the proffered substances, as well as for the sanctification of those who partake of them (= replacement of the Eucharist). Before the words of the prayer: **"Do Thou Thyself bless"**, the priest makes the sign of the cross over the substances, yet not with the hand alone, but with one of the loaves, signifying the heavenly Bread, "whereby [also] he shows that Christ accomplished the same, having taken in like manner into His hands five loaves" [^2364]; at the enumeration of the substances the priest points unto them with his hand, whereby the form of a cross is likewise produced. The prayer concludes with the glorification of those divine attributes through the manifestation of which the expected sanctification serves (among others, "All-holy, Good, and Life-creating...").

## History of the Rite

The Georgian MS:
"the cellarer [*kelar*] places upon the table three loaves, such as we customarily use for food, close unto them, or upon the same analogion, and wine";
and then concerning the signing with the loaf, as at present. Greek MSS Sevastyanov and No. 381:
"the cellarer (No. 381: the candle-lighter [*kandilāptēs*]) places upon the analogion 3 (No. 381: 5 loaves), whereof we eat at the refectory (No. 381 lacks this), as well as a vessel (*stamnion* [Gr. σταμνίον, printed: σταμνών], No. 381: *angeion* [Gr. ἀγγεῖον]) full of the very best wine (and in the prayer only concerning bread and wine) [^2365] (No. 381: + ripe wheat *hōraiou* [Gr. ὡраίου] and oil); and the priest comes forth from the sanctuary with the censer and censes crosswise, then the superior only."
Printed Greek is like Sevastyanov, only with 5 loaves and + "and a little oil in some vessel (*angos* [Gr. ἄγγος])". All these MSS describe the blessing of the other loaves with one loaf as does the present Typikon.
Slavic MSS Nos. 328 and 678:
"the cellarer (the paraecclesiarch) sets forth upon the lectern 5 loaves (a dish whereon is a little wheat and atop it 5 loaves), whereof we eat at the refectory (prepared for this purpose, each weighing a litra), likewise a vessel full of beverage and wheat from the granary and oil (and on both sides of the dish two cruets of wine and oil)."
The Old Believer Typikon is like No. 678, but at the beginning:
"there is an analogion in the church prepared for [this]; the paraecclesiarch sets it in place, and the cellarer *(Orig. p. 605)* —";
it speaks also of the blessing of the other loaves with one loaf before the prayer.

Concerning this blessing, the majority of MSS and editions agree with the present practice, yet certain ones, for example Moscow Synodal Library No. 332/385 of the 16th c.:
"taking the bread with the left hand, with the right he makes a cross upon it."
From the Order [*Diataxis*] of Patriarch Philotheus the present Typikon borrows verbatim, concluding with the position of the oil, and further therein:
"the priest with the deacon stand outside the Beautiful Doors"; concerning the censing, it is like the present Typikon, but: "round about the loaves cruciformly, then the abbot, and again the loaves, from the front only; and when the priest approaches, the deacon stands at his right hand, holding the censer with the left hand, and with three fingers of the right the orarion, and upon the completion of the troparion, indicating with the orarion the five loaves, he says: 'Let us pray to the Lord', and the priest [says] the prayer."
So too in the *Sluzhebnik* of Peter Mohyla, but after "Let us pray to the Lord" +
"and the priest, taking one bread lying on top into his right hand, says with compunction: O Lord Jesus Christ... Who didst fill. And he sets the bread in its place atop the four, and turning his hand palm upward, he indicates the loaves, saying: bless these loaves",
and so forth.
The Moscow *Sluzhebnik* of 1602:
"the paraecclesiarch sets in place a small table prepared for this, and the cellarer places upon it a dish, whereon is a little wheat and atop it 5 loaves prepared for this, and two cruets on both sides, one having olive oil, and the other wine; then the priest censes round about the table, then the abbot only, and having returned the censer, he says the prayer with a loud voice for the blessing of the loaves: O Lord Jesus Christ... Who sanctifiest all things, O Christ our God: The priest, taking one bread from above, blesses therewith the other loaves in the form of a cross, saying: And unto Thee the glory... amen" (1647: "and the singers: amen").
The Moscow *Sluzhebnik* of 1658:

"and the cellarer sets forth upon the analogion 5 loaves, whereof we eat at the refectory; likewise also a flagon [*ruchka*], filled with the finest wine; and the priest, taking one bread in his hands and having formed a cross upon it, prays this prayer with a loud voice" [^2366].

# "BLESSED BE THE NAME OF THE LORD" (*Budi imya Gospodne blagoslovenno*)

In correspondence with the Liturgy, out of which it was born, Great Vespers concludes with a threefold prayer-sequence, consisting of a psalm-verse, a psalm, and a priestly blessing, having one common theme—blessing. The verse **"Blessed be the name of the Lord..."** from Psalm 112:3 [LXX; Masoretic Ps. 113:2] (cf. Job 1:21) corresponds unto the blessing of the name of God at the beginning of each service and reminds that with the end of the day the glorification of God does not come to an end, but will continue for ever, most immediately throughout the upcoming night (for which reason at Vespers without a vigil this verse is not appointed). Thus, together with the following *(Orig. p. 606)* Psalm 33, **"I will bless the Lord at all times"** [LXX; Masoretic Ps. 34], this verse constitutes a very skillful transition unto Matins. Containing David's ecstatic thanksgiving unto God for deliverance from imminent peril (under one of the circumstances of Saul's persecution), Psalm 33 depicts all the blessings of complete trust in God, inviting one directly to taste of this goodness in order to become convinced of it, and especially by this expression is suited unto the present moment. Of the psalm, which at the Liturgy is appointed in its complete form, here only half is pronounced (of the 22 verses—11, through "shall not lack any good thing"), the more poetic portion of the psalm, which thereafter passes into moral instruction. Moreover, verse 11 [LXX 33:11 / Masoretic 34:10], wherewith the psalm here concludes: **"The rich have become poor and suffered hunger..."**, is suited unto the upcoming meal. Unto our blessing of God in the verse **"Blessed be the name"** and in Psalm 33, God answers with His blessing through the priest. This blessing, so natural and necessary at the end of the service, is imparted not by the usual formula "Peace be unto all", but with that fullness (abundance) and definitiveness as at the Liturgy: "The blessing of the Lord be upon you, through His grace (not a general blessing solely according to love for mankind, but grace-filled through the power of redemption and the mysteries) and love for mankind, always, (more specifically:) now and ever...".

## History

The "blessing" of the Lord, corresponding unto the verse **"Blessed be the name of the Lord"**, was at the end of almost all Liturgies. Thus, at the Coptic Liturgy of Basil the Great of the 2nd redaction, immediately before communion the priest says: "Blessed be the Lord unto the ages, amen"; according unto the 1st redaction: "Blessed be the Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, and the Holy Spirit, amen"; at the Liturgy of the Apostle Peter following communion: "Blessed is our God always, now and ever, and unto the ages of ages"; according unto the most ancient copy of the Liturgy of the Apostle James (*Messanensis* of the 10th c.), before the communion of the laity: "Blessed be the name of the Lord our God." According unto later copies of the same Liturgy (*Rossanensis* of the 11th c. and later), the verse **"Blessed be the name"** is already appointed. It is likewise appointed at the end of the Liturgy of the Apostle Mark, of the Roman [Mass] at a hierarchical service (entering here into the composition of the solemn final blessing of the people), at the beginning of the Ambrosian (Milanese) and Lyonese rites, in the blessing of the people by a newly consecrated Pope [^2367], and in Protestant worship (see below, Protestant Vespers). — Psalm 33 is appointed in the Liturgy of the *Apostolic Constitutions* [^2368] during communion, and its 9th verse (**"O taste and see..."**) is the Communion Hymn at the Liturgy of the Apostle James. — The blessing of the priest at the end of the service was always considered an indispensable attribute of the service. In the 4th–5th centuries in various places such a blessing was imparted through the laying on of hands by the bishop (Introductory Chapter, pp. 136, 141, 142), whereunto all bowed their heads, and the bish*(Orig. p. 607)*op read a special prayer corresponding unto the present prayers of the bowing of heads. With the increase of worshippers in temples, the individual blessing of each person had to be replaced by a general blessing of all. In the West it was considered no less, if not more, an indispensable attribute of every service, and especially of Vespers, than in the East. The Council of Agde (*Concilium Agathense*) of 506, Canon 30, requires "that the people, upon the completion of the prayer towards evening, be dismissed by the bishop with a blessing." In the *Life of Caesarius, Bishop of Arles* († 542), it is related that "it was established that at a known time four men should go forth to meet him; with them he proceeded unto Vespers in the basilica of St. Stephen, since upon the conclusion of Vespers he gave a blessing unto the people" [^2369]. The blessing at the end of services was preserved even by Protestants of all confessions and sects, not only Anglicans, but also Lutherans, Reformed, Presbyterians, Irvingites, Anabaptists, and Moravian Brethren [Herrnhuters].

## Manner of Execution

This tripartite concluding prayer-sequence of Vespers is performed with the following particulars. **"Blessed be the name of the Lord"** is sung ("we sing") in Tone 4, the usual tone of festal prokeimena, corresponding moreover unto the tone of the dismissal troparion for Sunday. As a prokeimenon, for which purpose it as it were serves with respect to Psalm 33 (corresponding unto the antiphon in Western worship), this verse is sung thrice, naturally alternately by the choirs. "Then Psalm 33, **'I will bless the Lord at all times'**, and we speak it unto 'shall not lack any good thing'" — an indefinite expression, which can be understood both in the sense of the singing of the psalm, and in the sense of its reading: singing is required both by the solemnity of the moment and by the analogy of all the other psalms of Vespers, which are all required to be sung (ordinarily a psalm is read). "And the priest, having gone, stands before the Royal Doors, looking towards the west", unto the people—for the purpose of imparting the blessing unto them. "And upon the completion of the psalm he says: The blessing of the Lord be upon you... And the reader [says]—amen." "Amen" is appointed to be pronounced by the reader, since immediately thereafter the reading (from the Apostle) is appointed (where the latter is omitted, there the amen is sung).

### According unto Ancient Typika

The Georgian MS:
"**'I will bless the Lord...'** unto 'shall not lack'; the priest stands before the holy doors, turns, and says: 'The blessing of the Lord be upon you...' and immediately follows the reading."

Greek and Slavic MSS and Greek printed editions:
"and after the amen we say the 33rd Psalm (MSS: + 'unto the middle'), **I will bless the Lord at all times** unto the word 'shall not lack' (MSS + Glory, and now)" and further as at present, but instead of "he says" the Greek hath: "he prays (*epeuchetai* [printed: *epeuchetoa*, Gr. ἐπεύχεται]): 'The blessing of the Lord... ages' and immediately the reading."

The Order [*Diataxis*] of Patriarch Philotheus:
"when **'I will bless the Lord'** is spoken by the brethren, the priest with the deacon enters into the holy sanctuary (*bēma* [Gr. βῆма]); the brethren speak the psalm unto 'shall not lack'; and the priest within *(Orig. p. 608)* the holy sanctuary exclaims: 'The blessing of the Lord... ages.' And thus they divest themselves of their sacred vestments and depart."

Thus, the verse **"Blessed be the name"** was not appointed.

The Moscow *Sluzhebniki* of 1602 following the text of the prayer of blessing (with "amen"):
"thereafter we sing: Blessed be the name — 3 in Tone 4, then Psalm 33, I will bless the Lord — we speak it unto 'shall not lack'," further as at present, but instead of "upon you" — "upon all of you" and with "amen" pronounced by the priest.

The *Sluzhebnik* of Peter Mohyla of 1629:
"The choir: Amen, and immediately Blessed be the name 3, and the psalm I will bless the Lord unto 'shall not lack'; and the priest, standing before the holy doors, awaits the completion of the psalm; and upon completion he says: The blessing of the Lord... And the reader having uttered: Amen...".

Likewise the Moscow [edition] of 1647, but regarding **"Blessed be the name"** — "in Tone 4", regarding the psalm "we speak", "he stands in the Royal Doors", "upon all of you".

The Moscow [edition] of 1658:
"and after the amen immediately Blessed be the name 3, and we speak I will bless the Lord — even unto — and the priest having gone forth stands before the holy doors looking towards the west, and upon the completion of the psalm the priest prays, saying: The blessing... ages, and the dismissal takes place."

The Old Believer Typikon is like ours, only regarding **"Blessed be the name"**, as also Psalm 33 — "we speak", with an indication of the tone, and "The blessing of the Lord be upon all of you" [^2370].

## According unto the Present Constantinopolitan Order

Following the dismissal troparion — the deacon: "Let us pray to the Lord", the choir: "Lord, have mercy"; the hierarch or priest from the solea blesses the people, exclaiming: "The blessing of the Lord and His mercy come upon you, through His grace and love for mankind, always, now and ever, and unto the ages of ages" [^2371].

In the present Greek *Euchologion* the same — yet without "Let us pray to the Lord", "Lord, have mercy" [^2372].

# THE GREAT READING (*Chtenie Velikoe*)

There is now introduced into the structure of the vigil a new element of divine worship—the reading (*anagnōsis* [Gr. ἀνάγνωσις]). Such a reading is performed at the Sunday all-night vigil 7 times, and at a festal vigil 6 times: after Vespers, after the 1st and 2nd Kathismata, after the Polyeleos, after the 3rd and 6th Odes of the Canon, and after Matins—the last being only on Sunday. Having as their purpose the instruction and edification of the worshippers, these readings serve at the same time to refresh attention and afford rest for the body, since they are listened to while seated. They are of diverse content: whereas the first, at the Sunday vigil, is taken from the Holy Scriptures, the next four are taken from Patristic homilies upon the New Testament, the sixth from the lives of the saints, and the seventh is moral-ascetical—the *Catecheses* of St. Theodore the Studite. Consequently, the most important of these readings is the first, which is therefore called the "Great Reading" [*chtenie velikoe*], although in volume it is smaller than all the rest. From the Holy Scriptures there is taken for this reading that portion which, while being most important and most profitable for a Christian, is rarely known to anyone with the desired thoroughness—namely, the Acts, *(Orig. p. 609)* the Apostolic Epistles, and the Apocalypse, that is, the entire New Testament with the exception of the Gospel, which, in addition to being more or less familiar to everyone, would be inconvenient to hear while seated and with the freedom necessary for rest (for we are bound to hear it standing upright ['Let us attend / Stand upright' — *prosti*]). For each reading there falls 4–5 chapters. The Acts of the Apostles are required to be read only during the Paschal season [from Pascha unto Pentecost]; concerning the Epistles, however, on the Sunday of All Saints it is appointed that their reading should begin on that Sunday with the General Epistle of the Apostle James; consequently, they are read in the Biblical order, concluding with the Apocalypse (during Great Lent) [^2373]. On Palm Sunday and Cheesefare Sunday other readings are appointed, as also at the concurrence of the Twelve Great Feasts. On the Sunday before the Nativity of Christ there is appointed "a reading in the Apostolic commentaries".

## Its Origin

The custom of reading consecutively through the whole of the Holy Scriptures at services, at least of the New Testament, derives its origin from the most ancient times of the Church and was borrowed by her from the synagogue, where the entire divine service was reduced almost exclusively unto reading. In the 1st–6th centuries no distinction was made in importance between the reading of certain sections of Holy Scripture and others, and every reading, with the possible exception of the Gospel, was listened to while seated; from the 4th century they began to select for readings shorter sections suited unto the day, imparting unto their reading a solemn setting. Owing unto this, many portions, especially of the Old Testament, for lack of time were left unread at divine services. The ascetics returned the Church in this regard unto the former practice: deprived of temple services, they replaced them with the singing of the Psalter and the consecutive reading of the whole of Scripture, reading through at a single sitting entire large books, such as, for example, Isaiah and the Epistle to the Romans. With the foundation of the first monasteries, in those of them that followed the order of the cathedral-parochial service (the monasteries of Palestine and Syria), alongside the traditional short readings adapted unto the day, they endeavored, imitating the practice of the ascetics, to conduct also a continuous reading of the Bible in large sections, entire epistles, for example on Sinai (see Introductory Chapter, pp. 59–61, 104, 105, 161, 167, 189–191, 295). In ancient Western worship, reading was allotted scarcely less, if not even more, space than in the East: there not one of the services was devoid of at least a short reading from the New Testament under the name of *capitulum* or *capitellum*, while at Matins reading occupied as much space as the chanting of the Psalter; furthermore, two special services were assigned unto reading: one after the 1st or 3rd Hour under the name of *capitulum*, and the other after Vespers before Compline—*(Orig. p. 610)* the *collatio* [^2374] (Introductory Chapter, pp. 304–307, 309–319); the latter, evidently, corresponds completely in placement unto the reading under consideration at our Vespers, but its subject matter consisted of Patristic homilies.

## Order of the Great Reading

Concerning the order of this reading the Typikon states:
"The reader [says]: **Amen** (following 'The blessing of the Lord...'), and announces the beginning of the reading. And the priest: **Through the prayers of our holy fathers**. And the priest and the deacon divest themselves of their sacred vestments and depart. And thus all sit down, each in his own place."
By the "beginning of the reading", which is pronounced by the reader prior unto the exclamation of the priest: **"Through the prayers of our holy fathers"**, there is evidently understood the title of the book being read, in the form, for example: "The Reading from the Acts of the Holy Apostles" or "The Reading from the General Epistle of Peter" (as at the Paremias). The priest's exclamation serves as a fitting reminder that the practice of this reading traces back unto the holy ascetics. It goes without saying, and as is stated in the practice—rarely observed anywhere, however— of these readings (in Russia—at Solovki Monastery, at Valaam, and in a few other monasteries), that this reading must be performed not in a chanting tone (*naraspév*), like the Epistle and Gospel, but in an ordinary, even conversational voice, with the necessary intonations: it replaces a sermon, an instruction. The reader stands facing or half-turned toward the people.

## Ancient Typika on the Great Reading

According unto the Evergetis Typikon, this reading took place between the pannychis and Matins, "amounting unto 8 folios" [^2375].
The Georgian MS:
"there is a reading of the text (a Georgian word signifying the original text in distinction from commentaries and paraphrases) of the Acts of the Holy Apostles; it is meet to know that from Pascha unto the Sunday of All Saints the Acts of the Holy Apostles are read, and on the remaining Sundays of the year the 7 General Epistles and 14 Pauline Epistles and the Apocalypse."
Likewise, with the exception of the word "text", Greek and Slavic MSS, Greek printed editions, and the Old Believer Typikon.
The Order [*Diataxis*] of Patriarch Philotheus:
"when the reading is set forth, the priest pronounces the verse: **Through the prayers of our holy fathers**." The Moscow *Sluzhebniki* do not speak of the reading, except that "when they begin to ring for the third hour (at the 3rd tolling?), then the reader leaves off the reading, and upon the conclusion of the third ringing, the psalm-reader says: **Amen**, and **Glory to God in the highest**."
The *Sluzhebnik* of Peter Mohyla:
"And the reader, having uttered: **Amen**, immediately having read the inscription of the reading, says: **Bless, father**. The priest: **Blessed is our God always, now and ever, and unto the ages of ages**. The reader: **Amen**. And he reads as much as is required. And thus the priest and the deacon divest themselves—" [^2376]. *(Orig. p. 611)*

# FRACTION AND CONSUMPTION OF BREAD AND WINE (*Khlebolomlenie i pocherpanie*)

During this reading the worshippers not only restore their strength for the further vigil by sitting, but are also refreshed by partaking of the blessed bread and wine. In the church there thus takes place, as it were, a supper, accompanied, like every monastic meal, by reading, and that of an especially lofty nature. Taking place within the temple, unto the sound of the divinely inspired Scriptures, this is the holiest of meals. It is truly the agape of antiquity.
"The cellarer (*kellaritēs* [Gr. κελλαρίτης], the supervisor of the storeroom), having taken from the blessed loaves and broken them into pieces (cut them into slices), distributes them upon a dish unto the brethren, and ladles out a cup (*potērion* [Gr. ποτήριον]) apiece of (blessed) wine unto all equally, from the superior unto the lowest who are in the monastery. — And when the cellarer has distributed unto the brethren the bread and a cup of wine apiece, on account of the toil (*dia ton kopon* [Gr. διὰ τὸν κόπον]) of the vigil (because of fatigue from the vigil), as we have received from the beginning from the holy fathers, he then departs and makes the customary prostration together with those who served with him (who assisted him in the distribution), two in a rank (the refectory servers who assisted the cellarer stand in pairs before the solea, where they make prostrations) before the holy doors (thanking God for the completed ministration) and unto both choirs one apiece (asking forgiveness for shortcomings), and they depart (unto their places)."
Following the partaking of the blessed bread and wine, the Typikon further observes, it is forbidden to consume any food ("to taste anything") in view of the morrow's communion. In view of this also, this partaking occurs at vigils only from September 1 unto March 25; at summer vigils, however, the blessed loaves are not tasted, but are eaten at the morrow's meal before other food (this is in view of the fact that the Vespers of the vigil, beginning after sunset, in summer, owing unto the brevity of the night, may end too late at night).
"And the blessed loaves have diverse gifts (*charismata* [Gr. χαρίσματα]), that is to say (i.e.), they stay (*pauei* [Gr. παύει]) burning heat (*pyreton* [Gr. πυреτόν], high fever) in those who drink them with water, and shaking ague (*phrikas* [Gr. φρίκας], chills/ague), and heal every infirmity (*malakian* [Gr. μαλακίαν], weakness) and every disease; and in addition unto these, they drive away mice (*sētas* [Gr. σῆτας], which signifies also 'moths') from crops (*gennēmatōn* [Gr. γεννημάτων], granary grains) and expel other noxious pests."

In the *Sluzhebnik* this notice is abridged:
"blessed bread is an aid against all evils, if it be received with faith",
and there is added a warning unto the priest, that he bless not the blessed substances a second time at another vigil, but distribute the bread unto the people and eat it himself at the table before other food, consume the wine with reverence, anoint with the oil at the end of Matins or put it into food, and sow or grind the wheat.

## Ancient Typika on the Blessing of Loaves

The Georgian MS:
"The cellarer breaks one of the blessed loaves and gives it unto the brethren, as well as a cup apiece of wine on account of fatigue, as this has been handed down unto us by the fathers; the brethren bow unto the sanctuary, unto the right and unto the left, and go forth from the church. From this time forth, in view of the communion of the Holy Mysteries, they must not drink water. Blessed bread hath manifold grace: specifically, when taken with water, it expels fever and heals every infirmity; it destroys also the worms harmful unto wheat."
Greek MSS and printed editions are as the present Typikon, only *(Orig. p. 612)* instead of "to taste anything"—"to drink water", and they lack "and expel other noxious pests", and sometimes instead of *gennēmatōn* [Gr. γεννημάτων]—*hōreiōn* [Gr. ὡρείων], "from granaries".
Slavic Typikon of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 328/383 of the 14th c.:
"they have diverse grace, they heal infirmities, and drunk with water it drives away the onset of diseases and heals all bodily debility; wheat and other fruits it delivers from noxious pests."
No. 678/386 of the 15th c. is as the present one. MS of the Kyiv Academy Museum Aa 194 of the 16th c.: "two cups apiece", and lacks "mice from crops they drive away".
The Greek printed *Euchologion* is as our *Sluzhebnik*, without the warning unto the priest.

The Moscow *Sluzhebniki* of 1602 and 1647: "to drink water or taste anything else", and they lack mention of the gifts.
In the *Sluzhebnik* of Peter Mohyla there is nothing even concerning the partaking. The Moscow [edition] of 1658 is in everything like the present *Sluzhebnik*.
The Old Believer Typikon is like ours [^2377].

## Historical Foundation of the Evening Blessing of Loaves and Wine

The prototype of this "meal", as has long since been observed by many, was the agape. At the latter the food was frequently as simple as that offered by the present Typikon for consumption at the vigil (Introductory Chapter, pp. 51–52, 75–77). Probably oil and wheat were also added unto the substances being blessed (and they were added, as we have seen, not without hesitation and not all at once) not without thought of the ancient agape, and likewise, probably under the influence of the very ancient practice of blessing oil. In the liturgical monuments of the 4th and neighboring centuries there are prayers for the blessing of water and oil, which were brought into the temple, apparently, alongside the bread and wine for the Eucharist, on which account prayers for their sanctification were placed following the order of the Liturgy. Such a place they occupy in the Syriac *Testament of our Lord Jesus Christ* (*Testamentum Domini Nostri Jesu Christi*), where they are cited with the note: "if the priest sanctifieth oil for the healing of those who suffer, then, placing its vessel before the altar, he saith with compunction"; the prayer beseeches God, Who hath granted us the Holy Spirit, Christ, Who hath sanctified us, made us wise, given us consciousness of sins, the power of His Spirit, the Healer, Who hath given unto the worthy the grace of healing, to send down upon the oil the fullness of His beneficent mercy, that it may relieve the laboring, heal the sick, and sanctify those who come unto faith; "this prayer is said also over water". The *Apostolic Constitutions* beseech the Lord of Sabaoth, Who hath given water for drinking and purification and oil to make the face cheerful, to sanctify these substances through Christ, to grant them "power effective for health, banishing diseases, driving away demons, and expelling every deceitful snare". The prayer in the Euchologion attributed unto Serapion, Bishop of Thmuis (4th c.), "concerning those who offer oil and water", "blessing" these substances "in the Name of Christ", likewise entreats for them "healing power", so that through the drinking of them and anointing with them "every burning heat (*pyretos* [Gr. πυρετός]), everything demonic, and every disease may be repelled" [^2378]. Mention of blessed loaves is made in the *Spiritual Meadow* [*Pratum Spirituale*]: Abba *(Orig. p. 613)* Sergius the Sinaite, having given such bread unto a lion lying upon the road and hindering his mules from passing, commanded him to get off the road, which the beast duly performed [^2379].
The second part of our Vespers, by its proximity unto the Liturgy, resembles the 2nd part (from the Entrance onward) of Chanted Vespers (Introductory Chapter, p. 342), only there the assimilation was unto the beginning of the Liturgy, whereas here it is unto the end.

# NON-ORTHODOX VESPERS (*Inoslavnye vecherni*)

Instituting a comparison of our Vespers according unto the themes of its hymns and prayers with non-Orthodox evening services, we find in the latter the following most significant differences (the points of agreement have been indicated in the exposition of the rite).

Armenian Vespers hath at the beginning Psalm 54:17–18 [LXX; Masoretic Ps. 55:16–17]: **"As for me, I cried unto God, and the Lord heard me; evening and morning and at noon will I tell and declare it, and He shall hear my voice"**, Psalm 85 [LXX; Masoretic 86] **"Bow down Thine ear, O Lord"**, Psalm 139 [LXX; Masoretic 140] **"Deliver me, O Lord"**, Psalm 120 [LXX; Masoretic 121] **"I have lifted up mine eyes"**, Psalm 90 [LXX; Masoretic 91] **"He that dwelleth in the help of the Most High"**, Psalm 122 [LXX; Masoretic 123] **"Unto Thee have I lifted up mine eyes"** (in our rite, at Daily Vespers), Psalm 53 [LXX; Masoretic 54] **"Save me, O God, in Thy name"** [^2380]; thus, all the psalms of our Sixth Hour, one of the Ninth Hour, and one from the Midnight Office entered into Armenian Vespers.

Coptic Vespers: Psalm 130 [LXX; Masoretic 131] **"Lord, my heart is not exalted"**, 131 [LXX; Masoretic 132] **"Remember, O Lord, David"**, 136 [LXX; Masoretic 137] **"By the waters of Babylon"**, 137 [LXX; Masoretic 138] **"I will give thanks unto Thee, O Lord"**, 145 [LXX; Masoretic 146] **"Praise the Lord, O my soul"**, 146 [LXX; Masoretic 147:1–11] **"Praise ye the Lord, for a psalm is good"**, 147 [LXX; Masoretic 147:12–20] **"Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem"**, the Gospel of Luke 2:25–30 on the Meeting of the Lord, the Creed [*Credo*], the 1st prayer with thanksgiving for the past day and with a petition to accept the evening doxology, to deliver from the snares of the evil one, and to grant a peaceful evening and night; the 2nd prayer for the forgiveness of the sins of the day, restful sleep, a guardian angel, and deliverance from evil and the torment of the devil [^2381].

Abyssinian [Ethiopian] Vespers: Psalm 117 [LXX; Masoretic 118] **"Give thanks unto the Lord"** and the "Songs of Ascents"—Psalms 119–128 [LXX; Masoretic 120–129] (**"Unto the Lord in mine affliction"**, in our rite the customary Kathisma at Daily Vespers); the Gospel of Mark 1:29–34 on the healing of Simon's mother-in-law and the evening healings of the Savior; **"Glory to God in the highest... goodwill"**; a petition for forgiveness through the prayers of the Theotokos; **"We worship Thee, O Christ, with Thy Good Father and the Holy Spirit, for Thou hast come and saved us"**; our 4 penitential stichera: **"I would fain blot out with tears"** [*Khotekh slezami*]; from the service of the Great Canon the stichera: **"My whole life"** [*Vse zhitie moe*], **"With the weight of heedlessness"** [*Tyazhestiyu nebrezheniya*], **"I have become an offense"** [*Bykh pretknovenie*]; our Theotokion **"Rejoice, O Pure One"** [*Raduisya Chistaya*]; **"It is good to give praise"**; penitential sessional hymns from the Psalter after the 17th Kathisma: **"I have sinned against Thee, O Savior"** [*Sogreshikh k Tebe Spase*], **"I cry unto Thee"** [*Zovu k Tebe*]; the Martyr's hymn [*martyrikon*] **"They who desired not earthly pleasures"** [*Izhe zemnyya slasti ne vozzhelevshe*]; the Theotokion **"O Virgin Theotokos Mary, preserve Thy flock"** [*Bogoroditse Devo Marie sokhrani stado Tvoe*]; penitential troparia: **"As the prodigal son"** [*Yako bludnyi syn*], **"I pray Thee like the publican"** [*Molyutisya yako mytar*]; a prayer unto the Lord Jesus with confession of the sins of the day and a petition for amendment, with the addition *(Orig. p. 614)* of a petition unto the saints and the Theotokos for intercession on our behalf; 2 prayers unto God the Father as the Creator of the day, with thanksgiving for the past day and a request for a peaceful night; a prayer for kings, resembling **"Establish, O God"**, and **"Thou Who at all times"** [^2382]. Thus the entire service is of a penitential character (Abyssinian Matins is of a more laudatory and supplicatory content).

Roman Vespers hath 5 consecutive psalms from among Psalms 109–147 [LXX; Masoretic 110–148], and thus Sunday Vespers hath Psalms 109–113 [LXX; Masoretic 110–114/115] with antiphons: **"The Lord said"** [*Dixit Dominus*] before Psalm 109, and **"The Lord said unto my Lord: Sit Thou at My right hand"** (v. 1) after it; for Psalm 110 [LXX; Masoretic 111], its v. 7: **"Faithful"**, **"Faithful are all His commandments, confirmed unto the age of the age"** [Lat. *Fidelia omnia mandata ejus: confirmata in saeculum saeculi*]; for Psalm 111 [LXX; Masoretic 112], v. 1: **"In His commandments"**, **"In His commandments he shall greatly delight"**; for Psalm 112 [LXX; Masoretic 113], v. 2: **"Blessed be the name of the Lord"**, **"Blessed be the name of the Lord from henceforth and for evermore"**; for Psalm 113 [LXX; Masoretic 114–115], v. 26 [v. 18]: **"We that live"**, **"We that live will bless the Lord"**; the *capitulum* (2 Cor. 1:3–4)—the glorification of God, the Father of Christ, for comfort in every affliction (probably the Resurrection is in view); the hymn *Lucis Creator* [^2383] unto God as the Creator of light and of day, which were created on this day of the week (the hymns for Vespers of each day glorify the work of creation of that day, on Monday—the creation of heaven, etc.; cf. in Jewish worship, Introductory Chapter, p. 11); the responsory: **"Let my prayer be set forth, O Lord, as incense before Thee"** (Ps. 140:2 [LXX; Masoretic 141:2]); the Canticle of the Theotokos, **"My soul doth magnify the Lord"** [*Magnificat*], with the **Glory to the Father** [*Gloria Patri*] [^2384].
