In addition, a sessional hymn is easier to listen to, since it is listened to while sitting, and its protracted singing is not so tiring for the worshipers as such singing of a troparion would be. Besides its protractedness, the melody of the Sunday sessional hymns is distinguished from the troparion melody by greater...

...evenness and tranquility; from them breathes, moreover, a certain sorrow concerning the burial of the Savior; although they glorify the Resurrection of the Savior, like the troparia, yet this glorification passes in them through the remembrance of the burial and death of the Savior (**"Life lay in the grave and a seal was set upon the stone; as a sleeping King, soldiers guarded Christ"**—sessional hymn of Tone 6 after the 2nd Kathisma; cf. **"The noble Joseph"**—sessional hymn of Tone 2); for this reason the melodies of the sessional hymns approximate in character the melodies of stichera, full of deep contemplation and tender contrition. In general, they dispose the soul more unto tranquil meditation, such as is required for the impending readings, and give more rest to the soul than the joyful, but stirring melodies of the troparia. They serve also as a transition from the joyful hymns of **"God is the Lord"** and the troparia unto the readings, which constitute the least solemn and most monotonous part of the Vigil. Of the merit of the Sunday sessional hymns according to their melody speaks also the fact that these melodies are independent and have no model melodies (*prosomoia*, *podobny*), with the exception of the sessional hymns after the 2nd Kathisma: Tone 1 is patterned on the model **"While the stone was sealed"** (*Kameni zapechatannu*), Tone 3 on **"Awed by the beauty of thy virginity"** (*Krasote devstva*, the Theotokion to the sessional hymn), Tone 4 on **"Speedily anticipate"** (*Skoro predvari*, the Theotokion of the Sixth Hour on Great Lent Wednesdays and Fridays, taken as mournful in contrast to the joyful troparion melody of Tone 4).

*(Orig. p. 637)*

As regards the comparative merit of the sessional hymns according to their content with other hymnographic compositions, in this respect they stand on an equal footing with the troparia and surpass the stichera and canons in poetic height. In places they strike by the power of their expressions (**"Death was fiercely despoiled,"** **"The tomb opened, Hades weeping,"** **"No longer, O death, dost thou hold dominion"**—Tone 3 after the 1st Kathisma), by the vividness of depiction (Hades saith: **"I tremble at the flesh of the incorruptible hypostasis, I behold the Invisible One secretly contending against me, therefore even they whom I hold cry aloud: Glory, O Christ, to Thy Resurrection!"**—Tone 3 after the 2nd Kathisma), and by the depth of psychological analysis of the persons involved in the event of the Resurrection (the Myrrh-bearing Women at the tomb think within themselves: **"Can it be that He is risen, Who even before the Passion proclaimed the Resurrection?"**; after the Resurrection, **"Peter cried aloud unto Thee: The women took courage, but I was afraid; the thief theologized, but I denied Thee; wilt Thou, then, call me henceforth to be a disciple, or wilt Thou show me again as a fisher of the deep?"**—Tone 5 after the 2nd Kathisma; Mary Magdalene saith unto the Jews: **"Either give me my Lord, or cry aloud with me: O Lord, glory to Thee!"**—Tone 6 after the 1st Kathisma). Of the high merit of the Sunday sessional hymns speaks also the fact that several of them serve as troparia or sessional hymns of the greatest feasts: of Holy Saturday—**"The noble Joseph,"** **"Unto the Myrrh-bearing Women"** (with additions); of St. Thomas Sunday—**"While the tomb was sealed."**

In view of such merits of the Sunday sessional hymns according to their melodies and content, they are never canceled at the Sunday service,...

...even upon the concurrence with Sunday of the Meeting of the Lord (*Hypapante*) and the Twelve Great Feasts of the Mother of God; they are then sung in their entirety, even with their Theotokia, whereas at least the latter it would have been natural to replace with the sessional hymns of the feast.

Of Sunday sessional hymns after each kathisma two are appointed, just as on great feasts after each kathisma there are two sessional hymns, or else, if one, it is sung twice, evidently with the aim of affording singing unto each of the two choirs. In this connection they are linked by a refrain, so that the first is sung "simply" and the second with a refrain. As such a refrain for the sessional hymns after the 1st Kathisma serves the verse of Psalm 9:33 [LXX; Masoretic 10:12], as it were inviting or summoning the Savior unto the Resurrection: **"Arise, O Lord my God, let Thy hand be lifted up, forget not Thy poor unto the end"**; and after the 2nd Kathisma—the opening verse of that same psalm—the vow of the faithful for the fulfillment of this sublime prayer of theirs: **"I will give thanks unto Thee, O Lord, with my whole heart, I will tell of all Thy marvelous works"** (these same verses are the prokeimenon and its verse for Tone 7). Out of the series of psalmic verses that can be applied unto the Resurrection of the Savior, precisely these were selected for this present place, because the direct glorification of the Resurrection has not yet begun at Matins (it begins only with the Gospel and **"Having beheld the Resurrection of Christ"**), and because here a somewhat mournful and penitential tone is required (**"forget not Thy poor"**). Unto the two sessional hymns after each kathisma is joined, through **"Glory... Both now..."**, a Theotokion, which customarily concludes every series of Sunday hymns, as well as hymns in honor of the saints.

The Theotokia of the sessional hymns, like the Theotokia of the troparia, are dedicated unto the mystery of the Incarnation and just as rarely as those dwell upon the Resurrection *(Orig. p. 638)* of the Savior, upon the relationship of the Mother of God unto that event; the latter occurs in the Theotokia of Tone 2 after the 1st and 2nd Kathismata, Tone 6 after the 2nd Kathisma, Tone 7 after the 1st and 2nd Kathismata, and partly Tone 1 after the 2nd Kathisma and Tone 5 after the 1st Kathisma. Some of these present Theotokia strike by the power of their expressions, the depth and originality of their thoughts; such are, for example, the Theotokia of Tones 3 and 4 after the 1st Kathisma: the 1st, **"Awed by the beauty of thy virginity"** (*Krasote devstva*), conveying the thought that at the spiritual beauty of the Most Holy Virgin Gabriel himself was awestruck and was at a loss what to say unto Her, how to name Her; the 2nd, **"Joseph was astonished"** (*Udivisya Iosif*), depicting the feelings and reflections of Joseph at the Nativity of Christ, how he had to recall the types of the seedless birth (the fleece and the bush) and, being convinced, began to prove unto the priests of Jerusalem (who, it is implied, had brought an accusation against him for failure to fulfill the obligation he had assumed) that a seedless birth is possible. By a remarkable coincidence, the melodies of these two Theotokia are also the most beautiful and beloved ...by the church typikon: they are time and again appointed as model hymns (*prosomoia*, *podobny*) unto sessional hymns, even on the greatest feasts: for example, the sessional hymns on the Nativity of Christ after the 2nd Kathisma, Theophany after the 1st, the Annunciation after the 3rd have as their model melody **"Awed by the beauty of thy virginity"** (*Krasote devstva*); on Theophany after the 2nd Kathisma, and likewise on the Nativity of Christ and the Annunciation after the Polyeleos—**"Joseph was astonished"** (*Udivisya Iosif*). Of the high merit of the sessional Theotokia bears witness also the fact that certain of them have been taken into other services, even of the greatest feasts; thus, the Theotokion of Tone 3 after the 2nd Kathisma, **"Incomprehensible and Indescribable"** (*Nepostizhimago i neopysannago*), serves as the sessional hymn of Matins of the Nativity of Christ after the 2nd Kathisma; the sessional Theotokion of Tone 2 after the 2nd Kathisma, **"All-blessed art thou"** (*Preblagoslovena esi*), serves constantly as the Theotokion for the Praise Stichera of Sunday Matins. And the Theotokion of Tone 8 after the 2nd Kathisma—the concluding kathisma unto all—**"All of creation rejoiceth in thee"** (*O Tebe raduetsya*), serves as the Megalynarion (*Zadostoynik*) of the Liturgy of St. Basil the Great, for which reason 'we sing it not sitting, but standing, and with fear and reverence.' On account of the high merit of the Theotokia, they are almost never omitted at the Sunday service, even upon the concurrence with a Twelve Great Feast of the Mother of God, although, as we have seen, they speak almost nothing of the Resurrection, but are of general content.

The sessional Theotokia are replaced only by troparion Theotokia—namely, as is stated concerning this in Chapter 52 of the Typikon, if the troparia at **"God is the Lord"** are sung with a Theotokion not of the current tone, then this Theotokion is sung after the 1st Kathisma, while the regular one is omitted (since the Theotokia after the 1st Kathisma are superior [**"Joseph was astonished,"** **"Awed by the beauty of thy virginity,"** **"Gideon prefigured"**], it is better to transfer them unto the 2nd Kathisma and omit those appointed there, excepting, of course, the Theotokion **"All of creation rejoiceth in thee"**) [^2436].

*(Orig. p. 639)*

### Sunday Sessional Hymns According to Ancient Typika (*Voskresnye sedal'ny po drevnim ustavam*)

Sessional hymns are already indicated by the well-known description of the Sinaitic Matins (Introductory Chapter, p. 295) under the name *kathismata anapausima* (Gr. καθίσματα ἀναпаύσιμα), which in Slavonic is inaccurately translated as 'Sunday kathismata' (*kafizm voskresnykh*); it should rather have been translated: 'restful sessional hymns' (for resting, see below concerning the readings).

In the *Hypotyposis* they are called *troparia tou kathismatos* (Gr. τροπάρια τοῦ καθίσματος) [^2437].

In the Holy Sepulchre *Order of Passion and Paschal Week*, the designation 'sessional hymn' (*kathisma*), besides its present usage, is applied unto all troparia: after **"Now lettest Thou..."** (*Nyne otpushchaeshi*), and at **"God is the Lord"** [^2438].

The Evergetis Typikon after the 1st Kathisma had a 'Sunday sessional hymn' ...and after the second—a 'hypakoe' (*ypakoi*), because it did not have the Blameless (*Amomoi*).

The Studite typika speak indistinctly concerning sessional hymns.

Of the MSS of the Jerusalem Typikon: the Georgian MS speaks of one sessional hymn with a Theotokion after each kathisma; the ancient Greek MSS: 'we say the Sunday sessional hymn of the tone, the first, and if there be more sessional hymns, we say the verse: **"Arise, O Lord, help us..."**, and we likewise sing the other; but if not, **Glory... Both now...** and the Theotokion'; later MSS and the printed Greek add: 'and again the psalm verse: **"I will love Thee, O Lord,"** and again the Sunday sessional hymn and the Theotokion'; the Slavic MSS are like the present one, but later ones do not indicate the verses. The Old Believer Typikon gives the 1st verse as in the Greek. In the Western divine service an analogy unto the sessional hymns is constituted by the responsories, although they follow after the readings (Introductory Chapter, p. 307); they correspond for the most part unto the content of the reading, yet at times are common unto different readings; the Sunday ones do not differ in character from the weekday ones.

### Readings After the Kathismata (*Chteniya po kafizmam*)

After the sessional hymn follows the reading prepared by it. The readings of Matins are of an entirely different kind from the reading at Great Vespers: the latter is taken, on Sunday at least, from Holy Scripture; the former—from patristic writings. The rule for these readings is set forth in Chapter 10 of the Typikon. According unto it, the readings serve as commentaries of St. John Chrysostom or Blessed Theophylact on the New Testament *(Orig. p. 640)* (the commentaries are read on that Evangelist from whom the Gospel at the Divine Liturgy is taken), from Symeon Metaphrastes, and the *Margarites* (*Pearl*). The length of the reading is not defined, but if one divides all the books named therein among the readings of the entire year, there will fall upon a single reading about 10 octavo pages. Neither in the present place of the Typikon nor in Chapter 10 is it indicated from which book the reading is taken at which place of Matins; it is only noted concerning the reading after the 1st Kathisma that it takes place 'in the Commentary Gospel' (*Tolkovoe Evangelie*) and concerning the reading after Ode 6 of the Canon that the *Prolog* is read then. Nor is the order of the reading indicated here; it is given in Chapter 35 for the trapeza: the reader pronounces the 'preface,' that is, the name of the author and the title of the book, while the superior or the priest on duty exclaims: 'By the prayers of him whose reading this is' (that is, 'By the prayers of Saint *N*, O Lord Jesus Christ our God, have mercy on us'). In ancient manuscripts of liturgical readings, after the title of each reading there is the addition: 'Bless, father,' unto which the exclamation of the priest serves as the response.

### Their History (*Istoriya ikh*)

Already Canon 17 of the Council of Laodicea prescribes: 'Psalms should not be joined together in a continuous sequence in the services, but a reading should take place in the interval after each psalm.' Balsamon says that this is prescribed for rest. The readings at Matins in the well-known description of the 7th-century Sinaitic Vigil are from the Catholic Epistles, taken in course. The *Hypotyposis*, the *Diatyposis*, and the Studite typika, while mentioning readings at the same places of Matins as today, do not indicate the content of the Sunday readings. Among non-Orthodox traditions, readings are especially developed in the Armenian divine service, where they are called 'exhortations' (*uvehshchanie*); of such 'exhortations' there are even 2 at the Hours, 5 at the Midnight Office (= the 1st part of Matins), and up to 3 at Matins in the strict sense (Introductory Chapter, pp. 299–301). In ancient Western rules readings were likewise very highly developed, especially in the Rule of St. Benedict (ibid., pp. 310ff.), where it is noted concerning them: 'at vigils books of both the Old and New Testaments are read, and commentaries upon them composed by the most renowned orthodox teachers and ecumenical fathers.' At the present Roman Catholic Sunday Matins there are 9 readings: the first three from the Old or New Testament (Epistles), the second three from the Fathers, the 7th the Gospel, and the 8th and 9th its homiletic exposition; in length each reading is less than half a duodecimo page; before the reading a blessing is implored: 'Command, O Lord, a blessing (*Iube Domine benedicere*)'; the blessing before each reading is varied, with the response Amen [^2439].

*(Orig. p. 641)*

# THE BLAMELESS OR THE POLYELEOS (*Neporochny ili Polieley*)

### The Blameless (*Neporochny*)

The second part of Matins draws near its conclusion, and therewith, following the general rule of our services, solemnity must increase. Now there arrives the most sublime section of this part and, according unto the customary view, the most solemn moment of the entire Matins and of the whole Vigil—the singing of the Polyeleos or the Blameless (*Neporochny*), with the Gradual Antiphons (*anabathmoi*), concluded by the reading of the Gospel. Yet concerning the Polyeleos, which at the ordinary Sunday Vigil is appointed to be sung comparatively rarely—for a little over 3 months in the course of the year—the Typikon makes no mention whatever in the present place. After the 2nd Kathisma and its reading, it says here, 'we sing the Blameless.' Taking thus the place of the festal Polyeleos at the ordinary Sunday Vigil, the Blameless (*Amōmos*, Gr. Ἄμωμος) is fully suited for such a substitution. Thus is named Psalm 118 [LXX; Masoretic 119], **"Blessed are the blameless in the way"** (*Blazheni neporochnii*), after its second word, which expresses the theme of the entire psalm, and therefore in antiquity was prefixed unto it during singing as an antiphon or melodic model (as even now in the Order of Burial). Representing an ecstatic hymn unto the Law of God, the psalm depicts the ardent love of the righteous man for this Law, or, more precisely, toward God for His so perfect and beneficent gift unto mankind. This greatest of psalms, containing 176 verses, in the Hebrew text consists of 22 strophes beginning in alphabetical order with all the letters of the alphabet; in almost every strophe, consisting of 8 verses, the name Jehovah [YHWH] is used once (at least 22 times in all), and the Law is called by various names: 'law,' 'commandment,' 'statutes' (properly 'ordinances'), 'testimonies' (that is, revelations), 'judgments' (that is, decrees), 'precepts' (in Slavonic likewise 'commandments'), 'ways,' 'words'—all this, of course, with the epithet 'Thy,' that is, 'God's'; by these are designated various aspects of the Law of God. The righteous man finds no words to depict his devotion unto this Law and his zeal for it: for him it is dearer than all treasures and good things, higher than all earthly wisdom; he meditates upon it day and night, prays for heavenly illumination to comprehend it, is ready to suffer for it, and well-nigh paid for it with his life. With such a content, the psalm is applicable, first of all, unto the Savior, unto the entire work of His life, for which there is given here the most touching depiction that can possibly be conceived; and secondly, the psalm is applicable unto every Christian, as sketching a complete ideal for him. The psalm ...breathes a remarkable warmth, acting with irresistible charm upon a heart in any degree capable of religious feelings, and surpassing in this respect the other psalms. All this prompted the church order to make Psalm 118 [LXX; Masoretic 119], which constitutes the 17th Kathisma, the funeral hymn over the Savior, introducing it into Holy Saturday Matins, which it fills more than halfway—just as it is sung over every Christian in the Order of Burial. Adjoining the kathismata as the last of them, and moreover adapted, in contrast unto the first two kathismata, unto the commemorations of the day, the psalm *(Orig. p. 642)* at this place of Matins well prepares the subsequent joy of the Resurrection. In general, the relationship of the Typikon unto this psalm is exceptional, answering fully unto its high merits: the kathisma which it alone constitutes is not considered regular; when the Psalter is sung twice a week, as in Great Lent, the 17th Kathisma is excluded from the ordinary alternation, from which even the 1st Kathisma is not excluded; of all the kathismata, it alone is not omitted at the end of Passion Week, when kathismata are entirely absent; furthermore, it serves as the opening psalm of the Midnight Office (weekday)—a service celebrated at the most contrite hour of the night.

### Method of Execution (*Sposob ispolneniya*)

In execution at church services, Psalm 118 [LXX; Masoretic 119] is divided, like other kathismata, into three parts, or 'Glories' (at the burial service sometimes into two), named after their opening words: **"Blessed are the blameless"** (*Blazheni neporochnii*), **"Thy hands have made me"** (*Rutse Tvoi sotvoriste mya*), and **"Look upon me"** (*Prizri na mya*), which gradually decrease in length: the 1st Glory, verses 1–72, depicts preeminently the firmness of the righteous man in the Law; the 2nd, verses 73–131, asks for consolation in persecutions; the 3rd, verses 132–176 [printed 177], asks for victory in conflict.

The Blameless is appointed to be sung in Tone 5—of course, in that melody of this tone wherewith are sung the 'Sunday troparia' immediately adjoining the psalm—**"The assembly of the Angels"** (*Angel'skiy sobor*). The melody of Tone 5 represents a union of tender contemplation, reaching at times unto quiet sorrow, with joy—yet a joy not so much exultant as deep and serene, and therefore most suited unto the event of the Resurrection, which cost the Savior so much sorrow and the shadow of death. Therefore in this tone (only in another, special melody of it) is sung the troparion and the most important stichera of Pascha (**"Sacred Pascha"**). The Typikon does not indicate more particularly how to sing this psalm, perhaps because it is self-evident that it must be sung, like ...other psalms, alternately by the two choirs by verses, and, of course, with the inserted 'Glories,' excepting the concluding 'Glory,' which is placed already after the troparia **"The assembly of the Angels."** Such a manner of singing considerably shortens the execution (under skillful singing, when not only are there no pauses between the singing of both choirs, but one choir begins without awaiting the complete finish of singing by the other). In view of the considerable length of the psalm and the duration of the Sunday Vigil, no refrains are appointed for the psalm such as it has after each verse, for example, at the burial service. In place of such refrains, there is added at the end of the psalm a series of troparia with the subjoining unto them of the most characteristic verse in the psalm, expressing its primary thought: **"Blessed art Thou, O Lord, teach me Thy statutes"** (*Blagosloven esi, Gospodi, nauchi mya opravdaniem Tvoim*). By this addition the thought is instilled that, properly, the entire psalm ought to be sung with the addition unto each verse of a Sunday troparion (as on Holy Saturday), and if this is not done, it is solely from lack of time.

*(Orig. p. 643)*

### History of the Blameless (*Istoriya Neporochnykh*)

Psalm 118 [LXX; Masoretic 119] under the name 'Blameless' (*Amōmos*, Gr. Ἄμωμος) occupied a very prominent place at Sunday Matins according unto the Typikon of the Great Church of Constantinople, both in its most ancient form, in the 10th–11th centuries (see Introductory Chapter, p. 339), and in the so-called Chanted Office (*asmatikos akolouthia*): it constituted the central and larger part of this Matins; it was sung here in three staseis (*statii*) with the refrain on the 1st and 3rd of **"Alleluia,"** and on the 2nd—**"Give me understanding, O Lord,"** with censing and a solemn entrance into the temple at the conclusion of the psalm (ibid., pp. 345–346).

The Studite typika did not have this kathisma at Sunday Matins, restricting themselves unto the 2nd and 3rd Kathismata [^2440]. They had it on Saturday, wherein it was for the most part sung without Alleluia (see below, 'Concerning the Saturday Service'), consequently, as with us on Sunday [^2441].

The Jerusalem Typikon concerning the Sunday Blameless: the Georgian MS: 'after the 2nd Kathisma and its reading, **"O give thanks unto the Lord"** with 3 Alleluias (Psalm 135 [LXX; Masoretic 136], that is, the Polyeleos, see below), the Sunday sessional hymn, the reading, and the Blameless, during which the priest censes'; the most ancient Greek MSS: 'we sing the Blameless in Tone 5, at which the priest also censes' [^2442]; later Greek: 'then the Blameless'; Slavic MSS (14th–15th centuries): 'we recite the verses of **Blessed are the blameless** with refrains in three staseis; but after the third stasis, not having said **Glory... Both now...**, he says the troparion of Tone 5 **The assembly of the Angels**'; later MSS: 'we sing ...the Blameless in Tone 5'; the Old Believer Typikon: 'we sing the Blameless in Tone 5' [^2443].

### The Polyeleos (*Polieley*)

According unto Chapter 17 of the Typikon, on Sundays from the Apodosis of the Exaltation, that is, from September 22, until the Forefeast of the Nativity of Christ, December 20, and from the Apodosis of Theophany, January 14, until Cheesefare Sunday, instead of the Blameless there is sung the *Polyeleos*, that is, Psalm 134 [LXX; Masoretic 135], **"Praise ye the name of the Lord"** (*Khvalite imya Gospodne*), and Psalm 135 [LXX; Masoretic 136], **"O give thanks unto the Lord"** (*Ispovedaytesya Gospodevi*). The grounds for such periods are:
1) the Polyeleos, occupying more time than the Blameless, is sung preeminently on autumn and winter Sundays, when the nights are longer and, consequently, the Vigil must be started earlier and ended later;
2) the Polyeleos is canceled from December 20 unto January 14 owing unto the concurrence in this period of great feasts having a Polyeleos more solemn than the Sunday one, whereby the impression of the latter would be weakened;
3) in Great Lent the Polyeleos is canceled on account of the mournful character of this period.

Psalms 134 and 135 [LXX; Masoretic 135 and 136] are homogeneous in content. They invite Israel unto the glorification of God the Creator (134:6; 135:5–9) and Provider (134:7; 135:25) for the election of Israel as the people of God and for all the mercies shown *(Orig. p. 644)* unto him throughout the whole of his history, especially for the deliverance from the Egyptian bondage (134:8–10; 135:10–16) and the settlement in the Promised Land (134:10–12; 135:17–20); these mercies obligate Israel to be faithful unto God and to shun idolatry (134:15–18). The homogeneity of the psalms reaches in places unto literal identity in expressions (134:10–11 and 135:17–20). Both psalms breathe the most ecstatic joy, pouring forth in an irrepressible stream of gratitude; but the second psalm, developing the thoughts of the first, is more ecstatic and powerful than it (**"praise"** and **"give thanks"**; 134:5: **"our Lord is above all gods"** and 135:2–3: **"unto the God of gods,"** **"unto the Lord of lords"**; 134:3: **"for the Lord is good,"** 135:1: **"for His mercy endureth unto the ages"**); special solemnity is imparted unto the second psalm by the accompaniment of each verse thereof with the refrain **"For His mercy endureth unto the ages,"** which is repeated, consequently, 26 times and sounds with particular force in verses 17–20, where it divides into 4 parts a single grammatical sentence (**"Unto Him that smote great kings, for His mercy endureth unto the ages; and slew mighty kings, for His mercy endureth unto the ages; Sehon, king of the Amorites, for His mercy endureth unto the ages; and Og, king...**

...**of Bashan, for His mercy endureth unto the ages"**). — According unto Symeon of Thessalonica, the Polyeleos psalms are 'a triumphal song proclaiming the marvelous works of God, especially the passage of our souls out of the Egypt of sin and delusion unto faith in Christ, our deliverance from Pharaoh and the Egyptians, that is, the devil and demons, the deliverance of the Church from Diocletian, Maximian, and the Apostate, and other most ungodly rulers, as from Amalek, Sehon, Og, and those like unto them—and after trials and labors, settlement in the Promised Land and the heavenly inheritance through Jesus' [^2444].

The order of singing the Polyeleos psalms is not indicated in the Typikon and other liturgical books. Musical tradition prescribes to sing them with the refrain of Alleluia after each verse: in some melodies this Alleluia is sung thrice, in others after the first psalm once and after the second thrice, wherein after the first half of the verse it is sung once, and after the second twice, or vice versa. The melody for the Polyeleos psalms is not tonal, even if it be idiomelic (*samoglasny*) (as, for example, for the Prooemiac Psalm or **"Blessed is the man"**), but entirely independent, distinguished by special solemnity, exultation, and majestic slowness (the Polyeleos psalms are more than twice as short as the Blameless).

### Its History (*Istoriya ego*)

The Polyeleos, though it is unknown in what sense, is indicated by the 7th-century Jerusalem Canonarion in the Georgian version at the Paschal Vigil 'in Tone 8 with Alleluia,' as well as by later recensions of the Constantinopolitan-Hagia Sophia Typikon, for example, on the Exaltation (Introductory Chapter, p. 340). In a monument with a clearly expressed character of this Typikon—in the Kondakar of the Annunciation Monastery (wherein there is the so-called *asmatikon*—a species of chant of unknown purpose, but applicable only unto the Chanted Office)—Psalm 135 *(Orig. p. 645)* is set to musical notation in different tones: Tone 1 from verse 1 through 4, Tone 2—from verse 5, Tone 3—from verse 9, Tone 4—from verse 13, Tone 5—from verse 17, Tone 6—from verse 21, Tone 7—from verse 23, Tone 8—from verse 25 [^2445].

In the Studite-Alexian Typikon Psalms 134–136 [LXX; Masoretic 135–137], although sung only in course among the other psalms of the 19th Kathisma wherein they are included—consequently, always on Friday at Matins—nevertheless had a particularly solemn execution, a special melody of Tone 4 or 6, a refrain of Alleluia differing in quantity for each of these psalms, and were called the Polyeleos (Introductory Chapter, p. 365). Thus, according unto this typikon, the Polyeleos occurred every Friday and never otherwise. Presumably, Matins of the most ancient type, when on Sunday it had no kathismata, likewise had no Polyeleos; therefore it was an adjunct only of the Sunday Matins ...of the Forty Days [Great Lent]; and today the complete Polyeleos—with Psalm 136 [LXX; Masoretic 137]—occurs only before the Forty Days. Western Studite typika appoint Psalm 135 or both as festal psalms at Matins alongside others, sometimes with special refrains, akin to our megalynaria (*velichaniya*) (Introductory Chapter, p. 366). The Jerusalem typika in ancient Greek MSS make of these psalms a usage analogous unto the Studite-Alexian (ibid., p. 376), but speak of the Polyeleos only on feasts (as does also the Evergetis Typikon) and during the period of 3 kathismata (from September 20 unto Great Lent) [^2446].

According unto Arseny Sukhanov, in the East 'he who says the Psalter, that same one at the analogion at the choir stall says **Lord, have mercy** thrice, **Glory... Both now...**, then the two psalms which are at the Polyeleos, at the end **Glory... Both now...**, and they do not sing those psalms' [^2447].

In the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra the Polyeleos psalms are sung in the following composition: **Praise ye the name of the Lord, alleluia; praise the Lord, O ye servants, alleluia** (3). **For the Lord is great, and our Lord is above all gods, alleluia** (3) (and so forth). **O Lord, Thy name endureth unto the ages, and Thy memorial from generation to generation. Blessed be the Lord out of Zion... O give thanks unto the Lord, for He is good, alleluia** (2). **For His mercy endureth unto the ages, alleluia** (and so further 'alleluia'). **With a strong hand and a high arm. And He hath redeemed us from our enemies. O give thanks unto the God of heaven.**

### Censing at the Blameless and Polyeleos (*Kazhdenie na Neporochnykh i polielee*)

Both the Blameless and the Polyeleos that replaces it are accompanied by censing, which in divine worship marks the most solemn and sacred moments. Symbolizing, as always, the power and God-pleasingness of prayer, which truly reaches during the singing of these psalms the highest degree of intensity; symbolizing likewise the grace of the Holy Spirit attracted by such prayer; contributing unto the elevation of the spiritual mood by the pleasant fragrance of incense, censing in the present case has further a relationship unto the commemoration associated with this part of Matins: it recalls that sweet-smelling myrrh which 'with tears of compassion' the Myrrh-bearing Women blended at this hour of the night of the Resurrection. Concerning censing at the Blameless, in the continuous order of the Typikon it is only noted that 'at them the priest censes.' This brief indication in *(Orig. p. 646)* the rubric to the chapter of the Typikon under consideration (the 2nd 'Notice' [*Zri*]) is supplemented:

'the priest with the deacon only (not concelebrating, as at the megalynarion, see below) vest in the sacred vestments (from the preceding discourse in this rubric it is clear that the priest vests in the phelonion) and the deacon takes ...a candlestick with a burning candle (usually in place of this a single candle, but a large one), while the priest takes the censer, and having censed round about the holy table and the whole altar, they go forth through the north doors, and he censes the Royal Doors and on both sides the holy icons and on the analogion, then the superior and the choirs and the standing people, as is customary, and they enter again through the doors of the south side.'

Consequently, the Royal Doors are not opened during this censing, in accordance likewise with Chapter 23 of the Typikon, according unto which the Holy Doors in the first half of Matins are opened only for the reading of the Gospel, which is still far off (the hypakoe and the reading) and the preparation for which (the bell ringing) begins only with the Gradual Antiphons (*anabathmoi*). In like manner is the censing performed, according unto the aforementioned rubric of the Typikon, 'and on other days, [when] a megalynarion is sung unto anyone apart from a vigil,' that is, at the Polyeleos to a saint without a vigil. But at the Polyeleos of a feast or of a saint with a vigil, this censing is performed already with greater solemnity:

'an analogion is set (a reading table with a slanted top, by virtue whereof the icon placed upon it is visible unto all) in the midst of the temple, and upon it is placed the festal icon of the Day of the Lord, or of the Mother of God, or of the Saint (male or female); and the superior (the sole place at the Vigil where he takes direct part in the sacred ministration) vests in the sanctuary (altar), and all the concelebrants in phelonia according unto custom, and having gone forth from the altar through the opened Royal Doors, they take their stand on both sides round about the analogion.' The saint, whose icon is surrounded by the ministers of the altar, stands as though visible in the temple in the midst of the worshipers, responding thereby unto their desire (expressed in a hymn unto St. John the Baptist: 'Come and stand with us') [^2448].

If the icon depicts an event, then it is, as it were, reenacted among the faithful, while the clergy, as the most worthy, are present at its very accomplishment. Thus the glorification of the saint or event in this place of the Vigil reaches the highest degree of immediacy, when all the faithful, headed by the clergy, surround the very author of the celebration and converse with him face to face, 'as though one were speaking unto his friend.' 'And the superior distributes candles unto the concelebrants and unto the holy people standing in the temple.' The candle in the hand of the worshiper signifies the spiritual burning of the whole being in ...the feeling of love toward the Author of the triumph, and likewise befits the memory of the saint, as the annual anniversary of his repose. In present practice, the holding of candles by the people during the Vigil has been preserved only for two days of Passion Week and the Palm Sunday and Paschal Matins connected therewith; at the Polyeleos of Vigils, however, it has been preserved for the priests; moreover, it is replaced by the burning of the chandelier (*panikadilo*), concerning the kindling of which the Typikon nowhere says anything. After the distribution of candles the superior, "preceded by the deacon with a burning candle, censes first round about the icon upon the analogion," as the focal *(Orig. p. 647)* sanctuary at this moment,

"and goes into the altar, and there censes the Holy Table and the entire altar, and all the holy local icons in the temple, and then the presiding clergy on both sides, and the right choir of chanters and the left; thereafter he censes passing through all the standing people, and again the Holy Doors, and only two icons—of Christ and of the Mother of God, and that upon the analogion. At the same time (during this censing) they sing the Magnification (*velichanie*), with selected verses from the Psalms of David (on Sunday thereafter—the troparia **"The assembly of the Angels,"** see Chapter 3 and September 8, if on a Sunday). After this customary singing, the Little Ektenia is said by the deacon, and the sessional hymns are sung (prior unto them—the Sunday Hypakoe), and all the clergy enter (with the beginning of the reading) into the holy altar and divest themselves of the sacred vestments, only the priest holding the weekly turn remaining in vestments for the reading of the Gospel."

Customarily the censing begins after the singing of the Magnification for the first time by the clergy.

### "The Assembly of the Angels" (*Angel'skiy sobor*)

After the Blameless or the Polyeleos there are sung the troparia **"The assembly of the Angels"** (*Angel'skiy sobor*), which stand in close connection with the Blameless. They are sung with the most characteristic verse of Psalm 118 [LXX; Masoretic 119], expressing its main thought, namely verse 12: **"Blessed art Thou, O Lord, teach me Thy statutes"** (*Blagosloven esi, Gospodi, nauchi mya opravdaniem Tvoim*). By this is replaced the appending of a troparion unto every verse of the psalm. Constituting thus one whole with this kathisma, these present troparia likewise conclude with the customary conclusion of a kathisma: **"Glory... Both now..."** subjoined unto the final two troparia, and **"Alleluia, alleluia, alleluia, glory to Thee, O God"** (thrice). The troparia are sung in the same Tone 5 in which this (17th) Kathisma is appointed to be sung. (The troparia are located in the appendices unto the Octoechos, ...the Horologion, and in the Heirmologion). They—more precisely, four of all six, the primary ones—depict the feelings experienced by the 'assembly' (*dēmos*, Gr. δῆμος) of the Angels and by the Myrrh-bearers at the time of the death and Resurrection of the Savior; the 5th glorifies the Holy Trinity, and the 6th—the Mother of God.

### History of the Troparia "The Assembly of the Angels" (*Istoriya troparey "Angel'skiy sobor"*)

The troparia **"The assembly of the Angels"** are of Jerusalem origin. In the well-known Jerusalem *Order of Passion and Paschal Week* of the 9th century according unto MS 1122, in the service of Palm Sunday there are troparia 2–6 of them, while unto the 1st the opening one is close (**"The assembly of the Angels was astonished, beholding Thee mounted upon a colt"**); the corresponding three troparia of Holy Saturday here each begin with **"The assembly of the Angels,"** and the 3rd is very close unto the present first (**"...being numbered; while Adam exulting with Eve cried aloud: I am the lost sheep, call me back, O Savior, and save me"**) [^2449]. Yet unto the Studite and Evergetis typika these troparia, apparently, are unfamiliar.

The Georgian MS of the Jerusalem Typikon in the order of the Sunday Vigil says concerning them: 'at the Blameless, three Sunday stichera of Tone 5'; the Greek MSS and printed editions: 'after (*apo*, Gr. ἀπό) the Blameless (No. 381: is said: **Blessed art Thou, O Lord**, and are sung) the Sunday troparia of Tone 5, **The assembly of the Angels**, and the rest'; the Slavic MSS: 'after the third stasis (of the Blameless), not having said **Glory... Both now...**, are said the troparia of Tone 5, **The assembly of the Angels**.' The Greek text *(Orig. p. 648)* [gives] the following variants with the Slavonic: 2—'with merciful tears'—*sympathōs* (Gr. συμπαθῶς), 'spoke unto the myrrh-bearers'; 4—'O Savior, heard (*enēchounto*, Gr. ἐνηχοῦντο) the Angel (Jerusalem Order + clearly) speaking' [^2450].

### The Little Ektenia at the Polyeleos (*Malaya ekteniya na polielee*)

After that torrent of praise and joy which the Blameless with their troparia, and especially the Polyeleos, represent, there arises the need for a prayer of supplication, refreshing likewise the attention that has been so long occupied with songs of praise. The Little Ektenia after the Polyeleos or the Blameless answers precisely this purpose. Either of these, moreover, as a kathisma must have it thereafter. The exclamation of this ektenia: **"For blessed is Thy Name, and glorified is Thy kingdom, of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit..."** (almost identical with the concluding doxology of the 8th Matins Prayer) indicates by its opening words the content of Psalm 118 [LXX; Masoretic 119] and directs the mind of the worshippers unto the consoling thought of the Kingdom of glory in harmony with (setting the tone for) the present rejoicing. From this exclamation joy fairly breathes forth, and it is so adapted unto this occasion that it is nowhere else used in the services, with the exception of Paschal Matins, at which it is appointed after Ode 8 ...of the Canon, and in an extended form—at Holy Saturday Matins after the 1st Stasis of the Blameless. Concerning this ektenia speaks only the Sluzhebnik.

### The Exclamation of the Polyeleos Ektenia in Antiquity (*Vozglas polieleynoy ektenii v drevnosti*)

In old Greek Euchologia the exclamation is: **"For blessed and glorified is Thy most honorable and majestic Name"**; in MSS of the Slavic Typikon prior unto the 15th century: **"For Thou art a God of mercy..."**; in the Slavic Sluzhebnik, Venice, 1544: 'after the 3rd Kathisma the exclamation: **"For blessed and glorified,"** after the 4th Kathisma: **"For holy and glorified art Thou"**'; in the Sluzhebnik of Peter Mohyla: the 1st after the Blameless and after the 3rd Kathisma, 'when it is read,' the 2nd 'if a Polyeleos happens on a Sunday' (consequently, a Polyeleos occurred even along with the Blameless, with an ektenia after both the one and the other); in the Moscow Sluzhebnik of 1602 (Old Believer) and 1647: 'after the Blameless: **"For blessed and glorified,"** but if there is a Polyeleos unto a saint, after the Many-Merciful: **"For Thou art our sanctification"**.' From the Moscow 1658 edition and later Greek editions, it is as today [^2451].

### The Hypakoe (*Ipakoi*)

Now, according unto the general order of kathismata, of which the Polyeleos or the Blameless is one, a sessional hymn ought to be sung. But at Sunday Matins the sessional hymn after so great a kathisma as this is replaced by a more solemn hymn—the Hypakoe (*hypakoē*, Gr. ὑπακοή). Derived from the verb *hypakouō* (Gr. ὑπακούω), to listen attentively, at times to answer, to respond, this word (which outside liturgical language is used only in the New Testament in the meaning of 'obedience') in the capacity of a liturgical term has the meaning of 'refrain.' According unto the idea of the Hypakoe, therefore, it ought to be a refrain (of the people) unto the verses of the Blameless, *(Orig. p. 649)* and, taking the place of the sessional hymn after them (or after the Polyeleos), differs from it also in that, like the 'kathisma' unto which it is subjoined, it has no permission for listening unto it sitting. On account of all this, it is also shorter than a sessional hymn. Besides Sunday Matins, it is used only on the greatest of the Twelve Great Feasts and days similar unto them (the Nativity of Christ, Theophany, Palm Sunday, Pascha, the Dormition, June 29 [Ss. Peter and Paul], Thomas Sunday, the Sunday of the Forefathers and of the Fathers), but then already after Ode 3 of the Canon. Its melody is close unto that of the sessional hymns.

### Its History (*Istoriya ego*)

In the 4th century, the chanting in response unto each verse of a psalm of any verse was called *hypēchein* (Gr. ὑπηχεῖν), *hypakouein* (Gr. ὑπακούειν), and this responsive verse was called *hypakoē* (Gr. ὑπακοή). St. Athanasius the Great speaks of psalms having as their *hypakoē* 'Alleluia'; St. John Chrysostom indicates as *hypakoai* (Gr. ὑπακοαί) unto certain psalms their verses, for example unto Psalm 117 [LXX; Masoretic 118] the verse **"This is the day."** Blessed Augustine calls such responsive singing *respondere* [^2452]. Consequently, the Hypakoe originally corresponded unto the Latin responsory, the psalm verse that accompanied a reading (from Holy Scripture or the Fathers); and the present Hypakoe always precedes a reading and is quite brief. Unto non-biblical hymns the designation 'Hypakoe' was not yet applied in the 7th century: it is not mentioned in the well-known description of the Sinaitic Matins. In the Jerusalem *Order* of the 9th–10th centuries there are our present Hypakoai of Palm Sunday and Pascha under this title [^2453]. According unto the Studite-Alexis Typikon, the Hypakoe (*upakoi*) in exceptional cases, however (though here is a trace, presumably, of an ancient general practice), was sung thus: the first time by the chanter, then by the people; the chanter chanted the psalm verse unto it, the people again the Hypakoe, and the chanter—its conclusion [^2454].

### Sunday Hypakoai (*Voskresnye ipakoi*)

The majority of the Sunday Hypakoai, namely of Tones 1–5 and 8, celebrate the visit of the life-bearing tomb by the Myrrh-bearing women—correspondingly unto the Troparia of the Blameless, unto which they so directly adjoin, and unto that hour of the night when they are sung (for which reason, besides Matins, they are sung also at the Midnight Office). The remaining ones depict the fruits of the Resurrection. Each subsequent one continues the description of the preceding. With brevity there is united here power of expression (for example, the beginning of that of Tone 1: **"The repentance of the thief plundered Paradise"**).

### According to Ancient Typika (*Po drevnim ustavam*)

The author of the Sunday Hypakoai is unknown. The earliest mention of them is in the Studite-Alexis and Evergetis typika: in both they were sung after the kathismata; in the former at times after the 1st, at times after the 2nd Kathisma; in the latter—after the 2nd [^2455]. The Georgian and Greek MSS of the Jerusalem Typikon: 'and the Hypakoe'; the earliest Slavic MSS: 'and there is sung *(Orig. p. 650)* the Hypakoe'; later ones (MS of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 678 of the 15th century) omit 'is sung.' In the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra it is read.

### The Polyeleos Reading (*Polieleynoe chtenie*)

The Hypakoe, like the sessional hymn, constitutes, properly speaking, a hymnographic introduction unto the patristic reading that follows after it, which on Sunday, as also after the kathismata, ought to have as its subject the exposition of the Gospel or Epistle of the Divine Liturgy. On Sundays with which special commemorations are joined, in place of this there is the 'reading of the feast.' The reading here, being a pause necessary for the rest of the singers and hearers in that stream of hymns which, beginning with the Polyeleos, extends unto the Gospel, constitutes the conclusion customary for psalmody.

# THE ANABATHMOI (*Stepenny*)

Psalm singing is now replaced by Christian singing imitative thereof, and the reading that concludes such singing is the greatest here. We mean the Anabathmoi (*Hymns of Degrees*) and the Gospel. The Anabathmoi (*anabathmoi*, Gr. ἀναβαθμοί), in popular parlance called antiphons on account of their manner of singing, as the title shows, constitute an imitation of Psalms 119–133 [LXX; Masoretic 120–134], inscribed **"Songs of Degrees"** (*pesni stepeney*). Such an inscription of the psalms (from the Hebrew 'ascents' [*ma'aloth*], Vulgate: *graduum*) is explained today in that these psalms were sung by festal pilgrims in Jerusalem upon ascending its heights, or by bands of those returning from the captivity (formerly the title was explained in that these psalms were sung upon the steps of the stairway from the temple Court of the Women into the Court of the Israelites—on the ground that the rabbis compared these psalms unto the 15 steps of that stairway). Under the impression of the recent calamities of the chosen people, these psalms frequently speak of the value unto the latter of Jerusalem and the temple, and inspire a feeling of steadfast hope in God, capable of sweetening the bitterness of all afflictions. It is these psalms that formed the foundation of the gradual antiphons (*stepennye antifony*). For each tone there are 3 gradual hymns (*stepenna*), with 3 antiphons in each, only for Tone 8 are there 4 gradual hymns. Each antiphon is sung twice, once by the right and once by the left choir. The Anabathmoi of Tones 5–8 are parallel (as are the tones) unto the Anabathmoi of Tones 1–4, and imitate in Tones 1 and 5 Psalms 119–121 [LXX; Masoretic 120–122], in Tones 2 and 6—122–124 [LXX; Masoretic 123–125], in Tones 3 and 7—125–127 [LXX; Masoretic 126–128], in Tones 4 and 8—128–132 [LXX; Masoretic 129–133]. They contain a prayer for the correction and purification of the soul, and express hope for this correction; since this is attained through the grace of the Holy Spirit, every 3rd verse (antiphon) is dedicated unto His glorification. More particularly, the Anabathmoi either contain a prayer unto God that He enlighten 'me' with virtue, save from passions, from the fire of sin, from the devil, or they strive to impart unto hope in God steadfastness and unto love for Him strength, describing the grace of the Church, the sweetness of the eremitic life and of prayer in the temple (which on Sunday replaced for the ancient monk the prayer of the cell—**"Concerning them that said unto me: We will go into the courts of the Lord"**).

Thus the Anabathmoi *(Orig. p. 651)* have a generally edifying (not specifically Sunday), ascetic content, just as in general into the Sunday service much generally edifying material has been introduced, in view of the fact that the Church looks upon Sunday not only as a day for the glorification of this event, but also as a day wherein the Christian, occupied the entire week with worldly cares, can reflect upon his soul. Yet even with such a content, the Anabathmoi are knit together with the commemoration of the Resurrection, reminding us of ...being buried together with Christ in order to be co-resurrected with Him (cf. the Epistle of Holy Saturday [Rom. 6:3–11]). The melody of the antiphons is more complex than the troparic and sessional melodies; in it sounds forth the triumph of victory over the passions. A special beauty is imparted unto their singing by the repetition of each verse by both choirs without refrains, excepting the final verse (in honor of the Holy Spirit), which, as concluding, has the refrain **"Glory... Both now..."**, by virtue of which the glorification of the Holy Spirit is preceded by the glorification of the Holy Trinity. The number 9 for the antiphons of each tone could have been chosen on the basis of the vision of St. Ignatius, that 9 ranks of Angels alternately chanted praise unto the Holy Trinity.

### History of the Anabathmoi (*Istoriya stepenn*)

The Anabathmoi in their style differ so much from the Damascene hymns of the Octoechos that already Nikephoros Kallistos, and following him Nicodemus the Hagiorite, considered St. Theodore the Studite to be their author [^2456], and they are inscribed with his name, apparently, in a MS of the Bodleian Library. And in content they correspond unto the entire direction of the literary activity of St. Theodore (nevertheless modern Byzantinists do not place them among his works). They are mentioned by the *Hypotyposis* at the present place of Sunday Matins [^2457]. According unto the Alexis-Studite Typikon, at festal Matins, which had neither the Blameless nor the Polyeleos, this was the most solemn part. According unto this Typikon, the Anabathmoi were sung with the verses of the Gradual Psalms: in each gradual hymn 1 antiphon without verses beforehand, then 4 verses of the psalm, with the 1st accompanied by 'Alleluia' and *nenenaika* [melismatic syllables], antiphon 2, four other verses of the psalm with the same additions unto the 1st verse, and antiphon 3 (unto the Holy Spirit) [^2458].

### The Peal for the Gospel (*Zvon k Evangeliyu*)

The Anabathmoi by their ascetic content purify and 'elevate' the soul, and thereby prepare the worshippers for the hearing of the Gospel. Concerning the impending reading of the latter, announcement is made during the singing of the Gradual Antiphons by the ringing 'on the bells' (*v kampany*), that is, a festive peal (*trezvon*). This ringing indicates that 'their sound has gone forth into all the earth'—the proclamation of the Gospel. Only the Gospel of Sunday and festal Matins has a bell-ringing before it, whereas that of the Divine Liturgy has none, because the latter often has no *(Orig. p. 652)* connection with the commemorated event and because at the Divine Liturgy a more sacred moment is marked by ringing. Practice transfers the ringing for the Matins Gospel unto the beginning of the Polyeleos [^2459]. 'And the priest and the deacon, having entered into the sanctuary, vest according unto custom'—if there were no Polyeleos, for ...which it was necessary to vest, or if the vestments were removed for the reading.

### According to Old Typika (*Po starym ustavam*)

The Georgian MS: 'the lamp-lighter rings upon the iron; the priest and the deacon vest'; the Greek: 'the lamp-lighter (*kandilaptēs*, Gr. κανδηλάπτης) departs and gives the signal upon the iron'; the ancient Slavic: 'the lamp-lighter having gone forth gives the signal upon the iron, while the priest in the altar vests (in sacred robes)'; later ones (from the 15th century): 'the paraecclesiarch having gone forth strikes upon a single bell...'; the Old Believer: '+ or upon the iron semantron' (it says nothing concerning vesting) [^2460].

# THE MATINS PROKEIMENON (*Prokimen utreni*)

A more direct preparation for the Matins Gospel than the Anabathmoi is served by the Prokeimenon. The Matins Prokeimenon always contains a glorification of the commemorated event, whereas the Vesperal Prokeimenon has no relation unto it (with a few exceptions). This, consequently, is always a festal prokeimenon. It has not such a melody as the Vesperal and Liturgical prokeimena (for which reason it is usually sung in recitative), yet being not an independent chant like the Vesperal one, but serving merely as a preparation for the Gospel, it is never sung with such solemnity as certain Vesperal prokeimena, that is, it is always sung only 2 1/2 (and not 4 1/2) times. And the exclamations before it are less complex. 'And the deacon says: **"Let us attend. Wisdom."** The canonarch then announces: **"The Prokeimenon, a Psalm of David, of Tone..."**,' that is, the canonarch pronounces: **"The Prokeimenon, a Psalm of David, Tone N."** Thus here before the prokeimenon there is no imparting of peace and no second **"Let us attend,"** because both the one and the other will take place before the Gospel. It is incomprehensible why at Matins alone it is directed to name whence the prokeimenon is taken (**"A Psalm of David"**); however, the same, apparently, is directed to be done both for the prokeimena of Lenten Vespers and for the Liturgical ones if they are taken not from the Psalter; thus, before the prokeimenon **"My soul doth magnify the Lord"** there is added 'the Canticle of the Theotokos,' and before the prokeimenon **"Blessed art Thou, O Lord God of our fathers"**—'the Canticle of the Fathers.' In the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra **"A Psalm of David"** is not proclaimed.

*(Orig. p. 653)*

### According to Ancient Typika (*Po drevnim ustavam*)

In the Greek Typikon concerning the prokeimenon there is silence (the Georgian does not even mention it); the Slavic of the 14th century: 'Deacon: **Let us attend**; Priest: **Peace be unto all**; We: **And to thy spirit**; Deacon: **Wisdom**; the chanter says: **A Psalm of David**; Deacon: **Let us attend**; the chanter sings the prokeimenon of the current tone and we sing the same, then the chanter sings the verse and we the prokeimenon, and again the chanter the prokeimenon, while we sing near the end of the prokeimenon, then the chanter sings the conclusion.' In later ones there is silence.

In the Moscow Sluzhebnik of 1602 and 1647, the Old Believer Sluzhebnik and Typikon: + **Peace be unto all** and a 2nd **Let us attend**; in the remaining Slavic and Greek ones there is silence [^2461]. Inasmuch as the prokeimenon is a remnant of the Old Testament reading, which in antiquity always preceded the New Testament ones, since it was, as it were, a chanting reading of the Psalter (Introductory Chapter, p. 162), and before a reading it was always announced ...whence it was taken, then, presumably, the same was previously always done before the prokeimenon as well.

Under Arseny Sukhanov in the East the Matins Prokeimenon was sung by the choirs thrice (entire) without any exclamations or verses [^2462].

### Sunday Matins Prokeimena (*Voskresnye prokimny utreni*)

The Prokeimenon of Sunday Vespers is likewise dedicated unto the event of Christ's Resurrection, but it does not so directly relate unto this event and speaks not concerning it with such clarity as the Matins Prokeimenon, in which for the most part there is the very concept of 'resurrection.' This is because it prepares for the Gospel of the Resurrection. In addition, from the Vesperal Prokeimenon the Matins Prokeimenon differs in that it is not one and the same for each Sunday, but changes according unto the tones. Thus, of Sunday Matins prokeimena there are 8. For them there are chosen from the Psalms preeminently those verses where there is spoken of that special, direct action of Providence which the ancient Hebrew figuratively termed the rising up, the 'arising' (Heb. *qūm*), of the Lord as if from the couch of His customary rest—a word rendered in the Septuagint by *anistēmi* (Gr. ἀνίστημι), which signifies, besides rising from a couch, also resurrection. Namely, the Sunday Matins prokeimena and their verses are taken from the following psalms:

Tone 1: **"Now will I arise, saith the Lord"**—from Psalm 11:6, 7 [LXX; Masoretic 12:5, 6].
Tone 2: **"Arise, O Lord my God, in the decree"**—Psalm 7:7, 2 [printed 8, 2; LXX 7:7, 2; Masoretic 7:6, 1].
Tone 3: **"Say among the nations that the Lord reigneth"**—Psalm 95:10, 1 [LXX; Masoretic 96:10, 1].
Tone 4: **"Arise, O Lord, help us"**—Psalm 43:27, 2 [LXX; Masoretic 44:26, 1].
Tone 5: **"Arise, O Lord my God... for Thou dost reign"**—Psalm 9:33, 2 [LXX; Masoretic 10:12, 9:2].
Tone 6: **"O Lord, stir up Thy might (that is, Christ)"**—Psalm 79:3, 2 [LXX; Masoretic 80:2, 1].
Tone 7: **"Arise, O Lord my God... forget not"**—Psalm 9:33, 2 [LXX; Masoretic 10:12, 9:2].
Tone 8: **"The Lord shall reign for ever"**—Psalm 145:10, 1 [LXX; Masoretic 146:10, 1].

The theme of the prokeimena of Tones 3 and 8 coincides with the Vesperal Prokeimenon. In Tone 8, as concluding, most appropriate is 'for ever,' as indeed in general the series of prokeimena gives a certain development of thought (Tone 1 is only the promise *(Orig. p. 654)* of the Resurrection and in general of salvation, concerning which the Lord speaks openly, 'unhesitatingly,' *parrēsiasomai*, Gr. παρρησιάσομαι). As verses unto the prokeimena, as is generally done, there are taken the opening verses of those psalms wherefrom the prokeimena are drawn (a remnant of the practice when along with the responsive singing of the prokeimenon the entire psalm was sung); the exception is the Prokeimenon of Tone 1, where a verse was chosen more suited unto the prokeimenon: **"The words of the Lord are pure words"**— ...in correspondence with **"saith the Lord."**

### Their History (*Istoriya ikh*)

In the Holy Sepulchre *Order* (*Akolouthia*) of the 9th–12th centuries, from among the present prokeimena under the title *epakouston* (Gr. ἐπακουστόν; while the vesperal and liturgical prokeimena are given under the name 'prokeimenon'), there are assigned Tones 3 and 5 (or 7) at Paschal Matins, Tone 8 at Matins of Bright Tuesday, Tone 4 on Wednesday, and Tone 7 on Thursday [^2463].

In the earliest manuscript copy of the Studite-Alexis Typikon of the 11th–12th centuries, there is a section: "Sunday Matins prokeimena before 'Let every breath,'" wherein the present prokeimena are cited, ending with Tone 5 (the section is unfinished, as are others in this manuscript [^2464]).

# THE GOSPEL (*Evangelie*)

### "For Holy Art Thou" (*Yako Svyat*)

For the hearing of the Gospel our Typikon prepares not only through chants, but also through prayers. The second mode of preparation is more essential than the first, and therefore follows after it. The prayerful preparation, like the chant preparation (the prokeimenon and "Let every breath"), has two stages, and at this first stage it is limited unto the invitation **"Let us pray to the Lord"** (*Gospodu pomolimsya*), the response **"Lord, have mercy"** (*Gospodi pomiluy*) (an as yet indefinite prayer), and the exclamation indirectly indicating our need for sanctification and to this end glorifying God Who is Holy in His saints: **"For holy art Thou, O our God, and Thou restest in the saints, and unto Thee do we send up glory, to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit..."** (*Yako Svyat esi Bozhe nash...*).

### Origin (*Vozniknovenie*)

Without doubt, here is a remnant of an earlier prayer for the worthy hearing of the Gospel; in a certain Georgian Euchologion this prayer is appointed precisely before **"Let every breath"**; it begins like our present one (**"Shine in our hearts"** [*Vozsiyay v serdtsakh nashikh*]), but has the exclamation: **"For Thou art the illumination and the sanctification..."** [^2465]. There is such a prayer also in other manuscript Sluzhebniks at this place.
*(Orig. p. 655)*

### "Let Every Breath" (*Vsyakoe dykhanie*)

Now follows the second and definitive stage of the hymnographic and prayerful preparation for the Gospel. The hymnographic part of this preparation consists in the singing, according unto the order of a prokeimenon (with a canonarch), of the verse **"Let every breath praise the Lord"** (*Vsyakoe dykhanie da khvalit Gospoda*), the final (6th) verse of the final (150th) Psalm, with its 1st verse: **"Praise God in His saints..."** (*Khvalite Boga vo svyatykh Ego...*). Serving as just as direct a preparation for the Gospel as the liturgical Alleluiarion (the prokeimenon at the Divine Liturgy serves as preparation for the Epistle, for which reason at Matins likewise it cannot be the immediate preparation for the Gospel), this verse summons all living beings unto the glorification of the Lord—a glorification that became possible and was realized only after the proclamation of the Gospel unto "every creature" (cf. the 1st Matins Gospel; cf. the verse unto the prokeimenon for the Apostles: **"The heavens declare the glory of God"** and ...the present verse: **"in the firmament of His power"**). Being the final verse of the Psalter, this verse worthily concludes the present 'psalter' division of Matins.

### History (*Istoriya*)

Historically, the precedence of this verse before the Gospel is explained by the fact that formerly the Gospel at Matins (the sung Asmatic Office) was read after the Praises (Lauds) psalms and the Great Doxology.

According unto the Studite Typikon, **"Let every breath"** was sung in the tone of the preceding prokeimenon [^2466].

The Greek manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon are silent; Slavic manuscripts of the 14th–15th centuries specify:

"After the Amen the chanter begins **'Let every breath'** in the current tone, and we sing the same in the same tone. The deacon censes only the altar. Then the chanter the verse: **'Praise God in His saints.'** And we: **'Let every breath.'** Then the chanter: **'Let every breath,'** and we: **'praise the Lord'**"; later ones: "**'Let every breath'** in the same tone."

The Old Believer: "The canonarch: **'Let every breath'** in Tone 6" [^2467].

### "And That We May Be Accounted Worthy" (*I o spodobitisya*)

The prayerful part of the present preparation for the Gospel consists in the invitation from the deacon: **"And that we may be accounted worthy to hear the holy Gospel, let us pray to the Lord"** (*I o spodobitisya nam k slyshaniyu svyatago Evangelia, Gospodu pomolimsya*) (cf. the indefinite invitation at the preceding stage) and the threefold (cf. the single one at the preceding stage) **"Lord, have mercy."** At the Divine Liturgy there is no such special supplication, because the Gospel is read with less solemnity, frequently pertains less unto the commemorated event, and is prepared for by the reading of the Epistle.

### Origin (*Vozniknovenie*)

Already the opening "And" in this exclamation of the deacon indicates that this is a fragment of a formerly more extensive supplication. Indeed, Georgian and ancient Greek manuscripts state: "The deacon (Greek: the priest) says the Little Ektenia, then proclaims: **'And that we may be accounted worthy,'**" which later Greek sources omit; but Slavic manuscripts of the 14th–15th centuries add: "Again *(Orig. p. 656)* and again; the priest the exclamation: **'For unto Thee is proper,'** deacon: **'And that we may be accounted worthy to hear worthily the holy Gospel, in peace to the Lord God let us pray'**" ...let us pray." An exclamation of the same recension is found also in Old Believer editions, but with "worthily" before "to hear," and "the Lord God" (there is no ektenia) [^2468].

### Pre-Gospel Exclamations (*Predugotovitel'nye k Evangeliyu vozglasy*)

Having implored of God help for the worthy hearing of the Gospel through so fervent and prolonged a prayer, the faithful are invited on their own part likewise to take measures toward such hearing. An invitation unto this is made to them several times, by the priest and the deacon alternately. It begins with the warning of the deacon concerning the "wisdom" hidden within the Gospel, which requires most directly a special posture of the body (**"Wisdom! Stand upright, let us hear the holy Gospel"** [*Premudrost', prosti, uslyshim svyatago Evangelia*], the genitive case, according to the Greek, governed by "let us hear"—*orthoi* [Gr. ὀρθοί], *prosti*—"upright," "erect") for the hearing thereof (most immediately *prosti* requires standing upright during the Gospel in contrast unto other readings), and then also a special disposition of soul—peace, concerning which the priest not only reminds them, but also graciously imparts it (**"Peace be unto all"** [*Mir vsem*]), while the faithful (in prayer) desire the same for him (**"And to thy spirit"**). Now the heading unto the Gospel reading is proclaimed, which is uttered as an inseparable part of the Gospel always by the one who reads the latter himself—consequently, at Matins by the priest—in the form: **"The reading from the Holy Gospel according to N"** (Gr. ἐκ τοῦ κατὰ with accusative, literally: "From the Gospel according unto N, the reading"), unto which the choir responds with a joyful glorification of the Lord: **"Glory to Thee, O Lord, glory to Thee"** (*Slava Tebe, Gospodi, slava Tebe*) (this verse is absent from the Greek Euchologion), repeated also after the reading of the Gospel. Just before the reading of the Gospel itself, the faithful are summoned unto attention by the brief **"Let us attend"** (*Vonmem*), which is pronounced by the sacred minister who is not reading the Gospel, in order to separate this exclamation from the holy words of the Gospel.

### Their History (*Istoriya ikh*)

Originally, the preparation for the Gospel consisted, presumably, only of a prayer, similar unto the present **"Shine in our hearts"**; only such a prayer is contained in the earliest manuscripts of all liturgies. But very early the Gospel began to be preceded also by exclamations similar unto the present ones; their antiquity is proved by the agreement in this regard among various recensions of liturgies, even Western ones. Thus, the Alexandrian Liturgy attributed unto the Evangelist Mark, in an 11th-century manuscript, contains such exclamations:

— "Deacon: Bless, Master. Priest: The Lord bless and strengthen [us], and make us hearers of His holy Gospel, Who is blessed God now and ever... Deacon: Stand upright (*stathete*, Gr. σταθῆτε). Let us hear the holy Gospel. Priest: Peace be unto all. People: And to thy spirit" [^2469].

In the Roman Liturgy (Mass), after the prayer *Munda cor meum* ("Cleanse my heart"), the celebrant says:

"Command, Lord, a blessing" (*Jube Domne benedicere*), "The Lord be in my heart," "The Lord be with you" (*Dominus vobiscum*), "And with thy spirit" (*Et cum spiritu tuo*), "The continuation (*Sequentia*)" or "The beginning of the holy Gospel according to (*secundum*) N," "Glory be to Thee, O Lord" (*Gloria tibi Domine*); after *(Orig. p. 657)* the Gospel: "Praise be to Thee, O Christ" (*Laus tibi Christe*), and the prayer "By the words of the Gospel" (*Per evangelica dicta*).

At Matins before the Gospel there is the verse:

"Command, master (*domne*), a blessing. Blessing: May the reading of the Gospel be our salvation and protection (*Evangelica lectio sit nobis salus et protectio*). Response: Amen. The reading of the holy Gospel according to N" [^2470].

In the Milanese (Ambrosian) Liturgy, it is as in the Roman, but before the Gospel there is in addition **"Lord, have mercy"** thrice [^2471].

In the Mozarabic Liturgy:

The celebrant: "The Lord be always with you," the choir: "And with thy spirit," "The reading of the holy Gospel according to N," "Glory be to Thee, O Lord"; after the Gospel: "Amen," "The Lord be...", "And with...", "Praise. Alleluia" [^2472].

In the Liturgy of the Apostle James according unto a 10th-century manuscript:

"Stand upright, let us hear the holy Gospel. Peace be unto all. From N. Let us attend." In the 11th century: "Stand upright, let us hear... Peace be unto all. Let us attend unto the holy reading"; after the Gospel: "Peace be unto thee. Glory to Thee, O Lord." In the 14th century: "Let us attend unto the holy reading. Peace be unto all. Stand upright, let us hear the holy Gospel"; after the Gospel: as in the 11th century [^2473].

In manuscripts of the Liturgies of Basil and Chrysostom prior unto the 16th century, for the most part only a prayer is indicated; from the 16th century, it is as at present, ...yet seldom **"Glory to Thee, O Lord, glory to Thee"** before the Gospel, and still more seldom after it [^2474].

### Typikon for the Reading of the Matins Gospel (*Ustav chteniya utrennego Evangelia*)

The Gospel at Matins is read not by the deacon, as at the Divine Liturgy, but by the priest, in view of the fact that he should "first nourish with the divine word those whom at the Divine Liturgy he will nourish with the mystical Bread," as Christ also did, and as He commanded the Apostles to do ("Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them..."—Matt. 28:19) [^2475]. The priest at the Divine Liturgy has higher functions than the reading even of the Gospel. Moreover, at Sunday *(Orig. p. 658)* Matins the Gospel is more important than the liturgical one, because it directly relates unto the event of the Resurrection (in such a relationship stand the Matins and Liturgical Gospels also of certain other feasts, for example the Nativity of Christ; cf. Pascha). In view of this, the Matins Gospel is read in the altar upon the Holy Table, whereas the liturgical one is read in the center of the temple upon an analogion. This is especially fitting for Sunday Matins, because the Holy Table symbolizes the Tomb of the Savior.

### Historical Note (*Istoricheskaya spravka*)

The Gospel at Sunday Matins in the order of the Asmatic Office as well, at least according unto Symeon of Thessalonica and manuscripts of the 14th–15th centuries, was read by the priest, but upon the ambo; in ancient Western monasteries—by the abbot (Introductory Chapter, pp. 347, 310). According unto certain 16th-century manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon, it was read in the midst of the temple [^2476].

### The Sunday Matins Gospels (*Voskresnye utrennie Evangelia*)

The narrative of all four Evangelists concerning the Resurrection of the Savior is divided for reading at Sunday Matins into 11 pericopes (*zachalos*), presumably because into such a number of parts this narrative naturally falls; perhaps the "eleven" Apostles were kept in view as the closest witnesses of the Resurrection. From the series of Gospels there is omitted only the account of the Evangelist Matthew that most circumstantially describes the very moment of the Resurrection, and is therefore reserved for Pascha (for the Liturgy of its Eve [Holy Saturday]). Thus, all the Gospel readings speak rather of the appearances of the risen Savior than of the Resurrection itself. The cycle of Sunday Gospels, called the 'pillar' (*stolp*), is repeated approximately six times in the course of ...the year: the 1st pillar begins on the Sunday of All Saints, the 2nd after the Feast of Elijah, the 3rd after the Exaltation [of the Holy Cross], the 4th during the Nativity Fast, the 5th after Theophany, and the 6th during the Great Fast (Lent). Tables of these pillars, indicating with which tone each Gospel coincides, are placed in the Liturgical Gospel Book, the Octoechos, and Chapter 54 of the Typikon. For the Sundays of the Pentecostarion (Flowery Triodion), the Matins Gospels follow in a special order.

### History (*Istoriya*)

The Sunday Matins Gospels in their present composition are already contained in manuscripts of the Liturgical Gospel of the 8th century, for example the Greek manuscript of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 42, XLIII, 11, fols. 241–246 [^2477]. Mention of the rotation of the 11 Sunday Gospels exists in the Studite Typikon of the 11th century, the Evergetis, and in Georgian and Greek manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon [^2478]. At Roman Sunday Matins there is a Gospel not relating unto the Resurrection. According unto the Typikon of the Great Church in the Asmatic Office, the Gospel at Sunday Matins was read after the Great Doxology (Introductory Chapter, p. 347), but according unto the Studite *(Orig. p. 659)* and others—at its present place; in the earliest recensions of the Studite Typikon, however, perhaps after Ode 6 of the Canon [^2479]. According unto the present Typikon of the Great Church of Constantinople—after Ode 8 of the Canon [^2480].

# FROM THE GOSPEL UNTO THE CANON (*Ot Evangelia do kanona*)

### "Having Beheld the Resurrection of Christ" (*Voskresenie Khristovo*)

With the reading of the Gospel, the festal joy of the worshippers reaches its zenith and pours forth no longer in merely Sunday hymns, but in purely Paschal chants. After the Gospel there are appointed at Sunday Matins two hymnographic compositions from the service of Pascha: **"Having beheld the Resurrection of Christ"** (*Voskresenie Khristovo videvshe*) and **"Jesus having risen from the grave"** (*Voskres Iisus ot groba*). True, of the Paschal hymns these are the most restrained in joy: they are of Tone 6, a tone which in its troparic and canonic melodies is the most mournful, and in its sticheraric melody, in which these present hymns are sung, is a tone of quiet joy, barely liberated from beneath grief.

In content as well, the hymn **"Having beheld the Resurrection of Christ,"** beginning with words highly appropriate unto the moment (during the reading of the Gospel the faithful have spiritually beheld the Risen One with the Apostles), dwells rather upon the counterpart of the Resurrection—the Crucifixion. The hymn does not so much exult over the Resurrection (cf. the Paschal Canon and **"A Pascha sacred and worthy of all honour"**) as it meditates in concentrated fashion upon the significance of the event for Christ (it revealed His Divinity and sinlessness) and for us (it brought joy unto the world, destroying death), being thus of dogmatic content, and invites unto the glorification of the event (having in view the long series of subsequent hymns in its honour: the Canon). At the same time, this is the largest of the Paschal hymns and the most complete and comprehensive, for which reason it replaces throughout Bright Week all introductory psalms. It consists of seven strophes, bound together not so much grammatically as by unity of thought; each of these strophes could be (and perhaps was) an independent chant (cf. **"O Gladsome Radiance,"** above, p. 558), just as one of the strophes serves as such an independent chant (**"Thy Cross do we adore, O Master..."** [*Krestu Tvoemu poklanyaemsya...*]).

### Ancient Use (*Drevnee upotreblenie*)

Of the antiquity of the hymn **"Having beheld the Resurrection of Christ"** testifies the presence of a similar text in the Latin Church at the Liturgy of Great (Good) Friday: **"Thy Cross do we adore, O Lord, and Thy holy Resurrection do we praise and glorify: for behold, by the wood of the Cross joy is come into the whole world"** (*Crucem tuam adoramus, Domine, et sanctam resurrectionem tuam laudamus et glorificamus...*) [^2481]. The hymn **"Having beheld the Resurrection of Christ"** is mentioned in the well-known 9th-century Jerusalem Paschal *Order* (*Akolouthia*) not only as a Paschal chant, but also as an ordinary ...Sunday *(Orig. p. 660)* chant after the Gospel: on Palm Sunday there is appointed here, in place of **"Having beheld the Resurrection of Christ,"** a special parodic (that is, patterned upon it) hymn [^2482]. — The hymn **"Having beheld the Resurrection of Christ"** bears a distinctly Jerusalem coloration, having in view, presumably, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre (the *Anastasis*—**"let us worship the holy Resurrection of Christ"**) and the Cross behind it (the frequent mention of the Cross). Yet even the earliest manuscripts of the Studite Typikon contain it at Sunday Matins, although immediately after the Gospel there was here a prokeimenon: **"In the nights lift up your hands"** with the verse: **"The Lord bless thee out of Zion"** [^2483] (Psalm 133:2, 3 [LXX; Masoretic 134:2, 3]).

— Under Arseny Sukhanov in the East, this hymn "they recited divided between both choirs line by line," as also Psalm 50 with its concluding refrains (**"Glory... Both now... Through the prayers of the Apostles... Have mercy on me, O God... Jesus having risen from the grave..."**), making six such strophes in the hymn [^2484]. Did not its strophes originally serve as troparia unto the verses of Psalm 50? According unto the present Greek Euchologion, **"Having beheld the Resurrection of Christ"** is "recited by the superior or appointed monk"; according unto the Hieratikon—by the hierarch or by a priest standing in the choir [^2485].

### Psalm 50 (*50-y psalom*)

The Psalter portion of Matins is already drawing toward its very end, and it requires here the most powerful and at the same time most expressive chord, most naturally in the form of one of the psalms with which this entire central part of the most important of the daily services is filled. Hardly could a more felicitous choice have been made, therefore, than placing Psalm 50 [LXX; Masoretic 51, *Miserere*] here. No psalm was written under such exceptional and harrowing circumstances as this; none answers more than this unto the fundamental disposition of a Christian—repentance (**"Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand"**) [^2486]—nor expresses it with such power. And the contrast in which it stands unto the preceding prolonged jubilation further heightens this impression: it is, as it were, a skull brought into a festive banquet.

### Manner of Execution (*Sposob ispolneniya*)
