In the manner of executing Psalm 50 at Matins, the Typikon, apparently, makes no distinction from **"Having beheld the Resurrection of Christ"**: "Thereafter (after the Gospel) we say **'Having beheld the Resurrection of Christ'** and Psalm 50." Moreover, this hymn, as well as the refrains **"Glory... Through the prayers of the Apostles..."** and so forth, as well as the hymn **"Jesus having risen from the grave,"** having as its refrain the 1st verse of the psalm, stand in such close connection with it that ...it is most natural to chant it as well, and of course, in the tone of these hymns surrounding it, that is, Tone 6, the tone of grief and repentance. The chanting, as for other chanted psalms, ought to be antiphonal, by verses between the two choirs.
*(Orig. p. 661)*

### Its Constant Use at Matins (*Vsegdashnee upotreblenie ego na utrene*)

Already under St. Basil the Great, Psalm 50 constituted an essential, concluding part of Matins (Introductory Chapter, p. 148). In the earliest recensions of the Typikon of the Great Church of Constantinople, this is the most important, and likewise the second, part of Matins (ibid., p. 340). The earliest manuscript copies of the Studite Typikon (the *Hypotyposis* and *Diatyposis*) did not cancel it even for Paschal Matins. Almost all non-Orthodox morning offices also possess it: the Abyssinian, Maronite, Nestorian, and ancient Latin; the Armenian and the present Latin have it only on weekdays (the latter at Lauds—ibid., pp. 299–319), but at the First Hour there is always a series of verses from this psalm [^2487].

According unto the Typikon of the Great Church of Constantinople, it was sung at Matins with the refrain of a troparion unto the verses—either one or several (ibid., p. 340).

Greek manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon express themselves concerning Psalm 50: "it is said"; certain Slavic manuscripts of the 14th century concerning **"Having beheld the Resurrection of Christ"** and **"Glory..."** specify "it is recited," "in Tone 6" (concerning the second), concerning Psalm 50 are silent, and concerning **"Jesus having risen"**—"we chant" [^2488].

According unto the *Diataxis* (*Order*) of Patriarch Philotheus: "Psalm 50 with singing" [^2489].

Under Arseny Sukhanov in the East, the psalm, like **"Having beheld the Resurrection of Christ,"** "they recite divided between both choirs line by line," making 18 such lines in the psalm (the verses in it being 19), while on weekdays "the psalm-reader recites it" [^2490].

According unto the present Greek Euchologion, the brethren chant it melodically; according unto the Hieratikon—the choirs chant it [^2491].

In the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra it is read.

### Refrains unto Psalm 50 (*Pripevy k 50-mu psalmu*)

The mournful character of this psalm for Sunday Matins is sufficiently softened by the Sunday, and indeed directly Paschal, hymns surrounding it (**"Having beheld the Resurrection of Christ"** and **"Jesus having risen from the grave"**), which according unto the concept ought to serve as refrains unto each of its verses. At the same time, it too, bursting with its penitential tone into the most luminous part of the Vigil, tempers its joy. In order to soften the transition from the grief of this psalm unto the joy of the hymn that immediately follows, **"Jesus having risen from the grave,"** which returns this cycle of hymns unto their beginning ...(**"Having beheld the Resurrection of Christ"**), the refrains unto the concluding doxology of the psalm are not Sunday verses, but a prayerful turning in the spirit of the psalm in thought unto the foremost witnesses of the Resurrection and partakers of its joy—the Apostles and the Theotokos [^2492]: **"Glory: Through the prayers of the Apostles, O Merciful One, cleanse the multitude of our transgressions"**; **"Both now: Through the prayers of the Theotokos..."** The refrain unto the 1st verse of the psalm repeated here is the troparion in Tone 6: **"Jesus having risen from the grave..."** (*Voskres Iisus ot groba...*), which, with power in its conciseness and a certain victoriousness in its expressions and melody (an *idiomelon* in Tone 6), depicts both the external and the internal aspects of the commemorated event.
*(Orig. p. 662)*

### Their History (*Istoriya ikh*)

The present execution of Psalm 50 is the most integral remnant of the ancient manner of chanting for every psalm, when it was required to conclude each psalm with a doxology unto the Holy Trinity and to append a refrain unto every verse (Introductory Chapter, p. 157).

According unto Canon 12 of the Fourth Council of Toledo (633): "at the end of all the psalms we say: Glory and honor to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit unto ages of ages" (cf. Introductory Chapter, p. 217). Such is the practice even now in Roman Catholic worship [^2493].

As regards the appending of troparia as refrains unto the verses of the psalms, in the Typikon of the Great Church of Constantinople such refrains were especially customary for Psalm 50 (Introductory Chapter, p. 340). The hymn **"Jesus having risen"** is not mentioned in the 9th-century Jerusalem *Order* (*Akolouthia*) alongside **"Having beheld the Resurrection of Christ."**

In Slavic manuscript Typika of the 14th century, after **"Jesus having risen"**: "**Glory.** Standing in the temple of Thy glory, O Lord, we seem to stand in the heavens. **Both now.** O Virgin Theotokos, heavenly portal, open unto us the doors of Thy mercy" [^2494].

The Old Believer Typikon: "For the sake of the prayers... have mercy on us, O God my Savior"; in **"Having risen"**—"life and peace" [^2495].

In the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra: **"Through the prayers of the holy Apostles..."**, **"Through the prayers of the Most Holy Theotokos..."**

### The Veneration of the Gospel (*Tselovanie Evangelia*)

During Psalm 50 and the hymns surrounding it, the veneration (kissing) of the Gospel takes place. This is a powerful and at the same time childishly simple expression of joy, when one kisses even an inanimate object that has brought us joy. But the Holy Gospel is not merely such an object: it represents ...in itself, as does also the Cross, the Lord Himself, by its carrying out from the sanctuary as from the tomb signifying His appearance after the Resurrection. Therefore the kissing of the Gospel, as also veneration paid unto it, "passes to the Prototype" and serves as a greeting of the Savior upon His Resurrection. However, here too joy does not exceed bounds nor rise unto the boundlessness of Paschal joy, which expresses itself also in the mutual kissing among the faithful.

### Origin of the Custom (*Vozniknovenie obychaya*)

According unto the Sinai Kanonarion of the 9th–10th centuries, at Paschal Matins after the reading of the Gospel the priest brings out the latter unto the people and greets them; all kiss one another [^2496]. According unto a certain 13th-century Triodion at Paschal Matins it is indicated: "and they kiss the Holy Gospel, and the ektenia and dismissal" [^2497]; consequently, the Paschal greeting (*christosovanie*) here was reduced unto the veneration of the Gospel, as is now done at ordinary Sunday Matins.
*(Orig. p. 663)*

### The Order of Veneration (*Chin tselovaniya*)

The Typikon sets forth in detail the order for the veneration of the Gospel. The Gospel is brought out through the Holy Doors (as a sign of the glorification of Christ, whereas at entrances it is brought through the north door as a sign of humiliation—as are likewise the Cross and the Plashchanytsia [shroud]) by the priest, and not by the deacon; as at entrances, in an unloosed phelonion (see above, p. 551), the priest holding the Gospel at his breast (the deacon, as subordinate, holds it higher—before his face), as a sign of love for Christ. The priest is preceded, as at all entrances, by two candlesticks with candles. The priest halts in the midst of the church; the candlesticks are placed at his sides so that, burning before the Gospel, they do not hinder the kissing thereof. Unto the Gospel there first approaches the superior—in contrast unto the rest of the brethren, who approach in pairs—alone, and makes two bows before the Gospel prior to kissing it and one afterward: not prostrations to the ground, the Typikon notes parenthetically, but small bows (metanias), bowing the head so far as to touch the ground with the hand, because on Sunday, on Despotic feasts, and throughout the entire Pentecostarion knees are not bent (Canon 20 of the First Ecumenical Council is meant). After the veneration of the Gospel, the superior makes a slight bow ("a semblance of a bow") first toward the left choir, because he himself stands on the right side and can bow toward the right choir "as he departs unto his place." After the superior, the brethren approach the Gospel in pairs ("two by two") according unto seniority ("by rank") ...and bow before the Gospel just as the superior does, and in place of bows toward the choirs they make a bow toward the superior. The Typikon presumes the veneration to conclude together with Psalm 50: the chanting of the entire psalm would provide sufficient time for this.

### Development of the Order (*Razvitie china*)

Georgian and early Greek manuscripts merely mention the kissing (*aspasmos*, Gr. ἀσπασμός) of the Gospel. Later Greek manuscripts specify:

"While it (Psalm 50) is being recited, they kiss the Gospel: first the superior alone, making bows (a bow?) before it as it is held by the priest standing upon the *omphalion* [^2498]; then the brethren by rank, two by two, they likewise making in similar fashion bows (a bow?) before the kissing, and another after the kissing, and one toward each of the two choirs. And after this, when the priest has blessed the people with the Gospel, there is said... Save, O God" [^2499].

Slavic manuscripts of the 14th century specify:

"And after the kissing of the Gospel the priest or deacon censes the Gospel and both choirs" [^2500].

According unto the *Order* (*Diataxis*) of Patriarch Philotheus and the present Greek Euchologion:

"The priest, having lowered his phelonion and bearing the Holy Gospel before his breast, goes forth and halts in the midst of the church, and the reader or *eutaxios* (see above, p. 492, note 1) stands at his right, holding a candlestick with an arranged lamp, and there takes place the kissing of the Holy Gospel by the brethren according unto custom; *(Orig. p. 664)* on other feasts, however, there is no kissing, but only on Sunday" [^2501].

According unto certain manuscript Typika of the 16th century the Gospel was placed upon an analogion [^2502].

According unto certain 16th-century monuments, prior unto the kissing they made a prostration to the ground with the prayer:

"With fear and love do we draw near unto Thee, O Christ, and we believe Thy words: with fear on account of sin, and with love for the sake of salvation"; after the kissing, the prayer: "We believe, O Lord, in the Holy Gospel; O Christ God, help us and save ...our souls" [^2503].

Other manuscript Typika of the 15th and 16th centuries do not provide an order for the veneration.

— The Sluzhebnik of Peter Mohyla agrees with our Typikon regarding the bringing forth of the Gospel, but concerning the veneration states: "according unto custom."

The Moscow Sluzhebnik of 1602 (= Old Believer) and of 1647:

"First the hegumen alone kisses the Gospel, making 2 metanias to the waist before the Gospel while the Gospel is held by the priest standing before the Holy Doors, the deacon standing with a candle at the priest's side; and after kissing it he makes 1 bow to the waist, and toward each choir he casts one prostration to the ground"; concerning the brethren, as at present, but with the addition: "if there be no superior, the brethren likewise make one bow toward each choir" [^2504].

The Old Believer Typikon:

"First the hegumen alone kisses the Gospel, having made a metania before the Gospel while the Gospel is held by the priest standing before the Holy Doors, and thereafter the brethren two by two, they likewise making one bow before the kissing and only one bow after the kissing, and one toward each choir—and after the kissing he blesses" [^2505].

According unto the Hieratikon:

After the Gospel the hierarch, if he is present, blesses the people with the Cross during the singing of *Eis polla* [Gr. Εἰς πολλὰ ἔτη]; when the choirs in chanting Psalm 50 reach the verse **"For behold, Thou hast loved truth..."** (*Se bo istinu vozlyubil...*), the priest carries out the Gospel unto the middle of the temple and presents it for veneration unto the hierarch or the present priest, and in order unto all the people, and then places it upon the *proskynetarion* [Gr. προσκυνητάριον] and enters the sanctuary; moreover, during the kissing of the Gospel by the hierarch the 1st choir sings *Eis polla*, the 2nd sings the specified verse slowly, and the hierarch blesses the people with his right hand [^2505].

### "Save, O God" (*Spasi Bozhe*)

Every psalm or group of psalms must have following it a prayer in the form of an ektenia or another form. Psalm 50, ...in accordance with its exceptional position at this part of Matins, likewise has following it a prayer in a distinctive form—that of a truncated litiya ektenia. Such a prayer, so fitting also unto this place in Matins—the conclusion (cf. at Vespers) of one of its parts—is the prayer **"Save, O God, Thy people"** (*Spasi, Bozhe, lyudi Tvoya*), which, like an ektenia, is proclaimed by the deacon "at the customary place" and has a priestly exclamation. Unto this brief "litiya" the response, naturally, is not "Lord, have mercy" dozens of times, but only 12 times. And the exclamation here (**"Through the mercy and compassions and love for mankind..."** [*Milostiyu i shchedrotami i chelovekolyubiem...*]), more so than in simpler ektenias, appeals unto the mercy of God, designating the latter—*(Orig. p. 665)* like the exclamation at the most sacred part of the Divine Liturgy (after the Our Father)—by three synonyms (only here with "mercy," whereas there, in view of the Mystery being accomplished, with "grace"), and naming the Persons of the Holy Trinity with special distinctness. The prayer, as well as the exclamation, boldly addresses God the Father directly in the Name of His Son.

### According unto Ancient Typika (*Po starym ustavam*)

In place of the prayer **"Save, O God,"** certain 16th-century Georgian manuscript Euchologia appoint after the Gospel and Psalm 50 an entire ektenia (a remnant of the most ancient practice).

Thus, the Euchologion of the Tiflis Church Museum No. 450 indicates here the following ektenia:

"In peace let us pray to the Lord. For the mercy shown unto us, let us pray to the Lord. That every transgression, voluntary and involuntary, may be forgiven us. For those who rise early for Matins, who chant and give glory. Protect us. Commemorating our Most Holy... Exclamation: Through the mercy..." The Euchologion of the Imperial Public Library No. 208: "In peace let us pray to the Lord. For the peace from on high. For the peace of the whole world. For this holy temple. That the Lord God may have mercy upon us. That we may be delivered. And for all. Protect us. Commemorating our Most Holy... Through the mercy and compassions" [^2506].

The ektenias are of a penitential character, corresponding unto Psalm 50 and the litiya prayers. In the first of the named Euchologia there is a section: "Festal ektenias proclaimed at Matins after the reading of the Gospel"; each petition in these ektenias is prefaced by a glorification of God for the celebrated event—for instance, at the Nativity of Christ: "O Christ God, born of the Virgin"; they are appointed for 12 feasts that do not coincide with our Twelve Great Feasts [^2507].

The Georgian manuscripts appoint the prayer **"Save, O God"** to be proclaimed by ...the deacon; Greek manuscripts unto the priest, later ones among them specifying: "within the sanctuary or before the Holy Doors"; Slavic manuscripts of the 14th century—unto the priest or deacon before the Holy Doors, later ones—unto the priest; the *Order* (*Diataxis*) of Patriarch Philotheus: "the deacon in the customary place with a loud voice."

The Moscow Sluzhebnik of 1602 and 1647: "the deacon having stood before the Holy Doors (1602 adds: with a loud voice)—if there be no deacon, the priest himself says it, standing before the Holy Table"; the Sluzhebnik of Peter Mohyla: "the deacon upon the ambo"; the Moscow Sluzhebnik of 1658 and the Old Believer Typikon: "the deacon." The present Greek Euchologion appoints the deacon; the Hieratikon—the priest, adding: "The choirs: Lord, have mercy 12 times by threes."

Slavic Typika of the 14th century: *Kyrie eleison* [^2508].

# THE KANON (*Kanon*)

With the Kanon begins—or rather, the Kanon constitutes—the third of the four parts of Matins, completely different in character from the other parts, especially from the preceding second part. As that part consisted primarily *(Orig. p. 666)* of psalms, so this part does not have a single psalm, but consists of the so-called "Biblical Odes" (*bibleyskie pesni*), the verses of which are alternated with hymns of later Christian composition; whereas hymns of the latter kind in other parts of Matins occupy very little space in comparison with the biblical material (the psalms), here they are allotted a more prominent position, so that the Biblical Odes appear rather as something appended unto them. Nevertheless, the Biblical Odes regulate, by the number of their verses, the quantity of hymns of later composition, and also determine in a certain measure their very content, serving for them, consequently, as a rule, a model, a norm—whence also the name of this part of Matins: "Kanon" (*kanon*, Gr. κανών). The chant melody of the kanon in complexity is intermediate between the sticheraric and the troparic.

### The Word "Kanon" and Its Present Application (*Slovo "kanon" i ego nastoyashchee primenenie*)

*Kanōn* [Gr. κανών] (perhaps cognate with *kanna* [Gr. κάννα], a reed)—strictly speaking, is a straight stick, entering, for example, into the construction of shields, weaving looms (such use of the word is found in Homer), or scales (Pollux), serving for measuring (Sophocles); hence a measure (Euripides), a rule (Lycurgus), a prescription (Demosthenes); among ecclesiastical writers: a rule in general (Clement of Rome), the rule of faith (Clement of Alexandria), a rule of the Church (Council of Ancyra), a canon of a Council (Basil the Great), of the Fathers (Socrates, Sozomen), the collection of divinely inspired books (Athanasius the Great); and finally: a church service, an office (Basil the Great, Evagrius, Palladius), more precisely—the total quantity of psalms that a monk was required to chant in a twenty-four-hour period (whence the designation of Typika as Kanonaria) [^2509], in particular—Matins (John Moschos), or the Vigil (Dorotheus). With its present liturgical meaning, the word emerges firmly only from the 9th century, first appearing, apparently, in Theodore the Studite [^2510]. It could have acquired such a narrow meaning both because the kanon constituted a significant, central part of Matins, and also because this is a genre of church hymnody possessing the most strictly sustained and definite literary form.

### The Biblical Odes of the Kanon (*Bibleyskie pesni kanona*)

The foundation of the kanon, its principal part (with the exception of a few kanons), is composed of the Biblical Odes (*ôdai*, Gr. ᾠδαί). These are songs chanted by Old Testament prophets and righteous ones on the occasion of the greatest events in their lives and in that of all Israel. Being, therefore, outpourings of the highest religious inspiration, they constitute the finest portion, the flower of biblical poetry, and may be placed higher than the psalms. Of such odes there are 11 recorded in the Bible: two of Moses, those of Deborah, Hannah, Habakkuk, Isaiah, Hezekiah, Jonah, the Three Holy Children, Zacharias, and the Mother of God. But from among them there did not enter into the composition of the kanon the Ode of Deborah (Judges 5), on account of its martial character and the specialized nature of its content, and the purely personal prayer of Hezekiah (Isaiah 38:11–20). The 9 odes taken as the foundation of the kanon yielded *(Orig. p. 667)* also the 9 odes of the kanon, according unto the number of the 9 Angelic ranks; yet from the Ode of the Three Holy Children two were made, while the two New Testament odes were united into a single 9th ode of the kanon. By the content of each Biblical Ode there is determined the theme and its unfolding throughout the non-biblical composition of each ode of the kanon, not to mention that its verses are always appended as refrains unto the troparia of the Matins kanon (with the exception of Matins of Holy Week and Bright Week). Therefore this content is of the most essential significance in the kanon. Here it is in brief:

In the First Ode of Moses (Exodus 15:1–19), **"Let us sing unto the Lord"** (*Poim Gospodevi*, Heb. "I will sing"), there is glorified the victoriousness of the Lord (in comparison with the military weakness of Israel) against Pharaoh, the obstinacy of the enemy and his overthrow, from which the conclusion is drawn that the God of Israel is higher than all gods, and His present great work must produce an overwhelming impression upon all nations.

In the Second "Rebuking" Ode of Moses (Deuteronomy 32:1–43), **"Attend, O heaven, and I will speak"** (*Vonmi, nebo, i vozglagolyu*), after the glorification of the Lord for His righteousness, there are depicted His benefactions unto Israel—in their election, the Exodus from Egypt, and their establishment in the Promised Land; the unfaithfulness of the people and the terrible punishments impending on account of it, which are to end, however, not in the destruction of the people, but in mercy, in vengeance upon all the enemies of God and of His people, and in the cleansing of the land and people of God, all of which will demonstrate the unity of the true and almighty God.

The Ode of Hannah (1 Samuel [1 Kingdoms] 2:1–11), **"My heart is established in the Lord"** (*Utverdisya serdtse moe v Gospode*), entirely breathing joy at the granting unto her of a son, depicts the sweetness of unwavering hope in the One Holy God, against Whom as it is useless to contend, so it is beneficial to place trust in Him, since He does all things in the world according unto His will, is almighty, endures no self-exaltation in man, judges the earth righteously, and will strengthen the (future) anointed ones— ...the kings of Israel.

The Ode of the Prophet Habakkuk (3:1–19), **"O Lord, I have heard Thy report"** (*Gospodi, uslyshakh slukh Tvoy*), depicts the impending appearance of the Lord ("revive Thy work in the midst of the years," LXX: "in the midst of two living creatures shalt Thou be known," according unto certain Fathers: between the two testaments) for judgment upon the oppressors of the chosen people (the Chaldeans), like unto the Theophany at Sinai and the wonders of the Exodus ("God shall come from the south," Heb. Teman—southern Idumaea; according unto the Fathers—from Bethlehem; "and the Holy One from the mountain overshadowed by the forest," Heb. "from Mount Paran"; according unto the Fathers—Zion), an appearance destined to be accompanied by terrible elemental upheavals and tribulations, which will serve as punishment for the ungodly and therefore ought not to dismay one who firmly trusts in God.

The Ode of the Prophet Isaiah (Chapter 26), from which the greater part is taken for the kanon, verses 9–19, beginning with the words **"From night my spirit awaketh early"** (*Ot noshchi utrenyuet dukh moy*), chants the future longed-for land of the righteous, from which all the ungodly will be removed and upon which there will take place what is impossible according unto natural laws: the dead, who generally do not return to life, after certain spiritual labors of the righteous people resembling the pangs of childbirth, will revive from the dew of God (in Hebrew only "thy dead") unto the joy of all born of earth.

The Ode of the Prophet Jonah (2:3–10 [LXX; Masoretic 2:2–9]), **"I cried in my affliction unto the Lord"** (*Vozopikh v skorbi moey ko Gospodu*), sung as if from the tomb by one buried alive, progressively depicts all the horrors of the prophet's plight: first externally—the deep of the waters, then internally—the proximity of death; moreover, along with the deepening of the colors in this description, there ever grows *(Orig. p. 668)* the prophet's hope of deliverance, which in the 3rd part of the ode supplants all other thoughts.

The Ode of the Three Holy Children (Daniel 3:26–88 [LXX; Greek additions]), **"Blessed art Thou, O Lord God of our fathers"** (*Blagosloven esi, Gospodi Bozhe otets nashikh*), which is not found in the Hebrew Bible, in its first and larger part, used as the 7th Ode of the kanon (vv. 26–56), glorifies the God of the fathers for the righteous punishment of His people with captivity and entreats mercy and deliverance for the sake of the covenant with the forefathers; thereafter (following an insertion of a narrative character concerning how the furnace was heated ever more fiercely and how an Angel descended into it, an insertion likewise not omitted in the 7th Ode of the kanon) it glorifies the Lord as the God of the fathers, glorified in His temple and in the heavens. The second, smaller part of the ode (vv. 67–88), **"Bless the Lord, all ye works of the Lord"** (*Blagoslovite, vsya dela Gospodnya*), serving as the 8th Ode of the kanon, invites all His "works" unto the glorification of the Lord, beginning with the Angels and descending, as along a ladder, through the diverse spheres of creation, down unto human beings and Israel in its various classes.

The Canticle of the Most Holy Theotokos (Luke 1:46–55), **"My soul doth magnify the Lord"** (*Velichit dusha moya Gospoda*), joyfully from the depths of her soul glorifies the Lord because in her ...low estate He granted unto her worldwide majesty, as the Holy One Who hath ever shown mercy unto them that fear Him, casting down the proud (perhaps Herod is borne in mind) even from thrones and exalting (unto them) the humble, enriching the hungry and depriving the rich of all things; moreover, this mercy is not unto her alone personally, but unto all Israel, according unto the promise made unto the patriarchs. It is remarkable how the canticle moves entirely within the circle of Old Testament conceptions (being close unto the Ode of Hannah) and speaks the language of the sacred books with the highest poetic inspiration.

The Canticle of Zacharias (Luke 1:68–79), **"Blessed be the Lord God of Israel"** (*Blagosloven Gospod' Bog Izrailev*), glorifies God for granting salvation unto His people in the house of David, according unto the prediction of the prophets and the covenant with the fathers, which salvation will consist in deliverance from enemies and the righteous service of the people unto God—as a consequence of the activity of the Forerunner and the "Dayspring from on high."

The Odes are arranged in the kanon approximately in chronological order; only the Ode of Habakkuk has been transposed with the Ode of Jonah, perhaps in order to take a more moving biblical ode for the 6th Ode of the kanon as concluding that division. At the same time, one cannot fail to notice that joyful odes have occupied the odd positions, while mournful ones have occupied the even positions (cf. the Six Psalms), with the exception of Odes 7 and 8, where for this principle it would have been necessary to place the end of the ode before its beginning.

### History of Use (*Istoriya upotrebleniya*)

In the Old Testament Temple, at the additional (festal) sacrifice on the Sabbath, the rebuking Ode of Moses was chanted—apparently one-sixth of it in turn—while at the evening sacrifice Exodus 15 was chanted, verses 1–10 and 11–19 in turn [^2511].

A monument dating probably from the 3rd century, the *Testament of Our Lord Jesus Christ* (*Testamentum Domini Nostri Jesu Christi*), indicates at Matins an ode of Moses and one from the Prophets, four songs in all together with a psalm (Introductory Chapter, p. 86).

Hilary of Poitiers (4th century) mentions the Biblical Odes *(Orig. p. 669)* [^2512]. According unto Verecundus (4th century), in the African Church they were chanted with the same tone and melody (*sono cantuque*) as the psalms, and from among them there were used the following: the 2 odes of Moses, Deborah, Jeremiah: **"Remember, O Lord"**, Azariah, Hezekiah: **"I said in the midst of my days"**, Habakkuk, Manasseh, and Jonah [^2513]. But especially customary was the Ode of the Three Holy Children: it is indicated for Matins by the 4th-century work of Pseudo-Athanasius *On Virginity* (*De virginitate*) [^2514]; it alone also enters into the composition of the ancient sung Asmatic Matins (Introductory Chapter, p. 346).

In the well-known description of Sinai Matins of the 7th century there are indicated at it the "Odes of Moses" (that is, the Biblical Odes, just as all psalms are called "of David") and, undoubtedly, all 9 current ones (ibid., p. 295).

In the Greek Psalter of the Imperial Public Library from the collection of Bishop Porphyrius of 862, after the kathismata, alongside the most important songs and prayers, the Biblical Odes are placed; 1–7 are designated *ôdai* [Gr. ᾠδαί], the 8th *hymnos* [Gr. ὕμνος], 9, 10, and 11 (the Theotokos, Zacharias, and Simeon the God-receiver)—*euchai* [Gr. εὐχαί] [^2515].

Among non-Chalcedonian traditions, Coptic Matins has no Biblical Odes; Nestorian has only the 2 Odes of Moses; the Abyssinian (Ethiopian) has the Odes of Moses, the 3 Holy Children, and Simeon the God-receiver [^2515].

Armenian Matins (properly speaking, the Midnight Office) has the Odes of the 3 Holy Children, the Theotokos, and Zacharias; among the Armenians there is also one ode each at the Third Hour, Vespers, and the "Service before Sleep" (after Compline), the latter having portions of the Odes of Habakkuk, the 3 Holy Children, and Simeon the God-receiver. Among the Maronites: Matins has 7 odes, Vespers 4, the Hours 3 or 2, Compline 2. Among Western rites, the Roman rite already under St. Benedict had at the concluding, most important part of Matins (Lauds) in turn (beginning from Sunday): the Odes of the 3 Holy Children, Isaiah (from ch. 12), Hezekiah, Hannah, Moses 1, Habakkuk, Moses 2 (the Theotokos—at Vespers); the Ambrosian rite—Zacharias or Moses 2, Moses 1, the Three Holy Children (only on Sundays and feasts); the Mozarabic rite—one ode in turn, but differently from the Roman (Introductory Chapter, pp. 299–303, 315–318).

### Manner of Execution (*Sposob ispolneniya*)

The Biblical Odes in the kanon are used in three scopes: in their entirety in Great Lent (though not all daily), in an abbreviated form on weekdays, and in an even more abbreviated form on Sundays, feasts, forefeasts, afterfeasts, and on Saturdays. In the first and second cases, the Biblical Ode is first chanted by verses alternately by the two choirs without refrains until there remains a sufficient number of verses unto which the heirmos and troparia of the kanons are to be appended as refrains (usually 12 such verses are needed, or 14 with "Glory" and "Both now"; sometimes in Lent only 2); in the last case, the entire ode is chanted with the troparia of the kanon appended as refrains. To judge the degree of abbreviation of the odes for weekday and festal use, one must compare the number *(Orig. p. 670)* of verses of each of them in its complete form, in which the ode is used in Great Lent, with the number of verses in its abbreviated forms. At the same time, it must be noted that the division of the odes into verses for liturgical use for the most part does not correspond unto their division into verses in the Bible: long ...biblical verses are broken into two or more parts.

Ode 1 in the Bible: 19 vv.; in Lent: 19; on weekdays: 12; festal: 10.  
Ode 2 in the Bible: 43 vv.; in Lent: 65.  
Ode 3 in the Bible: 11 vv.; in Lent: 16; on weekdays: 12; festal: 10.  
Ode 4 in the Bible: 19 vv.; in Lent: 30; on weekdays: 12; festal: 10.  
Ode 5 in the Bible: 11 vv.; in Lent: 15; on weekdays: 12; festal: 10.  
Ode 6 in the Bible: 8 vv.; in Lent: 11; on weekdays: 10; festal: 10.  
Ode 7 in the Bible: 31 vv.; in Lent: 34; on weekdays: 12; festal: 10.  
Ode 8 in the Bible: 22 vv.; in Lent: 20; on weekdays: 12; festal: 10.  
Ode 9 of the Theotokos in the Bible: 10 vv.; in divine worship: 8.  
Ode of Zacharias in the Bible: 12 vv.; in Lent: 12; on weekdays: 10; festal: 10.

The abbreviation is carried out in such a way that from the ode those verses are omitted that are less poetic and whose absence does not disrupt the flow of discourse nor disturb the principal thought; for example, from Ode 1 there are omitted—for weekday use: "His chosen horsemen, captain-commanders, He drowned in the Red Sea"—a thought already contained in the preceding verse: "His host hath He cast into the sea"; or the verse: "Thy right hand, O Lord, is glorified in strength..."—a general thought; for festal use there are omitted the verses: "The waters grew thick as a wall... the enemy said: I will pursue, I will overtake..."—on account of the detailed description of the event. From Ode 5 only 1 1/2 verses are omitted; from Ode 6—1 verse. The first verse is never omitted, nor likewise the last, by reason of which the ode preserves also its external structure.

The weekday execution of the Biblical Odes bears the title **"Let us sing unto the Lord"** (*Gospodevi poim*), and the festal **"We sing unto the Lord"** (*Poim Gospodevi*) (see Chapter 18 of the Typikon). The odes in the indicated three scopes are placed in the Heirmologion; in the Followed Psalter, however, only in the Lenten scope. Unto the Heirmologion the chapter of the Typikon under examination likewise refers: "and after the Amen (unto the exclamation: Through the mercy and compassions) we begin the heirmos of the Sunday kanon... And unto the 1st troparion the refrain: Glory, O Lord, to Thy holy resurrection. Then the refrains of the Sunday odes (written in the Heirmologion)."

### Manner of Execution in Antiquity (*Sposob ispolneniya v drevnosti*)

In the ancient Western Church also, the Biblical Odes were chanted with a more solemn melody than the psalms [^2516]. One may think that originally the Biblical Odes were chanted with a short refrain unto each verse, and such a manner of chanting them was not abandoned even when kanons appeared: prior unto the heirmos or troparia the entire ode was chanted with this refrain, and the troparia were chanted either without refrains, or with special refrains not taken from the ode, or, finally, with the repetition of the concluding verses of the ode as refrains. A trace of such ...execution at present is Ode 2 and the Canticle of the Theotokos, as also the manner of chanting the kanon in *(Orig. p. 671)* Holy Week and Bright Week (the services of which have preserved the greatest number of traces of ancient practice) [^2517]. Traces of ancient responsorial refrains unto the Biblical Odes are preserved in certain Greek and Slavic manuscripts (of the Moscow Synodal Library), which also indicate "antiphons" unto the psalms, identical with those in the "Kanon of Antiphons of the Psalms of the Great Church of God" of the 6th-century Monophysite pseudo-patriarch Anthimus of Constantinople. These refrains are: for Ode 1 none is indicated; for Ode 2: "Glory to Thee, O God"; 3: "Have mercy on me, O Lord"; 4: "Hear me, O Lord"; 5 and 6: "Show bounty unto me, O Lord"; 7 and 8: "Be merciful unto me, O Lord"; 9 and 10: "Blessed art Thou, O Lord" [^2518].

Later, in the Studite Typikon, refrains (*otpely*) were composed for the odes, distinctive for each in accordance with its content. They are indicated, for instance, in the Horologion of the Sophia Library at the St. Petersburg Theological Academy of the 13th century, No. 1052; some of them—namely, for some reason only the refrains of Odes 2, 4, and 7—are indicated by the most important manuscript of the Studite Typikon of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 330/380 (with the note that Ode 2 is chanted on Tuesday, if "God is the Lord" does not occur, Ode 4 on Thursday, and Ode 7 on Saturday); these refrains coincide with the verses placed in the present Followed Psalter as epigraphs unto the odes (with the exception of Ode 2):
1. **"Let us sing unto the Lord, for He is gloriously glorified"** (*Gospodevi poim, slavno bo proslavisya*).
2. (vv. 1–14): **"Glory to Thee, O God"** (*Slava Tebe, Bozhe*); (vv. 15–22a): **"Preserve me, O Lord"** (*Sokhrani mya, Gospodi*); (vv. 22b–39): **"Righteous art Thou, O Lord"** (*Praveden esi, Gospodi*); (vv. 39b–43): **"Glory to Thee, O God"** (*Slava Tebe, Bozhe*).
3. **"Holy art Thou, O Lord, and my spirit praiseth Thee"** (*Svyat esi, Gospodi, i poet Tya dukh moy*).
4. **"Glory to Thy power, O Lord"** (*Slava sile Tvoey, Gospodi*).
5. **"O Lord our God, give us peace"** (*Gospodi Bozhe, mir dazhd' nam*).
6. **"As Thou didst save the prophet Jonah, save us, O Lord"** (*Yako proroka Ionu spasi mya [nas, Gospodi]*).
7. **"O God of our fathers, blessed art Thou"** (*Otets nashikh Bozhe, blagosloven esi*).
8. **"Praise the Lord, all ye works, and exalt Him unto all ages"** (*Gospoda poyte, dela, i prevoznosite vo vsya veki*).
9. "Praise of the Holy Theotokos; if according to the order of Tone 1: **All generations call thee blessed** (and further refrains for the 8 tones) (**We magnify the Theotokos in songs**)" [^2519].

In the Studite Typikon, apparently, the verses of the odes were appended as refrains unto each heirmos and troparion of the kanon (concerning August 14: "they appoint the verses according to the number of verses of the kanons"), so even on great feasts; consequently, there was no difference between *Gospodevi poim* and *Poim Gospodevi* [^2520], for which purpose all the odes, with the exception of the long ones—Odes 2, 4, and 7—were divided, it must be, into 14 verses, while these latter odes, it must be, were abbreviated for feasts, as is shown by the above-cited note concerning Odes 2, 4, and 7 of the Studite-Alexian Typikon, and were chanted in their entirety on weekdays (Ode 2 on Tuesday, etc.).

According unto the Evergetis Typikon on great feasts: "we say not *Gospodevi poim*, but the heirmos twice"; but if they occur on ...Sunday: "we say *Gospodevi poim* and appoint 16 (verses from?): **Thy right hand, O Lord, is glorified**", *(Orig. p. 672)* on an ordinary Sunday: "we appoint always 14: **The waters grew thick as a wall**" [^2521]. **"Poim Gospodevi"**, thus, is an innovation of the Jerusalem Typikon, and that from its earliest redactions; thus, a Georgian manuscript notes concerning the Sunday kanon: "in place of *Poim Gospodevi* (?) we say the heirmos" [^2522]; Greek manuscripts and printed editions of the Typikon: "we say not *Gospodevi poim*, but the heirmos"; Slavic manuscripts of the 14th century: "we appoint 14 verses and with the heirmos from: **He sent His Spirit and the sea covered them**—the odes however we say not"; later manuscripts (15th c.): "the chant however (still later, 16th c.: the odes however; Old Believer Typikon: of the odes however) we say not *Gospodevi poem*, but immediately the heirmos" [^2523].

In a manuscript likewise of the 14th century, but of a later redaction, there already appears the present chapter on *Gospodevi poim* [^2524].

In the time of Arseny Sukhanov in Greece there was already the present abbreviation of the odes, but identical for feasts and weekdays (such as is now for feasts) [^2525], and thence, it must be, it was introduced into our Heirmologion.

### Refrains (*Pripevy*)

Almost universal practice, at least in Russia, replaces the verses of the Biblical Odes, with the exception of Great Lent, with special refrains unto the kanon; thus, unto the Sunday kanon there is used the refrain: **"Glory, O Lord, to Thy holy resurrection"** (*Slava, Gospodi, svyatomu voskreseniyu Tvoemu*); unto the Cross-Resurrection kanon: **"Glory, O Lord, to Thy Precious Cross and resurrection"** (*Slava, Gospodi, Krestu Tvoemu chestnomu i voskreseniyu*); unto the Theotokos kanon and the Theotokia in the first two kanons: **"Most Holy Theotokos, save us"** (*Presvyataya Bogoroditse, spasi nas*); unto the kanons of the saints from the Menaion: "Holy [rank and name], pray to God for us" (*Svyaty... moli Boga o nas*).

Notwithstanding the wide dissemination of such a practice, it is difficult to find any justification for it. Is any refrain possible better than such verses, for example, of the Biblical Odes: **"The dead shall rise and they that are in the tombs shall awake, and they that are on the earth shall be glad"** (Isa. 26:19), or: **"And let my life ascend out of corruption unto Thee, O Lord my God"** (Jonah 2:7), or, finally, all the verses of the 8th Ode with the concluding refrain in each: **"Praise the Lord and exalt Him unto all ages"** (Dan. 3:57ff.)?

Moreover, non-biblical refrains divide the kanon into very unequal parts, owing unto the fact that in a single kanon there occur two or three identical refrains (and the third is a Theotokion). Finally, it is not always possible to compose a rhythmic refrain; in general, since the liturgical books scarcely appoint refrains (they appoint them occasionally only for the kanons of Compline), there is opened here a wide field for the arbitrariness of each reader and for uncalled-for ...creativity. But in view of the fact that the practice of refrains is exceedingly ancient and widespread, and there is little hope for an early triumph in this domain of the requirements of the Typikon, we shall indicate here the refrains sanctified by the liturgical *(Orig. p. 673)* books themselves and provide several directives concerning their composition. (Where the verses of the Biblical Odes are appended unto the kanons, these directives will be suitable for Molebens).

Besides the cited refrains of the Sunday and Theotokos kanons (the second is indicated by the Octoechos for Compline, see Chapter 1, Sunday), the liturgical books provide also the following refrains: **"Christ is risen from the dead"** (*Khristos voskrese iz mertvykh*); **"Glory to Thee, our God, glory to Thee"** (*Slava Tebe, Bozhe nash, slava Tebe*) (Holy Week, see Triodion and Typikon, Compline of Palm Sunday); **"O Most Holy Trinity, our God, glory to Thee"** (*Presvyataya Troitse, Bozhe nash, slava Tebe*) (Sunday Midnight Office, see Octoechos Tone 1, Sunday); **"Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me"** (*Pomiluy mya, Bozhe, pomiluy mya*) (see Triodion and Typikon, Compline of Monday of the 1st week of Lent); **"Venerable fathers, pray to God for us"** (*Prepodobnii ottsy, molite Boga o nas*) (see Triodion and Typikon, Cheesefare Saturday); **"Venerable father Andrew, pray to God for us"** (*Prepodobne otche Andree, moli Boga o nas*); **"Venerable mother Mary, pray to God for us"** (*Prepodobnaya mati Marie, moli Boga o nas*) (Triodion, Compline of Wednesday of the 1st week of Lent); **"Holy Hieromartyr Euthymius, pray to God for us"** (*Svyashchennomucheniche Evfimie, moli Boga o nas*) (December 26).

These models demonstrate that a refrain ought to consist of 2 strophes of approximately equal length, as for example:

*Venerable father Andrew,*  
*Pray to God for us.*

By such a rule one ought to be guided in the composition of refrains. Consequently, in the case of two or more saints it is no longer necessary to name them. In like manner one ought not to encumber the first strophe with the addition unto the saint's name of his epithets, not only such as are indifferent unto his glory, as "Tyro" (= recruit), "warrior", "gardener", but even honorary ones: "the Great", "the Theologian", "Chrysostom", "Wonderworker". Nor are multiple designations of the saint's sanctity required—that is, alongside "venerable" to place also "holy", for which reason one does not say "holy hieromartyr N", but simply "hieromartyr".

On this foundation the following refrains may be permissible for the diverse choirs of saints: "Holy Archangels and Angels, pray to God for us"; "Holy Apostle N, pray to God for us"; "Holy Apostles, pray..."; "Holy Prophet N, pray..."; "Holy Prophets, pray..."; "Holy Martyr N, pray..."; "Holy Virgin-Martyr N, pray..."; "Holy Martyrs, pray..."; "Holy Hieromartyr N, pray..."; "Holy Venerable-Martyr N, pray..."; "Holy Hierarch father N, pray..."; "Holy Fathers, pray..." (unto several hierarchs); "Holy Venerable father N, pray..."; "Holy Venerable mother N ...pray..."; "Holy Venerable fathers, pray..."; "Holy Righteous N, pray..."; "Holy Righteous [woman] N, pray...". The composition of refrains for certain saints presents great difficulties (more than two strophes are required). Thus, for example, unto John the Baptist ("Holy Prophet and Forerunner of the Lord John, pray..."); unto Equals-to-the-Apostles ("Holy Equals-to-the-Apostles N and N, pray..."); unto princes ("Holy right-believing Prince N, pray...").

The register of these refrains may be supplemented further by the following: for Feasts of the Lord, their forefeasts and afterfeasts: **"Glory to Thee, our God, glory to Thee"**; for Feasts of the Theotokos: **"Most Holy Theotokos, save us"**; for Lenten kanons of the Triodion: **"Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me"** (excluding the 1st and 3rd Sundays of Lent, where there is **"Glory to Thee, our God, glory to Thee"**).
*(Orig. p. 674)*

### Antiquity of the Practice (*Davnost' praktiki*)

When the custom of replacing the verses of the Biblical Odes in the kanon with other refrains arose may be judged from the fact that in 16th-century monuments these refrains are already indicated. Thus, for example, in certain 16th-century Typika for the Nativity kanon there is indicated the refrain **"Glory, O Lord, to Thy Nativity"**, for the Theophany—**"...to Thy Theophany"** [^2526]. In a certain 17th-century Typikon there are sections: "On the refrains in the Octoechos on weekdays, how to speak them in the kanon" and "Rubric on the refrains in the kanons unto the saints" [^2527].

It is not surprising that among the Old Believers also they are accepted. In the *Short Practical Typikon* of the Old Believer Bishop Arseny, refrains are indicated with the following variations from those recommended above: "Glory, O Lord, to Thy resurrection"; "Glory, O Lord, to Thy Cross and resurrection"; "Most Holy Lady Theotokos, save us"; "Glory, O Lord, to Thy Precious Cross" (Exaltation and 3rd Sunday of Lent); "Glory, O Lord, to Thy Ascension, Transfiguration, Nativity, Theophany, Meeting" (in afterfeasts this or "Glory to Thee, our God, glory to Thee"); unto the Guardian Angel: "Holy Angel of Christ (or + my Guardian), save me, thy sinful servant"; "Holy and great John, Forerunner of the Lord, pray..." (January 7, August 29, and at the Findings: + "Baptist"); in refrains unto saints the naming of two and three is permitted; with two, the dual number is also used, but the plural is recommended: "Holy glorious supreme Apostles Peter and Paul, pray..."; "Holy glorious Apostle and Evangelist John the Theologian, pray..."; unto a prophet one may add "+ glorious"; "holy great martyr", "venerable father", "holy right-believing" or "passion-bearing prince" [^2528].

In the time of Arseny Sukhanov in the East the Sunday refrain was: **"Glory to the holy resurrection, O Lord"** or **"Glory, O Lord, to Thy ...resurrection"** [^2529].

# THE HEIRMOS AND TROPARIA (*Irmos i tropari*)

More than the Biblical Odes, the significant portion of the kanon in terms of volume is constituted by the hymns of later composition—the heirmos and troparia.

The heirmos (*heirmos*, Gr. εἱρμός, link, chain), as its very name indicates, its position at the head of the troparia, and its customary content, serves as a link between the Biblical Odes, which have no relation unto the commemorated event, and the troparia, dedicated exclusively unto the latter. The heirmos accomplishes this by discovering an analogy between the event sung in the Biblical Ode and that being celebrated, paraphrasing the ode in accordance with this—that is, it sings the particular commemoration in adaptation unto the content of the Biblical Ode, as far as possible in its very words.

At the same time it serves as a model both in melody and in rhythmic structure for the troparia: in the troparion there must be as many *(Orig. p. 675)* strophes and of the same length and as many musical lines as in the heirmos.

As regards the quantity of heirmos and troparia, by the very idea of the heirmos there ought to be one for each ode of a single kanon; the quantity of troparia, however, is determined by the number of verses in the Biblical Ode that may serve as refrains unto the troparion. Since these odes are of diverse lengths, as the norm for the quantity of troparia there were taken the shortest odes—those of Jonah and Zacharias, each yielding 13 verses; on account of the oddness of this number, inconvenient in antiphonal chanting, as the normative number for the troparia, including the heirmos in their number, there was taken the number 14, since the number of verses in each ode is augmented by the two parts of the minor doxology obligatory at the end of each ode, as also at the end of each psalm (see above, p. 661): "Glory" and "Both now".

This normal quantity of troparia with the heirmos is maintained on the majority of days of the year—on all ordinary weekdays, on Sundays, and on the majority of feasts. Only on the greatest feasts is this quantity increased unto 16, and under special circumstances reduced unto 12, 10, and even 6 and 4 (the latter two cases not at Matins).

But very rarely does this entire series of troparia constitute a single kanon: as a consequence of the confluence on almost every day of the year of several commemorations, this number is divided among several kanons, in which case there falls unto the share of each 8, 6, 4, 3, or 2 troparia (sometimes with the heirmos). Thus, the entire kanon at Matins may be for 16, 14, 12, and 10 (only on Great Thursday), and the kanons entering into its composition individually for 8, 6, 4, 3, and 2. A peculiarity in ...the structure of the kanon is also that Ode 2 is usually omitted in it, except on Tuesday of Great Lent and certain Saturdays connected with Great Lent; this is done on account of the profound sorrowfulness and wrathfulness of this ode, and also, perhaps, because of mankind's perpetual unfavorable view of the number 2.

### History (*Istoriya*)

The earliest writer of kanons, and consequently the founder of this genre of church hymnody, might be recognized as St. Sophronius, Patriarch of Jerusalem (7th c.), and the original form of the kanon might be considered the triodion (Introductory Chapter, p. 331), had not the view been expressed at present, with considerable foundation, that the triodia attributed unto St. Sophronius belong unto St. Joseph the Hymnographer (9th c.) [^2530].

However, refrains in the form of troparia unto the Biblical Odes are already indicated by the well-known description of the Sinai Matins of the 6th–7th centuries (Introductory Chapter, p. 295); it is remarkable that in this description the refrains unto Ode 8 stand out from the rest, although they bear the identical name of "troparia"; it is possible that the refrains unto the remaining odes had the form of the above-indicated (p. 671) short and uniform verses for each ode (for Ode 1 **"Let us sing unto the Lord, for He is gloriously glorified"**, for Ode 2 **"Glory to Thee, O God"**, for Ode 3 **"Holy art Thou, O Lord, and my spirit praiseth Thee"**, etc.), and only for Ode 8 were in honor of the commemorated event (cf. the significance that *(Orig. p. 676)* the Ode of the 3 Holy Children has at sung Asmatic Matins—Introductory Chapter, p. 346); if so, then the original form of the kanon was the single-ode kanon (*monoodion*).

The *monoodion* gradually grew into a two-ode kanon (*diodion*) through the appending of Ode 9 unto Ode 8: a certain 9th-century Georgian Menaion on the majority of days of the year has *diodia* of Odes 8 and 9, providing full kanons only on the greatest feasts and *triodia* for the Triodion period [^2531].

In addition unto Odes 8 and 9, they gradually began to append troparia unto the daily ode of the day: on Monday unto Ode 1, etc.; thus arose the *triodion*, which, like the *diodion*, was for a time, it must be, the exclusive form of the kanon; a trace of such practice is the present *triodia* at Compline in the forefeasts of the Nativity of Christ, Theophany, and especially the Transfiguration. A peculiarity of this period in the development of the kanon was the small number of troparia in each ode of the kanon (the aforementioned Georgian manuscript has 2–3 of them) and the absence of heirmos.

The first to begin writing large and full kanons was, it must be, St. Andrew of Crete. As his Great Kanon demonstrates, he, apparently, strived to make the quantity of troparia for ...each Biblical Ode correspond unto its length. He also, it must be, introduced the heirmos; it is remarkable that his heirmos are very close unto the Biblical Odes, often being a paraphrase of them. Ode 2 at that time was not excluded from the kanon (as is shown by the Great Kanon, where it is preserved for all four days, as also by his triodia for Great Saturday), nor likewise under John of Damascus [^2532].

The later exclusion of Ode 2 from the kanon was caused, perhaps, by the circumstance that when the heirmos diverged from the Biblical Odes, the poets found it difficult to give the heirmos of Ode 2 a celebratory or festive character, or did not consider it proper to introduce into a joyful feast the sorrowful and menacing motifs of this ode. Moreover, the acrostic—a frequent literary device in Greek kanons (e.g. from the acrostic *Klēmentos* [Gr. Κλήμεντος] there resulted the meaningless *Kēmentos* [Gr. Κήμεντος]) [^2533]—demonstrates that already St. Cosmas wrote no troparia for Ode 2; perhaps unto the latter belongs the initiative of its exclusion from the kanon.

In view of the fact that the odes from antiquity were used, like the psalms, with the addition at the end of "Glory" and "Both now", for a long time in the kanon a Trinity strophe (*Triadikon*) and a Theotokion (*Theotokion*) were considered obligatory; so in all the kanons of Andrew of Crete; in the time of John of Damascus only the Theotokion is already considered obligatory, and his kanons even of the great Despotic feasts originally possessed them; they were omitted by later editors. Cosmas here also introduced an innovation, beginning frequently to write kanons without Theotokia.

A great difference is observed between Andrew of Crete, on the one hand, and John of Damascus and Cosmas, on the other, in the volume of their kanons: in the latter they are many times shorter, and for great commemorations are limited unto two or three troparia. This was, it must be, in order to afford space for the compositions of other creators or for the purpose of antiphonal repetition.

In the 9th century, when the Triodion through the activity of St. Theodore the Studite and his brother Joseph, and the Octoechos and Menaion through St. Theophanes and Joseph the Hymnographer, were brought unto their present form—through the composition of kanons for the vast majority of ordinary days—there was fully developed also the present customary type of kanon with 4–6 troparia, which volume became established *(Orig. p. 677)* in view of the perpetual necessity of combining several kanons on a single day.

Significant importance was not yet attached unto the quantity of troparia in the kanon in the 9th century, as is shown by the indifference toward this in the *Hypotyposis*. But already the *Diatyposis*, and especially complete copies of the Typika—Studite, Evergetis, and Jerusalem, consequently from the 10th–11th centuries—perhaps in view of the extraordinary increase in this genre of liturgical literature and the necessity here of some regulation, began to measure the importance of a feast by the number of troparia in the kanon and the doubling of the heirmos and troparia, whereupon almost immediately in this regard there were established the present norms for the quantity of troparia in the kanon (see Introductory Chapter, p. 367).

# THE KANON OF SUNDAY MATINS (*Kanon voskresnoy utreni*)

The kanon of Sunday Matins, in regard unto its heirmos and troparia, consists of 4 parts and is usually composed of 4 kanons: the Sunday Resurrection kanon, the Cross-Resurrection kanon, the Theotokos kanon, and the daily Menaion kanon, of which only the first is with an heirmos.

In this manner, unto the celebrated event only half of the kanon is dedicated, since the Theotokos kanon glorifies the Mother of God without relation unto the Resurrection (in contrast, for example, unto certain Theotokia at "God is the Lord").

The reason for such duality in the composition of the Sunday Matins kanon is that on a simple Sunday, recurring so frequently, the soul of the worshiper cannot be so filled with the celebrated event as on an annual feast in honor of an event (such a view of the character of the celebration of the Lord's Day was expressed already in the 3rd century by Origen—see Introductory Chapter, p. 112). With these intentions even the second kanon in honor of the Resurrection is dedicated not unto this event exclusively, but together unto the Crucifixion of the Savior, whereby joy concerning the Resurrection is tempered.

In the following—Theotokos—kanon the diverting of the mind from the celebrated event, necessary for its refreshment, goes still further: the content of this kanon has with the celebrated event, the Resurrection, only that connection that there is glorified the foremost participant therein (in like manner as a separate kanon unto the Theotokos is appointed at Matins of Wednesday and Friday).

Finally, the 4th kanon leaves the Resurrection altogether and occupies itself with the other commemoration of that day.

Being sung directly only by the first of the 4 kanons, the event of the Resurrection does not occupy that kanon entirely either: of its four strophes (3 troparia and the heirmos) only the two middle ones speak of the Resurrection; likewise of the 3 strophes of the Cross-Resurrection kanon.

The most prominent part of the kanon is its heirmos, which opens the kanon. The heirmos of the Sunday kanon likewise has no relation unto the celebrated event. But it must be observed that the heirmos of other feasts rarely have such a relation; thus, for example, of the heirmos of the Nativity of Christ only half (of the first kanon) directly glorify the event; of the 8 heirmos of the Meeting only 2 do so; of the 16 heirmos of the Transfiguration—1; as regards the kanons unto saints, only the heirmos unto Gregory the Theologian on January 25 glorify him directly.

Consequently, in this regard *(Orig. p. 678)* Sunday yields only unto the greatest feasts. But not setting for themselves the goal of glorifying a single event, even so great a one, the heirmos of the Sunday kanon receive instead all the richer and more diverse content, striving to embrace all the spiritual needs and to touch all the cords of the worshiper's heart. The heirmoi of a laudatory character in the Sunday kanon almost alternate in each tone with heirmoi of a prayerful, sorrowful character. At the same time, the former strive to encompass the entire system of Christian doctrine, speaking first of the creation of the world (for the most part the 3rd heirmos, because the 1st develops the theme of its Biblical Ode), of the Incarnation of the Son of God (for the most part the 4th, sometimes the 4th and 5th, sometimes also the 3rd), of the Church (the 3rd or 4th heirmos); making use of the motifs of the Odes of Isaiah and Jonah, they depict the striving of the soul toward the light of Christ (the 5th heirmos) and supplication for deliverance from the abyss of sin and suffering (the 6th heirmos). Speaking of all this, the heirmoi of the Sunday kanon do not lose sight of their Biblical Ode, with which they must connect the troparia following them, and they express their relationship unto it, if not by direct references (in the 4th heirmos the Prophet Habakkuk is frequently mentioned, in the 6th—Jonah), then by the manner of expression: in the 3rd heirmos the expressions "be established" [*utverdisya*] are frequent; in the 5th—"enlightenment" [*prosveshchenie*], "light" [*svet*]; in the 6th—"abyss" [*bezdna*], "sea" [*more*], "surging" [*volnenie*]. The 1st, 7th, and 8th heirmoi, however, are not limited unto such a distant connection with the Biblical Odes, but occupy themselves entirely with the theme of these odes in view of the exalted prototypical significance of the events celebrated therein. The 9th heirmos, moreover, not only in the Sunday kanon but in almost all kanons, is dedicated exclusively unto the glorification of the Mother of God.

As regards the troparia, in the first kanon—the Resurrection kanon (*anastasimos* [Gr. ἀναστάσιμος])—they occupy themselves not so much with a picturesque description of the event as with explaining its meaning, uncovering its inner essence; the Theotokia of this kanon, however, are of general content—glorifying the Mother of God without reference unto the event of the Resurrection (in contrast unto the Theotokia of the Paschal kanon). The Cross-Resurrection kanon (*stauroanastasimos* [Gr. σταυροαναστάσιμος]), glorifying the Resurrection of the Savior, so to speak, through the prism of His suffering, compensates thereby for the impossibility for many to hear the services of Wednesday and Friday, which are specifically dedicated unto the latter commemoration—an impossibility that applied not only unto laymen, but also unto hermits; the Theotokia of this kanon are likewise of general content. The Theotokos kanon of Sunday Matins, although, like the Theotokia troparia of the two preceding kanons, it glorifies Her entirely without reference unto the event of the Resurrection, nevertheless differs essentially from the corresponding kanons at Matins of Wednesday and Friday and at all Small Complines in that it possesses not a sorrowful-penitential character, but a joyful-laudatory one, and is directed toward an equally detailed explanation of the significance for us of the mystery of the Incarnation of Christ, just as the two preceding kanons explain the mysteries of the Resurrection and death, whereby the comprehensiveness of Christian edification from the kanon is attained.

*(Orig. p. 679)*
### Time of Origin

The first Sunday kanons undoubtedly belong unto John of Damascus. Judging from the fact that the oldest copy of the Alexis-Studite Typikon makes no mention of the Cross-Resurrection kanon and apparently presupposes only a single Sunday kanon [^2534], one may think that the Cross-Resurrection kanons are of later origin than the former. Nevertheless, they are mentioned under the name of the second Sunday kanon, or at least presupposed, by later (from the 13th century) manuscripts of the Alexis-Studite Typikon. All manuscripts of the Studite Typikon and the Evergetis do not know the Theotokos kanon; it is mentioned only by manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon, beginning from the oldest [^2535]. The manuscripts of the Octoechos, at least the Slavic ones, present significant variations among themselves and with the present Octoechos (corrected in the 17th century according unto Greek printed editions) in the composition of the troparia of all three kanons of Sunday Matins: most frequently different troparia or a different number of them (compared with the present Octoechos) appear in the Theotokos kanon, which some Octoechoi (*Parakletika*) of the 14th–15th centuries lack altogether; there is less difference in the Cross-Resurrection kanon, and least of all in the Sunday kanon, but even here the Theotokia are often different, and at times troparia of the present Cross-Resurrection kanon are found in the Sunday kanon, and vice versa. Not infrequently there are different heirmoi in the Cross-Resurrection and Theotokos kanons [^2536].

### Unto How Many Stanzas for Each Kanon?

In accordance with the degree of proximity of the various kanons of Sunday Matins unto the celebrated event, the volume in which they are chanted is determined—that is, the number of troparia in them, or according unto the technical expression: *unto* (*eis* [Gr. εἰς]) how many (verses) they are chanted. The first kanon, the Sunday kanon, at ordinary Sunday Matins unencumbered by any concurrences, is chanted unto 4, including the heirmos, which is chanted once; the Cross-Resurrection kanon is chanted unto 3, the Theotokos kanon unto 3, and that of the Menaion unto 4; the three latter kanons are without heirmoi. Here it is understood of itself that if for such a number there are insufficient troparia in the Octoechos, as sometimes happens with the Cross-Resurrection and Theotokos kanons, then it is necessary to double the first troparion [^2537] (the first, as the most important). This is the standard order for combining kanons at Sunday Matins. Yet it is applicable in rare cases, since for the most part the Menaion—which, however, is not even always chanted on Sunday—has more than one kanon, most frequently two, or has a kanon unto more than 4. Cases of the latter kind are provided for in subsequent chapters of the Typikon—3, 4, and 5 [^2538]. Nowhere in the Typikon is *(Orig. p. 680)* provision made for the most frequent case, when there are two kanons in the Menaion; since two kanons have 8 troparia, it is most natural in this case to be guided by the rubric for a great (vigil) saint falling on Sunday and having a kanon unto 8; according unto this rubric, given in Chapter 3 of the Typikon, the Sunday kanon is chanted unto 4, the Cross-Resurrection kanon is omitted, the Theotokos kanon is chanted unto 2, and the Menaion unto 8. Such a rubric is likewise given for this case by the "Brief Explanation" [*izʺyavleniem vkrattsē*] printed at the beginning of the General Menaion.

### According unto Ancient Typika

The Studite Typika do not specify in what quantity the one or two Sunday kanons then in use were chanted, nor the kanon of the Menaion, which according unto these Typika was likewise chanted alongside the Sunday kanons [^2539].

The Evergetis: "The 1st Sunday kanon unto 6, the 2nd unto 4, and the saint unto 4; if it be a great saint, both Sunday kanons unto 4 and the saint unto 6" [^2540].

The Jerusalem Typikon: the Georgian manuscript does not define the quantity; the Greek manuscripts and printed editions likewise do not, but add: "If the saint of the Menaion is celebrated, the Cross-Resurrection kanon of the Octoechos is omitted; and at the kanon of the saint we appoint 6 verses from **'Until Thy people pass over'**" (*Dondeže proidut lyudie Tvoi*).

The oldest Slavic manuscripts: "The Sunday kanon with heirmos unto 4, and the Cross-Resurrection without heirmos unto 4, and the Theotokos unto 2, and unto the saint in the Menaion unto 4"; later ones—of the 15th and 16th centuries: "Two Sunday kanons, and of the Theotokos, and of the saint," without definition of the quantity, as in the Greek ones; "if the Typikon appoints unto the saint unto 6, then we chant the Sunday kanon with heirmos unto 4, and the Cross-Resurrection unto 2, and the Theotokos unto 2 (later, 15th cent.: the Sunday unto 4 and the Theotokos unto 4) and the saint unto 6 (in still later, 16th cent.—there is nothing concerning a saint unto six); but when in the Menaion it is unto the saint unto 8, the Cross-Resurrection is omitted, and the Theotokos is unto 2, and the saint unto 8 (later: if the saint who is in the Menaion is celebrated, we omit the Cross-Resurrection kanon which is in the Octoechos, and chant the Sunday kanon unto 4, and the Theotokos unto 4, and the saint unto 6—and we recite the verses from **'Until the people passed over'** [Exodus 15:16]); likewise also unto two saints, if there are two kanons; likewise it is in forefeasts or between feasts" (that is, in the Menaion unto 8; in later manuscripts—absent) [^2541].

The Old Believer Typikon: Sunday 4, Cross-Resurrection 2, Theotokos 4, Menaion 4; if the saint is unto 6, Theotokos unto 2; unto 8, as with us, with the addition that it is likewise for 2 saints, and in forefeasts and afterfeasts [^2542].

The Constantinopolitan Typikon: "The Sunday kanon and that of the occurring Saint"; the *Hieratikon*: "The Sunday kanons unto 4 and the Menaion unto 4" [^2543].

The Greek Octoechos: "If the saint is celebrated *(Orig. p. 681)* unto 6 or 8, the Cross-Resurrection kanon is omitted" [^2544], against which the Old Believer Typikon states: "If the saint who is in the Menaion in course is celebrated unto 6, we do not omit the Cross-Resurrection kanon" [^2545]. In practice, the Old Believers at a minor saint chant, as with us—the Cross-Resurrection unto 3 and the Theotokos unto 3 [^2546].

### Katavasia

The troparia of the kanon, in their content, depart too far from the Biblical Odes with which they are connected by the heirmos; and thus, in order to restore their connection with these odes, their long series concludes, just as it opened, with an heirmos. Such a return of the ode of the kanon unto the heirmos is called a *katavasia* (*katavasia* [Gr. καταβασία] = *katabasis* [Gr. κατάβασις])—a descent, a returning (of an army from an expedition). On the greatest feasts the katavasia consists in the repetition of the opening heirmos; on lesser feasts, including Sunday, the heirmos of another, kindred or proximate feast serves as the katavasia; on weekdays the heirmos of the last kanon serves as the katavasia, and occurs only after the most important odes—the 3rd, 6th, 8th, and 9th; finally, during Lent the katavasia sometimes even replaces the heirmos, that is, the heirmos is chanted only in the capacity of a katavasia.

### History

The Studite Typika require the chanting of the heirmos of the same or a proximate feast at the end of each ode only on great feasts—sometimes even two heirmoi—yet they do not call this a katavasia, but express it simply: "and at the end the heirmos," or: "and again the heirmos" [^2547], and once: "in place of the *perisse*" [*v peris mesto*] [^2548]; the Alexis-Studite Typikon, however, calls the hypakoe a *katavasia* [^2549]. The Evergetis Typikon knows the present term *katavasia*, but likewise requires it only on great feasts [^2550]. So too do the oldest manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon [^2551]. In Greece, the katavasia of Odes 1–8, apparently, is chanted in its entirety after Ode 8.

### The Katavasia "I Will Open My Mouth"

Sunday Matins naturally has a katavasia of the festal type—that is, after each ode of the kanon. But even festal katavasia, as observed above, possesses various degrees. The most solemn is the repetition as katavasia of the heirmoi of the feast itself, moreover of both if the feast has two kanons. Such a katavasia is possessed only by the greatest of the Despotic Great Feasts and the Dormition. All other feasts have *(Orig. p. 682)* as katavasia the heirmoi of another feast, for the most part the nearest of the great feasts, with the aim of increasing their solemnity by such a katavasia.

Sunday belongs, by type of katavasia, unto feasts of the latter kind. The heirmoi of the proper kanon of Sunday Matins bear no relation unto the celebrated event and therefore are not suitable for a katavasia (for which reason they are not doubled at the beginning of the kanon). For the Sunday katavasia heirmoi in honor of the Mother of God were chosen—for the identical reason that a separate kanon unto Her is appointed at this Matins, and because every series of ecclesiastical hymns customarily concludes with a hymn in Her honor. More specifically, for the Sunday katavasia there were chosen from the heirmoi of Theotokos feasts the heirmoi **"I will open my mouth"** (*Otverzu usta moya*), used on all feasts of the Theotokos—yet not in the form in which these heirmoi are used on any of the Great Feasts of the Theotokos, when their text is adapted unto the celebrated event, but in the form in which they serve as the heirmoi of the majority of secondary Theotokos feasts, principally in honor of icons of the Mother of God, and consequently with a general glorification of Her as the Mother of God. In this form their content fully corresponds unto that purpose with which there is introduced into the Sunday service this glorification. In these heirmoi, after a general invitation of the faithful to chant the wonders of the Mother of God—that is, instances of Her constant miraculous aid unto us (instances that serve as the reason for Her so frequent and fervent veneration, and in particular for veneration on every Lord's Day) (1st heirmos), and after a supplication that She accept this glorification (3rd heirmos), the doctrine concerning the mystery of the Incarnation from Her of the Son of God (5th heirmos) is unfolded on the foundation of the prophecy of Isaiah 19:1 (4th heirmos) and the prototypical saving of the 3 Holy Children (7th and 8th heirmoi)—whom the faithful are summoned to welcome directly with the clapping of hands on this feast as much of Her as of Her Son (6th heirmos), on a feast celebrated likewise in the heavens (9th heirmos). Such a katavasia, however, occurs only on Sundays that are unencumbered by any special concurrences.

### Time of Introduction

The katavasia **"I will open my mouth"** for the kanon of Sunday Matins is not mentioned not only by any redaction of the Studite Typikon (the Alexis-Studite appoints it together with the heirmoi of Palm Sunday as the katavasia for its temple on March 12) [^2552] and the Evergetis Typikon, according unto which, apparently, on Sundays as on weekdays there was no katavasia, but it is not mentioned either by any of the ancient manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon—Georgian, Greek, Greek printed, and Slavic of the 14th–15th centuries; an indication of this katavasia is found only in Slavic manuscripts of the 16th century [^2553].

Under Arseny Sukhanov [^2554] it was used in the East; but it is not mentioned by the present Greek liturgical books—the Octoechos, the Typikon of the Great Church, and the *Hieratikon*, nor by the Old Believer Typikon. In *(Orig. p. 683)* practice, however, among the Old Believers it is used during the identical periods (with minor exceptions) as with us [^2555].

### Order of Chanting and Melody of the Kanon

The kanon, like every series of hymns, is chanted alternately by both choirs so that all the verses of the Biblical Odes and all the troparia with the heirmoi in each ode are distributed equally between the choirs, for which reason the number of these verses and troparia is always even. If before the heirmos a portion of the Biblical Ode without refrains is appointed, one choir (the beginning choir) chants the 1st verse of the ode, the other chants the second, and so forth; then the first choir chants the verse of the Biblical Ode appointed as the refrain unto the heirmos, and immediately after this the heirmos; the second choir chants the next verse of the ode and the 1st troparion, and so forth, and at the end "Glory"—the penultimate troparion, and "Both now"—the Theotokion. If before the heirmos no Biblical Ode is appointed, as occurs on Sundays, feasts, and certain other days (when **"Let us sing unto the Lord"** [*Poim Gospodevi*] is appointed), the first choir chants the heirmos, the 2nd choir—on days other than Sunday—chants the heirmos a second time, but on Sunday chants the refrain **"Glory to Thy Holy Resurrection, O Lord"** (*Slava, Gospodi, svyatomu voskreseniyu Tvoemu*) and the troparion, again the first choir chants the 1st verse of the Biblical Ode and the second troparion, and so forth [^2556]. Owing unto the fact that the chanting of the troparion begins with the chanting of the refrain, the refrain and troparion constitute a single whole: the troparion represents, as it were, the development of the thought of the refrain, its application unto the celebrated event. And the refrain is chanted in such a manner that the most characteristic sounds of the troparion (and heirmos) melody are preserved in it, namely, of its final musical strophe. Since for this strophe only the concluding words of the refrain are needed, its first and greater part is chanted in recitative and identically for all tones (a pattern of such execution of the refrain familiar unto everyone is **"We praise, bless, and worship the Lord..."** [*Khvalim, blagoslovim, poklanyaemsya Gospodevi...*] before the katavasia of Ode 8). As for the troparia themselves, they must be chanted entirely like the heirmoi, for which reason the heirmos is indicated before each kanon, even if the kanon is chanted without heirmoi. Inasmuch as the chant of the kanon is distinct from the sticheraric and troparic chants (for dismissal troparia and at "God is the Lord"), and since the entire kanon normally constitutes a series of 112 strophes (14 × 8), there is introduced by it into Matins an indefinitely long stream of this distinctive, complex melody, interrupted only twice by the troparic melody (the Sessional Hymns and Kontakia after Odes 3 and 6).

### When and Why Did They Cease Chanting the Troparia of the Kanon?

Already at the time of the Stoglav Council (1551) there was, apparently, a significant distinction in the manner of executing, on the one hand, ecclesiastical hymns, and on the other—the Introductory Psalms, kathismata with the Sessional Hymns and troparia connected with them, and kanons, as may be deduced from the following expressions of the Council concerning both manners of execution: "And as for the rest of ecclesiastical *(Orig. p. 684)* chanting, everything is to be performed according unto the Typikon: the Doxology to be chanted, and the katavasia chanted with the choirs coming together; but at Vespers and at Matins the psalms and the Psalter are to be spoken quietly and unhurriedly, with all attentiveness; likewise the troparia and Sessional Hymns they should recite according unto the rite and unhurriedly, and thereafter read, and of psalms and the Psalter at one and the same time they should not speak, nor canonarch two kanons together" [^2557].

Yet until the middle of the 17th century and somewhat later, both the kathismata and the troparia of the kanons were in one way or another chanted, as is evident from the ever-spreading custom of so-called polyphonic chanting (*mnogoglasie*): since chanting absolutely everything at the service lengthened it exceedingly, they began at one and the same time to chant—one the Six Psalms, another "God is the Lord" and the troparia, a third the kathismata, a fourth one kanon, a fifth another kanon, while the deacon at this time was reciting litanies, and so forth. "Give heed, holy master," wrote a certain Agathonikos unto Archbishop Sophrony of Suzdal in the 17th century, "unto the voice of the Apostle, that he shows those who all speak at once to be as ones possessed; is it not evident among us, when in two voices, and in three, and in four, and in five, and at times in six and in seven, not only unbelievers, but also a believer who loves piety and ecclesiastical good order, will say of us: are we possessed?" [^2558] This circumstance must have brought about also the legislative prohibition on the part of one of the Moscow Councils of the 17th century against chanting the entire kanon.
