Arseny Sukhanov notes that in the East they chant every troparion of the kanon in its entirety, and not merely the ending [^2559]; consequently, in Russia during his time the transition from chanting the troparia unto reading them was taking place: they chanted only their endings. At present in the East they chant the entire kanon with its troparia, and not the heirmoi alone, for which reason the chanting of the kanon occupies the greater part of Matins there, although sometimes someone chants alone on each choir [^2560].

### Melody of the Kanons at Sunday Matins

However distinct in each tone the kanon melody may be from the sticheraric and troparic melodies, nevertheless the general character of the tone (indicated above, p. 539) is preserved in it as well; and since the kanon represents the longest series of hymns in the entire Vigil (on condition, of course, that the troparia are chanted), by its tone it imparts musical coloration unto the Vigil above all. For the character of the latter it is far from indifferent whether these 80 troparia of the Octoechos kanons ((4 + 3 + 3) × 8) at Sunday Matins are chanted in the most joyful tone (Tone 1), in a less joyful one (Tone 4), or in tones as mournful as Tones 6 and 2.

It must be observed, however, that the Cross-Resurrection and Theotokos kanons are chanted with a melody not entirely identical unto that of the Sunday kanon, but—for the sake of variety and greater correspondence unto their content—with another. Especially the first of these kanons, as following immediately upon the Sunday kanon, always differs significantly from it in melody, although this melody is in the identical tone. Specifically, the melodies for the Cross-Resurrection kanons are chosen to be more artistic *(Orig. p. 685)* and compunctionate than those for the Sunday kanon, while for the Theotokos kanon they are at times the identical ones as for the Cross-Resurrection, at times new ones again. This melody is indicated in the Octoechos in such a manner that before the troparia of the Cross-Resurrection and Theotokos kanons the heirmos or its opening words are inscribed: since these kanons are chanted without heirmoi, such an inscription has as its aim to show that the troparia of the kanon must be chanted after the model of the inscribed heirmos; consequently, it is the identical thing as the heading in the stichera and Sessional Hymns: "Prosomoion" [*podoben*]. Specifically, the Cross-Resurrection kanons are chanted according unto the melody of the following heirmoi: Tone 1 according unto the melody of **"Christ is born"** (*Khristos raždaetsya*); Tone 2 **"Untrodden, unusual"** (*Netrenu, neobychnu*); Tone 3 **"Let us sing a new song, O ye peoples"** (*Pēsn' novuyu poim lyudie*); Tone 4 **"I will open my mouth"** (*Otverzu usta moya*); Tone 5 **"Unto God the Savior"** (*Spasitelyu Bogu*); Tone 6 **"By the wave of the sea"** (*Volnoyu morskoyu*); Tone 7 **"He who covered the deep"** (*Pontom pokry*); Tone 8 **"Having traversed the water"** (*Vodu proshed*). In this manner, on a simple Sunday, under the exact observance of the Typikon, the church could resound with the thrillingly sweet melodies of Great Saturday, the Nativity of Christ, the Ascension, and Pentecost. The effect is heightened by the fact that the troparia of the Cross-Resurrection kanon, executed with these touching melodies, are likewise in their verbal expression close in places unto the heirmoi whose music they imitate. For example, the 1st and 2nd troparia of the Cross-Resurrection kanon of Tone 1 are constructed analogously unto the heirmos **"Christ is born"**: "Christ deifieth me becoming incarnate; Christ exalteth me humbling Himself; Christ maketh me passionless." But most frequently the troparia of the Cross-Resurrection kanon borrow from their originals the concluding words that constitute the final and richest musical strophe; thus, in Tone 1, Ode 3 concludes: "Who hast lifted up our horn, Holy art Thou, O Lord"; Ode 7: "Praised and exceedingly glorified is the God of our fathers"; Tone 6, Ode 3: "There is none holy save Thee, O Lord, crying aloud"; Ode 7: "O God the Redeemer, blessed art Thou"; Ode 8: "O children, bless; O priests, sing praises; O peoples, supremely exalt Him unto all ages"; Ode 9: "Unto Thee who with faith and love magnify Thee." It is noteworthy that not all Cross-Resurrection kanons imitate the heirmoi of such great feasts. For instance, for the kanon of Tone 2 one could have chosen as a model the heirmoi of Theophany; for Tone 3—the Meeting of the Lord; for Tone 4—Palm Sunday or the Transfiguration; for Tone 8—the Exaltation of the Cross. Yet this was not done.

As regards the Theotokos kanon, it seems, as it were, to hesitate to imitate such exalted models; and when the Cross-Resurrection kanon has a melody from heirmoi that are too festive, the Theotokos kanon is chanted unto the melodies of the Sunday kanon; thus, in Tone 1 it has the melody of **"Thy triumphant right hand"** (*Tvoya pobeditel'naya*); in Tone 5 **"The horse and rider"** (*Konya i vsadnika*); in Tone 6 **"As on dry land"** (*Yako po sukhu*); in Tone 7 **"By Thy nod"** (*Maniem Tvoim*) (excluding Ode 9, where it follows the model of the Cross-Resurrection kanon: **"Mother of God and Virgin"** [*Mati Bozhiya i Deva*]). Where the Cross-Resurrection kanon has a more modest model, the Theotokos kanon continues its melody: therefore in Tone 2 the Theotokos kanon likewise has as its model the heirmos **"Untrodden, unusual"**; in Tone 3 **"A new song"**; in Tone 4 **"I will open my mouth"** (a more suitable model could not exist here—in view of the katavasia). Only in Tone 8 do all three kanons have different models, although not for all odes (namely, excluding Odes 4 and 7).

*(Orig. p. 686)*
The customary katavasia of Sunday Matins, **"I will open my mouth"**, has a tone likewise fully corresponding unto Sunday joy: the 4th heirmos tone, in which this katavasia is chanted, is the tone for kanons on feasts of, so to speak, moderate solemnity: with it are chanted the kanons of more than half of the Great Feasts. Lacking that boundlessness in its joy possessed by Tone 1, especially in its Paschal and Nativity melodies, this tone for heirmoi nevertheless shimmers and glitters entirely with a light, triumphant joy; its somewhat rapid melody at times resembles the sound of the clapping of hands unto which one of the heirmoi of the Sunday katavasia invites.

### Historical Note

In Slavic manuscript Octoechoi, especially in the so-called *Parakletika* (an Octoechos containing only kanons) of the 14th and 15th centuries, not infrequently the heirmoi for the Cross-Resurrection and Theotokos kanons are indicated differently from those in the present printed Slavic Octoechos (which is in full agreement in this regard with the Greek printed edition), but the difference is less than in the troparia [^2561].

### Censing at the Beginning of the Kanon According unto Ancient Typika

As constituting an independent portion of Matins, as it were a distinct service, the kanon, like other services, had according unto ancient Typika a censing at its beginning. The *Diataxis* [*Chin*] of Patriarch Philotheos provides the detailed rite of this censing: "With the beginning of the kanon the priest comes forth and stands in the right choir at the customary place; and the deacon, having first received the blessing for the censer, censes first the sanctuary entirely, then goes out by the northern door and traces a cross before the holy doors, and censes first the icons on the right side all as they are set, and goes away unto the icon (*signon* [Gr. σίγνον]) of the monastery, and having traced a cross toward it, turns toward the west, and having taken a stand in the midst of the temple, traces a cross, and goes away and censes first the icon set upon the stasidion of the superior, then the superior and in order the brethren of the right choir; and after the censing of all the choirs (in the choir?), he takes a stand in the midst of the choir and, looking toward the south, makes a cross; and while censing and receiving a bow from those whom he censes, he likewise bows unto them a little; and having made a cross, he goes away unto the right (left?) choir and, having censed there the holy icons, censes also the brethren, beginning from the top from the icons and departing, as it were, toward the beautiful gates, receiving a bow, and in like manner himself bowing a little. Having finished also this choir, he again takes a stand in the midst, looking toward the north and making a cross, goes forth into the narthex and, having censed all there as well, enters through the beautiful gates and, having traced a cross toward the east, censes the superior and again in the midst traces a cross, and having censed the holy icons, enters and puts down the censer, goes forth, bows a little unto the superior from afar, and takes a stand at the customary place" [^2562].

An analogous censing is indicated by Slavic manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon of the 14th century:
"After the kissing of the Gospel, the priest or deacon censes the Gospel and both choirs—and says: Save, O *(Orig. p. 687)* God…" [^2563].

*Old Believer Sluzhebnik*:
"After Psalm 50 the deacon censes, and before him the candle-bearer walks with a candle" [^2564].

### Inter-Ode Breaks [Mesodia]

However diverse the melodies of the kanons at Sunday Matins may be, nevertheless such a vast stream of canticles (15 × 8 = 120) would exceed the capacity of even the most untiring attention were this stream continuous. In view of this, two large breaks are made within it, by which the kanon is divided into 3 (the sacred number) parts. Since the kanon in principle ought to have 9 odes, for these "inter-ode breaks" [*mezhdopesniya*] the place chosen is "after" (*apo tes* [Gr. ἀπὸ τῆς]—from, off, after) the 3rd and 6th odes. The inter-ode break (*mesodion* [Gr. μεσῴδιον]), in order to afford rest from the chanting of the kanon and to revive the attention of the listeners, must provide something completely opposite in character unto the kanon. The kanon is a hymn of praise with an especially intricate melody. The inter-ode break accordingly gives prayer instead of praise, reading instead of song, a simpler chant instead of an intricate melody. Thus the inter-ode break at the kanon consists of 3 parts: prayer, reading, and chanting. Since the parts into which the kanon is divided by the inter-ode breaks are analogous unto kathismata, more specifically, unto this composition of the inter-ode breaks was given the identical form possessed by the intervals between the kathismata, that is, they consist of the little litany, sessional hymns or the kontakia with ikoi replacing them, and a reading.

### Antiquity of the Mesodion

The well-known description of Sinai Matins of the 6th–7th century already mentions the inter-ode breaks after the 3rd and 6th odes of the kanon, wherein regarding them it is given to understand that they consisted of certain artistic hymns begun by the priest (Introductory Chapters, 295, 296). The *Hypotyposis* and *Diatyposis* mention only 2 readings at the kanon [^2565]; the Studite-Alexian Typikon, besides the readings after the 3rd and 6th odes, speaks of a sessional hymn after the 3rd ode and a kontakion after the 6th [^2566].

### Litanies after Ode 3 and Ode 6

The little litanies after the 3rd and 6th odes of the kanon can mark the exceptional position they occupy at Matins only by their exclamations. The latter, naturally, are new in comparison with the preceding ones. Yet at the identical time the exclamations here do not continue, as one might have expected, the development of thought of the preceding ones, but—in view of the fact that the kanon is regarded as a completely independent part of Matins, or as a service within a service—they begin a new train of thoughts. Specifically, the exclamation of the litany after the 3rd ode glorifies God simply only as God: "For Thou art our God…", while the exclamation after the 6th ode gives an exhaustive conception of Him as King and Savior: "For Thou art the King of peace *(Orig. p. 688)* (*eirenes* [Gr. εἰρήνης]) and the Savior…" The exclamations conclude the 5th and 6th morning prayers, and the 1st and 6th evening prayers.

Of these two litanies, the Typikon directs the deacon to pronounce the first, and the priest the second. This is because up to the 3rd ode the deacon still participates in the serving, having begun this participation with the Polyeleos or with the Blameless [*Amomoi*]; from the 3rd ode until the 9th, however, as a portion of the kanon less festive and filled with readings, the priest alone ministers. The pronunciation by the deacon of the litany after the 3rd ode with his removal from the litany after the 6th ode is consequently analogous unto according him, out of the 3 litanies at the evening kathisma, only the last. The litanies after the 3rd and 6th odes of the kanon are pronounced before the holy doors: the first because it is pronounced by the deacon; the second because after the litany of the 3rd ode (for the sessional hymn and the reading) the priest and deacon "are stripped of the sacred vestments, and having gone forth (from the altar), they stand in the customary places." For the identical reason it is noted in the Typikon only regarding the 1st litany that its exclamation is "within the altar."

### Variants of the Exclamations and Ancient Typika concerning the Litanies

The present exclamations unto these litanies are given by all manuscript Sluzhebniki, but the Greek for the 2nd litany has: "For Thou art the King of peace, and unto Thee the glory…"; so also the printed *Euchologion*, whereas the *Hieratikon* is as with us; up to the Moscow *Sluzhebnik* of 1658 inclusively: "… King unto the world [or: unto peace] and Savior of souls…"; only in the *Sluzhebnik* of Petro Mohyla: "unto peace" [*mirovi*]. The Georgian and Greek manuscripts do not speak of litanies; Slavic manuscripts of the 14th century indicate the exclamations as well, but from the 15th century onward they agree with the Greek; concerning the actions of the priest and deacon only the "Order of Patriarch Philotheos" speaks, and that with an addition concerning the priest's pronunciation of the litany: "uncovered" [^2567].

### Sessional Hymn and Reading after Ode 3

Since the kanon, whose foundation is constituted by the Old Testament canticles, is regarded as something analogous unto kathismata, at its inter-ode breaks after the little litany there follow after the 3rd ode a sessional hymn and a reading, and after the 6th ode a kontakion with an ikos, and likewise a reading. From this normal order at Sunday Matins a departure is made because, in addition to the Sunday kontakion and ikos, it is necessary to chant at the kanon also the kontakia and ikoi of the Menaion. Since after the 6th ode of the kanon the Typikon does not permit chanting more than one kontakion and ikos, the Menaion kontakion—and by implication also the ikos (of which the General Menaion speaks directly)—is transferred unto the 3rd ode, and after them is chanted the sessional hymn of the Menaion, "Glory… now and ever…" Theotokion, with which in the Menaion the sessional hymn is always supplied. Neither the Typikon nor even the General Menaion, which gives the rule for combining with the Sunday service two saints, indicates what is to be chanted after the 3rd ode when two saints coincide on Sunday, perhaps because it is taken for granted that one must chant for both the kontakia, ikoi, and sessional hymns after the 3rd ode. Thus it is directed to do in the Typikon under September 8 (if the afterfeast falls on Sunday). As regards the reading after the 3rd ode, its content is not more closely defined in *(Orig. p. 689)* the Typikon, but judging by the fact that in Chapter 10 of the Typikon a reading at Matins is required, besides the commentary on the appointed Epistle and Gospel of the day, also from the *Margarita* of Chrysostom and Symeon Metaphrastes, while for the commentaries the three preceding readings suffice, after the 3rd ode there must be a reading from these latter books (on Sunday—from the *Margarita*, as the most important book).

### According unto Ancient and Other Typika

Manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon all speak only of a sessional hymn after the 3rd ode, but this is because the kontakion of the Menaion according unto them was chanted after the 6th ode (see below). According unto the *Hieratikon*, if it is the commemoration of a celebrated saint, the reader reads (after the 3rd ode) the Sunday kontakion and ikos, then the 2nd choir chants the sessional hymn of the saint, and the 1st choir the Theotokion; if, however, a saint is not celebrated, the Sunday kontakion and ikos are read after the 6th ode, (and after the 3rd ode) the choir chants the sessional hymn of the saint and the Theotokion; if the kontakion and ikos of the saint are read after the 6th ode, the choirs chant their conclusions [^2568].

### Kontakion and Ikos after Ode 6

Like the kanon itself, the inter-ode breaks steadily increase in solemnity. In view of this, after the 6th ode there is appointed not a sessional hymn, but a kontakion and ikos—hymns close in melody unto sessional hymns, specifically of troparic melody, which is more solemn than the sessional melody. By this there is introduced into Matins a new genre of church hymn, hitherto unused at the Vigil, occupying in the hierarchy of hymnography the second rank—after the troparion; like the latter, depicting the very essence of the celebrated event, but usually from a different aspect than the troparion; if the troparion presents a picture of the external side of the event, the kontakion presents the internal, or vice versa (cf. the troparion and kontakion of Theophany, or of the Ascension, or of the Transfiguration). Moreover, the kontakion usually depicts the very essence of the celebrated event more fully than the troparion (cf. the troparion and kontakion of Pascha, of the Nativity of Christ), for which reason in those cases when at a church service room can be given unto only a single hymn of the feast, it is accorded unto the kontakion; so it happens always at the Typika [*Izobrazitel'nye*], at Small Compline on feasts, and at the Lenten Hours in Passion Week.

### History

*Kontakion* [Gr. Κοντάκιον] is derived from *kontos* [Gr. κοντός]—the rod upon which a scroll of parchment was rolled; the diminutive [Gr. κονδάκιον] is a scroll, a book in the form of a scroll [^2569], otherwise termed an *iletarion* [Gr. ἰλητάριον] [^2570] (*kondwaon* being a corrupted pronunciation); of such scrolls not a few have been preserved in the libraries of the East dating from the 10th–11th centuries, the epoch when books had already assumed their present form; perhaps upon such scrolls the most important books were transcribed, or else they were more convenient for liturgical chant use. *Ikos* [Gr. οἶκος], house; yet the Syriac *beth*, house, can also signify a stanza (as the Italian *stanza* means both room and stanza), and the ikoi are of specifically Syriac origin, and for *(Orig. p. 690)* each feast there was an entire sequence of them—up to 24, so that they precisely constituted a sequence of strophes. Concerning Romanos the Melodist (6th c.), the founder of this genre of church hymnody, and concerning the other composers of ikoi, as well as regarding their primordial form—see the Introductory Chapters, 329–331. According unto the Studite Typikon these were the most solemn hymns of festal divine services; in the most ancient manuscript of this Typikon of the 11th–12th century they alone are placed in the menologion section of the Typikon, exhausting it; for the most important days of the year in this manuscript there is given one kontakion and ikos each with an obligatory prosomoion [*podoben*] for each, while for great feasts the kontakion is set to musical notation; and before the conclusion of the ikos, which is always identical with the conclusion of the kontakion, stands the rubric in cinnabar: "the people" [Slav. *lyudie*] (that is, its ending is chanted by the entire congregation) [^2571].

### Sunday Kontakia and Ikoi

Sunday kontakia depict primarily the fruits of Christ's resurrection and its internal aspect, whereas the ikoi at times also provide a depiction of the historical event (Tones 5, 7, 8). Both serve as a complement unto the troparia, illuminating the event from those aspects from which it is not touched upon by the corresponding troparion.

For certain kontakia model melodies (prosomoia) are likewise indicated in the Octoechos: for the kontakion of Tone 1—**"When Thou shalt come"** (*Egda priideshi*—the kontakion of Meatfare Sunday); Tone 3 **"Today the Virgin"** (*Deva dnes'*); Tone 4 **"Thou hast appeared"** (*Yavilsya esi*—Theophany); Tone 5 **"The Word Co-beginningless"** (*Sobeznachal'noe Slovo*); Tone 8 **"As the first-fruits"** (*Yako nachatki*—the kontakion of All Saints).

### History

The Sunday kontakia and ikoi are the latest in time of origin among the Sunday hymns: mentions of them begin only in manuscripts of the 11th century, and they do not occupy their present position at Matins and the Hours even in certain manuscripts of the 16th century. The Evergetis Typikon does not yet know them: after the 6th ode of the kanon at Sunday Matins according unto this Typikon there is the kontakion of the saint, and if the saint hath no kontakion, then the Sunday sessional hymn, "the finest in the tone," "chanter and people," "Glory… now and ever…" Theotokion [^2572]. The Studite Typika likewise make no mention of the Sunday kontakion in the order of services, but the ancient manuscript of the Studite-Alexian Typikon contains a section: "Sunday kontakia and ikoi" (see below).

Georgian manuscripts: "After the 6th ode the kontakion of the Menaion, and if there is none, the Sunday sessional hymn" [^2573]; ancient Greek and printed: "the kontakion of the saint, if he hath one; but if not, of the Theotokos: **A protection of Christians** [*Predstatel'stvo khristian*], or another if thou wilt" (instead of the italics later: "and the ikos: **Stretch forth thy hands**—one must know that the Sunday kontakion is not said"); ancient Slavic manuscripts: "kontakion of the saint; if not, then the Sunday"; later from the 15th–16th century: "kontakion of the saint or **O Protection** [= *Predstatel'stvo*] **of Christians**" [^2574].

In the aforementioned manuscript of the Studite-Alexian Typikon the Sunday kontakia and *(Orig. p. 691)* ikoi present not a few variant readings from the present ones, and besides, the following different ones: ikos Tone 3 **"He Who from the tomb, Christ"** (*Izhe ot groba Khristos*); Tone 5 **"Of Thy three-day burial"** (*Tridnevnago Ti pogrebeniya*); kontakion and ikos Tone 7 **"From the gates of hades"** (*Ot adovykh vrat*), **"The tombs as Redeemer Thou didst empty"** (*Groby yako Izbavitel' istoščil esi*); model melodies are indicated for all kontakia and ikoi: for the kontakia identical with the present ones where the latter have model melodies; for Tone 2 **"Seeking the highest"** (*Vyshnikh ishcha*—kontakion of Symeon the Stylite); Tone 5 **"Being an imitator"** (*Podobnik syi*—unto Panteleimon); Tone 7 **"On the mountain Thou wast transfigured"** (*Na gore preobrazilisya*); model melodies of the ikoi from the identical feasts as for the kontakia, but for Tones 4 and 6 there stands only the word "prosomoion" [*podoben*] [^2575].

### The Prolog

Like the hymn after the 6th ode of the kanon, the reading at this place is likewise exceptional, not a continuation of the preceding readings, but a new one, specifically the Life of the saint celebrated on that day, drawn from a special collection termed the *Prolog* (*prologos* [Gr. πρόλογος], properly a foreword, since in all probability the title of the foreword was erroneously taken for the title of the book) or *Synaxarion* [^2576] (*synaxarion* [Gr. συναξάριον], collection). Dedicated unto the memory of the saint, replacing the entire service unto him if for any reason it is omitted on Sunday, this reading is regarded by the Typikon as especially important, not being omitted even on Sundays with special commemorations [^2577].

### History

The reading of Acts of the Martyrs on the commemoration day of the martyrs was already in custom in the 2nd–3rd centuries, and in the 4th century it attained universal dissemination (Introductory Chapters, 68, 174), constituting, of course, a prominent and significant part of the divine service of that period, which was modest in liturgical material for such days. Even the Studite-Alexian Typikon restricts the service unto certain saints unto the reading of their Life, directing on certain days that only the Octoechos be chanted. By an instruction unto such a reading alone the entire Typikon is exhausted here for certain days (neither stichera, nor kanon, nor troparion being mentioned), for instance October 13: "Holy Martyrs Carpus and Papylus. Their martyrdom is read"; October 20: "Holy Great-Martyr Artemius. His martyrdom is read" [^2578].

It is no wonder, therefore, that already in the 4th century collections of such "martyrdoms" appear, and later of Lives as well (Introductory Chapters, 174)—martyrologies (275ff.). When the number of saints multiplied, it became increasingly difficult to compile complete collections of their Lives or even to have at hand all their Lives; consequently, subsequent complete menologia (6th–8th c.) restrict themselves unto indicating the names of the saints, the place and time of their demise for their commemoration at the Liturgy (ibid., 320ff.), presuming, evidently, the reading of their Lives according unto availability. But from the 9th century onward attempts begin at collections of brief Lives of saints in several lines; such biographical notices are given among other things *(Orig. p. 692)* in the Typikon of the Great Church of Constantinople of the 9th century under each day of the month; these notices perhaps served as the basis for the *Menologion* [Gr. Μηνολόγιον] *of Emperor Basil* (11th c.), wherein the accounts are already more extensive; from the 11th century also there appear similar collections under the name of *Prologs*, the most ancient of which is the verse Prolog of Christopher of Mytilene (Introductory Chapters, 400–401).

The Slavic *Prolog* is close unto the later recensions of the Greek; consequently, it likewise has as its basis the aforementioned menologion of the Great Church, and especially that of Basil; it is more extensive than the latter (or makes use of a more expansive recension of it), but much briefer than the Lives of Symeon Metaphrastes and the *Chet'i-Minei* of St. Demetrius, omitting many data from the Lives, but also providing abundant details, in places important for the characterization of the saint and engagingly edifying. The Slavic *Prolog* preserved in manuscripts of the 12th–14th centuries had several printed editions, combining the verse Prolog with Basil's Prolog: 1st ed. 1641–1643, last 1792. Greek Synaxaria (likewise verse and non-verse) were printed and continue to be printed in the monthly Menaia (after the 6th ode of the kanon), the most complete being in the Menaia of the 1843 Venice edition (not only for the saints who have services, but also for others whose memory falls on that day); as a separate publication in Modern Greek the Synaxarion appeared for the first time in 1691, the last edition being that of Nicodemus the Hagiorite in 1819, with reprints in 1842 and 1868 with minor alterations [^2579].

The Studite Typikon attached special significance unto the reading of the Lives of the saints: at weekday Matins this was the sole material for reading; long Lives were read in succession across several Matins services, for example the Life of Antony the Great on January 13–17, and of Theodore the Studite on November 8–11 [^2580]. The Evergetis Typikon did the identical thing, but hath no reading after the 6th ode [^2581]. Jerusalem Typikon—Georgian manuscript: "After the 3rd ode there is a reading, and likewise after the 6th, if only time permits." Greek manuscripts and printed editions: "and a reading in the Synaxarion"; Slavic manuscripts: "and we read in the Synaxarion", later (from the 15th c.): "… in the Prolog" [^2582].

### The Eighth Ode

From among the other odes the Typikon singles out first of all, naturally, the 8th ode, as the concluding one among the Old Testament canticles, the closest unto the New Testament both in time of composition and in spirit. Its distinction from the others is effected by the fact that the Lesser Doxology concluding each ode (as also each psalm) is here formulated differently, specifically so that it may be close in manner of expression unto the text of the canticle, so that it may pour forth, as it were, from the lips of the confessing youths themselves. Since each verse of the canticle begins with the word "bless", instead of "Glory to the Father" the canticle hath at the end "Bless we the Father…" Moreover, the doxology in such an exceptional form, *(Orig. p. 693)* used nowhere else in divine worship, is placed not at the very end of the canticle, but before its last verse, whereby it is organically interwoven into the canticle. Thanks unto this, the last verse of the canticle, **"We praise, we bless, we worship the Lord…"** (*Khvalim, blagoslovim, poklanyayemsya Gospodevi*), acquires a new meaning, or more precisely, reveals its hidden meaning, that its three principal verbs can relate unto the three Persons of the Most Holy Trinity. This verse serves as the refrain unto the katavasia of the 8th ode, thanks unto which this katavasia likewise is singled out from among the others. Since the verse invites also unto worship, "always at the end of the 8th ode, when we wish to begin the 9th ode (consequently, as much on account of the impending 9th ode, which is even more important than the 8th), we all make a metania (a bow, on Sunday, of course, a small one, such as are further on explicitly required at the Canticle of the Theotokos) equally [all simultaneously], saying: **We praise, we bless, we worship the Lord**" [^2583].

### According unto Ancient Typika

Concerning the significance that was always attached unto the 8th ode in the series of the others—see above, p. 669.

Concerning bows at the 8th and 9th odes the Georgian manuscript of the Jerusalem Typikon hath nothing; ancient Greek and printed:
"One must know that at (*eis* [Gr. εἰς]) the 9th ode we make a bow (bows?) unto (*apo? heos eis* [Gr. ἀπό? ἕως εἰς]) the ground, the two choirs together";
later Greek adds:
"that is (*etoi?* [Gr. ἤτοι?]) at the end of the 8th ode, as well as after the end of the 9th ode";
ancient Slavic:
"and at the completion of that psalmody (that is, the **More Honorable**) both choirs make a bow unto the ground, if it be Sunday";
later Slavic:
"it is proper to know that at the 9th ode, while chanting the **More Honorable**, both choirs make a bow (still later: bows) unto the ground" [^2584].

### The Ninth Ode. Vesting for It

However distinguished from the series of the others the 8th ode may be, as the concluding word in the kanon from the Old Testament, yet by how much the New Testament is higher than the Old, by so much doth the Typikon exalt the 9th ode above the other odes. This is expressed first of all by the fact that for this ode "the priest and the deacon vest customarily," as they vest in the course of the Vigil only 2 other times: for the Entrance and for the Polyeleos or Gospel. In vestments they now remain until the conclusion of the service.

### According unto Ancient Typika

Manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon do not speak of this vesting, in all probability presuming it in view of the censing. The "Order" of Patriarch Philotheos states: "at (*eis* [Gr. εἰς]) the 8th ode the priest with the deacon makes a bow unto the superior, and they enter into the altar and the deacon vests customarily, and upon the completion of the 8th ode the deacon sings with a loud voice: **The Theotokos and Mother of the Light**—So going forth (the priest from the altar) *(Orig. p. 694)* he stands at the customary place, while the deacon censes all customarily and, having returned, stands at the appointed place" [^2585].

### "More Honorable than the Cherubim"

The Biblical canticles in the kanon, arranged approximately in chronological order, lead our thoughts ever closer unto New Testament times, whither the last, 9th ode definitively ushers us. Composed of the canticles of the Most Holy Theotokos and the Prophet Zechariah, it in its first part thus represents the greatest and holiest work in its author of the most exalted and inspired content (concerning the content, see above, p. 668). It is no wonder that the Typikon appoints for this canticle an exceptional execution and surrounds it with special reverence: whereas the other Biblical canticles serve as refrains unto the heirmoi and troparia of the kanon, the Canticle of the Theotokos occupies a completely independent position in relation unto the latter, and in general in the kanon, and possesses its own refrain, identical for all 6 verses into which it is divided for chanting. As such a refrain there serves the hymn **"More Honorable"** (*Čestnējšuyu*), in which with special expressiveness the Most Holy Virgin is confessed as the real, true (*ten ontos* [Gr. τὴν ὄντως]) Theotokos and with great boldness of faith is placed above the highest Angelic ranks. According unto tradition (in Nikephoros Kallistos, 14th c.), the Mother of God, appearing unto the composer of the hymn (St. Cosmas), with a joyful countenance said: "Pleasing unto Me are thy hymns, yet this one is more pleasing than all the others; pleasing unto Me are those who sing spiritual songs, yet never am I so near unto them as when they chant this new song of thine"; and those capable of mystical vision repeatedly saw thereafter the Mother of God blessing those who chanted this hymn [^2586].

### History

The Studite and Evergetis Typika do not indicate the manner of execution for the Canticle of the Theotokos, thereby giving reason to think that here there was no difference from the other Biblical canticles, that is, that the canticle was chanted as the others. The ancient manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon—Georgian and Greek—likewise say nothing concerning the manner of execution of the canticle in the order of Sunday Matins; only later Greek under September 8 note: "We do not chant the verses of the **More Honorable**" [^2587].

At Sunday Matins, concerning the "chanting of the verses of the **More Honorable**" for the first time is mentioned by the "Order" of Patriarch Philotheos and all Slavic manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon, beginning from the most ancient.
The "Order": "and the **More Honorable** is chanted according unto verses";
a manuscript of the 14th century: "the right choir begins the verse: **My soul doth magnify… More honorable…** Again the other choir repeats… After the 9th ode both *(Orig. p. 695)* choirs unite, and chant **It is Truly Meet**" (nowadays only at weekday Matins) [^2588];
manuscripts of the 15th–16th centuries: "at the 9th ode unto those chanting the **More Honorable**."

The hymn **"More Honorable"** is the heirmos of the 9th ode of the triode of Great and Holy Friday, **"Unto Thee I rise early"** (*K Tebe utrenyuyu*); consequently, it belongs unto St. Cosmas of Maiuma, who utilized for it the expression of St. Ephrem the Syrian concerning the Mother of God: "More honorable than the Cherubim and beyond compare of all the heavenly hosts" [^2589]. According unto tradition (of Nikephoros Kallistos), the hymn was composed on Great Friday itself [^2590].

As regards the fortune in the West of the **"Magnificat"** ("Magnificat", a loose translation of the Greek Μεγαλύνει, subjunctive instead of indicative), first of all it must be noted that certain Latin manuscripts of the Gospel and certain writers prior unto the 4th century read in Luke 1:46 "Elizabeth said" (*ait Elisabeth*), and not "Mary"; consequently, they attribute the canticle unto Elizabeth, for which certain modern scholars (for example, Harnack) find grounds both in the text of the canticle and even in our exclamation before the canticle: "The Theotokos… in songs let us magnify" [^2591]. The introduction of the canticle into liturgical use in the West is attributed unto Caesarius of Arles (†542) [^2592]. From Gregory the Great or, rather, Benedict, this canticle came to be used here at Vespers, which "as an evening sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving culminated in it, as in a spiritual sweet-smelling savour par excellence" [^2593], which is expressed also by the censing of the altar taking place at this canticle; such usage constitutes a parallel unto the Canticle of Zechariah at Matins (there the impending salvation, here the accomplished salvation) and the hymn **"Glory to God in the highest"** at the Liturgy, and corresponds unto the evening disposition of the believer, grateful for all the good received during the day. The *Magnificat* is always accompanied and concluded, and in the Ambrosian rite also preceded, by an antiphon appointed for the commemoration of the day (*proprium*) [^2594], which in antiquity was chanted after each verse of the canticle (Introductory Chapters, 307, 317). (In the Mozarabic rite the *Magnificat* is chanted only on certain feasts at *Laudes* with an antiphon before and after [^2595]—*ibid.*, 318). Among the Lutherans the *Magnificat* is likewise chanted at Vespers, but in German translation, with the sub-chanting unto each verse of a short hymn composed in adaptation unto the Biblical text, wherein sometimes one choir chants a verse of the Biblical canticle and the other chants this refrain.

### Melody

Concerning the melody for the **Magnificat** in the present place of the Typikon it is stated only: "chanting with a loud voice." Yet in the rule of September 1, which is distinguished in general *(Orig. p. 696)* by its detail, since this is the 1st day of the ecclesiastical year, the tone is also indicated for this canticle—the 6th (that this instruction possesses general significance for all days is evident from the tones of the kanon for September 1: 1st, 4th, and 8th) and, of course, in its kanonic melody. This is also natural, because the refrain unto the canticle is constituted by the heirmos from the kanon of Tone 6 (**"Unto Thee I rise early"**). Musical tradition shows, however, that this is not the ordinary kanonic melody of Tone 6, but a special, automelon [*samoglasny*] melody.

### According unto Ancient Typika

Greek manuscripts (late) of the Jerusalem Typikon and the "Order" of Patriarch Philotheos express themselves concerning the **More Honorable** only with the word "is chanted according unto verses" (στιχολογεῖται, —οῦμεν); Slavic manuscripts say "is chanted"; the tone is not indicated even in the rule of September 1. The Old Believer Typikon indicates the tone here as well (see below, p. 697). Among Catholics and Lutherans the *Magnificat* is chanted in the 9th tone and constitutes a favorite subject for artistic compositions [^2596].

### Before the Magnificat

The 9th ode of the kanon, or more specifically the Canticle of the Theotokos opening it, is singled out from the series of the others by a special exclamation of the deacon before it, inviting unto the glorification of the Mother of God: **"The Theotokos and Mother of the Light let us magnify in songs"** [^2597], whereby the necessity of special attentiveness unto the canticle is marked (cf. "Let us attend"). In the exclamation the Most Holy Theotokos is named Mother of the Light in correspondence with the glorification of God soon to follow for the appearance of the morning light. The exclamation is pronounced "after the censing of the holy table" (according unto Chapter 9—during the censing), usually upon going forth from the altar before the icon of the Mother of God.

### According unto Ancient Typika

The exclamation without the words "Mother of the Light" serves as an epigraph unto the Canticle of the Theotokos, just as all the other Biblical canticles have epigraphs (Ode 1: **"Let us sing unto the Lord, for He is gloriously glorified"**; Ode 3: **"Holy art Thou, O Lord, and Thee my spirit hymneth"**). In such a form (without "Mother of the Light") the exclamation is found in Slavic Sluzhebniki prior unto 1647 (the Moscow 1658 edition is silent concerning it) [^2598]. But in the "Order" of Patriarch Philotheos and in Slavic manuscripts (the Greek are silent) of the Jerusalem Typikon, as nowadays, the Slavic manuscripts add "Virgin" after "Mother", "in hymns" or completely without the latter [^2599].

Late Greek manuscripts:
"It is proper to know that at the 9th ode, if it be not a Feast of the Lord, then we always chant according unto verses the **More Honorable**, even if there be a Great Doxology"; "if, however, it be a Feast of the Lord, we chant the heirmos of the 9th ode, it being begun by the priest" [^2600];
the "Order" of Patriarch Philotheos:
"if not (if the **More Honorable** is not chanted according unto verses), there is chanted (it is unclear whether by the priest or the deacon) the beginning of the heirmos of the 9th ode of the feast." So likewise the Old Believer Typikon; but with the addition: "in the altar with a loud voice; here, however, the custom obtains that the priest exclaims instead of the heirmos: **The Theotokos in songs let us magnify**, and we chant *(Orig. p. 697)* the heirmos of the 9th ode" [^2601].

Concerning the proclaimer of the exclamation, Slavic manuscripts state: the priest before the holy doors after the censing of the altar; the "Order" of Patriarch Philotheos: "the deacon chants with a loud voice"; the Old Believer Typikon: "the priest, having censed the holy table, exclaims in Tone 6" [^2602].

### Bows at the "More Honorable"

The Canticle of the Theotokos is singled out not only from the series of the other odes of the kanon, but from the entire Vigil, by the fact that here alone the Typikon directly requires bows, inviting thereby also to express one's veneration of God in view of the approaching conclusion of the service and its festal hymns; yet in view of the prohibition of kneeling on Sundays—only small bows: "We make also small bows" (it is understood: at each verse). By this similar bows in other places of the service are not excluded, but they are simply not considered there as necessary as here, or in general for some reason are not indicated (perhaps through oversight). With great detail they are indicated in the order of weekday service, and by these instructions one can be guided for Sunday and festal services, replacing prostrations with small bows (as indeed the Old Believers do).

### According unto Ancient Typika

Ancient Typika required a single bow at the 9th ode (see p. 693), assigning it unto its conclusion, as is evident from the note concerning this bow at the Nativity of Christ and elsewhere even in the present Typikon. Subsequently this bow was moved back unto the beginning of the 9th ode, even unto the katavasia of the 8th ode; consequently, other bows were likewise required at the 9th ode itself, assigned more specifically unto the Canticle of the Theotokos. The last stage prior unto the present practice is represented by the Old Believer Typikon: "Be it known also this, that always at the end of the 8th ode, when we wish to begin the 9th ode, we all make a metania once, saying equally: **We praise, we bless…**—we chant according unto verses the 9th ode, chanting with a loud voice **More honorable than the Cherubim**, both choirs make a bow from the waist, and at the last one unto the ground."

### Censing at the "More Honorable"

Censing, being an intensification of prayer and contributing unto the elevation of a prayerful disposition, accompanies the most important parts of divine worship, and throughout the entire Vigil it is performed 4 times. This is the last time. As concluding, it, like all concluding hymns in each series of songs, is dedicated unto the Most Holy Theotokos; it is Her veneration, just as the censing at the Blameless [*Amomoi*] is the veneration of the risen Christ, and at the Polyeleos Megalynarion—of the celebrated saint. As less important than that censing, it is performed by a single deacon, or by the priest if no deacon serves. Hence the ambiguity in the Typikon:
"At the conclusion of the 8th ode, having censed the holy table, the deacon exclaims: **The Theotokos and Mother of the Light…**—The priest or deacon censes the holy altar and the whole church and all the brethren. After the 9th ode, having returned and given up the censer, *(Orig. p. 698)* he says the litany, and the exclamation is from the priest"
(at weekday service, when the deacon does not participate in the serving, this censing is directed to be performed by the priest—see Chapter 9 of the Typikon).

### According unto Ancient and Other Typika

The Georgian manuscript of the Jerusalem Typikon, as also the Greek and printed editions, makes no mention of censing at the 9th ode. The "Order" of Patriarch Philotheos:

"the deacon censes all customarily and, having returned, stands at the appointed place."

Slavic manuscripts of the 14th century:
"At the end of the 8th ode the priest makes the customary bow unto the superior, having entered into the altar censes the holy table and the whole sanctuary and the table of oblation and goes forth into the church; and upon the conclusion of the 8th ode, having taken a stand before the holy doors, censing the holy doors crosswise, he exclaims: **The Theotokos…**" and "censes the church" [^2603];
later manuscripts do not mention it, as also the present Greek, but the *Hieratikon* states:
"the deacon: **The Theotokos and Mother of the Light**, and having taken the censer, censes the holy table and the sanctuary and the whole temple" [^2604].

### The Litany after Ode 9

With the 9th ode the third and final division of the kanon concludes, which possesses a conclusion similar unto the preceding two divisions, that is, first of all the little litany. Its exclamation: **"For all the powers of heaven praise Thee"**, on the one hand, at the completion of the lengthy hymn represented by the kanon with its approximately 112 canticles, expresses a humble acknowledgment of the unworthiness of our praise in comparison with heavenly praise; on the other hand, it prefigures the theme of the subsequent part of Matins, linking as it were thereby the end of its 3rd part with the beginning of the 4th.

### Primordial Antiquity of Its Exclamation

Such an exclamation is possessed by the litany here in absolutely all monuments that indicate the litany.

### "Holy is the Lord our God"

If already the 6th ode had after itself a chant more solemn than the 3rd (a kontakion, and not a sessional hymn), then the 9th must have something yet more solemn, something exceptional.

Such indeed proves to be, on Sundays only however, a hymn without a title, but performed according unto the order of **"God is the Lord"**: **"Holy is the Lord our God"** (*Hagios Kyrios ho Theos hemon* [Gr. Ἅγιος Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν]), that is, Psalm 98:9 [LXX], the concluding words of this verse; a hymn having, like a prokeimenon, two verses: the 1st verse—the identical passage of the psalm, read with the preceding word: "For (*hoti* [Gr. ὅτι]) holy is the Lord our God"; the 2nd verse—the conclusion of the 2nd verse of the identical psalm: "over all the peoples", with the addition from the basic verse of the words: "our God." Intruding by its distinctive execution (according unto the indicated order with exclamation and chanting) into the smooth flow of the longer preceding and subsequent *(Orig. p. 699)* hymns, this brief hymn by its suddenness directs the special and intensified attention of the worshippers unto a single attribute of God, more than ever revealed unto the world by the Savior's death upon the Cross—an attribute foundational, awesome, and as it were formidable for us, the contemplation of which, however, affords the most exhaustive and most blessed penetration into the Godhead, as is evident from the fact that this attribute alone serves as the subject of the Seraphic praise unto God. This hymn, which was, as discussed below, an exapostilarion and nowadays at times replaces the exapostilarion (on Palm Sunday and Great and Holy Saturday), clearly serves, judging by the manner of its execution, as an identical preparation for the Sunday exapostilarion as **"God is the Lord"** serves for the troparion, whereby the Sunday exapostilarion is singled out from the series of the others. It is chanted (by the choirs alternately, thrice in all) with its preliminary exclamation in the appointed tone, that is, with its solo chanting in this tone, moreover not by the canonarch, but by the deacon, and with an identical chanting, naturally, of the verses as well (usually both the one and the other are simply exclaimed), with the silent participation of the priest. "Then (after the exclamation of the litany) the deacon exclaims: **Holy is the Lord our God** in the appointed tone. Verse 1: **For…**—The priest stands at the customary place."

### History

**"Holy is the Lord"** is the most frequent exapostilarion in the Studite and Evergetis (somewhat less frequently) Typika; for example, it is appointed in the former on September 1, 6, 7, 8, 13, 14, etc. [^2605]; in the latter—on September 4, 7, 8, 13, 14, etc. [^2606]. According unto both Typika this same exapostilarion (Evergetis: *hexapostilarion*), and it alone, was appointed on Sunday, wherein according unto the latter—it was chanted in the tone of the week [^2607]. Its appearance at this place of Matins is explained by the proximity of the end of Matins unto the Liturgy (cf. **"One is Holy"** at the Great Doxology; see Introductory Chapters, 86, 87; cf. the *Kaddish* prayer—with the Seraphic doxology—in the synagogue service—Introductory Chapters, 16, 17).

In the Georgian manuscript of the Jerusalem Typikon **"Holy is the Lord"** is still termed an exapostilarion, although the present exapostilarion is already also present.
In Greek manuscripts it is not explicitly mentioned.

Slavic manuscripts of the 14th century:
"Then (after the litany) the appointed monk chants the verse **Holy is the Lord our God** in the appointed tone, and recites the verses: **For… Over all…** And the choirs after each verse chant **Holy is the Lord our God**" [^2608].
Later manuscripts: "after the 9th ode **Holy is the Lord our God**" [^2609].
The "Order" of Patriarch Philotheos—nothing.
The Old Believer Typikon:
"After the 9th ode the priest says: **Holy is the Lord our God**, Verse 1:… Verse 2…" [^2610].
Under Arseny Sukhanov in the East:
"After the litany **Holy is the Lord our God** at the cliroi thrice, but the priest or deacon does not announce it at all" [^2611].
The modern Greek *Euchologion*—silent.
The modern Greek *Typikon* and *Hieratikon*:
"They chant" *(Orig. p. 700)* **Holy is the Lord our God** "twice" and **Exalt ye the Lord our God** "once" [^2612].

### The Exapostilarion [Svitylen]

The hymn **"Holy is the Lord"**, executed according unto the order of **"God is the Lord"**, serves as a preparation for the exapostilarion [*svitylen*], which occupies here, after the 9th ode of the kanon, an identical position unto that which the sessional hymn occupies after the 3rd ode, and the kontakion after the 6th. If the kontakion surpasses the sessional hymn in solemnity, then the very place of the exapostilarion at the conclusion of the kanon, after such an ode as the 9th ode, compels one to anticipate from it an even greater solemnity. The exapostilarion, indeed, occupies an exceptional position in divine worship. This is a hymn of Matins repeated nowhere else. As its very name shows (*svitylen* [Hymn of Light, Gr. φωταγωγικόν]), it hymns God as Light and the Giver of Light; thus, the exapostilaria of Lenten Matins are all filled with the concept of light (**"Thou Who art Light, O Christ, enlighten me through Thyself"**—Tone 8); weekday exapostilaria frequently make use of this concept (**"By Thy holy Angels"** or **"saints"**, **"Who hast enlightened the whole earth"**—exapostilarion of Monday and Saturday); so likewise the exapostilaria of the greatest feasts (the Nativity of Christ: **"Our Savior, the Dayspring from the East, hath visited us from on high, and we who were in darkness and the shadow have found the truth"**; Theophany: **"… hath enlightened those who sat sleeping in darkness and the shadow, for the unapproachable Light hath come and appeared"**; Pentecost: **"The Father is Light, the Word is Light, and the Holy Spirit is Light"**; the Transfiguration: **"O changeless Light, O Word, Light of the unbegotten Father, in Thy manifest light today on Tabor have we seen the Father as Light, and the Spirit as Light, guiding all creation by light"**). In truth, however, such content is not mandatory for an exapostilarion: usually they simply glorify the celebrated event (cf. **"Having fallen asleep in the flesh"**), for which reason exapostilaria are more frequently termed *hexapostilaria* [Gr. ἐξαποστειλάρια].

The designation "svitylen" [Hymn of Light] is invariably applied only unto Lenten exapostilaria, which all speak of light; whereas the hymns occupying their place at weekday, Sunday, and festal Matins in Greek liturgical books are called only *hexapostilaria*; in Slavic books, however, both one and the other; in relation unto weekday hymns the designation *svitylen* is applied in the Typikon, Chapters 9 and 16, while the designation *exapostilaria* is in the Octoechos and the Horologion [*Sledovannaya Psaltir'*]; unto Sunday hymns—the designation *svitylen* is in the Typikon here, while *exapostilaria* is in the Octoechos; in relation unto festal hymns—*svitylen* is in the Menaion, and *exapostilaria* in the Triodion.

The name "exapostilarion" (*exapostilarion* [Gr. ἐξαποστειλάριον] from *exapostello* [Gr. ἐξαποστέλλω]—I send forth, dispatch) is explained either by the fact that they glorify the sending forth of the Apostles unto the preaching, of which mention is indeed made in the Sunday exapostilaria (Mark of Ephesus) [^2613], yet only in the Sunday ones, and by no means in all of them; or, what is more probable, by the fact that for chanting it a chanter goes forth into the center of the church [^2614], which even nowadays is required for certain exapostilaria (see Great and Holy Monday). — The melody of the exapostilaria *(Orig. p. 701)* does not follow the melody of the tone, but is completely automelon [*samoglasen*] (close unto the kontakion melody), whereby the exapostilarion is likewise singled out from all the hymns of Matins. On great feasts it, like the troparion, is chanted thrice.

### History

The exapostilarion is mentioned in the *Hypotyposis* and *Diatyposis* [^2615]. In the Jerusalem *Akolouthia* of the 9th–12th centuries it is indicated at the present place of Matins, with the addition of a prosomoion [*podoben*] or the note "automelon" [*samoglasen*], sometimes with an indication of the tone [^2616].

### Sunday Exapostilaria

Sunday exapostilaria are distinguished from the other changeable hymns of the Sunday Vigil in that they are closely bound up with the content of the morning Gospel and therefore glorify the multifaceted celebrated event from a single aspect, moreover from an even more particular aspect than that unfolded in the Gospel: in them "it is spoken of the going of the myrrh-bearing women unto the Apostles and of the Apostles unto the Gentiles for the preaching of the Resurrection" [^2617]. An identical content, but apparently broader, among the hymns of Sunday Matins is possessed further only by the stichera at "Glory…" of the Praises [Lauds], which are close in placement unto the exapostilaria, and which for that reason are already directly termed "evangelical" [*eothina*]. Whereas festal exapostilaria are appointed to be chanted twice, sometimes thrice, the Sunday exapostilarion is chanted only once, perhaps because it is twice as long as all the other exapostilaria, or because **"Holy is the Lord"** is also, properly speaking, an exapostilarion. Sunday exapostilaria, like the exapostilaria of saints and in contrast unto great-festal exapostilaria, have, as do all Sunday hymns, a Theotokion. Whereas all Sunday Theotokia, excluding the unchangeable ones (after the troparia **"The Angelic Council"** and after the Praises stichera), glorify the Mother of God without relation unto the event of the Resurrection, very rarely hinting at the latter by isolated expressions, each exapostilarion Theotokion is entirely dedicated unto the depiction of that participation which She took in this event (**"With the disciples Thou didst rejoice…"**—Exapostilarion 1; **"When Thou didst see Thy Son risen from the tomb…"**—Exapostilarion 9; **"Unto the Lord Who rose on the third day from the tomb, O Virgin, pray…"**—Exapostilarion 10), with the sole exception of Exapostilarion 8. Such exceptional content of these Theotokia fully corresponds unto the exceptional character in the series of hymns of the exapostilarion, which, like the hypakoe and the kontakion, is chanted only once at the Vigil. The Sunday joy, as it were continually intensifying and more fully encompassing the whole being of the worshippers, toward the end of the kanon reaches that degree when the worshipper can no longer think of anything except the Resurrection; therefore thenceforth the Theotokia also (after the exapostilarion and the Praises) become resurrectional, while the final Sunday troparion hath no Theotokion at all. *(Orig. p. 702)*

If a saint hath an exapostilarion (and the latter is possessed also by many minor saints—see, for example, September 27), then at "Glory…" his exapostilarion is chanted, but at "Both now…": not the Theotokion of the Menaion exapostilarion (which always hath a Theotokion attached unto itself), but the Sunday Theotokion. Thus it is done even for great saints. This is in view of the special—resurrectional— content of these Theotokia. Only on Feasts of the Lord (which unite their service with the Sunday service), Feasts of the Theotokos, and their forefeasts and afterfeasts is the Sunday Theotokion of the exapostilarion replaced by their exapostilarion.

### History

The Sunday exapostilaria were composed (probably together with their Theotokia), as their inscription in the Octoechos likewise indicates, by the Byzantine Emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus (912–959), the son of Emperor Leo VI the Wise, the author of the morning evangelical stichera. Such authorship secured for them rapid dissemination (cf. **"Only-Begotten Son"**, the creation of Emperor Justinian): in the capacity even of model melodies [prosomoia] they are already indicated in the well-known Jerusalem *Akolouthia* of the 9th–12th centuries; judging by the fact that in all three instances of such indications the 1st Sunday exapostilarion (**"Let us go up with the disciples"**) is invariably named as the model melody [^2618], one may think that all 11 exapostilaria possessed a single melody. Mention is made of them, under the general name, however, of "exapostilaria", by the Studite Typika of Western recensions [^2619], but for some reason they are not known unto the Studite-Alexian and Evergetis Typika: perhaps they were excluded here from the service when the Gospel was transferred first unto the 6th ode of the kanon, and then before the kanon.

The Georgian manuscript of the Jerusalem Typikon: "exapostilaria: **Holy is the Lord**, the appointed evangelical sticheron (that is, exapostilarion, because the evangelical sticheron is placed further on at its own place) twice and the Theotokion once."
Greek manuscripts: "Sunday exapostilarion, of the saint if celebrated, and Theotokion."
Slavic manuscripts: "Then the canonarch says the Sunday exapostilarion, of the saint if there be one, of the Theotokos another" [^2620].
Under Arseny Sukhanov in the East: "They chant the exapostilarion of the Resurrection on the right choir, then on the other they chant another exapostilarion, if there be one; if not, then 'Glory… Both now…' Theotokion" [^2621].
The modern Greek *Euchologion*: "Sunday exapostilarion and of the saint if celebrated."
The modern Greek *Typikon*: "and the exapostilaria."
The *Hieratikon*: "the Sunday exapostilarion, as likewise the Theotokion; if, however, a saint is celebrated, after the Sunday one there is chanted that of the saint, then of the Theotokos from the Menaion."
Old Believer Typikon: as ours [^2622].
*(Orig. p. 703)*

### The Praises [Lauds]

The fourth and final part of Matins begins. It begins, like all services and portions thereof, with psalms. Naturally, the psalms chosen for this place are the final ones in the Psalter. In proportion unto the modest scope of this part of Matins, three were required here (cf. the Hours and Small Compline). These psalms proved to be Psalm 148, **"Praise the Lord from the heavens"**, Psalm 149, **"Sing unto the Lord a new song"**, and Psalm 150, **"Praise God in His saints"**. All of these psalms share one common theme: a summons unto the glorification of God, on which account their group is designated in the Typikon as 'The Praises' (*Ainoi* [οἱ Αἶνοι]): the first psalm invites all creation unto this, beginning with the angels; the second, Israel; the third, the temple, both heavenly and earthly. The appropriateness of these psalms here is evident: conscious of the insufficiency and unworthiness of their own praise of God, when it is already drawing toward its conclusion, the faithful transfer it unto more worthy (among others, unto the 'assembly of the saints') and unceasing performers. These are among the most joyful and ecstatic psalms, thereby forming a contrast unto the calm, contemplative, and often sorrowful initial psalms of the Psalter, on which account they likewise belong toward the end of the service, when the ever-mounting prayerful inspiration reaches its highest point. By reason of their joyous tone, the Praises psalms, alone of all the morning psalms, are not omitted even at Pascha.

### History of Use

Psalms 148–150 conclude the psalter portion of morning synagogal prayer [^2623]. They entered into the composition of Matins, constituting its conclusion, already under St. John Cassian (5th century), and that equally in the East and in the West (Introductory Chapter, 147). They are mentioned in the present place of Matins under their present name by the well-known description of the Sinai Vigil of the 7th century (ibid., 295); decisively all rites of Western divine worship from the most ancient times begin with them the final part of Matins, Matins in the proper sense, called after them *Laudes* (already under St. Benedict—ibid., 312–319); with them all Eastern non-Chalcedonian rites conclude Matins: the Armenian, Abyssinian, Nestorian (ibid., 299, 300, 303), and Jacobite, with the latter concluding Midnight Office with them as well [^2624].

*(Orig. p. 704)*

### Order of Chanting the Praises Psalms

The order of chanting the Praises psalms is set forth in detail in the Heirmologion and the Psalter with Supplement [*Sledovannaya Psaltir*]; in the Typikon, however, in the present place, it is stated briefly: 'on the Praises, **Every breath**, in the tone of the day.' This signifies, as is evident from the aforementioned detailed order of chanting these psalms, that the psalms must be chanted festally, that is, beginning not with the 1st verse of Psalm 148, as on weekdays, but this verse must be preceded by the final verse of Psalm 150: **"Let everything that hath breath praise the Lord"**, and moreover they must be chanted in the tone of the day, and not with a simple, recitative melody, as on weekdays. Thus, in their festal execution, the Praises psalms begin with the verse expressing their theme (just as the Blameless [Amomos / Kathisma 17] at a funeral begins with the words **"Blameless in the way"**, and on Great Saturday with the verse: **"Blessed art Thou, O Lord"**), and with the same they conclude, whereby their entire group, constituting as it were a single hymn, returns by its end unto its beginning in token of infinity and continuity.

The subsequent chanting of the Praises psalms on feasts and weekdays has in common that their first two verses possess a refrain from Psalm 64:2 [LXX 64:1]: **"Praise is due unto Thee, O God"** [*Tebe podobayet pesn Bogu*], analogous unto the refrain unto the psalms of **"Lord, I have cried"**—**"Hear me, O Lord"** (and in contrast unto the more solemn introductory psalm of the Vigil, which has a refrain after every verse). This refrain in the festal execution of the psalm is chanted once after each verse; on weekdays, however, as if in compensation for the absence of the introductory verse **"Let everything that hath breath"**, it is chanted twice after the first verse (that is, three times in all): after the 1st half of the verse, **"Praise the Lord from the heavens"**, and again after the entire verse [^2625], that is, entirely according unto the same order as the verse: **"Hear me, O Lord"** at **"Lord, I have cried"** (see above, p. 542). Not without reason are the first two verses of the Praises psalms marked with a special refrain: they are most appropriate here, since, inviting the angels themselves unto the glorification of God, they express thereby most forcefully the deficiency of all our praise hitherto, just as verses 1 and 2 of Psalm 140, accompanied by a refrain, speak of the insufficiency of our evening sacrifice.

The subsequent verses of the psalms are chanted without refrains alternately by both choirs, and in the Heirmologion the distribution of verses for such chanting is provided; this distribution coincides with the biblical division of the psalms into verses, except that in view of the length of the final—14th—verse of Psalm 148, half of verse 13 is joined unto verse 12, and the conclusion of verse 13 with verse 14 is broken into two parts, but the number of verses in the psalm remained the same (14, seven for each choir); of Psalm 149, eight verses are chanted without refrains (four unto each choir); beginning with the final verse of this psalm: **"To execute upon them judgment"**, unto the verses of the Praises psalms, of which there remains one in Psalm 149 and six in Psalm 150, the stichera on the Praises are joined, wherein before each of the stichera a verse of the psalm is chanted, but the last two verses of Psalm 150 are chanted as one, so that the number of refrains might come out even, and on account of the brevity of the final verse.

*(Orig. p. 705)*

By the Praises psalms with their stichera, therefore, the sticheric melody of the tone is introduced once again into the Vigil, and for the first time into Matins, after the dominance in the divine service first of the troparic-kathismatic melody and then of the kanon-melody. Thereby the Vigil in musical terms returns unto its beginning (the stichera at **"Lord, I have cried"**, the aposticha, and the Litiya stichera), forming a sacred circle of eternity. Having passed through a multitude of diverse melodies of the same tone (sticheric, troparic, sessional, antiphonal, prokeimenon melody, kanon, kontakion, exapostilarion), the Vigil enters anew into the first melody of this long series, the simplest of all, and by this simplicity of its, austere and majestic, perhaps most answering unto the Christian taste of the worshippers. This return unto the sticheric melody is prompted also by the natural subsidence of prayerful ecstasy after the heightened fervor which this ecstasy attained in the kanon (**"Come, let us clap our hands"**, **"My heart hath poured forth"**). This subsidence proceeds further, through the tranquil melody of the Great Doxology, into the serene prayer of two litanies, and finally into the simple reading of the First Hour.

### History of Use

According unto the Studite-Alexian (and perhaps also according unto the ancient Jerusalem) Typikon, the Praises psalms had refrains after each verse, specifically the following (in parentheses are variants from the Studite Typikon of the Horologion of the St. Petersburg Sophia Library No. 1052 of the 13th century): Psalm 148 up unto and including verse 6: 'Praise is due unto Thee, O God'; from verse 7 (8): 'Give glory unto God'; verse 12 (13b): 'Unto Him (Thee) praise is due (unto God?)'; Psalm 149 from verse 1: 'Glory to Thee, Holy Father'; from verse 6 (7): 'Spare us, O Lord (Spare us)'; Psalm 150 from verse 1: 'O Son of God, have mercy on us'; at verse 3 (and 4): 'Glory to Him Who hath given (shown) the light'; from verse 4 (5): 'Glory is due unto Thee, O Lord' [^2626]. The Old Believer *Chasovnik* indicates no refrains whatsoever unto the Praises psalms [^2627]. According unto the Roman rite, Psalms 148–150 have before them the antiphon 'Alleluia' (once) and after them 'Glory be to the Father... Alleluia' (thrice), but among themselves they are not separated, in contrast unto other psalms, by 'Glory be to the Father'; according unto the Mozarabic rite, they have before them: '*Lauda*, Praise the Lord from the heavens, Alleluia (twice). Praise Him in the highest, Alleluia (twice)' and the doxology likewise only at the end of the 3rd psalm.

### Stichera on the Praises

The stichera on the Praises (*eis tous ainous* [εἰς τοὺς αἴνους]) are not indispensable with the Praises psalms, but constitute in general an appurtenance of Matins of a semi-festal type, appearing sometimes for six-verse [*shesterik*] saints (see, for example, September 6 and 24, November 1, but October 3, January 16, 18, 19) and being absent on forefeasts, afterfeasts, and Saturdays, with certain exceptions; moreover, stichera on the Praises are permitted even at weekday Matins if it is necessary to transfer them hither from **"Lord, I have cried"** on account of insufficient space there (see the Typikon, Monday of the 1st week of the Great Fast, at Matins). The usual, normal number of stichera on the Praises is four; *(Orig. p. 706)* thus it is always, even on great feasts—Pascha, the Nativity of Christ (on Palm Sunday, six, on account of special considerations), excepting Sunday, when there are eight on account of special circumstances (see below). So few are appointed (one might say, the minimal number for antiphonal chanting: two unto each choir), perhaps in view of fatigue toward the end of the service.

### History

The stichera on the Praises under the name of 'troparia' are mentioned by the well-known description of Sinai Matins of the 7th century (Introductory Chapter, 295) and in the Hypotyposis of certain recensions [^2628]. In the Studite Typikon the normal number of stichera on the Praises was considered, apparently, to be six [^2629], but the Jerusalem Typikon from the most ancient manuscripts appoints four [^2630].

### Sunday Stichera on the Praises

The stichera on the Praises of Sunday Matins are singled out from the series of others by their number: there are eight of them, twice as many as for the greatest feasts: four called directly 'Resurrectional' and four 'Anatolian' [*vostochny*] (cf. p. 545). Serving as refrains for them are six verses of the Praises psalms, beginning from the 9th, the last, verse of Psalm 149, and, in addition, two psalm verses specifically selected for the event of the Resurrection and named in the Typikon (chapters 3, 4, and others) 'Resurrectional refrains'—the very same that serve as refrains unto the sessional hymns: **"Arise, O Lord..."** and **"I will confess Thee, O Lord"** (Psalm 9:33, 2 [LXX]). Having for themselves specifically festal verses, these latter stichera are properly speaking no longer Praises stichera, but aposticha, on which account for their chanting the choirs unite; this convergence takes place already at the final verse of the Praises psalms (at **"Let everything that hath breath"**), so that there result three aposticha stichera. In terms of content, the Praises stichera, especially the Anatolian ones, are somewhat longer and more complex than the stichera at **"Lord, I have cried"** and the aposticha; they not infrequently turn with reproach unto the Judeans who wished to conceal the Resurrection of Christ.

In contrast unto the stichera at **"Lord, I have cried"** and the aposticha, the Praises, as the concluding and most solemn stichera, have their own specifically Sunday Doxastikon [*slavnik*], which borrows its content from the Sunday morning Gospel and is therefore called the 'evangelical' or 'morning sticheron' [*heothinon*]; as with the exapostilaria, there are consequently 11 evangelical stichera. The tones selected for stichera 1–8 are Tones 1–8; for the 9th, Tone 5; for the 10th, Tone 6; and for the 11th, Tone 8; that is, for the final stichera the final tones are used, excluding the 7th, as heavy (grave) (cf. the tones for the days of Bright Week, where this tone is likewise omitted). The evangelical stichera on Sundays with special commemorations are replaced by others and transferred unto the end of Matins.

Likewise, in contrast unto the stichera at **"Lord, I have cried"** and the aposticha, the Sunday Praises stichera have a Theotokion of Sunday content, but common unto all tones: **"Most blessed art thou, O Virgin Theotokos"** [*Preblagoslovenna yesi*]. It enumerates all the fruits of the Resur*(Orig. p. 707)*rection (in three homogeneous pairs), glorifying their indirect Cause. For this Theotokion Tone 2 is chosen, as the most joyful tone in the sticheric melody (in it are chanted the stichera at **"Lord, I have cried"** at the Nativity of Christ and Theophany; cf. the parallel Tone 6 for **"Having beheld the Resurrection of Christ"**). In view of the great significance of this Theotokion, it is not omitted on Sunday even when the latter coincides with a Great Feasts of the Theotokos (it serves also as the Theotokion of Tone 2 after the 2nd Kathisma).

Departures from the indicated order in the chanting of the Praises stichera are made for great, polyeleos, and six-verse saints (see the Typikon, ch. 3, 4, and 5), for forefeasts and afterfeasts occurring on Sunday (see September 7 and 9), and for the Sundays of the Holy Fathers and of the Triodion (see October 11 and the Great Fast).

### History

The Sunday stichera, specifically the first four of them, are given by the well-known Jerusalem *Akolouthia* of the 9th–12th centuries [^2631] and, undoubtedly, are intended by the Hypotyposis of certain recensions, which prescribes that they be doubled, and by the Evergetis Typikon, which likewise prescribes that they be doubled and indicates their number as four [^2632].

The Studite-Alexian Typikon, which had, in addition unto the Praises stichera, at every festal and Sunday Matins separately (after the litanies) the aposticha as well, indicates three Sunday Praises stichera, placing the fourth, evidently, on the aposticha (on Triodion Sundays it was doubled) [^2633].

According unto the Old Believer Typikon, the verses are taken from verse 1 of Psalm 150, and **"Let everything that hath breath"** is a separate verse [^2634].

The evangelical stichera belong, as their present inscription likewise shows, unto Emperor Leo VI the Wise (886–911) and are appointed by the aforementioned Jerusalem *Akolouthia* for chanting immediately after the Gospel at 'Glory... Both now...' [^2635]. They are, perhaps, a remnant of the ancient custom of chanting the Gospel, preserved unto this day in the Roman Church (for example, on Palm Sunday in the procession Matthew 21 and John 12 are chanted; cf. our sticheron on Palm Sunday, **"Six days before Pascha"**). According unto the Asmatic Office [*pesnennoye posledovanie*], at the evangelical sticheron the entrance with the Gospel took place (Introductory Chapter, 347). — The hymn **"Most blessed art thou"** in the Typikon of the Great Church of Constantinople of the 9th century and according unto the Sinai Kanonarion (9th–10th centuries) serves as the entrance troparion at the Liturgy of the 3rd day of Pascha. It stands in the present place of Sunday Matins in the Evergetis Typikon [^2636] and in the Asmatic Office under Symeon of Thessalonica (Introductory Chapter, 347). But according unto the Studite-Alexian Typikon, here stands the Theotokion of the tone of the day [^2637]. In early printed editions and among the *(Orig. p. 708)* Old Believers: 'Blessed is God (cf. below: **"He Who is blessed, Christ our God"**, **"Glory to Thee, O Christ God, our hope"**) Who was thus pleased,' without 'Glory to Thee' [^2638].

### THE GREAT DOXOLOGY

The detailed glorification of God for His various particular benefactions is concluded at the Vigil with a general glorification of Him for all benefactions. In this glorification the inspiration of the worshippers, the strength and warmth of their feeling, reach a zenith at which the mind can no longer dwell on particulars, on these or those mercies of God, even though they be so great as our salvation through the death and resurrection of the Son of God, but is wholly immersed in thankful contemplation of all the height of God and of all our nothingness and unworthiness before Him. Such is the character of that doxology with which all the hymns of the Vigil are concluded, and which is justly called 'Great'.

### "Glory to Thee Who Hast Shown Us the Light"

Such an outburst of religious feeling as this doxology represents is most immediately evoked by the first glimmer of morning dawn arriving at this moment of the All-Night Vigil. If, 'having come unto the setting of the sun and beheld the evening light,' the faithful pour forth their feelings in so ecstatic a hymn as **"Glory, O Tranquil Light"** [*Phos Hilaron*], then the sight of the morning light being born out of the darkness of night must attune them yet more deeply and warmly unto the contemplation of God as the Uncreated Light (**"in Thy light shall we see light"**). The morning hymn is far longer and fuller than the evening hymn, and therefore begins with a direct thanksgiving unto God (in the evening hymn thanksgiving is indirect: 'we praise the Father and the Son...') for the morning dawn, which is expressed in the solemn exclamation: **"Glory to Thee Who hast shown us the light"**.

Unto whom it belongs to pronounce this exclamation is not indicated in the Typikon in the order of the Sunday Vigil; but in chapter 7 it is stated that this verse, like that preceding it at weekday Matins: **"To Thee praise is due"**, and the Great Doxology [^2639] itself (of course, if it is read), must be pronounced by the superior. On this ground, probably, the pronunciation of this verse at Matins was assigned unto the priest. Yet both this prescription of the Typikon and the close connection of the verse with the Great Doxology rather demand its pronunciation by the one who executes the Great Doxology as well, that is, at the Vigil (and festal Matins), by the choir (hence the vacillation in practice: in some places the verse is assigned to be pronounced by the deacon).

### According unto Ancient Typika

The verse was one of the refrains unto the Praises psalms (see above, p. 705). In the manuscript Horologion and the Old Believer *Chasovnik*: **"Glory to Him Who hath shown us *(Orig. p. 709)* the light"** [^2640]. In certain Greek manuscripts: **"Glory to Him Who hath shown the true light"** [^2641]. In the Greek Horologion: **"Glory to Thee Who hast shown the light"** [^2642].
