The printed Greek Jerusalem Typikon: 'it is necessary to know that after Ode 9 the priest says: **"Holy is the Lord our God"** and the beginning **"Glory to God in the highest"** at the Great Doxologies' [^2643].

### Content of the Great Doxology

The doxology itself begins with the angelic hymn at the birth of the Savior—whereby Matins, already drawing near its end, returns unto its beginning (a favorite device in ecclesiastical hymnody). Such a lofty, heavenly hymn sanctifies our lips (as also before Matins) for our own hymn, which begins with the words: **"We praise Thee"** (properly: 'we sing of Thee'—*hymnoumen* [ὑμνοῦμεν]), **"we bless Thee, we worship Thee"** (cf. with the conclusion unto the recent 8th ode of the kanon), recalling by their brevity and generality the greatest hymn of the Divine Liturgy (**"We sing unto Thee"**): just as there it is not specified for what we sing, bless, and thank the Lord and for what we pray unto Him, because we thank then for all things and pray for all things, and an enumeration would turn out to be endless, so neither is it specified here, but rather the supreme cause of our praise, worship, and thanksgiving is indicated: the great glory of God. Following this glorification of God in the hymn comes prayer unto Him, the transition unto which is served by a prayerful address unto all Persons of the Holy Trinity separately. From the Holy Trinity, prayer is directed principally unto our Intercessor in heaven, the Lamb of God (a favorite name for the Savior among ancient Christians), of Whom we ask mercy (the fundamental petition of all prayers of the Vigil—the litanies), conditioned among other things by the acceptance of these present prayers of ours (long and already drawing toward their end). For confidence in the success of this petition, it concludes with that solemn confession of Christ which is proclaimed at the Divine Liturgy immediately before the communion of the Holy Mysteries: '**[For Thou only art] Holy, [Thou only art] Lord, Jesus Christ, in the glory of God the Father**' (the existence of such a Son yet increases the unmeasured glory of God, though there would seem to be no room to increase it). Hereby concludes the first part of the Great Doxology, ending with its first 'Amen'.

The second part is no longer so joyful and ecstatic; moreover, like the 3rd part, it is almost entirely compilatory—composed of the words of Sacred Scripture. The glorification of God which fills it (**"Every day"**, consequently also on the day now dawning, **"will I bless Thee"**, because Thy name will be glorified forever—from Psalm 144:2 [LXX]; and earlier it was glorified: **"Blessed art Thou, O Lord God of our fathers"**—Daniel 3:26 [LXX 3:25]), is darkened here by the consciousness of our sinfulness, which could as it were disrupt and interrupt this everlasting glorification of God (cf. 'in the glory...' at the end of the 1st part) by a single sinful day, from which may God preserve us today. The second 'Amen'.

*(Orig. p. 710)*

The third part is already exclusively prayerful. Penitential sorrow here intensifies already to such a degree that the joyful glorification of God with which the Great Doxology began, and which ought to be its principal subject, scarcely breaks through here and there in isolated expressions (**"Blessed art Thou, O Lord"**—Psalm 118:12 [LXX]). This part also begins with prayer, and not with praise, in contrast unto the first two parts, with a prayer of general character for the mercy of God, tempered, however, by hope in God (**"Let Thy mercy, O Lord, be upon us, as we have hoped in Thee"**—Psalm 32:22 [LXX]). This general prayer then assumes a more definite character and is reduced unto a petition unto God—to teach us His statutes, a petition expressed in the words of Psalm 118: **"Blessed art Thou, O Lord: teach me Thy statutes"**, and repeated thrice—unto the three Persons of the Holy Trinity (and this repetition is made not with a variation in the text, as at Vespers in **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"**, but with literal precision, whereby the effect is intensified). Further, this still rather general petition is developed and elucidated: for the realization in life of the statutes of God, purification from sins and the ability to do the will of God are needed. Both can be granted only by God Himself, unto Whom one must have recourse for help, as all have always had recourse unto Him (**"Lord, Thou hast been our refuge in generation and generation"**—Psalm 89:1 [LXX]); from Him purification from sins is first implored (in the words of Psalm 40:5 [LXX]: 'I said'—an intensified petition: **"Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against Thee"**); and then yet more intensely (**"Lord, unto Thee have I fled..."**)—instruction in His will (Psalm 142:9–10 [LXX]). The prayer concludes with a firm assurance of its fulfillment, grounded (as in the exclamations after the litany: 'For Thou art...') upon the special closeness unto us of God (**"my God"**, Psalm 142:9, 10 [LXX]), the source of life and light (**"in Thy light shall we see light"**, that is, the morning light—a return unto the initial exclamation of the Great Doxology at its conclusion). By its final words: **"continue"** (prolong, *parateinon* [παράτεινον]) **"Thy mercy unto them that know Thee"**, together with the preceding: **"for with Thee..."** (Psalm 35:10, 11 [LXX]), the third part of the Great Doxology returns unto its beginning, wherein its initial petition for the mercy of God toward us ('let it be') is here intensified ('continue').

One cannot fail to observe that the indicated connection between the individual sentences of this long hymn is not very close; the transitions in it from one thought unto another are rather unexpected. The hymn consists, properly speaking, of disconnected prayerful and laudatory exclamations, of which each is too complete, too finished in itself, for there to be any need of continuation or supplementation thereof. All expressions are taken from Sacred Scripture, and from there the most powerful were chosen.

### History

The foundation of the Great Doxology is the angelic hymn at the birth of the Savior, and it was introduced into it, presumably, after the example of the Divine Liturgy, when the latter was transferred unto the morning and began at times to merge with Matins (Introductory Chapter, 88ff.); in the Liturgy of the Apostolic Constitutions this hymn *(Orig. p. 711)* is appointed immediately before communion [^2644], and in the Liturgy of the Apostles Addai and Mari [^2645] and our own—at the beginning. From the Divine Liturgy also, presumably, was borrowed into the morning hymn the phrase **"We praise Thee, we bless Thee"**: at the Matins of the *Testamentum Domini* of the 3rd century a similar expression, but yet closer, almost unto literal identity, unto the present **"We sing unto Thee"** at the Divine Liturgy, constitutes the response of the people unto individual parts of the episcopal or priestly morning prayer (Introductory Chapter, 86). Finally, the third borrowing of the Great Doxology from ancient liturgies is the invocation: **"O Lamb of God, that takest away the sins of the world..."**; according unto St. John Chrysostom: 'not in vain do we make commemoration of the departed at the holy mystery and add prayer for them unto that Lamb Who takes upon Himself the sin of the world' [^2646]; the communion verse at the Liturgy of St. Peter: **"O Lamb of God, that takest away the sin of the world, have mercy on us"** [^2647]; at the Roman Mass after the commingling of the Body and Blood in the chalice (after the Our Father shortly before communion) the priest pronounces: **"Lamb of God, that takest away the sins of the world, have mercy on us"**—twice, and: **"Lamb of God, that takest away the sins of the world, grant us peace"** [^2648]; the Roman litany concludes with the same threefold invocation with the endings: 'spare us', 'graciously hear us', 'have mercy on us, O Lord' [^2649]. (Unto the widespread liturgical application from antiquity of this invocation catacomb depictions of the Savior in the form of a lamb may also have contributed).

Concerning the morning hymn **"Glory to God in the highest"** mention is made by Pseudo-Athanasius in the work *De Virginitate* [On Virginity]; the beginning of the hymn cited by him exhibits the following variants from the present text: it lacks 'we praise Thee' and 'we glorify Thee'; the fragment concludes with the words: 'we worship Thee and the rest' [^2650].

The *Apostolic Constitutions*, in the appendix unto Book VII, provide the following text of the hymn, entitling it in certain manuscripts "Morning Doxology":
"**Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will among men** (*Slava v vyshnikh Bogu i na zemli mir, v chelovetsekh blagovolenie*). **We praise Thee, we sing unto Thee, we bless Thee, we glorify Thee, we worship Thee, through the great High Priest, Thee, the true God, the only unbegotten, the only unapproachable, for Thy great glory. O Lord, Heavenly King, God the Father Almighty; O Lord God, Father of Christ, the spotless Lamb Who taketh away the sin of the world. Receive our supplication, Thou that sittest upon the Cherubim. For Thou only art holy, Thou only art the Lord Jesus, Christ of the God of all created nature, our King; through Whom unto Thee be glory, honor, and adoration**" [^2651].
In this manner, the monument refers even the second "**O Lord God**" unto God the Father and not unto Christ, and by virtue of this and the omission of "**O Holy Spirit**", it directs the prayer solely unto the Father [^2652]. In the Latin Church, where the Great Doxology *(Orig. p. 712)* is appointed according unto all rites at the beginning of the Mass after the Introit, almost immediately before the Epistle (in the Mozarabic rite also as a hymn for the Nativity of Christ), it likewise corresponds unto the first strophe of ours (concluding with "**in the glory of God the Father**") and contains the following variants compared with ours: "good will unto men" (*hominibus bonae voluntatis*); (**we praise**—*laudamus*, **we worship**—*adoramus*); unto "**we give thanks unto Thee**" the Mozarabic adds: "we speak a hymn unto Thee", and in the same: "for Thy great glory"; "**O Lord**" (1st time) + "**God**" (**Almighty**—*omnipotens*, as in the Creed); "**O Christ**" Mozarabic + "**Most High**" (*altissime*); there is no "**O Holy Spirit**"; instead of "sin"—"sins"; "**Thou only art Lord**" = Mozarabic + "**Thou only art Most High**"; instead of "**Jesus Christ**" (2nd time) the vocative case + "**with the Holy Spirit**". The hymn is contained in the *Codex Alexandrinus* of the Holy Scriptures and others as an appendix unto the Psalms, and in the ancient "Order" [*Posledovanie*] for the feast of Basil the Great, Gregory the Theologian, and John Chrysostom [^2653] in the present festal form with the following variants: "sin"—"sins"; "**have mercy on us, Thou that takest away the sins of the world, receive our prayer**" is absent from the "Order"; instead of "**in this day**"—"this day" in the codices; "**Let Thy mercy, O Lord, be upon us, according as we have hoped in Thee**" is found only in the "Order"; "**Blessed art Thou, O Lord**", as also at present, thrice.
In the most ancient Slavic manuscripts it is not indicated that "**Blessed art Thou, O Lord**" is said thrice [^2654].
According unto the Studite Typika of certain recensions, the Great Doxology on feasts as well consisted of two parts, as at present on weekdays, and these parts were separated by the Augmented Litany, after which was sung the portion beginning from "**Vouchsafe, O Lord**" (*Spodobi, Gospodi*) (Introductory Chapter, 368). A trace of such a practice is found also in early-printed Books of Hours [*Chasoslovy*], for instance Moscow 1602 (= Old Believer) and Lviv 1642, where the doxology is given only in our present weekday form (though, of course, entirely continuously), with the rubric (in the second Book of Hours) beneath "**Blessed art Thou, O Lord**": "if the doxology be sung, thrice thus; but if it be read, say this: **Blessed art Thou, O Master... Blessed art Thou, O Holy One...**" [^2655].
Nevertheless, the festal form of the doxology is, apparently, more ancient, and the morning hymn "**Vouchsafe, O Lord**", detached from it, is indebted, presumably, unto imitation of Vespers. The festal form could have developed within the confines of the Great Church of Constantinople and the Holy Sepulchre, and therefore prior unto the Studite Typikon, certain recensions of which know it, while the Studite-Alexian applied it, presumably, only on Great Saturday and Pascha; from the practice of the Holy Sepulchre this form was transmitted unto the Jerusalem Typikon.
The text of the Great Doxology brought from Greece by Arseny Sukhanov lacked "**have mercy on us; Thou that takest away the sins of the world**" [^2656]; the present Greek *Horologion* is as ours, differing only in punctuation: "... **Son of the Father,** *(Orig. p. 713)* **Thou that takest away the sin of the world, have mercy on us; Thou that takest away the sins of the world, receive our prayer; Thou that sittest at the right hand of the Father, and have mercy on us**" [^2657].
Slavic manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon: "Thou that takest away the sins of the whole world—Thou that takest away the sins of the world" and have no amen [^2658].
Early-printed Books of Hours have "sins" in the plural both times [^2659].

### The Trisagion (Great)

Begun with an angelic hymn, the Great Doxology likewise concludes with an angelic (according unto tradition) hymn: "**Holy God...**" (*Svyaty Bozhe*). Apart from the Divine Liturgy, this is the only place in the church service where the Trisagion is sung rather than read, independently and according unto a special order: not only thrice, but with the refrain **Glory... Both now...**, and with a repetition one and a half times more after this refrain. The absence of the prayers that customarily accompany it, even the **Our Father**, concentrates upon the hymn all attention and answers unto the laudatory and hymnographic coloring of this entire portion of Matins (cf. its designation in Western worship—*Laudes*).

### History

The Trisagion is not appended unto the Great Doxology by the aforementioned biblical codices that provide the latter, but only by the "Order" [*Posledovanie*], without the designation "thrice".
In one recension of the Typikon of the Great Church of Constantinople this Trisagion, at least on Great Saturday, was sung in Tone 2 [^2660].
According unto the Studite-Alexian Typikon this Trisagion occurred with the **Our Father** at the very end of Matins before the troparion and dismissal (as at Vespers) [^2661].
Hence Greek manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon state: "The Trisagion without the **Our Father**"; Slavic manuscripts: "afterwards in the tone, thrice **Holy God**, **Glory... Both now...**, **Holy Immortal**. Then again **Holy God** once. Then the priest the exclamation: **For Thine is the kingdom**." The Old Believer Typikon: "The Trisagion with singing without the **Our Father**, the priest saith: **For Thine is the kingdom**" [^2662].

### The Singing of the Great Doxology

In the present place of the Typikon nothing is said regarding the manner of executing the Great Doxology—whether it ought to be read or sung. Its chanting is indicated in the order for the Exaltation of the Cross: "while the Great Doxology is sung." That it must be sung is demonstrated also by its designation as "great", since in volume it is shorter than the weekday doxology, as well as by the existence from antiquity of a distinctive melody for it. The melody for the Great Doxology is idiomelon [*samoglasen*]; in it resounds a sense of exceptional tranquility, peace, and contentment in God. It is a quiet and slow melody. Concerning the singing of the Great Doxology on August 1 and on the 3rd Sunday of the Fast it is stated: "quietly and with voice," "in a quiet voice" [*tikhoglasno*].

*(Orig. p. 714)*

### According unto the Ancient Typika

The well-known description of Sinai Matins (Introductory Chapter, 295) mentions the solemn singing of the Great Doxology on feasts, when the priest began it. With exceptional solemnity it was sung according unto the Typikon of the Great Church of Constantinople, where the domesticus began it with a cross in his hands, taken up first by the priests, and then by the chanters (ibid., 347). But according unto the Studite Typikon of the Alexian recension it was chanted [^2663] in recitative ("*vly*"), like the Six Psalms, the Introductory Psalm, **"O Gladsome Light"** (*Svete tikhiy*), **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"** (*Spodobi, Gospodi*), and **"Now lettest Thou Thy servant depart"** (*Nyne otpushchaeshi*) with the Trisagion and troparion [^2664], while it was sung musically only on Great Saturday (Introductory Chapter, 368), but at Pascha as always ("quietly" [*potikhu*]) [^2665]. This singing was close unto reading; for this reason, even with the ascendancy among us of the Jerusalem Typikon, as a survival of the Studite the custom of reading the Great Doxology on feasts as well persisted stubbornly, concerning which Tsar Ivan IV complained unto the Stoglav Council, noting that they sing it in required cases only in such cities as Novgorod and Pskov [^2666].
Nikon of the Black Mountain considered the singing of the Great Doxology to be one of the principal peculiarities of the Jerusalem Typikon (Introductory Chapter, 368), which preserved these features from ancient cathedral practice, perhaps through the medium of the Typikon of the Holy Sepulchre. Yet Western Studite Typika likewise possess the term "Great Doxology" (see ibid.), as does the Evergetis Typikon, which remarks that it must be sung *litos kai hesychos* [λιτῶς καὶ ἡσύχως] (simply and quietly) [^2667].
Georgian manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon: "**Glory to God in the highest** with the voice"; Greek manuscripts: "the Great Doxology"; the most ancient Slavic manuscripts cite it in full (perhaps because in the Books of Hours it stood in weekday form), and one (Moscow Synodal Library No. 329/384): "the Great Doxology is sung in Tone 6" [^2668].
The "Order" [*Diataxis*] of Patriarch Philotheus: "with the beginning of the doxology the priest enters within the sanctuary, while the deacon at its conclusion pronounces the litany" [^2669].

### The Sunday Troparion

After the present Trisagion, which, in contrast unto all other Trisagia in the daily services, might be called great, at Sunday Mat*(Orig. p. 715)*ins, as at any festal Matins, a troparion follows, just as a troparion or kontakion is sung after every Trisagion (excluding that which forms part of the Usual Beginning): at the conclusion of Vespers and weekday Matins, at the royal portion of Matins, at all the Hours, at the Typika, at Small Compline, and at all three parts of Great Compline. This is already a second singing of the troparion during Matins, whereas the troparion is customarily sung during each daily service only once. Yet Matins is an exceedingly long service, and each of its three parts must possess a troparion or kontakion. In musical terms, Matins returns by the present troparion unto its beginning. Because the troparion at Matins is sung already for the second time, and because it takes place at the final and briefest portion of Matins, it is sung not according unto the full order, but according unto an abbreviated order, that is, not twice or thrice, but once; and the Sunday troparion, moreover, is sung without a Theotokion. The absence of the latter places the present Sunday troparion on a par with the troparia of the Twelve Great Feasts, which do not require a Theotokion alongside them. This troparion occupies an exceptional position among not only Sunday troparia, but also all other troparia in that it permits no combination with any other troparion whatsoever: even upon concurrence with a Great Feast of the Theotokos, "the troparion is of the Resurrection only" (see Typikon, September 8, "if on Sunday"). This is, presumably, in view of the special dignity of the present troparia, distinguished by a majestic simplicity and a certain triumphant quality. Examining the Resurrection of the Savior from the interior aspect (especially the 1st troparion), they provide a complete catalogue, potent precisely by its brevity, of all the boundless fruits of this event for us—a catalogue so fitting now, in conclusion of all the Sunday hymns of Matins. The 1st troparion is as it were more forceful and ecstatic, while the 2nd is fuller and more concrete. And of the melodies for the troparia, Tones 1 and 2 were selected. The 1st is sung under the odd tones, of which the 5th is close (in Greek, "plagal" / indirect) unto Tone 1; the 2nd under the even tones, of which the 6th is its "plagal". Moreover, the melodies of these troparia are idiomela [*samoglasny*], for which reason their tones are not indicated in the Book of Hours and the Octoechos, but only in the Typikon. In that they scarcely follow the tones, they are ranked higher than the "dismissal" (= also at **"The Lord is God"**) Sunday troparia, though, of course, yielding unto the directly Paschal hymns of the Vigil, **"Having beheld the Resurrection of Christ"** (*Voskresenie Khristovo videvshe*) and **"Jesus having risen from the tomb"** (*Voskres Iisus ot groba*), which do not follow the tone of the Sunday at all.

### Their History

According unto the inscription in the Greek *Euchologion*, the troparia belong unto St. John of Damascus. According unto the Typikon of the Great Church of Constantinople of the 9th century, the 1st troparion at Paschal Matins served as one of the only two troparia and hymns here in honor of the feast in general, being appointed specifically at Psalm 50, which occupied a central place at the Vigil (the other troparion, **"Unto the creature that boweth down"**, was the introit troparion); **"Having risen from the tomb"** (*Voskres iz groba*) stood at the Matins of Bright Monday. Exactly thus is it also in the Sinai Kanonarion. In both monuments the 1st troparion is in Tone 3 [^2670]. *(Orig. p. 716)* In the Jerusalem "Order" the 1st troparion at Paschal Matins occurs after the stichera **"A sacred Pascha"** (*Paskha svyashchennaya*) and **"Christ is risen"** (*Khristos voskrese*) (thrice) with the following variants: "hath come to pass" [*byst*] and "our" [*nasheya*] are absent; unto "of life" is added "unto Christ God"; absent is "by death" [^2671]. Regarding the order of singing troparia at the Asmatic Matins—Introductory Chapter, 347.
The Studite-Alexian Typikon knows these troparia and their present alternation, appointing them under the title of "the Sunday troparion" after the aposticha of Matins [^2672].
The Evergetis [Typikon prescribes] only **"Today salvation is come unto the world"** (*Dnes spasenie miru*) [Tone 3].
The Jerusalem Typikon in Georgian manuscripts: "one of the Sunday troparia"; ancient Greek manuscripts: "and the Sunday troparion, that is, **Having risen from the tomb** and **Today salvation is come unto the world**" (= printed editions: + "for they are sung one after the other") [^2673]; later Greek manuscripts transpose them and indicate which tone takes which, as at present [^2674].
Slavic manuscripts and the Old Believer Typikon: **"Today salvation is come"** in Tone 3, and **"Having risen"** in Tone 2, the alternation being as at present [^2675].
The present Constantinopolitan Typikon—only **"Today salvation is come"** [^2676].
The present *Euchologion*: **"Today salvation is come"** in Tone 4, for Tones 1–4, and likewise the *Horologion*, but **"Having risen"**—Tone 8 [^2677].
Among the Old Believers, in the 2nd troparion the word "of hades" is not read [^2678].

### The Concluding Litanies of Matins

### The Augmented Litany at Matins

The conclusion of Matins possesses the same composition as that of Vespers, yet this is fully the case only at weekday Matins in comparison with weekday Vespers. The conclusion of festal, and consequently of Sunday, Matins differs from the conclusion of such Vespers in that the Augmented Litany and the Litany of Supplication are not separated here by anything, but follow immediately one after the other, by virtue of which they merge into one great and majestic prayer, wherein the second complements the first, supplicating of God in detail all that is necessary for the persons for whom the Augmented Litany prays. Since these are secondary litanies at the Vigil, the Augmented Litany is shortened by the omission of the first two petitions, which contain an amplification of the thought of the 3rd (in the Great Litany and the Litany of Supplication, which likewise recur at the Vigil, such an abbreviation is impossible). Like the Great Litany and in contrast unto the less prominent Litany of Supplication, the Augmented Litany never changes its exclamation, even in the present case.

*(Orig. p. 717)*

### Its History

The "Order" [*Diataxis*] of Patriarch Philotheus and certain Georgian monuments (Introductory Chapter, 378) do not have the Augmented Litany at Matins, but only the Litany of Supplication [^2679]. When the Gospel was read at Matins after the Great Doxology, the Augmented Litany began with **"Let us all say"** (*Rtsem vsi*) [^2680] (cf. at present on Great Saturday).
Early-printed and present Greek *Euchologia*: "**Have mercy on us, O God... Again we pray for our brethren... Again we pray for the blessed founders... Again we pray for mercy, life, peace... For a merciful...**" [^2681].
In the Moscow *Sluzhebnik* of 1602 (= Old Believer), the *Sluzhebnik* of Peter Mohyla, Moscow 1647 and 1658, and the *Hieratikon*—as at Vespers, only beginning from **"Have mercy on us, O God"** [^2682]. The *Hieratikon*, concerning the founders, adds "blessed".

### Its Pronouncement

The Typikon appoints the Augmented Litany at Matins to be pronounced by the priest or the deacon (*Sluzhebnik*: deacon or priest)—the former, presumably, in the absence of a deacon.

### According unto the Ancient Typika

Manuscript Typika and the Old Believer Typikon—unspecified [^2683].
The "Order" of Patriarch Philotheus and the *Sluzhebnik* of Peter Mohyla—the deacon.
Greek printed *Euchologia* and the Moscow *Sluzhebnik* of 1658: "the deacon, if there be one" [^2684].

### The Litany of Supplication at Matins

The exclamation of the Litany of Supplication at Matins is no longer that of Vespers, just as in general the Litany of Supplication is always employed with a new exclamation. Its exclamation at Matins: "**For Thou art a God of mercy, compassion, and love for mankind**" (*Yako Bog milosti, shchedrot i chelovekolyubiya yesi*) contains the same thought as the vesperal exclamation ("**For Thou art a good God and lovest mankind**"), but in an intensified degree, and is close unto the exclamation of the Augmented Litany. After itself the Litany of Supplication here also, as always—at Vespers and the Divine Liturgy—has the bestowal of peace and the bowing of heads with the secret priestly "prayer at the bowing of heads," distinct from the corresponding prayer at Vespers and the Divine Liturgy, and containing within itself a petition for the forgiveness of sins voluntary and involuntary and for the granting of peaceful and supramundane blessings (greater than at Vespers, where it prays for preservation from sin, the devil, and evil thoughts). The exclamation of this prayer amplifies unto the ultimate degree the thought of God's mercy that was steadily heightened by the preceding exclamations: "**For Thine it is to have mercy and to save**" (*Tvoe bo yest yezhe milovati i spasati*).

*(Orig. p. 718)*

### Historical Note

At the Matins of the *Apostolic Constitutions* (4th–5th centuries) the Litany of Supplication is even more adapted unto the morning than the present one, and apart from this differs, though insignificantly, from the vesperal litany (Introductory Chapter, 137); the prayer at the bowing of heads there is of an entirely different content from the present one (137); yet in all manuscript *Euchologia* and other monuments the prayer at the bowing of heads is the present one (see above, p. 622).

### The Dismissal [Apolysis]

### The Order of the Dismissal

The order of the Dismissal (*apolysis* [ἀπόλυσις]) begins. For it the Holy Doors are opened (having been closed with the carrying of the Gospel into the sanctuary after the veneration before the kanon) [^2685], concerning which the Typikon makes no remark here, yet which is indicated in Chapter 7 in the order of Vespers (in ancient Typika this is noted here as well). The dismissal of Matins, which is at the same time the dismissal of the entire Vigil, must in its solemnity and scope correspond unto this longest of services, and therefore surpasses not only the dismissal of the Hours, Small Vespers, and Small Compline (termed the small dismissal), but also the dismissal of the Divine Liturgy.

### Preliminary Exclamations and Prayers

The order of the dismissal is preceded, like all the most important parts of the service (the reading of Holy Scripture, the prokeimenon, and the Eucharistic Canon of the Liturgy), by the exclamation: **"Wisdom!"** (*Premudrost*). This exclamation is pronounced here, as in other instances, by the deacon, concerning which, as something self-evident, the Typikon says nothing. That which enters into the order of the dismissal justifies the appropriateness of this exclamation here: the prayers chosen for it are the most sublime.
Unto such an admonition of the deacon regarding the approach of the time of dismissal, the choir musically requests the priest to begin the dismissal. Because the dismissal is a blessing upon the departure from the temple and a concluding glorification of God, the petition is expressed by the word: **"Bless!"** (*Blagoslovi*), the very word by which the priest is invited to begin the service. Only here this invitation is made not by the deacon, but more solemnly—by the choir, just as before the beginning of Matins for the exclamation: **"Glory to the Holy..."** (*Slava Svyatey...*).
After the deacon and the choir, the word belongs unto the priest, and in response unto the petition for a blessing the priest answers with a blessing, first of all, of the source of all blessing for us, Christ God, wherein the priest attributes unto Him, for the only time in the entire cycle of services, the greatest and most mystery-filled name, "**He Who is**" (*Sy* [ὁ ὤν]), Jehovah—that name which the ancient Hebrew feared to pronounce, substituting for it in the reading of *(Orig. p. 719)* Holy Scripture other names. In Christian boldness the priest, having cleansed his lips by so many prayers, now reverently and aloud pronounces this Name. In this manner, this final exclamation of Vespers and Matins, being almost literally identical with the initial exclamation of the church services:

"**Blessed is our God always, now and ever, and unto the ages of ages**," introduces into it two additions that render it still more majestic and tender: "**He Who is**" and "**Christ**". The union of "**He Who is**" with "**blessed**" was made, presumably, on the basis of 2 Corinthians 11:31: "**The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, Who is blessed unto the ages, knoweth**."
Having heard of the self-existence of Christ ("**He Who is**"), boundless for our intellect, the source and foundation of His eternity ("**always, now and ever**"), the choir, after the customary response unto the priest's exclamation, "**Amen**," prays for the manifestation on earth, in the degree possible for it, of this divine attribute, for its reflection in us through the "establishment of the Emperor," as the defender of the faith and of right order, and through him of the "holy Orthodox faith" and "Orthodox Christians."
The thought of Christ and of His self-existence cannot fail to evoke the thought of His birth on earth and of the Author of His Incarnation, Who is able also to assist by Her intercession our prayers unto Her Son. The priest accordingly turns unto Her for this assistance with the exclamation: "**Most Holy Theotokos, save us!**" (*Presvyataya Bogoroditse, spasi nas*), which, in addition to prayer, contains within itself also the greatest glorification of Her, since of Her we ask, as of Her Son, directly for salvation (which is promised in the dismissal), and not merely for prayers on our behalf and for our salvation (which alone we ask of other saints). Unto this laudatory prayer the choir answers already with a direct glorification of the Mother of God, and that with the most ecstatic of all hymns and the one most pleasing unto Her [**"More honorable than the Cherubim"**], substituting this hymn for prayer unto Her, just as the priest substitutes prayer for praise unto Her. The inverse of what preceded: there the priest praises, while the choir prays.
Now both unite in praise that returns unto Christ, and through Him unto the All-Holy Trinity. In view of the fact that the dismissal lying before the priest is directed toward instilling in those about to depart from the temple a steadfast hope in Christ, reaching unto full assurance of salvation ("**He will have mercy and save**"), the priest prepares for it: ("**Glory to Thee, O Christ God, our hope...**"). The choir takes up this glorification ascending heavenward and lifts it as it were still higher, unto the Tri-Hypostatic God Himself ("**Glory to the Father...**"), expanding this glorification likewise unto infinity ("**both now and ever**"), and joining unto it a final and fervent prayer unto God for mercy (**"Lord, have mercy"** thrice) and a second request unto the priest for a blessing upon departing from the temple: **"Bless!"** (*Blagoslovi*).

### The Dismissal in the Proper Sense

The priest makes the dismissal in the proper sense, consisting ...in the confession of Christ as true God and of our hope for mercy and salvation (though in the Greek, *σώσαι*—"may He save," etc.) from Him through the prayers of His all-pure (*panachrantou*) Mother, the apostles (according to the *Sluzhebnik*—see Vespers—*(Orig. p. 720)* there is also commemorated the "saint whose service is chanted"), and all the saints. At the beginning of the dismissal there is joined, or rather prefixed to the name of Christ, a brief commemoration of the celebrated event from His life, which on Sunday takes the form: **"He Who rose from the dead"** (*Voskresy iz mertvykh*), whereby the dismissal is transformed into a kind of concluding festal hymn (at Pascha an entire troparion is prefixed to it at the beginning).
To the dismissal no response of "Amen" is prescribed, presumably because the confirmation of the entire great promise that the dismissal imparts can be awaited only from the Divine "Amen" (Apoc. 1:18).

### History of the Dismissal

In the Studite-Alexian Typikon, the first exclamation is: **"Wisdom"** (*Mudrost*) [^2686] (*sophia*).
In the time of Arseny Sukhanov in the East, "the priest, opening the doors and turning toward the west, exclaims: *sophia*; those standing before him: *evlogison*" [^2687].
In a certain Euchologion (Patmos Library No. 105, 13th c.), the prayer of dismissal at Matins, addressed to God the Father, concludes: "Being blessed unto the ages, amen" [^2688].
Hence in Slavic manuscripts and the Old Rite Typikon: **"Blessed is our God, He Who is"** (*Syy blagosloven Bog nash*) [^2689]; in Slavic *Sluzhebniki* up to the Moscow edition of 1647 inclusive: **"Blessed and most glorified is Christ God, He Who is"** (*Syy blagosloven[-yy] i preproslavlen[-yy] Khristos Bog*) [^2690]; in ancient Greek manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon: "and the prayer: He Who is blessed" (*Syy blagosloven*).
According to the Studite-Alexian Typikon, instead of **"Establish, O God"** (*Utverdi Bozhe*), the choir answered to **"He Who is blessed"** (*Syy blagosloven*): **"Bless the Lord, ye holy ones; bless, father"** (*Blagoslovite, svyatii, Gospoda, blagoslovi, otche*), after which the dismissal followed immediately [^2691].
Regarding **"Establish, O God"** (*Utverdi Bozhe*) according to the typikon of the Great Church of Constantinople—see the Introductory Chapter, p. 344; Georgian manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon: "the prayer Establish, O God, according to the custom of all-night vigils" [^2692]; Greek manuscripts and printed editions: "then thus (*eith' houtos*) we establish (*stereoumen*) the sovereigns as usual, and we dismiss"; a 14th-century Slavic manuscript: "the singers [chant] Establish, O God, the Christian faith. They do not include the abbot (without commemorating the abbot?)..." [^2693]; a 16th-century manuscript adds: "and he commemorates the sovereign according to custom."
The *Diataxis* of Patriarch Philotheus: "and there is chanted Establish, O God, the sovereigns" [^2694].
The Moscow *Sluzhebnik* of 1602 (= Old Rite), 1647, and the Old Rite Typikon:
"Establish, O God, the Christian faith; preserve and have mercy upon the right-believing Tsar and Grand Prince [Name] (1647 adds: "and the right-believing Tsaritsa and Grand Princess [Name]");

save, O Lord, our Archbishop (Typikon: Patriarch) [Name] (*Sluzhebnik* adds: + and our father the abbot *(Orig. p. 721)* [Name], together with the brethren in Christ), and save all Christians, O Lord";
The *Sluzhebnik* of Peter Mohyla:
"Establish, O God, the holy Orthodox Christian faith unto ages of ages";
The Moscow *Sluzhebnik* of 1658:
"Establish, O God, the holy and Orthodox faith of Orthodox Christians unto age of age. Preserve, O Lord, and have mercy upon the right-believing Tsar and Grand Prince [Name], and the rest according to custom."
In the Greek *Euchologion*, the text is not cited; the *Hieratikon*:
"Establish, O God, the holy and Orthodox faith of pious and Orthodox Christians, with His Holy Church, unto ages of ages."
In the time of Arseny Sukhanov in the East, **"Establish"** (*Utverdi*) was pronounced by the patriarch [^2695].
Regarding **"Most Holy Theotokos, save us"** (*Presvyataya Bogoroditse, spasi nas*), the Georgian and Greek manuscript Typika are silent; Slavic manuscripts and the *Hieratikon* do not have it; the Old Rite Typikon: "thereafter: Wisdom, and the clerics chant More honorable."
The Moscow *Sluzhebniki* of 1602 and 1647:
"The deacon: Wisdom (1647 adds: if there be no deacon, then the priest himself says: Wisdom); (then) the priest: Most Holy Lady Theotokos, save us."
The Greek *Euchologion*, the *Sluzhebnik* of Peter Mohyla, and the Moscow 1658 edition are as at present.
In the time of Arseny Sukhanov in the East, **"More honorable"** (*Chestneyshuyu*) was chanted by the right choir, and **"Glory... Both now..."** (*Slava i nyne*) and the rest by the left choir.
**"Glory to Thee, O Christ God, our hope"** (*Slava Tebe, Khriste Bozhe, upovanie nashe*): 14th-century Slavic manuscript Typika and all *Sluzhebniki* up to the Moscow 1647 edition inclusive read without "Christ"; the *Sluzhebnik* of Peter Mohyla has: "to Thee" (*Ti*).
Regarding **"Glory... Both now... Lord, have mercy"** (three times), **"bless"** (*Slava i nyne. Gospodi pomiluy 3, blagoslovi*), Slavic manuscript Typika of the 14th century read: "the brethren say Glory... Both now... Lord, (have mercy?), bless, father."
The Moscow *Sluzhebniki* of 1602 and 1647, and in the time of Arseny Sukhanov in the East: **"Glory... Both now... Lord, have mercy"** (twice), **"Lord, bless"** (*Slava i nyne, Gospodi pomiluy 2, Gospodi blagoslovi*).

On the significance of the dismissal (in the strict sense) as the final prayer, which in antiquity was accompanied also by a blessing with the laying on of hands by the bishop (or priest) upon each person present in the temple—see the Introductory Chapter, pp. 148, 152ff., 343, and above in the present volume, p. 205.
Concerning the dismissal of Matins, the Studite Typika, as well as Georgian and Greek manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon, are silent.
The *Diataxis* of Patriarch Philotheus and the modern *Euchologion*:
"**May He Who rose from the dead** (modern text adds: + Christ our true God), through the prayers of His (*autou*) all-pure Mother, of the holy, glorious, and all-laudable apostles, and of all the saints, have mercy on us and save us, for He is good and the Lover of mankind."
A 14th-century Slavic manuscript of the Jerusalem Typikon:
"And the priest, standing in the holy doors and looking toward the west, says (No. 329/384 adds: + He Who rose from the dead) Christ our true God, through the prayers of His all-pure Mother and of the holy Bodiless Powers of Heaven, of the honorable and glorious Prophet, Forerunner, and Baptist John, and of the holy, glorious, and all-laudable apostles, and of the saint [Name] whose memory it is, and of all the saints, have mercy on us and save our souls, for He is good and the God Who loves mankind, amen."
The Moscow *Sluzhebniki* of 1602 and 1647:
"May He Who rose from the dead, Christ our true God, through the prayers of His all-pure Mother, and of our venerable and God-bearing fathers, and of all the saints (1647 adds: + for the sake of all the saints), have mercy on us and save us, for He is good and the Lover of mankind."
The Moscow *Sluzhebnik* of 1658:
"May He Who rose from the dead, Christ our true God, through the prayers of His all-pure Mother, of the holy, glorious, and all-laudable apostles, and of all the saints, *(Orig. p. 722)* have mercy on us and save us, for He is good and the Lover of mankind."
The *Sluzhebnik* of Peter Mohyla:
"May He Who rose from the dead, Christ our true God, through the prayers of His all-pure Mother, by the power of the precious and life-giving Cross, of the holy, glorious, and all-laudable apostles—and if there be a renowned saint, commemorate him also, naming his name—and of all the saints, have mercy on us and save us, for He is good and the Lover of mankind. And this after the First Hour and after the Ninth: May He Who rose from the dead, Christ our true God, through the prayers of His all-pure Mother, of our venerable and God-bearing fathers, and of all the saints, have mercy on us and save us, for He is good and the Lover of mankind. Admonition: Take heed, O priest, to observe that at every dismissal thou commemoratest also the saint whose day it is, in this manner: after 'our venerable and God-bearing fathers,' 'and of the Saint [Name] whose memory we celebrate today, and of all Thy saints,' and so forth. But if it have a Doxology, say thus: 'and of the Saint [Name] whose solemn memory we celebrate today, and of all the saints,' and the rest unto the end."
The *Hieratikon*:
"May He Who rose from the dead, Christ our true God, through the prayers of His all-pure Mother, by the power of the precious and life-giving Cross, through the intercessions of the honorable bodiless Powers of Heaven, through the supplications (*hikesiais*) of the honorable and glorious Prophet, Forerunner, and Baptist John, of the holy, glorious, and all-laudable apostles, of the holy, glorious, and right-victorious martyrs, of our venerable and God-bearing fathers, of our father among the saints John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople (or of Basil the Great, heaven-revealed Archbishop of Caesarea [^2696]), of the holy and righteous Ancestors of God Joachim and Anna, and of all the saints, have mercy on us and save us, for He is good, the Lover of mankind, and a merciful God. Through the prayers of our holy fathers, O Lord Jesus Christ our God, have mercy on us. The deacon: Amen" [^2697].

### The Polychronion (*Mnogolyetstvovanie*)

After the dismissal of festal Matins, the Typikon notes, "we chant many years for the emperor," that is, a prayer is chanted for the preservation for many years of the Emperor, the Empress, the Heir, the reigning house, the Holy Synod, the diocesan hierarch (and in a vicariate, also the vicar bishop), the superior of the monastery with the brethren, and all Orthodox Christians. This Polychronion, beginning with the word **"The most pious"** (*Blagochestiveyshago*) and concluding with the words **"O Lord, preserve them for many years"** (*Gospodi, sokhrani ikh na mnogaya leta*), is cited nowhere in the liturgical books (except the most recent among them: *Services for Each Day of the First and Passion Weeks* and the *Obikhod* of Bakhmetev); consequently, until recent times it was preserved in the oral musical tradition. It represents an abbreviation and simplification of the Polychronion after a moleben, just as this latter, in turn, is an abbreviation of the Polychronion of the Royal Hours, wherein of the several petitions of those Polychronia only the last is taken, and the participation of the priest and deacon therein is eliminated; the melody is likewise simplified and rendered recitative. On weekdays, when the First Hour is immediately joined *(Orig. p. 723)* to Matins, this chanting of many years is performed after it.

### History

Something very similar existed at the conclusion of the Asmatic Vespers (Introductory Chapter, p. 344). Manuscript Jerusalem Typika (and naturally also Studite ones) and the Old Rite Typikon make no mention of it.
In the time of Arseny Sukhanov in the East: "Amen. *Ton despotin kai archierea*... [The master and hierarch...]." Consequently, we have here the tradition of the Hagia Sophia Constantinopolitan typikon, occasioned by the presence of emperors at the services.
The present Polychronion is "as it were a hymn in honor of the tsar (with all titles), akin to those hymns cited in the work *De cerimoniis aulae Byzantinae* (10th c.), which were pronounced at the reception of the emperor, and by their content constitute a distinct genre, intermediate between troparia and works of the secular anthology of that era" [^2698].
In ancient Western orders of litanies of the 7th–8th centuries (English, Carolingian, German [*allemanis*], Colbertine), the following formulas were in use: "To [Name of the king], life (*vita*)!", or: "...life and victory!" (*vita et victoria!*), "health (*salus*) and life!"
At present among the Greeks, the substitute for such a Polychronion is the blessing pronounced by the priest as he passes through the church on his way home after the conclusion of the Liturgy:

**"Preserve, O Lord God, all pious and Orthodox Christians dwelling in this city (village or island) and parish, together with their wives and children"** [^2699].

## THE MORNING LITIYA (*LITIYA UTRENNYAYA*)

Like Vespers, Matins concludes with a litiya ("procession" [*iskhozhdenie*], Greek *litē*—not simply "we go forth") in the narthex, but far more brief, consisting only of the rite of going forth into the narthex and a single sticheron, if one does not include in this litiya the "Studite Catechesis" that follows it. The going forth is performed, it is understood, according to the same order as at the vesperal litiya, to which other descriptions of this litiya refer—in chapter 3 of the Typikon and under September 8. But since no actions are specified for the deacon at this litiya, his participation in the going forth is hardly necessary. The procession takes place during the chanting of an "idiomelon sticheron, as is customary," analogous to the sticheron at the vesperal litiya, that is, the sticheron of the temple. At those Matins services at which the Gospel sticheron is not chanted in its appointed place, it is chanted here instead of the sticheron of the temple (see Typikon, October 11, Sunday of the Fathers; December 11, Sunday of the Forefathers; December 17, Sunday of the Fathers; Sunday of the Publican and Pharisee). The indication of these rubrics of the Typikon that the Gospel sticheron at the morning litiya is preceded by **"Glory... Both now..."** (*Slava i nyne*) must have general application: that is, the sticheron of the temple at the morning litiya is likewise chanted with **"Glory... Both now..."**, whereby it is closely bound *(Orig. p. 724)* to Matins (and also in view of the fact that here there is only one sticheron, and there is no other place for **"Glory... Both now..."**). According to chapter 3 of the Typikon, if anointing with oil occurs at the morning litiya, as is prescribed when a great feast coincides with a Sunday, there is also read at it the prayer **"O Master, Great in Mercy"** (*Vladyko Mnogomilostive*) from the order of the vesperal litiya (cf. also September 8). No censing is performed.

### History

Western Studite Typika and the Evergetis Typikon do not specify anything of the kind after Sunday Matins [^2700], but the Studite-Alexian Typikon has a litiya here, canceling it only on occasion: concerning Meatfare Sunday:
"on that Sunday, as well as on Cheesefare Sunday, they do not go forth outside (later manuscripts: 'into the wing/aisle' [*v krylo*]), but after Matins the catechesis is read"; concerning the Sunday of the Prodigal Son: "they go forth into the church wing and chant for the founder (ktitor) a troparion (a funeral one?), unless it be a great feast, and the catechesis is also read" [^2701].
The Jerusalem Typikon—Georgian manuscript:

"At the conclusion of Matins we go forth to the litany, chanting the above-written idiomelon stichera; while chanting the stichera of St. John Chrysostom we enter into the church narthex, Glory... Both now... Theotokion. The deacon censes the brethren, and they pronounce the above-written great (litany) ectene, while we chant Lord, have mercy 25 times, the customary supplications, and the reading of the instruction of Theodore the Studite appointed for that day. After the instruction, the deacon exclaims: Hear us, O God... Peace be to all. Let us bow our heads. When we bend our knees, the priest prays: O Master, Great in Mercy... and in this manner we conclude all" [^2702].

Greek manuscripts and printed editions:
"After the dismissal we perform the litiya in the narthex, chanting the idiomelon sticheron of the saint, *while the above-written prayers are also exclaimed by the priest, that is, the ectenes and the rest, then this prayer: O Master, Great in Mercy* (the italics are absent in later manuscripts), and there is the complete dismissal."

Slavic manuscripts of the 14th century:
"We go forth into the narthex chanting the idiomelon (some add: + sticheron) of the saint whose church it is. The priest offers the customary prayers of the procession, as is written for the procession at Vespers. And at the conclusion we begin the First Hour";
later manuscripts (15th–16th centuries) read like the ancient Greek, but after the italicized passage add: "written at Great Vespers" [^2703]; one manuscript (Serbian, Moscow Rumyantsev Museum, Sevastyanov Coll. No. 1458) notes that this litiya is usually not performed, or is restricted to two prayers: **"Save, O God, Thy people"** (*Spasi, Bozhe, lyudi*) and **"O Master, Great in Mercy"** (*Vladyko Mnogomilostive*); the prayers are read when holy oil is distributed [^2704].

The Old Rite Typikon:
"And the procession into the narthex; and after the dismissal of Matins, if it be a feast of the Lord, both choirs having assembled, we chant Glory... Both now... and the Gospel sticheron of the current tone" [^2705].

*(Orig. p. 725)*

## THE STUDITE CATECHESIS (*OGLASHENIE STUDITOVO*)

The morning litiya, so brief in comparison with that of Vespers and at times entirely devoid of the prayers so essential to a litiya, receives in exchange for them an element of divine worship that is included by no means in all services, but only in the most important: namely, it has a reading. Being the last reading of the vigil, taking place no longer in the nave of the church, serving as a parting counsel for departure therefrom, and forming part of the shortest service, this reading occupies such an exceptional place among the seven readings of the vigil that it is not even directly assigned this title, but is called the "Catechesis" (*Oglashenie*), *katēchēsis*—a word that among classical writers bore the meaning of charming with tones [^2706], of oral instruction, and in ancient ecclesiastical usage acquired the meaning of instruction in the truths of the faith (in St. Cyril of Jerusalem), while in later times it came to mean exhortation or edification. In particular, this name was assigned to the long series of brief pastoral homilies of St. Theodore the Studite († 826), which he delivered to the brethren of his monastery and enjoined his successors to deliver several times a week—namely, for the most part on Sunday, Wednesday, and Friday. Very rarely touching upon doctrinal truths of faith, these homilies exhort the monastics to the strict observance of the monastic rule ("obediences"), to harmonious mutual relations, frequently linking these instructions to the events of the day (the passing of a brother, or observed transgressions). These instructions, presumably long after St. Theodore—perhaps by his disciples—were compiled into two collections: the *Small Catechesis*, consisting of 134 catecheses, and the *Great Catechesis* in three parts: I—87 catecheses, II—124, III—46. For liturgical use, the first collection, the *Small Catechesis*, was intended primarily, since the catecheses in it are arranged precisely: first across all Sundays of the year beginning with Thomas Sunday, after which follow catecheses for other days (Wednesdays and Fridays), thereby providing material strictly coordinated with the characteristics of the day for all days of the church year on which catecheses are appointed. Yet even among the catecheses in the *Great Catechesis*, there are frequently found those assigned to specific days of the ecclesiastical year—Sundays and others. There is no printed edition of the *Small Catechesis* in Church Slavonic. Of its manuscripts, there are known to us MS Moscow Synodal Library No. 715/159 from the end of the 17th century, which contains the first 127 discourses (with the omission of the 29th [^2707]), and MS Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra Library No. 45/23—a translation made from Latin in 1727 for the Lavra by Anthony, Metropolitan of Tobolsk and Siberia (in view of the impossibility of finding a Slavonic translation anywhere), which contains all 134 catecheses, with the addition of the 135th (for the 4th Sunday of Great Lent) and certain other writings of St. Theodore. For liturgical use, there may serve the collection of 95 catecheses of St. Theodore translated from Modern Greek into Slavonic and printed by Paisius Velichkovsky, drawn equally from the *Small* and *Great Catecheses*. In the aforementioned *(Orig. p. 726)* Kyiv manuscript, each catechesis occupies on average 1 1/2 pages in folio; in the Russian translation and edition, 1 1/2 octavo pages.

### Bibliography

Even in Greek there is no complete edition of the *Great Catechesis*; there is an edition only of its second part [^2708] and certain catecheses from other parts [^2709]. The most complete printed edition is therefore the Russian translation produced at the St. Petersburg Theological Academy from various Greek manuscripts [^2710]. The ancient Slavic translation (in places utterly unintelligible) of the second part of the *Great Catechesis* was published by the Imperial Archaeographical Commission in the *Great Menaion Reader* [*Velikiye Cheti-Minei*] under November 11 [^2711]. The *Small Catechesis* has three Greek printed editions [^2712]. The aforementioned collection in Modern Greek (Venice, 1770) and a similar one by Hieromonk Zachariah (1887) are paraphrases. The Slavonic translation of the former by Paisius Velichkovsky states in the preface: "they begin to be read from November 15"; before the 74th catechesis: "at the beginning of the Indiction the catecheses begin to be read every day, until the Precious and Life-Giving Cross, except for a Feast of the Theotokos; and after the Precious Cross, until November 14, on Sundays only. And having been completed up to the Holy Testament (concluding with the 'Testament' of St. Theodore), the book begins again from November 14"; the Russian translation of that same collection in the Optina Hermitage edition adds: "according to this order the instructions of St. Theodore are read in the Athonite monasteries even to this day" [^2713].

### The Order of the Catechesis

In the present place of the Typikon, it is not specified who is to read the catecheses of St. Theodore. This is indicated in the order for the Sunday of the Publican and Pharisee:
"If the abbot be there (in the narthex), they are read by him; but if not, then by the ecclesiarch, while the brethren stand and listen attentively."
For these homilies there must be precisely such an authoritative reader, because ...as they are filled with direct exhortations and reproaches to the brethren (beginning: **"My brethren and fathers"** [*Bratia moyi i ottsy*]). For the same reason, a "preface" (naming the author and the reading) is out of place before them, just as it is not pronounced before the Paschal Catechetical Homily of St. John Chrysostom at Paschal Matins, which corresponds exactly to the Studite catecheses. The abbot in this case represents the Venerable Father himself, and the catechesis is presented as issuing from the mouth of the saint himself, invisibly standing among the worshipers. Therefore, after the catechesis *(Orig. p. 727)* the worshipers respond to it with gratitude personally addressed to St. Theodore in the form of his troparion, Tone 8: **"Instructor of Orthodoxy"** (*"Pravoslaviya nastavniche"*), seek on November 11, "without a Theotokion," as noted in the Typikon rubric for the Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee.[^2714]

#### History

Concerning the profound antiquity of the custom for the abbot or someone else from the monastery administration to offer an instruction to the brethren several times a week, chiefly on Sunday, wherein discussion of it was also permitted (in Jerome's *Rules of St. Pachomius*, *catechesis* and *disputationes*)—see Introductory Chapter, pp. 193, 202, 213.

The catechesis in the strict sense is not mentioned by the *Hypotyposis*, *Diatyposis*, Evergetis Typikon, or Western Studite recensions, but only by the Studite-Alexis Typikon, and among the Jerusalem recensions in this present place, for some reason, only the most ancient manuscript—the Georgian (see above, p. 724); yet all mention it briefly under the Sunday of the Publican and Thomas Sunday.[^2715]

Old Believer Typikon:
"And then the Studite catechesis is offered, and the abbot reads it himself, or chooses one of the priests or of the senior brethren; and upon the completion of the reading, the clerics say the troparion, Tone 8: **'Instructor of Orthodoxy'** [*'Pravoslaviyu nastavniche'*], the end being sung; and the second choir says: **'Glory... both now...'**, Theotokion, in the same tone: **'Who for our sake was born'** [*'Izhe nas radi rozhdeysya'*]."[^2716]

### NON-ORTHODOX MATINS

In comparison with our own, non-Orthodox morning offices exhibit the following principal differences:

The Armenian Matins, consisting of the Midnight Office and "Dawn," has at the former: 7 prayers, 5 instructions, 5 divisions of the Psalter (of 8 in total), and several hymns; at the latter: 7 prayers (one with kneeling), 3 instructions (one of which is an "exhortation to prayer"), several hymns, and Psalms 112, 5, 114, 141, 53, and 85:17 [LXX].

The Coptic Matins, consisting of the Midnight Office and Matins proper, has at the former, besides our Psalms 3, 117, and 118 [LXX]: Psalms 6, 69, 85, and 116 [LXX]; the Gospel of Matthew 25 (concerning the ten virgins), Luke 7:36 (concerning the creditor and debtors), Luke 12:32 (concerning the expectation of the Second Coming), penitential sessional hymns, laudatory verses with **"Rejoice"** (*Chaire*) to the Mother of God, and a prayer; at the latter, it has at the beginning 19 psalms—besides our 62 and 142 [LXX], also 1–6, 8, 11–12, 14, 15, 18, 24, 26, 66, 69, and 112 [LXX]; the Gospel of John 1:1–16; the Creed; a series of brief prayer *(Orig. p. 728)* exclamations; and 2 prayers (Introductory Chapter, pp. 299–303).

The Abyssinian [Ethiopian] Matins of the ancient type has almost no psalms (only a few psalm verses); it opens with a long series of prayer invocations listing the works of creation and providence, appeals to various saints, an enumeration of their struggles, and the virtues of the Mother of God; it has two long series of readings from the New Testament—the first of 9 readings and the second of 4 (on the resurrection, light, vigilance, baptism, and the Second Coming), separated by the Canticles of Moses, of the Three Youths, and of Simeon the God-Receiver, and concluded by lengthy hymns to the Most Holy Trinity, to Christ, and to the saints, and a paraphrase of the Lord's Prayer (with frequent *Alleluia*).

The Abyssinian Matins of the later type (with Greek influence), consisting of the "Midnight Prayer," the "Prayer at the Third Hour of the Night," and the "Prayer at Cockcrow," has at the first service, besides our Psalms 118, 50, 117, and 3 [LXX]: Psalms 133, 6, 12, 69, 85, 90, 116, and 119–129 [LXX] ("the vesperal psalms"), the Gospel of Matthew 23:1–13 (on the Second Coming) and Luke 7:36–50 (the supper in Simon's house), the troparia **"Behold, the Bridegroom"** (*"Se Zhenikh"*) and penitential troparia, and a prayer to the Savior; at the second service, besides our Psalm 50 [LXX], the Canticles of Moses and of the Three Youths, and several litanies: "the compline psalms," Psalm 135 [LXX], a prayerful paraphrase of those two canticles (following them), and the Gospel of Matthew 25:31–46 (on the Last Judgment); at the third service, besides our Psalms 148–150 [LXX], a twofold Great Doxology, the Canticles of the Theotokos, of Zacharias, of Anna, of Simeon, and of Hezekiah: the Creed, several prayers to Christ and to the Mother of God, penitential troparia, and the Gospel: Luke 11:5–13 (concerning the friend asking for loaves at midnight), Mark 13:32–37 (concerning the unknown day of the Second Coming), and Matthew 25:14–30 (the parable of the talents).[^2717]

The Roman Matins has at Nocturns on Sunday Psalms 1–20, with the antiphon before Psalms 1–6: **"Serve the Lord"** (in the Paschal season: **"Alleluia"**), and after them: **"Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice unto Him with trembling"** (Ps 2:11; cf. our **"Blessed is the man"** in musical tradition); for Psalms 7–10: **"God is a righteous Judge / strong and longsuffering, and shall He bring on anger every day?"** (Ps 7:12 [LXX 7:11; Vulgate: *numquid irascitur per singulos dies*]); for Psalms 11–14: **"Thou, O Lord, / shalt preserve us and keep us"** (Ps 11:8 [LXX 11:8]); for Psalm 15: **"Of my goods / Thou hast no need; in Thee have I trusted, preserve me, O Lord"** (vv. 2, 1b, 1a [Ps 15:1–2]); for Psalm 16: **"By the words / of Thy lips I have kept hard ways"** (v. 4b [Ps 16:4]); for Psalm 17: **"I will love Thee, / O Lord, my strength"** (v. 1 [Ps 17:2]); for Psalm 18: **"There are no speeches / nor languages where their voices are not heard"** (v. 4 [Ps 18:4]); for Psalm 19: **"The Lord hear / thee in the day of affliction"** (v. 2 [Ps 19:2]); for Psalm 20: **"Lord, / in Thy strength the king shall rejoice"** (v. 2 [Ps 20:2]). After the first 14 psalms and after every three thereafter follow 3 readings, preceded by an "absolution" (*absolutio*)—a brief prayer for mercy, divine help, or forgiveness of sins—and a blessing (*benedictio*—see them above, p. 640); furthermore, Nocturns have at the beginning a hymn inviting to vigilance, nocturnal prayer, and virtuous deeds in general, and at the end the *Te Deum*; the opening hymn varies according to the liturgical season.

At *Laudes* on Sunday: Psalms 92, 99, 62, and without an intermediate *Gloria*, Psalm 66, with an antiphon *(Orig. p. 729)* before this group: **"Alleluia"** (1) and after them **"Alleluia"** (2); the Canticle of the Three Youths with the antiphon: **"The three youths by the command of the king were cast into the furnace, fearing not the flame of the fire, saying: Blessed art Thou, O God"**; Psalms 148–150 with an antiphon before them: **"Alleluia"** and after them **"Alleluia"** (3), without intermediate *Gloria*, having only the concluding one; a *capitulum* from Revelation 7:12 (a doxology) with the responsory: **"Thanks be to God"** (*Deo gratias*); a hymn, varying according to liturgical seasons, similar in content to the hymn at Nocturns,[^2718] with a verse following it: **"The Lord reigneth, He is robed in majesty,"** and the responsory: **"The Lord is clothed with strength and hath girded Himself with virtue"** (Ps 92:1; cf. our evening prokeimenon); and the Canticle of Zacharias (*Benedictus*).[^2719]

The Anglican Matins (around 11:00 AM) begins with an opening sentence pronounced by the priest: Ezekiel 18:27 (on the conversion of the wicked) or Psalm 50:19 [Ps 51:17] or a similar sentence (from among 11 choices); the priest delivers a brief exhortation to repentance and confession of sins; the congregation kneels and recites the formula of the General Confession, and the priest pronounces the General Absolution; he and the congregation kneeling recite the Lord's Prayer and the responsory: Priest: **"O Lord, open Thou my lips,"** People: **"And our mouth shall show forth Thy praise"** (Ps 50:17 [LXX 50:17; Ps 51:15]); Priest: **"O God, make speed to save us"** [*Bozhe v pomoshch nashu vonmi*], People: **"O Lord, make haste to help us"** (Ps 69:2 [LXX 69:2; Ps 70:1]); Priest: **"Glory..."**, People: **"Both now..."**; Psalm 94 [Venite] is read or sung, followed by two appointed portions from the 60 divisions of the Psalter; the priest reads the first "lesson" from the Old Testament, announcing before it: "Chapter [N] of the Book of [Name], verse [N]," and after it: "Here endeth the first lesson at verse [N]"; the *Te Deum Laudamus* is sung (in English) or the Canticle of the Three Holy Children (*Benedicite*); the second "lesson" from the New Testament; the Canticle of Zacharias (*Benedictus*) or Psalm 99 (*Jubilate Deo*); the Apostles' Creed or the Athanasian Creed; over the kneeling congregation the priest says: **"The Lord be with you,"** **"And with thy spirit,"** the Lord's Prayer, the responsory: **"O Lord, show Thy mercy upon us..."** (Ps 84:8 [LXX 84:8; Ps 85:7]); three collects: for the Church Militant, for peace, and for grace; an anthem; a litany or four prayers: for the Sovereign, the Royal Family, the clergy and people, and the **"Prayer of St. Chrysostom"** (= the Prayer of the Third Antiphon of our Divine Liturgy), and **"The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ..."** (2 Cor 13:13).[^2720]

Among Protestants there is no Matins, and daily services begin with the liturgy.
*(Orig. p. 730)*

### THE PRACTICAL FEASIBILITY OF THE ENTIRE ALL-NIGHT VIGIL TYPIKON
*(EXCURSUS)*

The celebration of the All-Night Vigil according to all the above-expounded requirements of the Typikon—with the singing, for example, of the entirety of Psalm 103 (with refrains to every verse), all 8 psalms of the First Kathisma, the prolonged singing of the two great Polyeleos psalms or the immense Psalm 118, and especially with the singing of the 120 irmosi and troparia of the Kanon, to say nothing of the multitude of stichera, sessional hymns, troparia, etc.—the celebration of a Vigil with such a massive volume of singing, and moreover with 7 readings, may appear decidedly unfeasible. And the practice of simultaneous chanting (*mnogoglasiye*) in the Russian Church during the 16th–17th centuries, that is, in the era when the All-Night Vigil concluded its historical development, would seem historically to confirm such an opinion. And yet, as if to provide a factual refutation of an opinion so disastrous for the Typikon, an experiment of such a Vigil was recently undertaken at the Kyiv Theological Academy—in all probability the first and only one in Russia since the 17th century (it is well known that in not a single Russian monastery today is the Kanon sung in its complete form, its troparia being merely read, just as nowhere is the entirety of the First Kathisma, the Polyeleos, or the Evlogitaria / Amomos [Psalm 118] sung).

The thought of such an All-Night Vigil originated two years ago simultaneously in the minds of two Academy professors: the Professor of Liturgics, Priest V. D. Prylutsky, and the author of the present book. Having deliberated on the matter, they decided that executing this intention would require an expenditure of a minimum of 300 rubles for two choirs (which, according to the principle of antiphonal singing upon which our entire liturgical order is constructed, must be of absolutely equal competence and balance) and not less than two months of rigorous preparation (rehearsals). When the aforementioned professors shared these aspirations with their like-minded colleague in liturgical scholarship, Bishop Gabriel of Akkerman (Chepur), he reproached them for their naivety, stating that this would require 3,000 rubles and 2 years of preparation.

The idea of an ideal All-Night Vigil, thus hovering in the air, sank into the hearts of two devout fourth-year students: Priest Z. T. Saplin (a native of Kursk) and I. A. Lagovsky (a native of Kostroma; the previously mentioned individuals were natives of Ryazan, Lithuania, and Kherson). They resolved to make of this Vigil a kind of vow-offering, and found among the student-singers about 20 individuals who expressed their readiness, at no small risk to their vocal cords, to sing even the entire night through, from 6:00 PM until morning. About 7 of these 20 were fourth-year students; next in number followed first-year students, then second-year, and finally third-year; ethnically, the performers were divided roughly equally between Great Russians and Little Russians [Ukrainians].

The All-Night Vigil was initially intended for the eve of December 5, as the feast of St. Sabbas the Sanctified; however, due to various considerations, November 10–11 was chosen—a Sunday with Tone 1, musically the richest. Rehearsals lasted about a month and a half. The site chosen for the Vigil was the small Holy Spirit *(Orig. p. 731)* Church of the Brotherhood Monastery (within whose precinct the Academy was situated). Benches were arranged along all the walls of the church. The Rector of the Academy, Bishop Innocent, who regarded the enterprise with great sympathy, consented—in order not to impede the complete execution of the Typikon requirements, which, as is well known, do not envision the hierarch's active presiding at the Vigil—merely to assume the position of the Abbot [Proestos] and restrict himself to the functions assigned to the latter in the Typikon (honor was paid to his episcopal rank in the church only upon the conclusion of the Vigil by the singing of *'Eis polla eti, Despota'* and the festive tolling of bells). He took his place in the center of the nave against the wall, wearing a monastic mantle. The celebrants of the Vigil were a fourth-year student, Hieromonk Antony (Romanovsky), and a fourth-year student, Hierodeacon Nektary (Trezvinsky).

At 6:00 PM, with the royal doors closed, the censing of the sanctuary began. Prior to this, the Rector invited those present to sit (unfortunately, there were by no means enough seats for everyone). After the censing of the sanctuary, the curtain and the holy doors opened, before which a student-novice in monastic habit holding a tall candle had taken his stand beforehand, fulfilling the duties of the paraekklesiarches. At the moment the holy doors opened, he exclaimed: **"Arise!"** [*Vozstanite*]. Through the holy doors came forth the hieromonk with the censer (without the deacon, wearing mantle and epitrachelion). In sepulchral silence, broken only by the clanking of the censer chains, an extensive censing of the entire three-aisled church was performed, during which the celebrants of the censing traced a sixfold wave-like path (along each side of the walls and pillars), the end of which brought them into the narthex; when they exited it following the censing, the paraekklesiarches exclaimed: **"Lord, bless!"** [*Gospodi blagoslovi*]. Those performing the censing proceeded to the holy doors, and having performed there the prescribed concluding censing of the principal icons, the priest made the opening blessing. Fulfilling the duties of the ekklesiarches, Priest V. D. Prylutsky sang solo: **"Amen. Come, let us worship..."** [*Amin. Priidite poklonimsya...*], and the beginning of Psalm 103 with the refrain. The psalm was sung verse-by-verse by two choirs with the prescribed refrains after each verse according to the Bakhmetev chant. Immediately after the exclamation, the royal doors were closed, and the priest came out and took his stand at the right end of the solea before an analogion and an icon, where he remained standing for nearly the entire All-Night Vigil. The unhurried singing of the psalm, with what seemed like an endless repetition of each of its three refrains, and with attention completely undistracted by anything (not even by a censing), revealed to the mind ever new insights in every verse. At verse 24 of the psalm (**"In wisdom hast Thou made them all"**), the priest approached the royal doors to read the Prayers of Light [Lucernarium prayers]. Rapture shone upon every face. The psalm was concluded at 6:35 PM.

**"Blessed is the man"** [*Blazhen muzh*] was likewise sung to the Bakhmetev chant with a threefold *Alleluia* after every verse; yet the singing of the first *Glory* (Stasis), that is, Psalms 1, 2, and 3, occupied only about 10 minutes. This was owing to the lively antiphonal execution: the second choir began its verse while the first was still finishing its own. The second and third *Glories* of the First Kathisma, that is, Psalms 4–8, were sung to the troparion melody of Tone 1 (the ordinary chant), that is, the manner in which the Typika psalms are sung at the Divine Liturgy. In this, it seems, the choir director made an error: they ought to have been sung to the sticheric melody, since the troparic melody begins at the Vigil only after *(Orig. p. 732)* **"Now lettest Thou Thy servant depart"** [*Nyne otpushchayeshi*] and thereafter dominates unchallenged (in the sessional hymns and hypakoe) almost until the Kanon.

On the other hand, a deeply moving feature was introduced into the singing of these 5 psalms: on the basis of the ancient Typikon for singing kathismata (see above, p. 633), each psalm verse was divided in singing between the two choirs, that is, the right choir sang the first half of each verse, and the left sang the second half. Since biblical poetry is founded upon the parallelism of members—where the second half of each verse contains a parallel thought to the first, developing and completing the thought of the first—this manner of chanting positively astonished the mind with unexpected insights and juxtapositions.

For example:
*Right choir*: **"Offer the sacrifice of righteousness,**
*Left choir*: **and hope in the Lord.**
*Right choir*: **Many say: Who will show us good things?**
*Left choir*: **The light of Thy countenance hath been signed upon us, O Lord."** (Ps 4:6–7 [LXX 4:6–7; Ps 4:5–6])
*Right choir*: **"All sheep and oxen,**
*Left choir*: **yea, and the beasts of the field."** (Ps 8:8 [LXX 8:8; Ps 8:7])

The litanies after the 1st and 2nd Stases were pronounced by the priest, and after the 3rd by the deacon.
Toward **"Lord, I have cried"** [*Gospodi vozzvakh*], the candles before the icons were lit, and the church immediately took on a more festive appearance; up to this point, only oil lamps had been burning, and there had been semi-darkness. **"Lord, I have cried"**, preceded by the intonation of the Tone, was sung to the Great Znamenny chant; portions of the first two verses were sung solo by a bass, while the entire choir responded at the appointed places (more frequently than in the ordinary chant) with **"Hear me, O Lord"** [*Uslyshi mya Gospodi*]. The remaining verses of Psalms 140 and 141 were chanted in recitative, as in the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra. The Sunday stichera were sung to the Bakhmetev chant, but the 6 Menaion stichera were sung to their appointed model melodies (*podobny*, according to the Lavra melody), on account of which the model melody was intoned before each group: before the first—**"As noble"** (*Yako dobla*), before the second—**"O most glorious wonder"** (*O preslavnago chudese*).

It is futile to describe to anyone who has not heard these melodies all their beauty, majesty, and compunction. Let us note only that upon the words of the sticheron to the Holy Martyr Stephanida: *"Bound unto two palm trees, thou wast torn asunder, / and didst fly up unto God like a sparrow,"* fell musical notes that expressed both the entire horror of this torment (the tearing asunder of the human body by two trees bent down and then released from men's hands) and the complete triumph over it achieved by the martyr's noble spirit, so that everyone capable of discerning these words and perceiving how their full horror was conveyed by the music could not help but tremble. The impression made by these melodies was heightened by the fact that the stichera, like all the chants at the Vigil, were sung without a canonarch (even in the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra, the finest idiomelon stichera [*samoglasny*], such as those for the Nativity of Christ, the Dormition, and the Annunciation, are sung without a canonarch). At the appointed place, the choirs came together in the center.

The Entrance, preceded by two immense candles borne by two monks in mantles, was performed only at 7:35 PM—that is, 1 1/2 hours after the beginning of the service, an amount of time within which, with energetic dispatch, an entire ordinary Vigil can be served. The prokeimenon, instead of being intoned, was sung solo by the canonarch (prior to its singing by the combined choirs to a modified *(Orig. p. 733)* Lavra melody), and its verses were likewise chanted by the canonarch, but in recitative (they ought to have been sung like the prokeimenon itself).

The departure for the Litiya (at 7:43 PM) was made through the north door with the royal doors closed, preceded by two candles carried by monks in mantles; the priest wore only the epitrachelion. The singers, having united their choirs and formed into ranks of four abreast, followed the priest singing **"Most glorious things today"** [*Preslavnaya dnes*], and at **"Glory... both now..."**—**"O Heavenly King"** [*Tsaryu Nebesny*] (the temple stichera). The Litiya procession advanced into the narthex itself, into which most of the worshipers also proceeded (the narthex proved to be quite commodious), including the Bishop. **"Lord, have mercy"** [*Gospodi pomiluy*] was counted by one of the singers. The Aposticha were sung (to a simple chant) by the combined choirs, who had formed a semicircle before the analogion. The royal doors were not opened even for the blessing of the loaves. Psalm 33, as later Psalm 50, was spoken aloud (following the rubric's direction: *"we say"* [*glagolem*]) by one of the choirs; the effect was exceedingly powerful.

After **"The blessing of the Lord be upon you"** [*Blagoslovenie Gospodne na vas*], the "Great Reading" took place. The analogion for the reader was placed at the left end of the solea, obliquely toward the iconostasis and the people. The continuous reading appointed for the day was the entirety of the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians. It was read by the Inspector of the Academy and Professor of the New Testament, Archpriest D. I.
