Bogdashevsky (without epitrachelion, of course), who sought by means of vocal inflection to invest into the text being read (the reading, like the others, was delivered in a natural conversational cadence, albeit in Church Slavonic) all the profound understanding accumulated through long years of scholarly research.

The concluding **"Amen"** of the Epistle was pronounced not by him, but, as the Typikon requires, by the reader of the Six Psalms—who, likewise according to the Typikon, in his capacity as the Abbot [Proestos], was the Rector-Bishop (who had also previously read **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"** and **"Now lettest Thou Thy servant depart"**). During the reading of the Epistle, the singers were given a prosphora and a cup of wine each, and the people received prosphora moistened with wine. With the beginning of the reading, the church was plunged once more into darkness (which lasted until **"God is the Lord, and hath appeared unto us"** [*Bog Gospod i yavisya nam*, Hebrew: "shone forth"]).

Matins began at 8:40 PM. The Great Litany was pronounced by the priest. **"God is the Lord"** was executed exactly like the prokeimenon (see above). The kathismata were read in the center of the church by a student. The sessional hymns were sung to the touchingly prolonged melody of the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra (which shares something in common with Passion chants; the Tone 2 sessional hymn being a genuine Passion chant, **"Noble Joseph"** [*Blagoobrazny Iosif*]). Chanting them while seated (*"seated we sing"* [*sedyashche poyem*]) could not be accomplished on account of the cramped space of the kliroses.

After the First Kathisma and its sessional hymns, the Rector read from the solea from Theophylact's *Blagovestnik* [Explanation of the Gospels] the commentary on the morrow's Gospel, titled: *"Homily of Blessed Theophylact, Archbishop of Bulgaria, on the Gospel according to Luke."* Due to the brevity of the Gospel reading (concerning the foolish rich man), the reading took up about two folio pages of spaced print.

The remaining readings were read by a second-year student, V. P. Afonsky (a native of Kyiv). Following the Second Kathisma, the Polyeleos, and the Third Ode of the Kanon, the commentary of the Apostle Paul upon the morrow's Epistle was read; this commentary occupied 5 folio pages of extremely fine print in two columns, and despite rather brisk reading it proved somewhat lengthy, on account of which it became necessary to abandon the original intention of reading from the *Margarit* [The Pearls] after Ode 3 of the Kanon, concerning which, moreover, the Typikon speaks very vaguely. *(Orig. p. 734)* The readings were directed by the author of the present book, for whom it required no small labor to track down the necessary Slavonic editions; and the "Studite Catechesis" required for the reading was discovered only in what was virtually a unique manuscript of the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra, the excerpting of which was delayed, making it necessary to translate it from Russian into Church Slavonic.

The pinnacle of the Vigil proved to be the Polyeleos. Sung to the majestic, distinctly triumphant melody of the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra, these 47 verses of the Polyeleos psalms seemed to form an unending hymn to the Creator and Provider. An inexplicable mystery seemed to breathe from the twofold mention of Og and Sihon (**"And Og the king of Bashan: Alleluia, alleluia; for His mercy endureth unto all ages: Alleluia"** [Ps 135:20; LXX 135:20]). The illuminated chandelier heightened the impression. And through all this, strangely, the royal doors remained continuously closed. For the singers, the Polyeleos was an extraordinary success. By common consensus, the Vigil here surpassed the boldest expectations. The fervor of the worshipers reached its apogee.

**"The assembly of the Angels"** [*Angelsky sobor*—the Evlogitaria of the Resurrection] was sung to the jubilant, rapid Lavra melody (resembling the hurried running of the Myrrh-bearing women to and from the tomb). The Hypakoe was sung solo to the melody of the sessional hymns by a fine tenor; an intense silence settled over the church, remarkably illustrating the very name of this chant (*"attention"* [from Greek *hypakoe*], or more accurately, *"refrain"*). And once again, a reading.

With the beginning of the Gradual Antiphons [Anabathmoi], the royal doors were opened, and they remained open until the Gospel was carried back into the sanctuary during Ode 1 of the Kanon. The Gradual Antiphons were sung to the Lavra melody, each twice. It was a majestic antiphonal dialogue between the kliroses. Psalm 50 was spoken in unison by the left kliros. Everyone was especially moved by the fact that the Gospel for veneration was held "upon his breast" by the priest, flanked by two candles.

The Kanon was begun at 10:45 PM and concluded at 12:50 AM. It was sung to the Bakhmetev chant, while **"I shall open my mouth"** [*Otverzu usta moya*—the Katabasia] at the coming together of the choirs was sung to the Lavra melody. The verses of the Biblical Canticles sounded especially powerful. Each ode of the Kanon seemed like something vast and unending. When those present saw that absolutely all 14 troparia of each ode were being sung, some began to fear for the vocal cords of the singers, all the more so since their ever-growing enthusiasm seemed to cause them to sing louder and louder. One venerable listener implored the organizers to curtail this "dangerous experiment." But that would have meant abandoning the enterprise at the very end. The kontakia, ikoses, and sessional hymns after Ode 3 were sung to the ordinary troparic melody, since there were seven of them in all; likewise the Sunday Kontakion and Ikos after Ode 6.

The reading after Ode 3 once again plunged the church into darkness, which persisted until the beginning of Ode 9, when the lighted candles remained unextinguished until the dismissal. During the reading of the Prologue, which comprised 10 folio pages, the author made a circuit of the seated congregation to observe the composition of the worshipers who had "endured unto the end" [cf. Matt 10:22]. He was struck by the substantial percentage of Academy students and educated women of various ages, from dignified matrons to teenage gymnasium students. There were also many educated men. In all, there were probably about 200 worshipers.

*(Orig. p. 735)*
The Exapostilaria [Photagogica] were sung solo, antiphonally, to the Greek troparion melody.

The Praises [*laudes*, *khvalitny*] stichera were sung to the ordinary chant, with the choirs coming together (*skhod*) at the appointed moment. The Doxology was sung to the Kyiv Caves Lavra melody. It was strange to see during the Great Doxology and the litanies following it the Royal Doors closed, opening only for the dismissal at the (first) **"Wisdom"** [*Premudrost'*].

After Matins the singers moved following the priest, preceded by two large candles (without a deacon), to the narthex for the litiya with the singing of **"The Holy Spirit was ever"** [*Dukh Svyatyy be ubo prisno*]. The Rector read the Studite Catechesis (half a sheet of writing paper)—concerning the purpose and benefit of catecheses. The singers thanked St. Theodore with his troparion. They read the First Hour in the same place. Everything ended at 1:50 AM.

It is difficult to convey in words what the listeners of this service felt—a service called by someone the "historical All-Night Vigil"—and especially its immediate participants. How unusual everything was in it is demonstrated by the following circumstance: the two leaders of the service, capable of reciting by heart the entire second chapter of the Typikon, so to speak, took turns losing their heads during the Vigil and had to cross-check each other as to whether this or that followed next. The majority of the service performers concluded the next day that they had been, as it were, intoxicated throughout the Vigil. There could be no question of any fatigue. One singer stated that without leaving the kliros he could have sung another such Vigil. One student, fond of sleep, several times left the church, undressed, and lay down in bed; but, unable to sleep because of the thought that just a few steps away such an original, unheard-of concert was taking place, he returned to church. One female university student prior to the Vigil had memorized all the psalms, stichera, kanons, and biblical canticles appointed to be sung. Those acquaintances of the leaders to whom an invitation to the impending Vigil had not been sent almost quarreled with them over this and extracted a promise that in the event of a repetition of anything similar they would be notified. And a repetition is possible...

In the event of a repetition, it is planned to chant everything in the Great Znamenny Chant, which will lengthen the Vigil by some 3–4 hours.

### THE FIRST HOUR

#### Its Relationship to the Vigil

Already from the Praises, that is, from the concluding portion of Matins, the Vigil diminishes its solemn intensity, transitioning first into the quiet and slow singing of the Great Doxology, and then into a long series of litanic petitions; the litiya after Matins with the reading that fills it stands in this regard yet another step lower, while the First Hour, completely devoid of singing, stands lower still. Both the one and the other are even transferred out of the nave into the narthex. Quiet prayer now caresses and refreshes the soul, exhausted by the prolonged ecstasy of festive hymns.

*(Orig. p. 736)*

#### Its Relationship to Matins

Falling at the very break of dawn (the first Eastern hour = 7:00 AM for us at the equinox), the First Hour stands in the same relationship to Matins as the Ninth Hour does to Vespers: both, coinciding in time, and partly in content, with these two paramount daily services, nevertheless possess each its own distinctive theological idea and do not repeat from those services a single chant or prayer.

#### Structure and Content of the First Hour

The theme of the First Hour is the thoughts and sentiments of the believer at the onset of morning; only certain passages of its psalms depicting the treachery of the enemies of the persecuted righteous one (as Psalm 5:11 [LXX 5:10]: **"There is no truth in their mouth... their throat is an open sepulchre..."**) permit also the association of the First Hour, according to the direction of the *Instructional Notice* [*Uchitel'noye izvestiye*] appended to the *Sluzhebnik*, with the commemoration of the trial of Christ before Pilate, which took place at this hour of the day.

The first psalm of the Hour, Psalm 5, **"Give ear to my words, O Lord"** [*Glagoly moya vnushi, Gospodi*], is a hope-filled morning prayer in the temple for the righteous and against the ungodly, who must be deprived of any participation in liturgical worship, wherein the psalmist turns from the ones to the others several times in balanced strophes (in all likelihood originally intended for antiphonal singing).

The second psalm of the First Hour, Psalm 89 [LXX 89; Ps 90], **"Lord, Thou hast been our refuge"** [*Gospodi, pribezhishche byl yesi ...nam"*, attributed (also by the Hebrew Bible) to Moses, depicts the brevity and arduousness of human life in comparison with the eternity of God, Who replaces generations of men upon earth like plants each morning, for our life before God is shorter than a single day; seeing the cause of this in the wrath of God against our sins, the singer prays for a swift ("in the morning") recompense by the mercy of God for former afflictions according to the number of their days and years.

In the final psalm of the Hour, Psalm 100 [LXX 100; Ps 101], **"Of mercy and judgment will I sing,"** the pious king in the form of a vow outlines the program for his conduct (at the beginning, the morning of his reign) both in private, domestic life, and in intercourse with men, toward subordinates and immediate servants, and toward the wicked, whom he will destroy every morning.[^2721]

Among the hymns and prayers of the First Hour, the Lenten troparion **"In the morning hear my voice"** [*Zautra uslyshi glas moy*] prays in general for the acceptance of morning prayer; the Theotokion **"What shall we name thee"** [*Chto Tya narechem*] constitutes a glorification of the Mother of God unrelated to the time of day, yet of the Theotokia at the Hours it is the most ecstatic, perhaps because the First Hour corresponds approximately to the time of the Savior's birth ("thou didst hold in thine arms the Son, the God of all"); this Theotokion is used nowhere else.

The verse of the Hour at the First Hour, in contrast to the other Hours, is twofold (as we shall see below, the First Hour in non-Orthodox Churches is distinguished from the others by its length and unique character); the first verse, **"Order my steps,"** taken from the midnight-matins Psalm 118 [LXX 118:133–135] *(Orig. p. 737)*, asks God for the direction of our conduct according to the commandments of God (implicitly, in the coming day) and for spiritual enlightenment; the second, from Psalm 70:8 [LXX 70:8], **"Let my mouth be filled with Thy praise,"** asks that throughout the coming day we may sing the glory of God.

The Lenten troparion after the Trisagion, of which at the First Hour, unlike the other Hours, only one is appointed, is dedicated to the Mother of God: **"The most glorious Mother of God"** [*Preslavnuyu Bozhiyu Mater'*], which serves also as a sessional hymn in Tone 6; on Wednesday and Friday to the Cross, **"Speedily anticipate"** [*Skoro predvari*]—a sessional hymn in Tone 4; on Saturday to the martyrs, **"As the firstfruits"** [*Yako nachatki*]—the kontakion to the martyrs in Tone 8. Only one troparion is appointed, perhaps in correspondence with the number of the Hour and on account of fatigue from Matins.

The exclamation at **"Thou Who at all times"** [*Izhe na vsyakoe vremya*] is the same as at the Ninth Hour: **"God be merciful unto us"** [*Bozhe ushchedri*].

The Prayer of the First Hour, attributed to St. Sabbas the Sanctified,[^2722] addressed to Christ, as is the prayer of the Ninth Hour alone besides this, asks Him, as the One Who enlightens (in baptism) and sanctifies every man coming into life, for spiritual enlightenment and correction through the intercessions of His Mother (the latter ...only in the prayer of this Hour; cf. the troparion after the Trisagion).

Liturgical practice has established that this prayer, unlike the other prayers at the Hours, is pronounced by the priest and not by the reader (in the Kyiv Caves Lavra—by the reader); and after it, in keeping with the special attention accorded at this Hour to the Most Holy Theotokos, they sing the kontakion to Her from the service of the Annunciation, **"To Thee, the Champion Leader"** [*Vzbrannoy Voyevode*], as possessing the most comprehensive laudatory and prayerful content. In the Kyiv Caves Lavra they do not sing it. As the concluding service in this group, the First Hour has a dismissal, termed therefore "complete" (*sovershennyy*), in common parlance "lesser" (*malyy*), at which among the saints only the choir of the venerable monastics is commemorated, because it is a monastic service.

#### History of the Hour

The First Hour was established in the 4th century[^2723] in Palestinian monasteries for ascetic purposes (Introductory Chapter, p. 147), wherein the concluding psalms of Matins—Psalms 50, 62, and 89 [LXX]—were introduced into its composition (*ibid.*). Concerning its subsequent development during the era when the Hours perhaps possessed a sung, musical character, nothing is known; judging from the fact that later sung offices appoint for it Psalm 5 [LXX],[^2724] one may surmise that from antiquity this psalm was part of the Hour's structure.

According to the most ancient Greek Horologion of the 8th–9th century, Sinai Library no. 863, the First Hour has after the usual beginning the troparion **"Having passed the night, I thank Thee, O Lord"** three times; 8 psalms: 5, 45, 66, 69, 89, 91, 100, 112 [LXX]; antiphons from Psalm 142:1, 2, 8–12 [LXX] with *Alleluia*; the troparion **"(O Christ,) True Light,"** preceded by its conclusion **"And direct"** (perhaps a refrain); **"Glory..."**—a troparion according to the day of the week: on Monday and Tuesday, **"Hear, O Lord, sinners who pray"**; on Wednesday and Friday, **"As having a multitude of compassions upon our humility"**; on Thursday, **"O Most Pure Theotokos, in despair at our grievous transgressions"**; on Saturday, **"O victorious martyrs"**; **"Order my steps"** (3 times), but for *(Orig. p. 738)* **"Let my mouth be filled"** no repetition is specified (as is also the case in other Hours); the Hour concludes with the Trisagion, the Creed, and the Our Father.

Horologia from the 9th century onward contain the First Hour in its present composition, differing only in the troparia after the Trisagion and the concluding prayers. Thus, the Slavonic Horologia of the Moscow Synodal Typography Library, nos. 46 and 48 (15th–16th c.), have the troparia **"Thou Who didst command light to exist throughout all creation"** and **"O Lord, we are Thy people"**; a manuscript of the Athonite St. Andrew Skete, no. 12 (11th c.), has only the troparion **"Speedily anticipate."** However, two manuscripts, namely St. Petersburg Public Library no. 57 and Sophia Library at the St. Petersburg Theological Academy no. 1052 (13th c.), appoint troparia after the psalms that differ from the present ones: specifically, on Saturday, "when there is no troparion" (for the day), **"Righteous Light"** and ...**"Truly all things are vanity."** As regards the prayers at the First Hour, in the Sung Office (*Asmatike Akolouthia*) it, like the other Hours, possessed 3 prayers of the antiphons, 1 of the dismissal, and 1 of the bowing of the heads (*kephaloklisia*); in certain monuments also a prayer behind the ambo (*opisthembonos*), and in some, prior to the latter, also a "morning" prayer (7 in total). In manuscript Horologia as well, the First Hour frequently contains several prayers; thus, in manuscripts of the Moscow Typography Library, nos. 46 and 48 (15th c.), there are 4 prayers, all differing from the present one: **"I thank Thee, O Lord my God, and I glorify Thee,"** **"Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God"** (no. 46: **"Thou Who at all times"**), **"Holy Father, Who the righteous Sun,"** and a "prayer concluding all singing: Merciful Lord, accept my sighs."

Sinai no. 12 (13th c.) and St. Petersburg Public Library no. 57 lack the third prayer. Sophia Library at the St. Petersburg Theological Academy no. 1052 (13th c.) contains of these only the first. Sinai no. 868 (13th–14th c.) and Moscow Typography Library no. 47 (15th c.) have no prayers. Sinai no. 855 (12th c.): **"Spotless, undefiled"** and **"Thou Who at all times,"** with a later hand adding: **"O Christ, the True Light"**; Sinai no. 870 (14th c.)—the present Prayer of the First Hour, with the addition of the present prayers of the Mid-Hour, wherein the latter (**"Thou Who sendest forth light"**) is read with uplifted hands.[^2725]

The Georgian manuscript of the Jerusalem Typikon does not mention the First Hour after the Vigil, observing after the litiya:
"and thus we conclude all"; likewise the ancient Greek manuscripts—after the litiya: "and the complete dismissal takes place"; according to later Greek: "and immediately (after the litiya) the First Hour and the catechesis, and the complete dismissal takes place."

Slavonic manuscripts indicate the First Hour after the litiya, observing that after **"More honorable than the Cherubim"** [*Chestneyshuyu*]:
"and all say: In the name of the Lord, father, bless. The Priest: Through the prayers of our holy fathers. And they say the prayer: O Christ, the True Light. Lord, have mercy (3). And the complete dismissal takes place."[^2726]

**"To Thee, the Champion Leader"** is nowhere indicated, yet one Typikon appoints this kontakion at the Hours on an *Alleluia* Saturday after **"With the saints give rest"** [*So svyatymi upokoy*] at **"Glory... both now..."**.[^2727]

*(Orig. p. 739)*

#### The First Hour on Sunday

The Sunday First Hour differs from weekday ones only in the troparia and kontakion. As at the other Hours, at the First Hour on Sunday there are appointed: the Sunday troparion; **"Glory..."**, of the saint; **"Both now..."**, the Theotokion of the Hour; and the kontakion of the Sunday only, since two kontakia are never appointed at an Hour, and the Sunday kontakion cannot alternate with a weekday kontakion: it can alternate only with a festal kontakion, beginning from one of Doxology rank (see Chapter 5 of the Typikon). If there are two saints on Sunday, it is understood (which, however, the Typikon does not provide for, but only the General Menaion) that their troparia alternate at **"Glory..."**.

*(Orig. p. 740)*

#### According to Ancient Typika

Greek manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon are silent on this matter.

Slavonic manuscripts of the 14th century:
"after the Our Father, the Sunday hypakoe of the tone of the day; if there is a kontakion in the order of the saint, then here we say the kontakion of the saint, and the Sunday hypakoe is not said" (Manuscript of the Moscow Synodal Library, no. 328/383, fol. 10).

Later manuscripts are silent.

The Old Believer Typikon directs concerning troparia as does our own:
"the kontakion of the saint, if he has one; if not, then we say the kontakion to the Mother of God, Tone 6: **'Protection [Steadfast Intercession] of Christians'** [*Zastupnitse (Predstatel'stvo) khristianom*] instead of the hypakoe of the tone... likewise at all the Hours we say the kontakion."

In practice among the Old Believers, according to our Typikon, only the Sunday kontakion alternates also with a six-verse [*shesterik*] saint.[^2728]

### THE THIRD HOUR

#### Content of the Hour

The Third Hour is always joined with the Sixth, forming with it a single service, which is placed in the same intimate relationship with the Divine Liturgy as the First Hour is with Matins and the Ninth Hour is with Vespers.

The general theme of the Third Hour is the natural prayer at the beginning of the day for the preservation of righteousness in conduct and the elimination of obstacles thereto—external ones on the part of enemies, and internal ones on the part of our own sinfulness. But in accordance with two commemorations associated for the Christian with this hour, this theme divides in two: according to the *Instructional Notice* of the *Sluzhebnik*, the Third Hour commemorates the trial of the Savior before Pilate, with the scourging and mocking, which took place precisely between 9:00 AM and 12:00 noon,[^2729] and the Descent of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles, which occurred precisely at this hour. The aforementioned general theme of the Hour is developed by its psalms, and especially by the verse of the Hour (consequently, its central focus), while of its two particular motifs, the first is presented in the first two psalms, and the second in the third psalm and in all the hymns.

The first psalm of the Hour, Psalm 16 [LXX 16; Ps 17], **"Hear, O Lord, my righteousness"** [*Uslyshi, Gospodi, pravdu moyu*], is a prayer for help in the name of the petitioner's righteousness, and above all in the name of the marvelous mercy of God—for help against enemies seeking both directly and indirectly to destroy the righteous one, as one who, by his elevated disposition, does not conform to their entirely worldly interests.[^2730]

The second psalm of the Hour, Psalm 24 [LXX 24; Ps 25], **"Unto Thee, O Lord, *(Orig. p. 741)* have I lifted up my soul"** [*K Tebe, Gospodi, vozdvigokh dushu moyu*]—an acrostic psalm—contains a series of prayerful appeals to God, not strictly connected but ever intensifying, for protection against enemies and guidance in fulfilling the at times difficult law, in the name of the eternal mercy of God toward the faithful.

The third psalm of the Hour, Psalm 50 [LXX 50; Ps 51]—the penitential **"Have mercy upon me, O God"** [*Pomiluy mya Bozhe*]—implores forgiveness and the complete cleansing of sin (wherein reference is made to the Old Testament rite of purification through washing, which gave rise to Christian baptism) in the name of the mercy of God, but also on the foundation of profound repentance, for the cleansing of inborn sinfulness; this prayer then intensifies into a prayer for the granting of the Spirit of righteousness and purity, and concludes according to custom with a vow: to convert the lawless and to glorify God instead of offering material ...sacrifices.[^2731]

The Lenten troparion of the Third Hour, commemorating the Descent of the Holy Spirit, asks that He not be taken from us, and that He be renewed within us; the Theotokion calls the Mother of God the vine that brought forth Christ, having obviously in mind the Savior's comparison of Himself to the vine (John 15), the branches of which are the Apostles (as the first to receive the Holy Spirit), and asks for prayers from them and all the saints (this hymn frequently serves as the Theotokion for great saints).

The verse of the Third Hour from Psalm 67:20 [LXX 67:19; Ps 68:19] contains an ecstatic glorification of God (**"Blessed be the Lord God, blessed be the Lord..."**—the same phrase twice with an insignificant variation, out of the fullness of emotion), a glorification that is due unto Him daily, and consequently on this newly begun, now fully unfolded day, and which is united with hope in His help in the work of salvation, the uniquely divine work.

Among the Lenten troparia after the Trisagion at the Third Hour: the first (Tone 8), **"Blessed art Thou, O Christ our God"** [*Blagosloven yesi Khriste Bozhe nash*], glorifies the event commemorated at this Hour; the second, **"A speedy and firm consolation"** [*Skoroe i izvestnoe*], asks for the abiding presence of Christ with us, resembling His abiding presence with the Apostles (after the Descent of the Holy Spirit); the Theotokion, **"The hope and protection"** [*Nadezhda i predstatel'stvo*], expresses hope in the help of the Mother of God and asks for mercy through Her unceasing (not merely at specific hours, as with us) intercessions.

The priestly exclamation of the Third Hour (after the prayer **"Thou Who at all times"**), as also of the Sixth, **"Through the prayers of our holy fathers,"** is of a more joyful tone than at the First and Ninth Hours, in view of the commemoration linked with the Hour and the proximity of the Divine Liturgy.

The concluding prayer of the Hour, likewise in view of this commemoration, is addressed distinctly to all three Persons of the Holy Trinity, Whom it implores for salvation. The prayer is attributed to St. Mardarius, an Armenian martyr under Diocletian, and was pronounced by him under torture that culminated in his death—a torture consisting of being hung upside down and burned with red-hot iron; to his fellow martyr, St. Eustratius, belongs the prayer of the Saturday Midnight Office, **"Magnifying I magnify Thee"** [*Velichaya velichayu Tya*].

*(Orig. p. 742)*

#### History of the Hour

In the rite of the Sung Hours, the Third Hour apparently contained Psalm 16 [LXX].[^2732] In all ancient Horologia, beginning with the celebrated Horologion of the Sinai Library of the 8th century (no. 863), the present psalms are appointed for the Third Hour. Likewise the troparia after the psalms; only the Horologia of the St. Petersburg Public Library no. 57 and Sophia no. 1052 (13th c.) appoint on "Saturday, when there is no troparion" (for the day), for the Third Hour the troparia **"Passion-bearers of the Lord"** (now a sessional hymn in Tone 2) and **"A dread ...mystery is death."

After the Trisagion, Sinai Horologion no. 865 (12th c.) has the troparia: **"O Heavenly King,"** **"As Thou wast in the midst of Thy disciples,"** and **"The great multitude of my sins, O Theotokos"**; the Horologion of the Athonite St. Panteleimon Library no. 71 (12th–13th c.) has for the second troparion **"When Thou didst descend,"** and for the third **"To Thee, the Champion Leader"**; Sinai no. 866 (12th c.) has for the second troparion **"When Thou didst descend,"** while Moscow Typography Library nos. 46 and 48 (15th c.) lack the second, having for the third **"Thee do we have as a rampart and haven."** The concluding prayer is absent in Sinai Horologia no. 863 (8th c.), 867 (12th–14th c.), and Moscow Typography Library no. 47 (15th c.). In Vatopedi Horologion no. 350 (12th c.) there is a brief prayer resembling the present troparion, **"Thou Who at the third hour"**; Sinai no. 870 (12th c.) contains the present prayer of the Mid-Hour; Sophia (St. Petersburg Theological Academy) no. 1052 has: **"O Compassionate God, Who comfortest us at every hour"** (moreover, at the beginning of the Hour, a "prayer beginning all chanting": **"Master, Lord Almighty, Who receivest from the Heavenly Hosts the Thrice-Holy Hymn"**—the same prayer appears at this place in Typography no. 47); Sinai no. 865 (12th c.) contains two prayers: the present prayer of the Mid-Hour and **"O Lord my Savior, why hast Thou forsaken me?"**; Typography nos. 46 and 48 contain that found in Sophia no. 1052 and **"O Righteous and All-Praised God"**; Khludov no. 123 (10th c.) contains this and the present prayer; Sinai no. 12 and St. Petersburg Public Library no. 57 (13th c.) contain three prayers: this same one, **"O Holy God, Comforter, Spirit of Truth,"** and **"O God Almighty and Father of Jesus Christ."**[^2733]

*(Orig. p. 743)*

### THE SIXTH HOUR

#### Content of the Hour

The Sixth Hour is dedicated to the commemoration of the Crucifixion of Christ itself (according to the *Instructional Notice* of the *Sluzhebnik*—of its circumstances from the bearing of the Cross until the darkening of the sun).

All the psalms of the Hour depict the persecution of the righteous one by enemies seeking his destruction.

The first psalm of the Hour, Psalm 53 [LXX 53; Ps 54], **"Save me, O God, in Thy name"** [*Bozhe, vo imya Tvoe spasi mya*], bearing the infrequent inscription "Instruction" (*Maskil*), asks God, for the sake of His very name (the preservation of its holiness), for salvation in a righteous cause from terrible enemies who forget God, expresses certainty in this, and offers a vow of thanksgiving.

The second psalm of the Hour, Psalm 54 [LXX 54; Ps 55], **"Give ear, O God, unto my prayer"** [*Vnushi, Bozhe, molitvu moyu*], is an agitated prayer to God in great affliction,[^2734] reaching even to the desire completely to abandon the city filled with violence and strife (guarded as if by an evil watch upon its walls), especially in view of a friend turned enemy;[^2735] a prayer for the destruction of the enemies, interwoven with the expression of complete certainty in salvation.

The third psalm of the Hour—Psalm 90 [LXX 90; Ps 91], **"He that dwelleth in the aid of the Most High"** [*Zhivyy v pomoshchi Vyshnyago*]—sketches in the form of an instruction all the benefits of complete trust in God (Who is called here by the most sublime titles), Who protects the one hoping in Him as with wings (perhaps an allusion to the Cherubim) from silently ambushing death (the snare of the fowlers), from all dangers of night and day that destroy thousands,[^2736] and from noxious beasts by means of Angels who do not allow him even to stumble against a stone; wherein a solemn assurance is given to us by God Himself, promising, moreover, to the one who trusts all earthly blessings and salvation.[^2737]

The Lenten troparion of the Hour, **"Thou Who on the sixth day and hour"** [*Izhe v shestyy den' zhe i chas*], commemorating the Crucifixion, asks for the forgiveness of sins and for salvation; the Theotokion **"Seeing that we have no boldness"** [*Yako ne imamy derznoveniya*] urgently implores the intercessions of the Mother of God in view of our sinfulness, redeemed by the sufferings of Her Son (the reflection on the latter being most general; in the Theotokion of the Ninth Hour it is more detailed).

The verse of the Hour (Psalm 78:8–9 [LXX 78:8–9]), **"Let Thy tender mercies speedily anticipate us,"** contains the prayer of a suffering soul for divine help and the purging of sins for the glory of the name of God.

The Lenten troparia after the Trisagion, **"Thou hast wrought salvation,"** **"To Thine immaculate Icon,"** speak of the Crucifixion, but the Theotokion is of such content only on Wednesday and Friday (**"Most praised art Thou, O Virgin Theotokos"** [*Preproslavlena *(Orig. p. 744)* yesi, Bogoroditse Devo*]), while on the remaining days it is of a prayerful, penitential content (**"Thou Who art a fountain of tender compassion"** [*Miloserdiya sushchi istochnik*]).

The priest's exclamatory blessing: **"Through the prayers of our holy fathers."**

The prayer of the hour, inscribed, as at the Ninth Hour, with the name of St. Basil the Great, **"O God and Lord of hosts"** [*Bozhe i Gospodi sil*], petitions God the Father, Who by the Cross of His Son tore up the handwriting of our sins (cf. the Lenten troparion) and vanquished the principalities and powers of darkness (cf. Ps. 90:6 [LXX]), to accept our thanksgiving and supplicatory prayers, to deliver us from sins and enemies, to "nail our flesh to Thy fear" (from Ps. 118:120 [LXX]) even unto abstinence from evil thoughts, and to wound our souls with love for Thee, so that, illuminated by His light (an allusion to noonday), we may offer Him unceasing confession and thanksgiving (not merely at fixed hours).

### History of the Hour
The Psalms of the Sixth Hour already in the most ancient manuscript Horologia coincide with the present ones. The same is true of the Lenten troparia following the Psalms. Only in the most ancient Sinaitic Horologion (Sin. gr. 863, 8th–9th c.) is this troparion, although close in text to the present one, more extensive; at *Glory...* another troparion is appointed according to the day of the week. The Horologia of the Imperial Public Library (No. 57) and the St. Sophia Library at the St. Petersburg Theological Academy (No. 1052, 13th c.) appoint for Saturday the troparia: **"Apostles, prophets, martyrs"** [*Apostoli, prorotsy, muchenitsy*] and **"Remember, O Lord, for Thou art good"** [*Pomyani, Gospodi, yako blag*]. Troparia after the Trisagion are absent in some Horologia (the same ones as for the other hours). The Horologia of the Moscow Synodal Typography Library (No. 46, 14th c., and No. 48, 15th c.) lack the second troparion; Sin. gr. 865 (12th c.) does not prescribe for Wednesday and Friday the special Theotokion **"Most praised art Thou"** [*Preproslavlena yesi*]. Some manuscripts lack the concluding prayer (the same ones as for the other hours); Vatopedi No. 350 (15th c.) has a concise prayer close to the Lenten troparion, as at the other hours; Synodal Typography Nos. 46 and 48 have two prayers: **"O Lord our God, Who hast vouchsafed us to pass through the midday"** [*Gospodi Bozhe nash, Izhe v pol dne spodobivyi preyti*] and **"O Christ our God, Who for the sake of our condemnation"** [*Khriste Bozhe nash, Izhe nashego radi osuzheniya*]; Sin. gr. 12 (12th–13th c.) and Public Library No. 57 (13th c.) likewise have two: the second of those noted and **"O Lord highest over all and for the sake of all"** [*Gospodi vyshli vsekh i vsekh radi*]; Sophia No. 1052 has only the first from the Synodal Typography; Sin. gr. 870 (13th c.) has the present prayer; Khludov No. 123 (15th c.), regarding the prayers of the Mid-Hour (*mesorion*), remarks that if there is no Mid-Hour, they are read at the hour (and likewise for the other hours)[^2738].
*(Orig. p. 745)*

## THE VARIABLE PARTS OF THE DIVINE LITURGY (SUNDAY)

The Divine Liturgy is so sacred, so "divine" a service that the Orthodox Church does not venture to alter it even for such great feasts as Pascha. It is sufficiently joyful even in its ordinary form for all feasts, for which reason during fasts it is entirely cancelled. In these respects it reflects upon itself the immutability and all-blessedness of God. Yet all this holds true only for the most essential portion of the Liturgy, for its "canon" (Anaphora), where it becomes the Mystery of the Eucharist. Only here does the Orthodox Church, in contrast to the Roman Catholic Church, not venture to alter so much as a single word for any feast. In the liturgical prayers that surround this most sacred portion, however—in the preparatory and concluding parts of the Liturgy—adaptation to the commemorations of the day is permitted and, one may say, increases in proportion to the distance of these parts from the "canon." In view of this, the beginning of the Liturgy is entirely distinct (not counting the litanies, which are identical with those of other services) for weekdays, for medium feasts, and for great feasts.

### The Typika (Typical Antiphons)
The Liturgy begins with three series of chants, rightly termed in the *Sluzhebnik* (*Hieratikon*), by reason of their manner of performance, "antiphons." It is precisely these antiphons that conform to the festive rank of the day. For Sundays and less momentous feasts, beginning with sixfold saints[^2739] up to and including the Great Twelve (*Dodekaorton*) feasts of the Mother of God, these "antiphons" are served by the so-called "Typika" (*izobrazitelnye*) and the "Beatitudes" (*Blazhenny*).

### Content of the Typical Psalms
Psalms 102 and 145 are called "Typika" (*izobrazitelnye*, τυπικά) not because, as was previously thought, they depict (*izobrazhayut*) the blessings of redemption, but rather, in all likelihood, because within the composition of the Liturgy only this part is subject to the regulation of the *Typikon* (the rule of the order), being capable of assuming varied "forms" (τύπος). These specific Psalms were chosen here because they represent an ecstatically joyful glorification arising from the depths of the soul ("Bless the Lord, O my soul," "Praise the Lord, O my soul," and likewise Ps. 103; cf. the Canticle of the Mother of God) and thanksgiving to God (so fitting for the Eucharist) for His tender mercy, manifested especially in the forgiveness of sins and help to the afflicted. Psalm 102 *(Orig. p. 746)*, **"Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me bless His holy name,"** glorifies God for healing from mortal sickness ("Who redeemeth thy life from corruption")[^2740], and then generally for His mercies toward Israel, and for His tender mercy in general and toward sins in particular, elicited in God, among other things, by the awareness of human insignificance; in conclusion, the Psalm depicts the sovereign dominion of God (thus gradually broadening the sphere of contemplation), summoning all Angels and all creatures to the glorification of God. Psalm 145, **"Praise the Lord, O my soul,"** glorifies God as our steadfast hope, in contrast to the unreliability of even the highest-ranking men, grounding this thought upon the creative power of God, His eternal truth, His constant benefactions to all who are oppressed, and His thwarting of sinners[^2741].

### History
Among non-Orthodox liturgies, whole Psalms at the beginning are found in the Nestorian Liturgy attributed to the Apostles Addai and Mari—Psalm 14 [LXX][^2742]—and the Coptic Liturgy attributed to Basil the Great—Psalm 50 [LXX] immediately before the Gospel[^2743].

The Roman Liturgy frequently employs excerpts from the Psalms as the *introitus* (entrance verse)[^2744].

The Liturgy of the Apostle James, the prototype of our own, apparently possessed at the beginning neither Psalms nor antiphons (the manuscripts indicate none)[^2745].

The Studite-Alexian Typikon forbids the Typical Psalms and the Beatitudes at the weekday Liturgy during the Apostles' Fast (Peter's Fast)[^2746].

The Western Studite (Calabrian) and Evergetis Typika prescribe the Typika for the Sunday Liturgy[^2747].

Manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon are silent (the Slavic ones speak of the Beatitudes). Manuscripts of Euchologia of the 16th century state: "After the litany of peace, the choir chants the 1st antiphon, or the Typika if it is Sunday; but if not, of the day... After the litany of peace, the second choir chants the second antiphon, or the second Typika if it is Sunday; but if not, of the day"[^2748].

### The Order of Chanting the Typical Psalms
The order of chanting the Typical Psalms is set forth in the *Heirmologion*[^2749] and the *Horologion* in the order of the Typika (*Izobrazitelnye*). They are appointed here to be chanted in Tone 8, in all likelihood as the most calm and solemn, wherein the troparic melody *(Orig. p. 747)* of this tone is intended, because only such is employed at the Liturgy (at the Beatitudes, the canonic melody is also used). Musical tradition diverges from this rubric: it assigns to the Typika the troparic melody of Tone 1, evidently presuming that they ought to follow the tone of the day (just as the Alleluiaria are always chanted in Tone 1). The silence of the *Horologion* regarding the tone likewise supports this supposition.

The Typika are chanted antiphonally. The distribution of verses for chanting between the two choirs is given in the *Heirmologion*. It coincides with the biblical division of verses, except that in Psalm 102, verse 6 is joined with 7, and 9 with 10, by virtue of which the total number of verses in this Psalm for antiphonal chanting amounts to 20 (instead of the 22 biblical verses); and in Psalm 145, verse 1 is joined with 2, by reason of which the verses amount to 9 (instead of the 10 biblical verses). The Psalms possess a refrain as well, but only at the beginning and the end. The refrain for Psalm 102 is the same as that for the neighboring and cognate Psalm 103 in the Bible, the Introductory Psalm of Vespers (the daily office closest to the Liturgy), namely: **"Blessed art Thou, O Lord"** (Ps. 118:12 [LXX]). This refrain is appended to the opening words of verse 1: **"Bless the Lord, O my soul,"** as in the Introductory Psalm and at *Lord, I have cried*, and to the entire 1st verse, but only when this verse is repeated at the end of the Psalm, after *Glory... Both now...*. In this way, the employment of the refrain with this Psalm is exceptional, applied in exactly this manner nowhere else, which corresponds to the uniqueness of the Divine Liturgy among the cycle of services. At the same time, this usage bears the character of singular simplicity: the refrain is purely scriptural (psalmic) and most concise; at *Glory... Both now...* there are no additions complicating this refrain to the Psalms as found at other services. Antiphonally chanted are not only the verses of the Psalm, but also *Glory... Both now...*; this latter is chanted in a "higher voice," likewise half by each choir, and the first choir chants again at the end the 1st verse with the refrain (at the place indicated above), thus returning the Psalm to its beginning. Psalm 145 is chanted according to a different order. Its refrain is served solely by *Glory... Both now...*, but in such a manner that *Glory...* is chanted before the Psalm, and *Both now...* after it, accompanied by the hymn **"Only-begotten Son"** [*Yedinorodnyi Syne*], wherein the chanting here is begun by the second choir, and by virtue of this the hymn falls to the first choir.

### Historical References
The method of appending the refrain to Psalm 102 resembles the antiphon in Roman Catholic worship (at the end of the psalm the complete verse, and before the psalm two or three opening words). Concerning *Glory... Both now...* at the end of the Psalms, see Introductory Chapter, p. 217.

### The Beatitudes: Content
After the 1st and 2nd antiphons have "depicted" the Kingdom of God (Ps. 102:19; 145:10 [LXX]) from the Old Testament perspective, the 3rd antiphon—during which the rite symbolizing the "entrance of the saints" into the Heavenly Kingdom is performed—provides the New Testament portrait of this Kingdom, naturally opening it with the prayer (of the Wise Thief, repeated also at the Great Entrance) for *(Orig. p. 748)* our admission into it. Inasmuch as there is no more vivid and touchingly joyful teaching concerning the Kingdom of God than that given by the Beatitudes, they are summoned here, elevating and intensifying the sensation of delight in the blessings of God that breathes within the Typical Psalms. At the same time, into the variable portion of the Liturgy, which is already drawing near to its end, extra-biblical hymnographic material is now introduced for the first time—in the form of special additional hymns to the verses of the Beatitudes, termed, like these verses, "Beatitudes" (*Blazhenny*, μακαρισμοί). They glorify the celebrated event, just as do the troparia of the canon, by which they are sometimes replaced, without reference to the accompanying biblical verses, with the exception of the 1st Beatitude, which, like the heirmos in the canon, bears such a reference, that is, it always speaks of the repentance of the thief crucified together with Christ.

### Melody
The Beatitudes are chanted to a special melody of the tone of the week, close to the troparic and canonic melodies. Thus, from the diverse melodies of the tone, the richest are taken into the Liturgy: the troparic, the canonic, and the prokeimenon melodies.

### Order of Chanting
For chanting, the Gospel Beatitudes, with the prayer preceding them: **"In Thy kingdom remember us, O Lord,"** and the concluding doxology to them (by analogy with the preceding Psalms), are divided into 12 verses[^2750], wherein the prayer with the 1st Beatitude is united into a single verse, while from the final Beatitude, by reason of its length, the promise is separated: **"Rejoice and be glad..."**, just as *Glory...* is separated from *Both now...*. The troparia are appended to the Gospel Beatitudes at the ordinary Sunday Liturgy, unencumbered by other sacred commemorations, not from the 1st verse, but, like the stichera at *Lord, I have cried*, from one of the subsequent verses, specifically from the 3rd, so that in total there are 10 of them, and without *Glory... Both now...*, 8—two more than at a weekday Liturgy. When there coincides with Sunday any commemoration possessing its own Beatitudes, the number of Sunday Beatitudes is reduced to 6 and 4, while the total number of Beatitudes may increase to 12, beginning from the 1st verse. Yet Beatitudes in the proper sense are possessed only by the Octoechos. For all other commemorations, the Beatitudes are served by odes of the canon, specifically the 3rd and 6th odes, or the 3rd ode alone. Such odes in the canon were selected, in all probability, because their numbering corresponds to the Third and Sixth Hours with which the Liturgy is celebrated, or because of a correspondence in the content of the biblical canticles underlying them with the Beatitudes (consolation in affliction)[^2751]. If on Sunday there falls one commemoration possessing an ode of the canon at the Beatitudes, the Sunday Beatitudes are chanted on 6 and the 3rd ode of the canon on 4; if there are two such commemorations, the Sunday Beatitudes are on 4 and each of the odes of the canon—the 3rd and the 6th—on 4 (concerning this, see Chapters 3, 4, and 5 of the *Typikon*, in the Menologion, for example *(Orig. p. 749)* September 1 and 9, in the Triodion, and in the Pentecostarion). The odes of the canon must evidently be chanted without a heirmos, since it is replaced by the first troparion (*blazhenna*) of the Octoechos (when only odes of the canon are chanted at the Beatitudes, then it is with a heirmos; see Sunday of Antipascha at Vespers, 2nd *Mark* [*Zri*]).

### "O Come, Let Us Worship"
The conclusion of the Beatitudes, which serve, as it were, as the chant of the Little Entrance at the Liturgy, being properly the "Entrance Verse" (*introitus* / *eisodikon*), is served by the chant: **"O come, let us worship and fall down before Christ,"** a verse that opens other services as well (conceptually, the Liturgy begins from here, from the Entrance, which is why before it the bishop takes no part in it), and which is so fitting for the Entrance, with the refrain: **"Save us, O Son of God, (on Sunday:) Who art risen from the dead (on weekdays: 'Who art wonderful in the saints'; on feasts of the Mother of God: 'through the prayers of the Theotokos'), who sing unto Thee: Alleluia."** Alleluia is chanted once, as is expressly stated in the *Sluzhebnik* and as is done at the corresponding festive refrain to the 2nd antiphon, and not thrice, because the hymn refers to the Savior alone, and not to the Holy Trinity, as does, for example, the Alleluia at Lenten Matins.

### Significance of the Beatitudes

Nowhere in the Liturgy is there such a convergence of specifically festive hymns as is presented by the Beatitudes with their 8–12 troparia. This is, one may say, the most festive part of the Liturgy, especially if one takes into account their melody—the richest in melody of all the tone melodies. It is not surprising, therefore, that the Typikon sometimes cancels even the antiphons of the Great Twelve Feasts of the Lord in order to preserve the Beatitudes. Thus, if the commemoration of St. John the Theologian falls on Ascension, the antiphons of the feast are omitted and the Typical Psalms are chanted solely so that at the Entrance the memory of the saint can be honored with the ode of his canon. The same is done if the patronal feast of a saint falls even on Pentecost[^2752].

### History of Usage
The Beatitudes within the structure of the Liturgy are so closely bound up with the Typika that they could appear within it only concurrently with them, consequently comparatively late (see above). Their presence at Matins of the Great Canon, of Great Friday, and in the Order of Burial—a service so close in structure to Matins—may argue that originally they were employed at that office. It is strange that Roman Catholic worship did not utilize so edifying and artistic a page of the Gospel.

*(Orig. p. 750)*

### Troparia and Kontakia
In the thought that at the entrance of the clergy into the altar there occurs the entrance thither of the saints as well, the Church naturally at this moment sings praises unto the saints, appointing after the Entrance troparia and kontakia to them. At the Divine Liturgy, sometimes (on weekdays) this is the sole place dedicated to the commemoration of the day. For this reason, from the hymns of the day the most general are chosen here, those expressing to the highest degree the essence of the celebrated event. Both troparia and kontakia are distinguished by precisely this character, often supplementing one another in content (see above, p. 689), which is why both here (and only here) are provided in combination with one another. This group of hymns endeavors to embrace all commemorations united with the day of the celebration of the Liturgy, to demonstrate that the bloodless sacrifice is offered on behalf of all and for all; on this ground, on weekdays at the Liturgy the troparion and kontakion of the day of the week are also chanted (on Monday, of the Bodiless Powers, etc.), which are chanted nowhere else—neither at Vespers, nor at Matins, nor at the Hours.

Finally, only here throughout the daily cycle of services are chanted the troparion and kontakion of the temple, in which alone the celebration of the Liturgy is possible. There results a series that is varied also in a musical respect, wherein the melody passes from one tone to another from minute to minute. Since the series of hymns by virtue of all this turns out to be lengthy, the troparia at the Liturgy (in contrast to Vespers and Matins) are not chanted more than once. The hymns are arranged according to the rank of importance of the commemorations, yet such that troparia precede kontakia. The conclusion to this series of hymns, according to the rule adopted for other cases as well, is served (in the majority of instances) by the kontakion of the Mother of God, identical for both festive and weekday Liturgies, **"O Protection of Christians"** [*Predstatelstvo khristian*], taken from the Molieben and containing an intensified supplication, united with glorification, to the Mother of God for aid and intercession (in accordance with the intercessory character of the Liturgy), which is why the kontakion is chanted in the plaintive Tone 6 (cf. **"With the saints give rest"** [*So svyatymi upokoy*], **"My soul"** [*Dushe moya*]).

In view of the fact that the order of troparia and kontakia at the Liturgy is determined by the importance of the commemorations, it cannot be identical for different temples, which is why it requires an especially complex regulation, such as is set forth in Chapter 32 of the *Typikon*. Here it is provided only for an ordinary Sunday, unencumbered by any special commemorations. The general rule of alternation is as follows: first come the resurrection hymns, then those of the temple, and finally those of the saints of the day. Yet this is adhered to strictly only for the troparia. Even for them, an exception is sometimes made from this order: since the Resurrection of Christ was the crown of His life, after the resurrection troparion and kontakion it would be superfluous to chant the troparion and kontakion to a temple of Christ[^2753] (in honor of some other event from the life of the Savior); therefore, following the resurrection troparion there is chanted only the troparion of a temple of the Mother of God or of a saint, and thereafter of the saint or saints of the day. The kontakia follow this same order, with the distinction that, since *(Orig. p. 751)* it is customary to assign *Both now...* to the Theotokion kontakion, here there is chanted, omitting its earlier turn, the kontakion of the temple if the temple is dedicated to the Mother of God; "if not," **"O Protection of Christians"**; and at *Glory...* the final kontakion is chanted—that of the saint of the day. The present passage of the *Typikon* gives no definite indication of what to chant at *Both now...* if the temple is of Christ. Chapter 52 of the *Typikon* indicates that in such a case one is to chant the resurrection kontakion at *Both now...*, transferring it hither from the 1st place. This ordinary order of chanting troparia and kontakia at the Liturgy undergoes changes indicated in other passages of the *Typikon*. Thus, in the presence of a great saint, and during forefeasts and afterfeasts, the troparion and kontakion of the temple patron saint are not chanted (Chapters 3 and 52); in the presence of a Polyeleos saint, they follow after the saint of the day (Chapter 4); when the service to the saint of the day is cancelled or transferred, his troparion and kontakion are not chanted (Sundays preparatory to Great Lent, of Great Lent, and of the Pentecostarion).

### History of Usage
Concerning the chanting of troparia and kontakia at the Sunday Liturgy according to the Studite Typikon, nothing is known.

According to the Evergetis Typikon: "the resurrection troparion and Theotokion."

According to the Slavic (the Greek are silent) manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon: "the resurrection troparion of the tone of the week; *Glory... Both now...* O Defender [= Protection] of Christians."

According to the present Greek *Typikon*: "the resurrection troparion, of the celebrated saint, of the saint of the monastery, and the kontakion"; according to the *Hieratikon*: the kontakion **"O Protection of Christians"**, except for forefeasts, afterfeasts, and the period of the Triodion, when the kontakion of that season is chanted[^2754].

According to the Old Believer Typikon, troparia and kontakia are chanted "to the temples" (that is, to the side-altar chapels as well); to a temple of Christ only the troparion is not chanted; at *Both now...* the kontakion to the temple of the Mother of God or of Christ; in a temple of Christ, **"O Protection"** [= *Zastupnitse*] is also permitted; the Typikon does not mention the resurrection kontakion, but in practice it is chanted[^2755].

### Prokeimenon and Alleluiarion
The most important variable parts of the Liturgy are the Epistle (*Apostol*) and the Gospel. Both, in view of this, possess before them an exceedingly complex preparation, whose variable elements before the former are served by the Prokeimenon, and before the latter by the Alleluiarion.

### The Prokeimenon
The Prokeimenon is chanted at the Liturgy according to the same order as at Vespers, though not of Sunday Vespers, but of any other, that is, 2 1/2 times, and with the same preliminary exclamations, with the exception of the final "Let us attend!", in all likelihood because it occurs before the reading, and repeating it before the Prokeimenon would rank the latter higher than the reading. In contrast to Vespers, the Prokeimenon varies at the Liturgy according to the tones, yet the melody of the tone is the same as at Vespers. Being distinguished *(Orig. p. 752)* in general by an exceptional melodic richness notwithstanding its brevity, this melody is exceedingly varied for different tones, for some assuming the most joyful coloration, as for Tone 8 (Tone 8 prokeimena of Pascha and the Nativity of Christ), and for others the most plaintive, as Tone 6 (the Prokeimenon for the departed) and Tone 7 (**"The rulers of the peoples"** [*Knyazi lyudstii*]).

### In the Western Church
In the Roman Liturgy (Mass), that which corresponds to our Prokeimenon is the *Graduale*, but it is chanted not before the Epistle (*epistola*), but after it. The *Graduale* received its name from the fact that it was chanted from that step (*gradus*) of the ambo from which the Epistle was read. It, like our Prokeimenon (see above, p. 562), replaced the chanting at this point of the Liturgy—between its scriptural readings—of an entire Psalm; the replacement occurred in the 5th–6th centuries: under Leo the Great, apparently, they still chanted an entire Psalm[^2756]—and was occasioned by the increasing complexity of the music. The order of chanting the *Graduale* closely resembles the chanting of our Prokeimenon, especially in its most ancient form; according to *Ordo Romanus II* (7th c.): "a single cantor begins the *responsum* (the 1st verse of the *Graduale*, subsequently repeated), and all in the choir respond, and likewise alone he chants the verse of the responsory; after this the choir chants again the 1st verse, and the cantor repeats it once more, but in a higher pitch; finally, the choir chants it a third time"[^2757]. The present rubric (*Graduale Romanum*, 1886) has shortened this order: two cantors begin the *responsum*, chanting from it only one or two opening words, while the choir concludes, and then two cantors chant the verse.

It is remarkable that the *Graduale* is not appointed during the period of the Pentecostarion from New Sunday (Antipascha) until Trinity Sunday; this the medieval liturgists explained by stating that in its tone it is too mournful a chant in comparison with the subsequent Alleluia, the preparatory hymn for the Gospel; it signifies the penitential preaching of John the Forerunner, whereas the Alleluia signifies the joyful Gospel of Christ; that it is nevertheless chanted during Bright Week they explained by stating that the newly baptized, who wore their white baptismal garments until Bright Saturday, were required during the course of this week to remain still in a penitential disposition[^2758]. In all probability, it was precisely the view of the *Graduale* as a mournful chant that displaced it from the specified period, without daring to touch Pascha itself.

### Sunday Prokeimena
Of the 8 Sunday Liturgical Prokeimena, only two are of supplicatory content: Tone 1, **"Let Thy mercy, O Lord, be upon us"** (Ps. 32:22 [LXX]), and Tone 6, **"Save, O Lord, Thy people"** (Ps. 27:9 [LXX]), one is of a hopeful character—Tone 5 (parallel both in a musical respect and in content to Tone 1: "even as we have hoped"): **"Thou, O Lord, shalt keep us..."** (Ps. 11:8 [LXX]), while the remainder are of a laudatory character, which is more fitting for the tone of the Sunday service; the most laudatory is Tone 4: **"How *(Orig. p. 753)* magnified are Thy works, O Lord..."** (Ps. 103:24 [LXX]); then, parallel in content, Tone 3: **"Sing praises to our God..."** (Ps. 46:7 [LXX]) and Tone 8: **"Make your vows (in Heb.: 'make vows') and pay them..."** (Ps. 75:12 [LXX]); finally, likewise parallel—Tone 2: **"The Lord is my strength and my song..."** (Ps. 117:14 [LXX]) and Tone 7: **"The Lord will give strength unto His people..."** (Ps. 28:11 [LXX]). The verses to the prokeimena, according to custom, are served by the opening verses of the Psalms from which the prokeimena are taken, except for Tone 2, where the verse is Psalm 117:18 [LXX].

### History
Of the Sunday Liturgical prokeimena, the "Jerusalem Order" of Holy Week and Bright Week of the 9th century provides the Prokeimenon of Tone 7 at Vespers of Bright Thursday; the Typikon of the Great Church of Constantinople of the 9th century gives the Prokeimenon of Tone 6 on the Tuesday of Pentecost. All prokeimena in present usage are provided by the Evergetis Typikon (11th–12th c.), with the sole peculiarity that the Prokeimenon of Tone 6 serves also for Tone 4[^2759].

### The Alleluiarion
Being accounted more sacred than the Epistle (*Apostol*), the Gospel must possess before it a most excellent preparation as well. If at Matins such a preparation for it is served by the Prokeimenon, then at the Liturgy, where the latter precedes the Epistle, the Gospel must possess before it something still more exceptional. Such indeed is the chant *Alleluia*, appointed before the Liturgical Gospel. According to the Apocalypse, this will be the heavenly song of eternity[^2760]. Except for "Amen," this is the sole Hebrew expression that the hand of the translator did not dare to touch, leaving it in the very sounds in which it was inspired by God; there breathes from it, therefore, a spirit of glossolalic mystery (Introductory Chapter, p. 41; cf. p. 34 ff.), prompting its employment, for example, at the Mystery of Baptism (similar to the *Kyrie eleison* at Ordination). Serving as the refrain of the most joyful (among the Hebrews, Paschal) Psalms in the Bible, the *Alleluia* steps forth as an almost invariable refrain of the Psalms in our divine worship, but this is almost the sole place (the other being at Lenten and memorial Matins) where it steps forth in the capacity of an independent chant possessing, on the contrary, refrains attached to itself, termed alleluiaria (*alleluiarion*, άλληλουιάριον); these are psalm verses having reference to the commemoration of the day, of which two are normally appointed for the threefold chanting of the Alleluia (each time thrice) (three verses only on Great Saturday). The verses, as in the Prokeimenon, are taken from a single Psalm, often contiguous ones.

### The Order of Chanting the Alleluia
The chanting of the Alleluia is prefaced by the exclamation: **"Wisdom!"**, which in its brevity is more eloquent than the complex exclamation before the Prokeimenon (cf. at the beginning of the Liturgy of the Faithful, before "Holy things to the holy," and at Baptism: "Let us attend!").

*(Orig. p. 754)*

The Alleluia is chanted with its verses according to the tones, to the melody of the Prokeimenon (in practice, usually to the melody of Tone 1), according to the very same order as the Prokeimenon, **"God is the Lord"**, and the Alleluia at Matins, which is why this order is nowhere explicitly prescribed—that is, the reader (having replied to the priest's "Peace be to thee" with "And to thy spirit") proclaims the tone of the Alleluia (**"Alleluia, in Tone N"**), after which the choir chants the Alleluia thrice; the reader chants (usually proclaims) the first alleluiarion verse, and the choir again chants the Alleluia thrice; the reader proclaims the second alleluiarion verse, and the choir chants the Alleluia thrice (this is done in the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra, although the verses are read). The solemnity of the moment is heightened by the censing taking place at that time, preparatory to the Gospel[^2761].

### History of the Gospel Alleluia and Alleluiarion
Concerning the antiquity of the pre-Gospel Alleluia, its existence in the Western Church in a form very close to our own can bear witness. The Alleluia before the Liturgical Gospel there consists of a twofold chanting of the Alleluia, then a single verse, and once again a single Alleluia; all this is chanted to a single melody according to the following order provided in the *Graduale Romanum* (which also contains the musical notes for the Alleluia of the various feasts): "If the Alleluia, Alleluia is said with a verse, first the Alleluia is chanted by two (cantors) up to the neume (so called from the rich melisma upon the final syllable—otherwise *jubilus*), while the choir repeats the Alleluia and appends the neume, prolonging the syllable *a*; two cantors begin the verse and the choir responds (= continues the verse); upon the conclusion of the verse the same two repeat the Alleluia, and the choir appends a single neume." The melody for this Alleluia, which was called the "lesser" (*alleluia minus*), in the Roman Church was always distinguished by exceptional vivacity, energy, and beauty. It is not chanted throughout the entire period of Great Lent and the weeks preparatory to it (from Septuagesima Sunday), on weekdays of Advent, during the Ember days (fasts of the Four Seasons), and on vigils. Introduced under Pope Damasus (4th c.), the Alleluia was originally chanted only during the Paschal season, and only Gregory the Great (6th c.) permitted it to be chanted on other feasts as well. In place of the neume, they subsequently began to substitute a special appropriate text, at first non-rhythmical and therefore termed *prosa*, and later entire metrical hymns, termed *sequentia*, in all likelihood because the Gospel following them has the exclamation before it: *"Sequentia Sancti Evangelii secundum N."* (one can hardly, following Thalhofer, see here an echo of the Greek ακολουθία); of such hymns in France and Germany by the 12th century there appeared up to 200, which entered into their local Missals, but into the official Roman Missal only five sequences entered: for Pascha, Pentecost, the Feast of Corpus Christi, the Seven Sorrows of the Mother of God on the Friday of the 6th week of Lent *(Orig. p. 755)* (*Stabat Mater*)[^2762], and the Requiem Mass (*Dies Irae*). These are entire hymns of some 8–10 strophes. They were chanted in some places by the whole choir, and in other places by individual cantors alternately. On the days of the Forty Days (*Quadragesima*) and those preparatory to it, and on penitential and memorial days, in place of the Alleluia before the Gospel there is chanted the so-called *tractus*, consisting of verses (2–5, sometimes half a Psalm and an entire Psalm, for example on the 1st Sunday of Lent—Psalm 90 [LXX], on Palm Sunday—Psalm 21 [LXX]), for the most part psalm verses adapted to the commemorations of the day, of which strictly speaking the first bears this name, while the others are termed "verses"; yet originally all of them were chanted from the ambo by a single cantor without interruption (= *tractim*; others identified the designation with *heirmos*) on the part of the choir, whereas later they began to chant such that two cantors began the verse and the choir continued; such chanting was compared to the singing of the turtledove, always solitary, in contrast to the alternating kind of ordinary, antiphonal or responsorial singing, likened to the cooing of doves (Luke 2:24 was also kept in view); for this reason alone the chanting of the *tractus* was termed the song of weeping and sorrow (*cantus fletus et tristitiae*), and the tones assigned to it were Tones 2 and 8[^2763].

According to the Mozarabic rite, the Alleluia (there termed *Lauda*) is chanted after the Gospel: first the Alleluia once, then a verse or several of them, and again the Alleluia; in Great Lent, beginning with the 2nd Sunday, the *Lauda* consists solely of verses without the Alleluia[^2764].

As for the Eastern liturgies, all of them, except for the Coptic, which has before the Gospel not the Alleluia but Psalm 50 [LXX], preface the Gospel with the Alleluia: in the Abyssinian (Ethiopian) Liturgy the priest pronounces the Alleluia thrice after 3 verses from the beginning of Psalm 33 [LXX]; in the Nestorian Liturgy the deacon who read the Epistle pronounces the Alleluia thrice and the cantors chant it[^2765].

Among Orthodox liturgical monuments, the most ancient mention of the Alleluia before the Gospel with an indication of the tone and one verse from the Psalm is found in the Jerusalem Kanonarion of the 7th century in the Georgian version[^2766].

Among ancient Orthodox liturgies, the Alleluia before the Gospel is mentioned by: the Alexandrian Liturgy of Mark the Evangelist according to an 11th-century manuscript: "the prologue of the Alleluia" (ό πρόλογος τοΰ αλληλούια); the Liturgy of the Apostle Peter: "Alleluia"; the Jerusalem Liturgy of the Apostle James according to a 10th-century manuscript: "the Alleluia" (with the article *to*); 11th century: "and the stichologia"; 16th century: "the chanter (*psaltes*) the Alleluia (with the article)" or without "the chanter"[^2767].

According to one of the most ancient manuscripts of the Liturgy of John Chrysostom:
"Deacon: Wisdom. Priest: Peace be to all. Deacon: Wisdom, let us attend! Then he says the alleluiarion"; according to another manuscript: "after the Epistle, the priest says: Peace be to all. Wisdom, stand upright! Cantor: A Psalm of David. Alleluia"; later manuscripts: "Deacon: Wisdom; Choir: Alleluia. A Psalm of David"[^2768].

The printed Slavic *(Orig. p. 756)* *Sluzhebniks*, Moscow, 1602 (= the Old Believer edition):
"Deacon: Let us attend, wisdom, let us attend! Reader: And to thy spirit. A Psalm of David. Alleluia. And the cantors chant: Alleluia."
The *Sluzhebnik* of Peter Mohyla, 1627:
"Deacon: Wisdom, let us attend! And the reader: A Psalm of David, naming the tone. Alleluia. And the cantors chant: Alleluia."
Moscow, 1647, the same as 1602, but "(they chant the Alleluia) 5 times: on the right side thrice, on the left side twice."
Moscow, 1658: "Reader: Alleluia. A Psalm of David."
Likewise the Greek printed editions. The *Hieratikon*: "The 2nd choir chants the Alleluia thrice"[^2769].

### The Sunday Alleluiaria
In contrast to the Sunday prokeimena, the Sunday alleluiaria are taken from the Psalms in their numerical order, and not in scattered succession: Tone 1, Ps. 17:48, 51 [LXX]; Tone 2, Ps. 19:2, 10 [LXX]; Tone 3, Ps. 30:2, 3 [LXX]; Tone 4, Ps. 44:5, 8 [LXX]; Tone 5, Ps. 88:2, 3 [LXX]; Tone 6, Ps. 90:1, 2 [LXX]; Tone 7, Ps. 91:2, 3 [LXX]; Tone 8, Ps. 94:1, 2 [LXX]. Not having, like the prokeimena and the Gospel for which they serve as preparation, a direct relation to the event of the Resurrection, the alleluiaria contain a general glorification of God. Not one of them, in contrast to certain of the Sunday prokeimena, possesses a supplicatory or mournful character. They at times depict the royal dignity of Christ (Tones 1, 4), at times express hope in God (Tones 3, 6), thanksgiving for mercies (Tones 5, 7), or generally the glorification of God (Tone 8).

### Their History
The present Sunday alleluiaria are found already in the Evergetis Typikon of the 12th century, with the distinction that here no alleluiaria are appointed for Tones 3 and 7 (perhaps there were no special melodies for them), but instead for Tone 2 there are two pairs, and the second is the present Tone 3, while for Tone 8 there are three pairs, of which the third is the present Tone 7, and the second is: **"Look upon me and have mercy on me"**, **"Order my steps"** (Ps. 118:132, 133 [LXX])[^2770].

### Prokeimena and Alleluiaria in the Concurrence of Two Commemorations
Neither the *Typikon* nor the other liturgical books give a direct indication of how to proceed when on a single day prokeimena and alleluiaria for two commemorations coincide. Yet this very silence presupposes that each of such prokeimena and alleluiaria must be chanted in full; and the circumstance that in some of such cases (for example, on the Sunday of the Fathers around October 11) at the second prokeimenon its verse is also given, resolves the question in a direction completely contrary to accepted practice—that is, when there are two prokeimena, one cannot chant the second without a verse, but must chant both the 1st and the 2nd with their verse, consequently the 1st twice, and the second 2 1/2 times; and the Alleluia, with 4 verses, 5 times, and each time thrice.

*(Orig. p. 757)*

## THE SCRIPTURAL READINGS (EPISTLE AND GOSPEL)

Following the Prokeimenon at the Liturgy comes the reading prepared by it from the apostolic epistles, termed concisely the "Epistle" (*Apostol*). It constitutes an almost exclusive property of the Divine Liturgy, appearing among other services only in those that were united or are unifiable with the Liturgy, or are structured after its model (at certain Vespers, certain rites of the Mysteries, etc.). The Epistle is taken from the apostolic epistles, including herein the Acts of the Apostles and excluding the Apocalypse. Besides the present place, the apostolic epistles—yet only the Catholic Epistles—are read also in the capacity of Old Testament readings (*paroimiai*), with less solemnity than here, according to the order of Old Testament readings; and thereafter at the Sunday Vigil after Vespers with still less solemnity, according to the order of patristic readings.

The Epistle is read by the reader or deacon from the ambo. The title of the reading is prefaced by the exclamation: **"Wisdom!"** The title is given in a more expansive form than for the Old Testament readings: not only the book is named, but also the author, by the formula: "The reading from the Epistle of the holy Apostle N unto N." Nowhere is a formula indicated for the Catholic Epistles and the Acts. Usually for the former they utilize the formula of the *paroimiai*: "The reading from the Catholic Epistle of N (of Peter, etc.)," and for the latter: "The reading from the Acts (others: Out of the Acts[^2771]) of the Holy Apostles" (see *Menaion*, August 9, 1st *paroimia*). In the case of paired epistles, the numbering is not pronounced (one does not say: "The reading from the first Epistle to the Corinthians") owing to the comparative indifference of this for the comprehension of the reading—on the ground that such numbering is not indicated in the titles of the epistles at the *paroimiai*. Following the exclamation: **"Let us attend!"**, the reading of the Epistle itself begins. If the Epistle is not from the beginning of the book, then in the Acts it begins with the words: "In those days"; in the Catholic Epistles: "Beloved"; in the Pauline Epistles: "Brethren"; and in his Pastoral Epistles: "Child Timothy" or "Titus" (excepting cases where such a beginning is impossible; see, for example, the Epistle of the 1st Sunday of Great Lent), wherein the connecting conjunctions with what precedes are omitted and other necessary textual adjustments are made. The apostolic reading concludes with the imparting of peace to the reader: **"Peace be to thee"**, and his response: **"And to thy spirit."**

The Liturgical Gospel is prefaced and concluded with the very same exclamations as that of Matins, with the distinction that if a deacon is serving, to whom in such a case the reading of the Gospel is committed (as to why, see above, pp. 657–658), then he, as taking upon himself in this instance a ministry exceeding his rank and properly belonging to the priest, requests from him a blessing for this (**"Bless, master, the proclaimer of the good tidings..."**, **"May God, through the prayers..."**), and upon the conclusion of the reading the priest imparts peace to him, marking thereby the exalted nature of the duty performed by him: **"Peace be to thee that announcest the good tidings."**

*(Orig. p. 758)*

### History
Concerning the development of the concepts of "Epistle" (*Apostol*) and "Gospel" (*Evangelion*), and concerning the readers of both in antiquity, see Introductory Chapter, pp. 61–62, 105–106, 168–169.

In the Mozarabic Liturgy always, and in the Nestorian on feasts, there is an Old Testament reading preceding the Epistle (as in antiquity; see Introductory Chapter, pp. 161–162); in the Coptic and Abyssinian Liturgies there are three Epistles: from the Pauline Epistles, the Catholic Epistles, and the Acts of the Apostles (see below; cf. *ibid.*); in the present Roman Mass, an Old Testament reading frequently replaces the Epistle (*epistola*).

In the Roman Liturgy, the subdeacon reads the Epistle, and the deacon reads the Gospel; in the Coptic, the deacon reads the Gospel "if he knows how to read"; in the Abyssinian and Nestorian, the priest reads it[^2772].

Manuscripts of the Liturgy of the Apostle James indicate preliminary exclamations only before the Prokeimenon (almost identical to our own; see above, p. 564) and do not mention them before the Epistle; the Liturgy of Mark the Evangelist according to an 11th-century manuscript, without mentioning the Prokeimenon, has: "Peace be to all. And to thy spirit. Let us attend!"

In Greek manuscripts and printed Greek Euchologia of the Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom, before the Epistle only the exclamation: "Let us attend!" is indicated; but in all Slavic editions of the *Sluzhebnik* it is as at present; and likewise in the Greek *Hieratikon*[^2773].

In the Roman Catholic Liturgy according to the Roman rite, before the Epistle its title is pronounced in the form: "The reading (*lectio*) of the Epistle of blessed Paul the Apostle to N," and after the Epistle (responded by the ministers): "Thanks be to God" (*Deo gratias*), which in the case of multiple Epistles is repeated after each; according to the Mozarabic rite, before the Epistle the priest says: "Keep silence (*Silentium facite*). The continuation (*Sequentia*) of the Epistle of Paul the Apostle to N; the choir responds: Thanks be to God"; after the Epistle, "Responsory: Amen"[^2774].

*(Orig. p. 759)*

### Exclamations before the Gospel
Concerning the exclamations before the Gospel, see above, pp. 656–657.

The opening words of the readings are literally similar to our own in the Roman Church: for the Acts: *"In diebus illis"*; for the Pauline Epistles: *"Fratres"* (the Catholic Epistles begin from Chapter 1); for the Gospel: *"In illo tempore"*[^2775].
