Thus, for the days of the Pentecostarion there have been chosen the most exalted Gospel and the Book of Acts, which recounts the events closest to the Resurrection of Christ, the Ascension, and the Descent of the Holy Spirit. Readings from the Catholic Epistles are not taken at all, owing to the lesser definiteness of their Christology in comparison with the Pauline Epistles (see Introductory Chapter, pp. 60–61); the Gospel of Mark, on account of its brevity, took its place after the two larger Gospels in the capacity of their supplement. In all other respects the books and their sections follow the order of the Bible; the exception for the Gospel pericopes is Matt. 15:21–28 concerning the Canaanite woman, which is placed last, and Luke 16:19–31 concerning the rich man and Lazarus, which is placed on the 22nd Sunday instead of the 28th, because the former was originally read before Great Lent (see below), while the latter, in all probability, was read on the Sunday nearest to the corresponding Menaion commemoration (St. Lazarus, October 17). As regards the Gospels in particular, one cannot fail to observe that the readings selected from them are distributed approximately evenly by topic between the teaching and the miracles of Jesus Christ, and that from another Gospel sections omitted in the first are taken; there are repeated from Luke in comparison with Matthew only the account of the Gadarene miracle (owing to the differences between Matthew and Luke), the parable of those bidden to the banquet, and the narrative concerning the rich young ruler, since in Luke these readings may be omitted on account of the Nativity of Christ; in Mark there are repeated in comparison with Matthew the accounts concerning the healing of the paralytic of Capernaum and of the mute and deaf boy—owing to the suitability of these readings for Lent and to the absence in this Gospel of anything new in comparison with Matthew and Luke.

### The Liturgical Shift (*Otstupka*)
The above-expounded annual cycle of Liturgical Epistles (*Apostols*) and Gospels is not precisely maintained every year, and is very frequently disrupted. This cycle provides readings for thirty-two weeks between Pentecost and the Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee. Yet in different years the number of these weeks varies, and this fluctuation depends upon the mobility of the Feast of Pascha. If in one year Pascha was very early and in the following year very late, then the number of weeks between Pentecost and the Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee will be greater than in the reverse case—that is, if in the first year Pascha was late and in the second early (which is called in the Liturgical Gospel *"within Pascha"* [*vnutr' Paskha*], that is, two Paschas within the course of an annual cycle, while the opposite case is called *"outside Pascha"* [*vne Paskha*]). Thus, between Pentecost and the Sunday of the Publican there can be both more than thirty-two weeks (more frequently) and fewer (rarely). If there is a shortage of Gospels, then on the Sunday after the Nativity of Christ, before the Theophany, and after it, only the Gospels specially appointed for these Sundays are read, while the regular pericopes of these weeks, as well as the regular pericopes falling on the Sundays of the Forefathers and the Fathers, are read in the surplus weeks, but in such a manner that on the Sunday preceding that of the Publican the Gospel concerning Zacchaeus is read without fail. If even these pericopes do not suffice for the surplus weeks, then on the Sunday preceding that of Zacchaeus the pericope (the 17th) of Matthew concerning the Canaanite woman is read. If there are fewer than thirty-two weeks, then the Gospels before Zacchaeus are omitted. The Epistles always accompany their respective Gospels *(Orig. p. 763)* (see the Typikon, January 7, 6th *Note*; cf. the 1st *Note*, and December 26 *Note*; see in the Liturgical Gospel the *"Account containing the number of Gospels for the entire year, and the reception of the Evangelists: whence they begin and where they cease"*).

### History of the Sunday Pericopes
As late as the 5th century, the selection of the Epistle and Gospel readings was left to the discretion of the presiding bishop or priest, although even then there are traces of a more or less fixed distribution of pericopes between feasts and Sundays (Introductory Chapter, pp. 164–168). The distribution of Epistle and Gospel readings among the days of the year is attributed to St. Sophronius, Patriarch of Jerusalem[^2776].

From the 6th–7th centuries there has reached us the Armenian Lectionary in an 8th–9th-century manuscript of the Bibliothèque Nationale in Paris, *MS Arm. 20*[^2777], which states of itself that it presents the practice of the Jerusalem Church, consistently indicating the holy sites of the Holy City for this or that divine service and frequently concurring with the data of the *Pilgrimage* of Silvia or Egeria (Introductory Chapter, pp. 138–139, 250 ff.). The readings indicated by this Lectionary for the Forty Days, Pentecost, and several fixed feasts for the most part do not coincide with the present ones (see below; for example, at the Paschal Liturgy the Gospel is the present one of Great Saturday, whereas the 1st pericope of John is absent), from which one may conclude that the Sunday pericopes as well, not given by this Lectionary, differed in the Jerusalem Church of that time from our present ones. They differed from the present ones somewhat later as well, as is demonstrated by the Greek Evangelistarion of the Library of Saint Catherine's Monastery on Sinai, *MS No. 210* of the 9th century. This Evangelistarion is precisely of the Jerusalem recension, because its Gospels for Palm Sunday and Holy Week coincide with another Evangelistarion of the same library, *MS No. 211*, of the Constantinopolitan recension, but bearing before the specified Gospels the rubric: *"It should be known that from hence begin the Gospels according to the Typikon of the Holy City, from the evening of Palm Sunday until the evening of the Liturgy of Holy Saturday."* Of the same—likewise Palestinian—recension with the two aforementioned monuments is a Syriac Lectionary of Old Testament readings (*paroimiai*) and Epistles in an 11th-century manuscript belonging to a private individual[^2778], reflecting the practice of the 8th–10th centuries. These incomplete collections present the following system of readings for the Sunday cycle:

- **Pascha (Easter Sunday)** — Armenian: 1 Cor. 15:1–11 (Appearances of the Risen Christ); Syriac: the present reading; Armenian and Sinai: Matt. 28:1–20 (The Resurrection).

Gradually this cycle of readings was subjected to influence and alteration under the impact of the Constantinopolitan lectionary system. Thus in the 12th century, as the well-known Jerusalem *"Order"* (*Akolouthia*) of Holy Week and Bright Week demonstrates, during these weeks certain Jerusalem readings yielded their place to Constantinopolitan ones—for example, on Easter Sunday at the Liturgy, not the ancient Gospel of Matthew, but our present Gospel of John[^2779]. Our present system of readings is Constantinopolitan, as is evident from the fact that it is presented in its current form by manuscript Epistles (*Apostols*) and Gospels of manifestly Constantinopolitan origin (with purely Constantinopolitan commemorations in the menologies, local rites, such as the Order of the Indiction [New Year], and the like). It is contained in its present form already in Greek manuscripts of the 10th century, for example *MS No. B1/5* of 985 from the St. Petersburg Theological Academy, and in an entire series of Greek manuscripts of the *Apostol* and Gospel of the 11th century—for example, in the *Apostol* and Gospel of the Kyiv Theological Academy Museum[^2780], and *MS No. 101* of the Imperial Public Library, where from the present *(Orig. p. 766)* order there are departures only for the weekday readings (in the latter manuscript the Gospel of the Canaanite woman is placed after the 16th reading from Luke)[^2781], and *MS Add. 1840* of the Cambridge University Library (11th–12th c.), where *"the readings from Matthew, Mark, and Luke differ greatly from the ordinary order, though in essence cognate with it"*[^2782]. The very same order is found also in the famous *Ostromir Gospel* of 1056–1057, where only Saturday, Sunday, and festal Gospels are given, both Matins and Liturgical, first of the movable cycle beginning from Pascha, and then of the immovable cycle (the remaining text being omitted)[^2783].

### Roman Catholic and Protestant Sunday Liturgical Readings
The system of Sunday Liturgical readings in the Roman Catholic Church:

- **Easter Sunday** — 1 Cor. 5:6–8 (Rising with Christ); Mark 16:1–8 (The Resurrection).
- **2nd Sunday of Easter (Low Sunday / Octave of Easter)** — 1 John 5:4–10 (The Faith that Overcometh the World); John 20:19–31 (The Unbelief of Thomas).
- **3rd Sunday of Easter** — 1 Pet. 2:21–25 (Christ, the Shepherd of Souls); John 10:12–16 (The Good Shepherd).
- **4th Sunday of Easter** — 1 Pet. 2:11–20 (Duties toward the Gentiles); John 16:16–23 (*"A little while"*).
- **5th Sunday of Easter** — James 1:16–21 (The Gift from Above); John 16:5–15 (The Departure unto the Father).
- **6th Sunday of Easter** — James 1:22–27 (Doers of the Word); John 16:23–30 (Prayer in the Name of Christ).
- **7th Sunday of Easter (Sunday after the Ascension)** — 1 Pet. 4:8–11 (Love and Service); John 15:26–16:4 (The Comforter).
- **Sunday of Pentecost (Whitsunday)** — Acts 2:1–11 (The Descent of the Holy Spirit); John 14:23–31 (The Comforter).
